Feed it a dataset with at least one **numeric or categorical column** to monitor, plus a **timestamp column** if you\'re tracking changes over time (highly recommended).\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| date | region | daily_revenue | error_rate |\n|------|--------|---------------|------------|\n| 2024-01-15 | North | 45000 | 0.02 |\n| 2024-01-16 | North | 12000 | 0.15 |\n\nThe node checks each row against your conditions and flags when thresholds are crossed.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Sensible Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|--------------|------------------|----------------|\n| **Metric Column** | The column to monitor | First numeric column | Choose the KPI that matters most (revenue, error rate, conversion) |\n| **Alert Condition** | Trigger logic: Above, Below, Between, Change % | Above | Use "Below" for downward thresholds, "Change %" to catch sudden shifts |\n| **Threshold Value** | The boundary that triggers an alert | None (required) | Set based on business rules—SLA limits, acceptable variance, historical norms |\n| **Comparison Window** | For "Change %" only: number of rows to compare against | 7 | Match your business cycle (7 for weekly, 30 for monthly) |\n| **Group By Column** | Split alerts by category (optional) | None | Essential when monitoring multiple products, regions, or models simultaneously |\n| **Cooldown Period** | Minimum rows between repeat alerts for the same condition | 1 | Increase to 24+ if you\'re monitoring hourly data but only want daily notifications |\n| **Alert Message** | Custom text included in the notification | Auto-generated | Personalize with context: "Revenue in {region} dropped to {value}" |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\nThe Alert node adds three new columns to your data:\n\n- **alert_triggered**: Boolean flag (TRUE when condition is met)\n- **alert_message**: Human-readable description of what happened\n- **alert_timestamp**: Exact moment the condition was detected\n\nYou\'ll also see a **visual summary panel** showing:\n- Total alerts triggered in the dataset\n- Timeline chart marking when alerts fired\n- Breakdown by group (if you used Group By)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Notification nodes** are the natural next step—connect to Email, Slack, or Webhook nodes to actually deliver the alert. The alert_triggered column makes it easy to filter: only send notifications when TRUE.\n\nYou can also branch to:\n- **Filter node** \u2192 isolate alerted records for deeper investigation\n- **Log node** \u2192 maintain an audit trail of all triggered alerts\n- **Dashboard node** \u2192 visualize alert frequency patterns over time\n\n### Quick Start\n\nHere\'s how to set up a revenue drop alert in under two minutes:\n\n1. **Connect your data source** containing daily metrics with a date column and revenue column\n2. **Drag an Alert node** onto the canvas and connect your data to it\n3. **Set Metric Column** to your revenue field\n4. **Choose "Below"** as the Alert Condition\n5. **Enter your threshold** (e.g., 15000 for minimum acceptable daily revenue)\n6. **Add Group By** if monitoring multiple regions/products\n7. **Connect an Email node** downstream and map alert_message to the email body\n8. **Run the workflow**—alerts trigger automatically on future data refreshes\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Filter out noise early**: If your metric is volatile, consider adding a Smooth or Rolling Average node *before* the Alert. Alerting on smoothed data reduces false positives dramatically.\n\n**Test with historical data first**: Run your alert logic against past data where you know anomalies occurred. This validates your thresholds before going live.\n\n**Use multiple alert nodes in parallel**: Don\'t try to cram every condition into one node. Create separate alerts for "revenue too low" and "error rate too high"—each with appropriate downstream actions.\n\n**Set meaningful cooldown periods**: Hourly data with cooldown=1 means 24 potential alerts per day for the same issue. Increase it to match how often you can realistically respond.\n\n**Include context in messages**: Use variable substitution like "Revenue in {region}: {value} on {date}" rather than generic "Alert triggered." Your future self will thank you at 3am.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Deployment Monitor\n\n**When to use:** Initial rollout of alerts on a new metric where you need immediate feedback use:** Mission-critical metrics (revenue, fraud scores, system health) where false negatives are costly and stakeholder trust depends on precision.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `threshold_type` | `statistical` (3.5 sigma) | Balances sensitivity with specificity |\n| `window_size` | `168h` | Full week captures weekly seasonality |\n| `evaluation_frequency` | `5min` | Near real-time without overwhelming system |\n| `lookback_period` | `90d` | Robust seasonal baseline and trend detection |\n| `cooldown_period` | `4h` | Prevents duplicate alerts for same incident |\n| `notification_channels` | `PagerDuty + Slack + email` | Redundant escalation paths |\n| `confirmation_checks` | `3 consecutive violations` | Eliminates transient spikes |\n\n**What you get:** Highly reliable alerts with <2% false positive rate and response latency under 15 minutes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires 90 days of clean historical data and may miss novel anomaly patterns outside learned distributions.\n\n### Recipe 3: Sparse Data Monitoring\n\n**When to use:** Low-frequency events like weekly batch jobs, monthly financial closes, or rare user actions where standard time-series approaches fail.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `threshold_type` | `percentage_change` | Works with irregular timestamps |\n| `window_size` | `last_5_events` | Event-based instead of time-based |\n| `evaluation_frequency` | `on_arrival` | Triggered by data appearance, not clock |\n| `lookback_period` | `20_events` | Statistical validity with limited samples |\n| `baseline_method` | `median` | Robust to outliers in small samples |\n| `notification_channels` | `email` | Matches low urgency of sparse events |\n\n**What you get:** Reliable anomaly detection for irregular data streams without time-series assumptions.\n\n**Trade-off:** Cannot detect temporal patterns or time-based degradation; purely event-to-event comparison.\n\n### Recipe 4: Silent Model Drift Detector\n\n**When to use:** Monitoring prediction confidence distributions, feature importance shifts, or data quality metrics that indicate model staleness before accuracy metrics degrade.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `threshold_type` | `KL_divergence` | Detects distribution shifts |\n| `divergence_threshold` | `0.15` | Sensitive to meaningful drift |\n| `window_size` | `7d_rolling` | Smooths daily noise |\n| `evaluation_frequency` | `daily` | Drift is gradual, not sudden |\n| `lookback_period` | `180d` | Captures seasonal model behavior |\n| `notification_channels` | `Slack (data-science channel)` | Technical audience for proactive action |\n| `alert_priority` | `low` "We caught most of these cases within 72 hours," he said, tapping the page, "but by then the money was already gone. We have a fraud model scoring every transaction. Why aren\'t we hearing about the high-risk ones immediately?"\n\nPriya knew the answer: their weekly fraud digest email buried critical signals in a sea of metrics. The model was working—it had flagged 89% of the fraudulent transactions—but no one was monitoring it in real-time. Marcus wanted an alert system that would notify the fraud team the moment suspicious activity spiked, not three days later when they reviewed the dashboard.\n\n**The Data**\n\nBack at her desk, Priya pulled hourly transaction summaries for the past six months. Each row represented one hour of activity across Everlight\'s payment platform:\n\n| timestamp           | total_transactions | high_risk_count | high_risk_pct | avg_fraud_score |\n|---------------------|-------------------|-----------------|---------------|-----------------|\n| 2024-01-15 14:00:00 | 1,847             | 23              | 1.24%         | 0.18            |\n| 2024-01-15 15:00:00 | 2,103             | 89              | 4.23%         | 0.31            |\n| 2024-01-15 16:00:00 | 1,992             | 91              | 4.57%         | 0.33            |\n| 2024-01-15 17:00:00 | 2,241             | 18              | 0.80%         | 0.16            |\n\nThe data was messy in the usual ways—occasional gaps during system maintenance, a spike of test transactions every Sunday at 3 AM that she\'d need to filter out, and one memorable week when a pipeline bug had logged everything as high-risk.\n\n**The Setup**\n\nPriya decided to monitor `high_risk_pct`—the percentage of transactions flagged as high-risk by their model. She opened her alerting framework and configured two conditions. First, an absolute threshold: if more than 3.5% of transactions in any hour scored as high-risk, send an alert immediately. That was roughly two standard deviations above the normal baseline of 1.2%.\n\nSecond, she added a relative threshold using a 24-hour rolling average. If the current hour\'s high-risk percentage exceeded 150% of the trailing average, that would trigger an alert even if the absolute number wasn\'t dramatic. This would catch gradual buildups that might indicate a coordinated attack.\n\nShe set the notification channel to post in the #fraud-ops Slack channel and configured it to suppress duplicate alerts for two hours after the first trigger—Marcus\'s team didn\'t need to be spammed every hour during an ongoing incident.\n\n**The Results**\n\nPriya ran the system in shadow mode for two weeks, logging what alerts *would* have fired without actually sending them. You can attach it to any complete analytical pipeline that produces outputs like predictions, reports, or updated datasets.\n\n**Input requirements:**\n- A completed workflow (any nodes that generate outputs you want to refresh periodically)\n- No specific column types required—Schedule works with whatever your workflow produces\n\nThink of Schedule as a timer you\'re setting on your entire analysis, not a transformation step within it.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Frequency** | How often the workflow runs (e.g., daily, weekly, hourly) | Daily at 6 AM | Match your business cadence: hourly for real-time dashboards, weekly for management reports, monthly for compliance checks |\n| **Start Date** | When scheduling begins | Today | Set a future date if you\'re preparing workflows in advance |\n| **Time Zone** | Which time zone to use for scheduling | Project default | Critical for global teams—schedule in your stakeholders\' time zone, not yours |\n| **Retry on Failure** | Whether to automatically retry if the workflow fails | Enabled (3 attempts) | Disable for workflows with non-idempotent operations (like sending emails) to avoid duplicates |\n| **Notification Recipients** | Email addresses to notify on success/failure | Project owner | Add stakeholders who need to know immediately if fresh data isn\'t available |\n| **Dependency Check** | Wait for upstream data sources to update before running | Disabled | Enable when your source data refreshes on its own schedule (e.g., warehouse loads at 5 AM) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nSchedule doesn\'t modify your workflow\'s outputs—it ensures they\'re generated on time. Here\'s what you\'ll see:\n\n**Execution History Panel**: A log showing when each run started, how long it took, and whether it succeeded. Color-coded rows (green for success, red for failure) make it easy to spot issues at a glance.\n\n**Next Run Indicator**: A timestamp showing exactly when the workflow will execute next, accounting for time zone and any active delays.\n\n**Performance Metrics**: Average runtime, success rate over the last 30 days, and total executions. These help you optimize workflow efficiency over time.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nSchedule nodes typically sit at the **end** of your workflow, not in the middle. However, you can connect notification or integration nodes after Schedule:\n\n- **Email Report** nodes to distribute results automatically\n- **API Push** nodes to send predictions to production systems  \n- **Data Writer** nodes to save outputs to databases or cloud storage\n\nThe key principle: Schedule triggers the entire chain, so anything connected after it becomes part of the automated routine.\n\n### Quick Start: Daily Sales Dashboard\n\n1. Build your complete workflow (data load \u2192 transformations \u2192 visualization)\n2. Drag a Schedule node onto the canvas\n3. Connect your final output node (e.g., Dashboard) to Schedule\n4. If your warehouse loads at 4 AM, don\'t schedule for 3 AM—you\'ll process stale data.\n\n**Start with longer intervals**: It\'s tempting to run workflows every hour, but this can mask underlying performance issues. Begin with daily runs, then increase frequency only when you\'ve proven stability.\n\n**Test with "Run Now"**: Before activating a schedule, use the "Run Now" button to manually trigger execution. This catches configuration errors without waiting for the scheduled time.\n\n**Monitor the first week closely**: New schedules often reveal unexpected data availability issues or runtime bottlenecks. Check execution logs daily for the first week.\n\n**Build in buffer time**: If stakeholders need results by 9 AM, schedule for 7 AM—not 8:55 AM. Workflows occasionally run longer than expected, and you\'ll want cushion for retries.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Schedule\n\n**When to use:** You\'re testing whether a scheduled workflow runs end-to-end before committing to production infrastructure.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `schedule_interval` | `None` | Manual trigger only; no automatic execution |\n| `max_active_runs` | `1` | Prevent overlapping test runs |\n| `catchup` | `False` | Skip historical runs; start fresh |\n| `execution_timeout` | `300` (5 min) | Fail fast if logic hangs |\n| `retries` | `0` | Surface errors immediately without retry masking |\n| `depends_on_past` | `False` | Each run independent for testing |\n\n**What you get:** Immediate error visibility with no background noise from retries or backfills, ideal for debugging scheduling logic.\n\n**Trade-off:** Zero fault tolerance means transient failures aren\'t handled; unsuitable for production environments.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Mission-Critical Production Pipeline\n\n**When to use:** Financial reporting, regulatory compliance, or SLA-bound deliverables where failures have business consequences.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `schedule_interval` | `0 6 * * *` | Daily at 6 AM when source systems are stable |\n| `max_active_runs` | `1` | Enforce sequential execution to prevent resource contention |\n| `catchup` | `True` | Backfill missed runs to maintain historical completeness |\n| `execution_timeout` | `7200` (2 hrs) | Generous buffer for complex transformations |\n| `retries` | `3` | Handle transient network/database failures |\n| `retry_delay` | `300` (5 min) | Allow upstream systems time to recover |\n| `sla_miss_callback` | `alert_function` | Proactive notification before business impact |\n| `on_failure_callback` | `pagerduty_escalate` | Immediate human intervention on persistent failure |\n| `depends_on_past` | `True` | Enforce chronological integrity for cumulative metrics |\n\n**What you get:** Maximum reliability with comprehensive failure handling and guaranteed execution order for dependent calculations.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower recovery from incidents due to sequential processing; requires manual intervention to reset cascading failures.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Cost-Optimized Cloud Data Refresh\n\n**When to use:** Refreshing dashboards from cloud warehouses where compute costs scale with query frequency and concurrency.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `schedule_interval` | `0 */6 * * *` | Every 6 hours to balance freshness vs. warehouse costs |\n| `max_active_runs` | `3` | Allow limited parallelism during catch-up without runaway costs |\n| `catchup` | `False` | Skip backfills—most recent data sufficient for dashboards |\n| `pool` | `low_priority_pool` (slots=2) | Limit concurrent warehouse connections |\n| `trigger_rule` | `none_failed_min_one_success` | Proceed if partial upstream success to avoid reruns |\n\n**What you get:** Predictable infrastructure costs with controlled concurrency and minimal redundant computation.\n\n**Trade-off:** Potential data gaps during outages; not suitable for audit-trail requirements.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Event-Driven ML Model Retraining\n\n**When to use:** Retraining models when data drift is detected or upstream feature stores signal significant updates—not on arbitrary time schedules.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `schedule_interval` | `@dataset` | Trigger on external dataset updates, not time |\n| `max_active_runs` | `1` | Prevent concurrent training runs corrupting model registry |\n| `execution_timeout` | `14400` (4 hrs) | Accommodate long training jobs |\n| `retries` | `1` | Retry once for spot instance preemption only |\n| `trigger_rule` | `all_success` | Require both data validation AND drift detection to pass |\n\n**What you get:** Training cycles aligned with actual data changes rather than arbitrary schedules, reducing unnecessary compute.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires mature data infrastructure with event propagation; adds complexity versus simple cron schedules.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was spending £180K annually on manual fraud review teams working weekends to assess Monday morning applications. sqlite_master WHERE type=\'table\';")\n    tables = cursor.fetchall()\n    \n    schema_parts = []\n    for (table_name,) in tables:\n        cursor.execute(f"PRAGMA table_info({table_name});")\n {col_name} ({col_type})")\n        \n        schema_parts.append(f"TABLE: {table_name}\\n" + "\\n".join(col_descriptions))\n    \n    return "\\n\\n".join(schema_parts)\n\nschema_description = Given a database schema \nand a natural language question, generate a valid SQLite query that answers the question.\n\nRules:\n1. Only use tables and columns that exist in the provided schema\n2. Return ONLY the SQL query, no explanations\n3. Use appropriate JOINs when data spans multiple tables\n4. Handle aggregations (SUM, AVG, COUNT, etc.) correctly\n5. Apply GROUP BY when using aggregations with other columns"""\n\ndef create_user_prompt(schema: str, question: str) -> str:\n    """Create the user prompt with schema and question."""\n    return f"""Database Schema:\n{schema}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nSQL Query:"""\n\n# ============================================================\n# Step 4: Generate SQL from natural language\n# ============================================================\n\ndef text_to_sql(question: str, schema: str, client: OpenAI) -> str:\n    """\n    Convert a natural language question to SQL using an LLM.\n    \n    Parameters:\n        question: Natural language question about the data\n        schema: Database schema description\n        client: OpenAI client instance\n    \n    Returns:\n        Generated SQL query string\n    """\n    response = client.chat.completions.create(\n        model="gpt-4o",\n        messages=[\n            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},\n            {"role": "user", "content": create_user_prompt(schema, question)}\n        ],\n        temperature=0.0,  # The node needs at least one table with column headers and data rows. There\'s no strict requirement on column types, but the clearer your column names, the better the results.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| order_id | customer_name | order_date | total_amount | region |\n|----------|---------------|------------|--------------|---------|\n| 1001 | Alice Chen | 2024-01-15 | 450.00 | North |\n| 1002 | Bob Smith | 2024-01-16 | 230.50 | South |\n\nThe node understands dates, numbers, categories, and text. Just make sure your column names are descriptive — `total_amount` works better than `col_7`.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Model Selection** | Chooses which LLM processes your questions | GPT-4 | Use a faster model like GPT-3.5 for simple datasets or when speed matters more than complex query handling |\n| **Max Results** | Limits how many rows appear in answers | 100 | Increase for comprehensive exports; decrease for quick previews |\n| **Enable Query Preview** | Shows the generated SQL before execution | On | Turn off once you trust the system, to streamline your workflow |\n| **Context Window** | How much of your previous conversation the model remembers | Last 5 questions | Increase for complex multi-turn analysis; decrease to save tokens on simple lookups |\n| **Strict Mode** | Requires exact column name matches | Off | Enable when working with similar column names (e.g., `revenue` vs `revenue_usd`) to prevent confusion |\n\n### What You Get Out\n\nThe node returns three things:\n\n**Answer Panel**: A natural language response to your question, like "The North region had the highest average order value at $387.50." This appears immediately below your question.\n\n**Results Table**: The actual data supporting the answer, formatted as a clean table you can sort, filter, or export. This appears when your question requests specific records or lists.\n\n**Generated Query**: The SQL or analytical logic created behind the scenes (if Query Preview is enabled). This helps you learn SQL or verify the interpretation.\n\nSome questions also trigger **automatic visualizations** — asking about trends over time produces line charts, comparisons generate bar charts, and distribution questions create histograms.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe Results Table output connects seamlessly to:\n\n- **Export nodes** when you want to save query results as CSV or Excel\n- **Visualization nodes** for custom charts beyond the auto-generated ones\n- **Statistical Analysis nodes** to run correlations or significance tests on the filtered data\n- **Another Ask Your Data node** to refine results further (e.g., "now show only customers from Q1")\n\n### Quick Start: First Analysis in 60 Seconds\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Ask Your Data node input\n2. **Type a simple question** in plain English: "What were total sales by region?"\n3. **Review the answer** in the Answer Panel and check the results table below\n4. **Refine if needed**: "Show only regions with sales over $10,000"\n5. **Export or visualize**: Connect the output to a Chart node or Export node\n\n### Practical Tips from Experienced Users\n\n**Be specific with time ranges**: Instead of "recent sales," ask "sales in the last 30 days" — the model can\'t guess what "recent" means to you.\n\n**Name your columns wisely upstream**: Spending 30 seconds renaming `col_A` to `customer_segment` before this node will save you minutes of rephrasing questions.\n\n**Use follow-up questions**: The context window remembers your conversation. After "What\'s the average order value?", just ask "Show the top 10 customers by that metric" — no need to repeat yourself.\n\n**Check the generated query when learning**: Even if you don\'t know SQL, watching the patterns helps you understand what questions work best.\n\n**Combine filters in one question**: "Sales over $500 in the North region during Q1" works better than three separate questions that you try to mentally combine.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data discovery sessions where speed matters more than precision, typically with "Topic 3" might statistically exist, but you decide it represents "onboarding confusion."\n\n**Run it multiple times**: Topic models have randomness built in. Think of these as example conversations you want your model to learn from.\n\n| Input Column | Output Column |\n|--------------|---------------|\n| "Summarise this product review: The coffee maker broke after 2 weeks..." | "Negative review: Product durability issue reported within 2 weeks of purchase." |\n| "Summarise this product review: Best purchase ever! Makes perfect coffee..." | "Positive review: Customer highly satisfied with product performance." |\n| "Summarise this product review: It\'s okay, nothing special but works fine..." | "Neutral review: Product meets basic expectations without standout features." |\n\nYour dataset should contain 50+ examples minimum, though 200–500 examples typically produce better results. Each row represents one training example showing the model exactly what good output looks like.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|------------------|------------------|----------------|\n| **Base Model** | Which pre-trained model to start from (e.g., GPT-3.5, Llama 2) | GPT-3.5-turbo | Choose larger models (GPT-4) for complex reasoning tasks; smaller models for speed and cost efficiency |\n| **Training Epochs** | How many times the model sees your entire dataset | 3 | Increase to 4–5 if the model hasn\'t learned patterns well; decrease to 1–2 if you notice it\'s memorising examples verbatim |\n| **Learning Rate** | How aggressively the model adjusts during training | Auto | Only change if you understand model training—too high causes instability, too low means slow learning |\n| **Batch Size** | How many examples processed together | 4 | Increase to 8–16 if you have ample GPU memory; larger batches train faster but use more resources |\n| **Validation Split** | Percentage of data held back for testing | 20% | Increase to 30% if you have abundant data and want robust evaluation; decrease to 10% if data is scarce |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\nAfter training completes, the node provides several outputs:\n\n**Fine-tuned Model ID**: A unique identifier you\'ll use to reference your custom model in downstream nodes. Save this—it\'s how you access your trained model.\n\n**Training Metrics Chart**: A line graph showing loss (error) decreasing over time. You want to see a steady downward trend that levels off. If it\'s still dropping steeply at the end, consider more epochs. If it increases, you may be overfitting.\n\n**Validation Results Table**: Shows sample predictions from your model on the held-back validation data, letting you spot-check quality before deploying.\n\n**Performance Summary**: Includes final loss values, training time, and token usage—helpful for estimating costs and comparing different fine-tuning runs.\n\n### Connecting to Downstream Nodes\n\nConnect your fine-tuned model to:\n- **Generate Text** node: Use your custom model for production inference\n- **Evaluate Model** node: Test performance against a holdout dataset\n- **A/B Test** node: Compare your fine-tuned model against the base model or prompt engineering approaches\n\n### Quick Start: Fine-tune a Customer Support Classifier\n\n1. **Prepare your data**: Create a dataset with "customer_question" and "category" columns containing 200+ labelled support tickets\n2. **Connect dataset** to the Fine-tune Model node input\n3. **Select columns**: Choose "customer_question" as input, "category" as output\n4. **Choose base model**: Start with GPT-3.5-turbo for cost-effectiveness\n5. **Leave other settings default** for your first run\n6. **Execute the node** and wait 10–30 minutes for training\n7. **Review the validation results** to check if categorisations look accurate\n8. **Connect to Generate Text** node to start using your model in production\n\n### Expert Tips\n\n- **Start small, iterate fast**: Begin with 100 examples and default settings. You\'ll learn more from quickly testing what works than from perfecting your first attempt.\n\n- **Balance your dataset**: If you\'re training a classifier, ensure each category has similar numbers of examples. An imbalanced dataset (e.g., 90% "positive", 10% "negative") will produce a biased model.\n\n- **Watch for overfitting**: If training loss drops to near-zero but validation loss stays high, your model is memorising rather than learning. Reduce epochs or add more diverse training data.\n\n- **Version your training data**: Keep track of which dataset version produced which model. You\'ll thank yourself when comparing model performance weeks later.\n\n- **Cost awareness**: Fine-tuning charges per token processed. A 500-example dataset with 100 tokens each, trained for 3 epochs, processes 150,000 tokens. **Manage Prompts** node doesn\'t strictly require an incoming data connection—you can use it standalone to create and test prompts. However, when you do connect data, it should contain at least one text column that you\'ll use as a variable within your prompt template.\n\n**Example input shape:**\n\n| customer_query | user_id | sentiment |\n|----------------|---------|-----------|\n| "Where is my order?" | 1001 | negative |\n| "Thanks for the quick delivery" | 1002 | positive |\n\nThis data flows through your prompt template, allowing you to inject dynamic values like `{customer_query}` into your LLM instructions.\n\n### Quick Start: Creating Your First Prompt\n\n1. **Drag** the Manage Prompts node onto your canvas\n2. **Open** the configuration panel and give your prompt a descriptive name (e.g., "customer_response_generator_v1")\n3. **Write** your prompt in the template editor using `{variable_name}` syntax for placeholders\n4. **Select** your LLM provider and model from the dropdown\n5. **Click** "Test" to validate your prompt with sample data\n6. **Save** the version—Heuristix automatically tracks this as version 1\n7. **Connect** downstream nodes to process the LLM responses\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Prompt Name** | Unique identifier and version tracking label | "untitled_prompt" | Always rename to reflect business purpose—makes governance easier |\n| **Prompt Template** | The actual instruction text sent to the LLM, with `{variables}` | Empty | Core configuration—write clear, specific instructions |\n| **LLM Provider** | Which AI service to call (OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, etc.) | Organization default | Change based on model capabilities or cost requirements |\n| **Model Version** | Specific model (e.g., GPT-4, Claude 3) | Latest stable | Pin to specific versions for production consistency |\n| **Temperature** | Creativity vs. consistency (0.0–1.0) | 0.7 | Lower (0.1–0.3) for factual tasks; higher (0.8–1.0) for creative content |\n| **Max Tokens** | Maximum length of LLM response | 256 | Increase for longer outputs; decrease to control costs |\n| **System Message** | Role/context instructions separate from the prompt | Empty | Set persona or rules that apply to all executions |\n| **Variable Mapping** | Links data columns to prompt placeholders | Auto-detected | Override when column names don\'t match template variables |\n| **Enable Versioning** | Automatic tracking of prompt changes | Enabled | Keep enabled for audit trails and rollback capability |\n\n### What You\'ll Get as Output\n\nThe node adds these columns to your dataset:\n\n- **prompt_response**: The full text returned by the LLM\n- **prompt_version**: Which version of the prompt template was used\n- **token_count**: Total tokens consumed (input + output)\n- **execution_time_ms**: How long the API call took\n- **model_used**: The specific model that processed the request\n\nYou\'ll also see a **performance dashboard** showing response time distributions, token usage trends, and version comparison metrics. The **test panel** displays side-by-side prompt/response pairs for quick validation before deployment.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect Manage Prompts to:\n\n- **Extract Entities**: Parse structured information from LLM responses\n- **Classify Text**: Feed responses into classification workflows\n- **Data Table**: Store and review outputs before further processing\n- **Export**: Push refined responses to production systems\n- **Another Manage Prompts node**: Chain prompts for multi-step reasoning\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n1. **Version before major changes**: Click "Create New Version" rather than editing in place when you\'re making significant prompt revisions—you\'ll thank yourself when you need to roll back.\n\n2. **Use system messages strategically**: Put unchanging context (company policies, response format requirements) in the system message rather than repeating it in every prompt template.\n\n3. **Monitor token costs in aggregate**: The dashboard\'s cost tracking is per-execution, but check the summary view weekly to catch runaway usage before it impacts budgets.\n\n4. **Test with edge cases**: Don\'t just validate with typical inputs—try empty strings, very long text, and unusual characters to see how your prompt handles boundary conditions.\n\n5. **Name variables descriptively**: Use `{customer_complaint}` instead of `{text1}`—your future self and teammates will understand the prompt logic instantly.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Explorer\n\n**When to use:** Initial discovery | `256` | Short responses reduce latency and cost |\n| `version_auto_save` | `false` | Manual saves only to avoid cluttering history |\n| `test_sample_size` | `5` | Minimal validation set for quick | support | "How to reset password" |\n| doc_002 | [0.11, 0.33, -0.08, ...] | billing | "Update payment method" |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Query Mode** | Whether to search using a text query (auto-embedded) or an existing embedding vector | Text Query | Use "Embedding Vector" when you already have query embeddings or want batch searches |\n| **Number of Results** | How many nearest neighbors to return | 10 | Increase for broader exploration (50-100); decrease for precision-focused use cases (3-5) |\n| **Distance Metric** | How similarity is calculated: cosine, euclidean, or dot product | Cosine | Use cosine for normalized embeddings (most common), euclidean for absolute distance sensitivity, dot product for raw similarity scores |\n| **Index Type** | Algorithm for search: HNSW (fast), IVF (memory-efficient), or Flat (exact) | HNSW | Switch to Flat for small datasets (<10k items) or when you need guaranteed exact results |\n| **Metadata Filters** | Pre-filter results by category, date range, or other attributes before vector search | None | Apply when you need "find similar items *within* a specific segment" (e.g., same department, recent items only) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Output columns added:**\n- **similarity_score**: A numerical measure of how close each result is to your query (0-1 for cosine, varies for others)\n- **rank**: Position in the results (1 = closest match)\n- All original columns from your input dataset for each retrieved item\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Results table**: Top N matches with scores, sorted by relevance\n- **Distance distribution chart**: Shows the spread of similarity scores to help you judge result quality\n- **2D embedding projection** (optional): Visual plot of query and results in reduced dimensional space\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node pairs naturally with:\n- **LLM Prompt node**: Feed retrieved documents as context for RAG applications\n- **Reranker node**: Apply a more sophisticated scoring model to refine your top results\n- **Filter node**: Further narrow results by business rules or thresholds\n- **Export node**: Send results to your application via API or database\n\nThe most common pattern: Vector Search \u2192 Reranker \u2192 LLM Prompt for production RAG systems.\n\n### Quick Start: Building a Knowledge Base Search\n\n1. **Connect your embedded documents** to the Vector Search node (from an Embeddings node or data import)\n2. **Set Query Mode to "Text Query"** and enter a sample question in natural language\n3. **Leave Number of Results at 10** and Distance Metric at "Cosine" for your first run\n4. **Run the node** and review the results table — check if the top results genuinely relate to your query\n5. **Adjust the number of results** based on how many relevant items you found (tighten if too noisy, expand if missing good matches)\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1**: Don\'t trust similarity scores in isolation. A score of 0.75 might be excellent in one domain and mediocre in another. Always manually review a sample of results to calibrate your expectations.\n\n**Tip 2**: If all your results cluster around similar scores (e.g., 0.82-0.85), your embeddings might be too generic. Consider fine-tuning your embedding model or adding metadata filters to sharpen retrieval.\n\n**Tip 3**: For production systems, start with HNSW indexing at 50-100 results, then add a reranker to reduce to your final top 5-10. This two-stage approach balances speed and quality beautifully.\n\n**Tip 4**: Use metadata filters *before* vector search, not after — it\'s dramatically faster and prevents wasting your result budget on irrelevant segments.\n\n**Tip 5**: When debugging poor results, try the 2D projection view. If your query vector sits far from all results, you may have a domain mismatch between query and document embeddings.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping on Laptop\n\n**When to use:** You\'re exploring a new dataset locally (< 100K vectors) and need fast iteration cycles to validate whether vector search will work for your use case.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `index_type` | `Flat` | No approximation overhead; exact search |\n| `metric` | `cosine` | Normalized similarity; forgiving of embedding scale |\n| `batch_size` | `1000` | Fits in memory without thrashing |\n| `ef_construction` | N/A | Not building graph index |\n| `nprobe` | N/A | No quantization cells |\n\n**What you get:** Sub-second queries on datasets up to 50K vectors with perfect recall; immediate feedback loop.\n\n**Trade-off:** Does not scale beyond ~100K vectors; no insight into production performance characteristics.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production RAG System\n\n**When to use:** Serving a retrieval-augmented LLM application with millions of document chunks where latency SLAs matter (p95 < 50ms) and recall quality directly impacts user-facing answers.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `index_type` | `HNSW` | Best recall/speed trade-off at scale |\n| `metric` | `dot_product` | Preserves magnitude signals in embeddings |\n| `M` | `32` | Balances graph connectivity vs memory |\n| `ef_construction` | `200` | High build-time quality; index built once |\n| `ef_search` | `100` | Tuned for 95%+ recall at p95 < 50ms |\n| `max_elements` | `10000000` | Preallocated capacity prevents reindexing |\n\n**What you get:** 95-98% recall with predictable 20-40ms latencies on 10M+ vectors; horizontally scalable.\n\n**Trade-off:** Index build time 30-60 minutes; 4-6GB RAM per million vectors; reindexing on schema changes is expensive.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Multi-Tenant SaaS with Metadata Filtering\n\n**When to use:** Each customer\'s data must stay isolated, and you\'re filtering 80%+ of the corpus before vector search (e.g., "find similar products in *this user\'s* catalog").\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `index_type` | `IVF_FLAT` | Supports efficient pre-filtering |\n| `nlist` | `4096` | Partition size matches tenant count order |\n| `nprobe` | `64` | Search 1.5% of partitions post-filter |\n| `metric` | `euclidean` | Metadata filters already scoped data |\n| `quantization` | `none` | Preserve precision after filter reduces candidates |\n\n**What you get:** Filter-then-search completes in 10-30ms even when 95% of vectors are excluded by tenant_id.\n\n**Trade-off:** Worse performance than HNSW when filtering is light (< 50% exclusion); requires careful nlist tuning per tenant distribution.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomaly Detection in Time-Series Sensor Data\n\n**When to use:** Finding unusual patterns in IoT streams where "anomalies" are behaviorally similar to each other but rare—vector search as a clustering proxy.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `index_type` | `Flat` | Need true k-NN distances for threshold calibration |\n| `metric` | `euclidean` | Actual distance magnitude signals anomaly severity |\n| `k` | `50` | Detect local density (not just nearest match) |\n| `use_faiss_gpu` | `true` | Real-time ingestion requires GPU acceleration |\n\n**What you get:** Millisecond detection of anomalous windows by comparing average distance to 50-NN baseline; no model training required.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires GPU infrastructure; concept drift needs periodic index rebuilding with recent normal behavior.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender with 200,000 historical applications struggled with fraud detection, relying on rigid rule-based systems that flagged legitimate customers while missing sophisticated fraud patterns. The data was messier than she\'d hoped—some descriptions were terse, others rambling, and there were plenty of typos and abbreviations that field adjusters had typed on mobile devices. Here\'s what a slice looked like:\n\n| claim_id | description | amount | region |\n|----------|-------------|--------|--------|\n| C-10293 | rear-ended at stoplight, bumper damage and taillight broken | 2847 | Northeast |\n| C-10294 | hail damage to hood and roof, multiple dents | 3921 | Midwest |\n| C-10295 | sideswiped in parking lot, driver door scraped | 1205 | West |\n| C-10296 | hit deer on rural highway, front end damage | 5832 | Midwest |\n| C-10297 | fender bender in parking garage, minor scratches | 890 | Northeast |\n\nSarah decided to focus on the description field. Her plan was to convert each claim description into a dense vector embedding using a pre-trained language model, then use vector search to find the most similar historical claims for any new inquiry. She chose the `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` model from sentence-transformers—it was fast, produced 384-dimensional vectors, and performed well on semantic similarity tasks without requiring GPU infrastructure.\n\nSetting up the vector search felt straightforward once she had the embeddings. Sarah indexed the full historical dataset of 400,000 claims using FAISS, Facebook\'s library for efficient similarity search. She configured it with an IndexFlatL2 structure initially—exact nearest neighbor search using L2 distance—because she wanted to establish a baseline before optimizing for speed. For the top-k parameter, she set k=5, reasoning that support agents would benefit from seeing the five most similar cases rather than being overwhelmed with dozens.\n\nHere\'s the core of Sarah\'s implementation:\n\n```python\nfrom sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer\nimport faiss\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\n\n# Load claims data\nclaims_df = pd.read_csv(\'claims_history.csv\')\ndescriptions = claims_df[\'description\'].tolist()\n\n# Generate embeddings using pretrained model\nmodel = SentenceTransformer(\'all-MiniLM-L6-v2\')\nembeddings = model.encode(descriptions, show_progress_bar=True)\nembeddings = np.array(embeddings).astype(\'float32\')\n\n# Build FAISS index\ndimension = embeddings.shape[1]  # 384 for MiniLM\nindex = faiss.IndexFlatL2(dimension)\nindex.add(embeddings)\n\n# Query example: new claim comes in\nquery = "crashed into another car at intersection"\nquery_vector = model.encode([query]).astype(\'float32\')\n\n# Search for 5 most similar historical claims\ndistances, indices = index.search(query_vector, k=5)\n\n# Display results with similarity scores\nfor i, (idx, dist) in enumerate(zip(indices[0], distances[0])):\n    similarity = 1 / (1 + dist)  # convert distance to similarity\n    print(f"{i+1}. requires **no upstream connections**—it is always the first node in any Heuristix pipeline. You configure it to read from external data sources including CSV files, Excel spreadsheets, databases, APIs, or cloud storage buckets.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | Description | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Source Type** | Format of input data (CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, SQL Database) | CSV | Match your data source format |\n| **File Path / Connection String** | Location of data file or database credentials | — | Always required; supports local paths and URLs |\n| **Delimiter** | Column separator for delimited files | `,` (comma) | Use `\\t` for TSV, `|` for pipe-delimited |\n| **Header Row** | Whether first row contains column names | True | Set False if data has no headers |\n| **Data Types** | Explicit schema definition for columns | Auto-detect | Override when auto-detection fails (e.g., ZIP codes as strings) |\n| **Missing Value Identifiers** | Characters treated as null/missing | `NA`, empty | Add custom indicators like `?`, `-`, `999` |\n| **Encoding** | Character encoding of source file | UTF-8 | Change to `latin-1` or `ISO-8859-1` for legacy systems |\n| **Skip Rows** | Number of rows to ignore from file start | 0 | Use when files contain metadata headers |\n| **Max Rows** | Limit on records to import | All | Set for testing large files or sampling |\n\n### Output Specifications\n\nThe Import Data node produces:\n\n- **Data Table**: The complete imported dataset with detected or specified column types\n- **Schema Summary**: Column names, data types, null counts, and cardinality for each field\n- **Import Statistics**: Total rows loaded, import duration, memory usage\n- **Data Quality Preview**: First 100 rows displayed in tabular format with flagged anomalies (unexpected types, encoding errors)\n\n### Downstream Connections\n\nConnect Import Data directly to:\n\n- **Data Cleaning** nodes (Handle Missing Values, Remove Duplicates)\n- **Exploratory Data Analysis** (Summary Statistics, Distribution Analysis)\n- **Feature Engineering** nodes when data is pre-cleaned\n- **Filter Rows** to subset data before heavy processing\n- **Join Data** to merge with other imported datasets\n\n### Platform Tips & Warnings\n\n\u26a0\ufe0f **Warning**: Always validate data types after import. At minimum, you need:\n\n- **A sequence column** (integer or datetime) — typically `observation_number`, `timestamp`, or `date`\n- **A metric column** (numeric) — the measurement you\'re monitoring (e.g., `defect_rate`, `response_time_ms`, `daily_sales`)\n\nOptionally, include:\n\n- **A group column** (string/categorical) — to create separate control charts by category (e.g., `production_line`, `region`, `operator`)\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| observation | defect_rate | line |\n|------------|-------------|------|\n| 1 | 2.3 | A |\n| 2 | 2.1 | A |\n| 3 | 5.8 | A |\n| 4 | 2.4 | A |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Metric Column** | Which numeric column to monitor | (required) | Select the KPI you want to track for stability |\n| **Sequence Column** | Order of observations | (required) | Use your timestamp or sequence number field |\n| **Group By** | Create separate charts per category | None | Enable when monitoring multiple lines, teams, or segments independently |\n| **Chart Type** | Statistical method used | I-chart (individuals) | Use X-bar & R for subgroups, P-chart for proportions, C-chart for count data |\n| **Sigma Level** | Width of control limits | 3 | Reduce to 2 for tighter sensitivity; increase to 4 to reduce false alarms in noisy processes |\n| **Baseline Period** | Number of initial observations to calculate limits | 20 | Increase to 30+ for volatile processes; ensure this period represents stable operation |\n| **Recalculate Limits** | Whether to update limits after detecting shifts | Off | Turn on for processes expected to improve over time (e.g., post-intervention monitoring) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Control chart plot** showing your metric over time with center line (mean) and upper/lower control limits (UCL/LCL) as dashed lines\n- **Points colored by status**: green (in control), red (out of control), yellow (warning patterns)\n\n**Output table** (adds these columns to your input data):\n\n| Column Added | Meaning |\n|-------------|---------|\n| `center_line` | Process mean during baseline period |\n| `ucl` / `lcl` | Upper and lower control limits |\n| `signal_flag` | Boolean: TRUE if point triggers a rule violation |\n| `signal_type` | Description: "Point beyond limits", "8+ points same side", "trend", etc. |\n| `zone` | Which sigma zone the point falls in (A, B, or C) |\n\n**Summary metrics panel:**\n- Percentage of points in control\n- Number and type of signals detected\n- Process capability estimate (if specification limits provided)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically connects to:\n\n- **Alert/Notification nodes** — trigger emails or Slack messages when `signal_flag = TRUE`\n- **Decision Tree or Rule Engine** — define different responses based on `signal_type`\n- **Time Series Forecast** — after confirming process stability, use for prediction\n- **Report Builder** — create executive dashboards showing quality trends\n\n### Quick Start: Monitoring Daily Defect Rates\n\n1. your baseline during known-stable periods** — don\'t include startup, major changes, or known incidents in your first 20 observations. Garbage in, garbage out.\n\n\U0001f3af **Not every red point requires action** — investigate the context. A single point slightly beyond limits might be noise; eight consecutive points on one side of center line indicates a real shift.\n\n\U0001f3af **Group by sparingly** — creating 50 separate control charts defeats the purpose. Group only by factors you can actually act on (which machine, which shift).\n\n\U0001f3af **Save your baseline limits** — when you confirm a process is stable, save those control limits and use them going forward rather than recalculating from recent data.\n\n\U0001f3af **Pair with process documentation** — control charts tell you *when* something changed, not *what* changed. Keep an intervention log to correlate with your chart signals.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Process Baseline\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploration of a new process when you need quick feedback on stability before investing in detailed analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Chart type | I-MR (Individuals-Moving Range) | No subgrouping required; works with single observations |\n| Control limits | 3-sigma | Standard detection threshold balancing sensitivity and false alarms |\n| Minimum observations | 20 | Enough for initial pattern recognition without waiting weeks |\n| Recalculation | Off | Static limits for consistent baseline reference |\n| Tests for special causes | Rule 1 only | Point beyond limits—fastest signal, least computation |\n\n**What you get:** A stable/unstable determination within days that tells you whether deeper investigation is warranted.\n\n**Trade-off:** You\'ll miss subtle process shifts detectable by Western Electric or Nelson rules and may not catch gradual trends.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Monitoring\n\n**When to use:** Established critical processes where detection failures have significant cost or compliance implications.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Chart type | X\u0304-R (X-bar and Range) | Separates within-subgroup and between-subgroup variation for better sensitivity |\n| Subgroup size | 5 | Optimal balance for detecting 1.5\u03c3 shifts per statistical power curves |\n| Control limits | 3-sigma | Industry standard for Type I error rate of 0.27% |\n| Minimum observations | 25 subgroups (125 points) | Statistical stability for reliable limit estimation |\n| Recalculation | Phase-based | Recalculate after confirmed process changes only |\n| Tests for special causes | All 8 Nelson rules | Maximum sensitivity to shifts, trends, cycles, and stratification |\n| Out-of-control response | Documented investigation protocol | Ensures traceability and learning |\n\n**What you get:** High-confidence signals with detailed pattern recognition that justifies intervention decisions under audit.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires disciplined subgrouping discipline and longer initialization period before monitoring begins.\n\n### Recipe 3: Low-Volume High-Value Process\n\n**When to use:** Manufacturing or service processes with fewer than 50 observations per year but high consequence of defects (aerospace components, custom medical devices).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Chart type | EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) | Superior sensitivity with small samples |\n| Lambda (\u03bb) | 0.2 | Detects 0.5\u03c3 shifts with minimal data |\n| Control limits | 2.7-sigma | Tighter limits compensate for smoothing, maintaining overall alpha |\n| Minimum observations | 15 | Lower threshold acceptable given EWMA\'s efficiency |\n| Target value | Engineering specification centerpoint | External reference when historical data is sparse |\n\n**What you get:** Actionable signals from limited data without waiting years for traditional chart validity.\n\n**Trade-off:** Autocorrelation in plotted points makes visual interpretation less intuitive than traditional charts.\n\n### Recipe 4: Early Detection of Cybersecurity Anomalies\n\n**When to use:** Monitoring authentication failure rates, API response times, or transaction volumes where adversarial actors create sudden but small shifts.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Chart type | CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) | Optimized for detecting small persistent shifts (0.5–1\u03c3) |\n| Reference value (K) | 0.5\u03c3 | Half the shift size you want to detect quickly |\n| Decision interval (H) | 4\u03c3 | Balances detection speed with false positive rate |\n| Sampling interval | 5 minutes | High-frequency monitoring for time-sensitive threats |\n| Recalculation | Daily | Adapts to legitimate pattern changes in user behavior |\n\n**What you get:** Detection of subtle attack patterns 5–10× faster than threshold alerting, often before damage occurs.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires domain expertise to distinguish adversarial shifts from legitimate business changes during investigation.\n\n## Business What is the most critical information still needed to answer this question using a proper decision rule?\n\nA) The sensitivity and specificity of the model at various threshold levels\n\nB) The cost of false negatives (missed readmissions) versus false positives (unnecessary interventions), along with intervention effectiveness\n\nC) A validation dataset to confirm the 92% accuracy holds on out-of-sample patients\n\nD) The probability distribution of readmission risk scores across the patient population\n\n**Answer:** B\n\n**Explanation:** A decision rule requires explicit specification of costs, benefits, and business constraints—not just predictive performance. ============================================================\n\ndef analyse_factorial(design_df, response_col, factor_cols):\n    """\n    Analyse a 2-level factorial experiment using effect results[\'Effect\'].append(effect)\n            results[\'Std_Error\'].append(se)\n            results[\'t_value\'].append(t_val)\n            results[\'p_value\'].append(p_val)\n    \n    return What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Design Experiment node doesn\'t require historical data to get started—it\'s a planning tool that *generates* your experimental design. However, you can optionally connect existing data to inform your design decisions:\n\n**Optional Input:**\n- **Historical performance data** with outcome metrics (conversion rate, response time, etc.) to estimate variance and effect sizes\n- **Factor lists** containing the variables you want to test and their possible levels\n\nIf starting fresh, you\'ll configure everything directly in the node parameters.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Design Type** | The experimental structure (Full Factorial, Fractional Factorial, Latin Square, etc.) | Full Factorial | Use Fractional when you have 5+ factors to reduce experiment size; use Latin Square when controlling for two blocking variables |\n| **Factors** | Input variables you\'re testing (e.g., email subject line, price point, page layout) | Empty list | Add each variable you want to test with its levels (e.g., "Price: [$9, $14, $19]") |\n| **Response Variable** | The outcome metric you\'re measuring | None (required) | Set to your primary KPI—conversion rate, revenue, engagement time, etc. |\n| **Number of Replicates** | How many times to repeat each treatment combination | 3 | Increase for noisy data or small effect sizes; reduce to save resources when effects are large |\n| **Blocking Variables** | Grouping factors to control for (day of week, user segment, etc.) | None | Add when you know certain variables create systematic variation but aren\'t your focus |\n| **Randomization Seed** | Controls random assignment order | Random | Set a specific number only when you need reproducible assignment sequences |\n| **Power Target** | Minimum statistical power desired (probability of detecting real effects) | 0.80 | Increase to 0.90 for critical decisions; 0.80 is the research standard |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\nThe node generates a complete experimental plan with several components:\n\n**Design Table:** Shows every treatment combination to run, with randomized assignment order. For example, if testing 2 subject lines × 3 prices, you\'ll see 6 unique combinations, each replicated according to your settings.\n\n**Sample Size Calculator:** Displays the total number of experimental units needed and the expected statistical power given your configuration.\n\n**Balance Check Visualization:** A matrix showing how factors are distributed across your design, helping you spot any unintended imbalances.\n\n**Assignment Schedule:** A downloadable CSV ready to implement, with columns for Unit_ID, Treatment_Combination, and any blocking assignments.\n\n### Quick Start: Testing Email Campaign Variables\n\n1. **Drag the Design Experiment node** onto your canvas\n2. **Set Response Variable** to "open_rate" or your success metric\n3. **Add your first factor:** Click "+ Add Factor," name it "Subject_Style," add levels: ["Question", "Statement", "Urgency"]\n4. **Add your second factor:** "Send_Time" with levels: ["9AM", "2PM", "6PM"]\n5. **Choose Design Type:** Keep "Full Factorial" (gives you all 9 combinations)\n6. **Set Replicates:** Start with 3 to ensure statistical validity\n7. **Click Generate Design** and review the assignment table—you\'ll need 27 total sends (9 combinations × 3 replicates)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Experiment Tracker:** Feed your assignment schedule here to monitor incoming results and track which units received which treatments.\n\n**Statistical Test:** Once data is collected, connect to t-test, ANOVA, or Regression nodes to analyze which factors significantly impacted your outcome.\n\n**Decision Matrix:** Compare treatment combinations against business constraints (cost, feasibility) to select the optimal configuration.\n\n### Pro Tips from Experienced Users\n\n**Start smaller than you think.** New users often design experiments with 6+ factors and hundreds of treatment combinations. Start with 2–3 factors you believe have the largest effects. You can always run a follow-up experiment.\n\n**Use blocking strategically.** If you\'re running a week-long test, add "Day" as a blocking variable to account for weekend vs. weekday differences—this increases precision without increasing sample size.\n\n**Check the correlation matrix** in your design output. If two factors are perfectly correlated in your design, you won\'t be able to separate their effects. The tool will warn you, but it\'s worth understanding why.\n\n**Save your design specs.** The node exports a JSON configuration file—keep it! Six months later when someone asks "how did we design that pricing test?" you\'ll be grateful.\n\n**Pilot before full deployment.** Run 10–20% of your planned sample first, check data quality, then complete the full design. This catches implementation bugs early when they\'re cheap to fix.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototype Test\n\n- **When to use:** You need directional evidence quickly with minimal setup—early-stage features, low-traffic pages, or internal tool changes where perfection isn\'t required.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Higher tolerance for false positives speeds decision timeline |\n| `power` | 0.70 | Accept 30% miss rate on true effects to shrink sample size |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 10% relative lift | Only catch large, meaningful changes worth acting on |\n| `sample_ratio` | 1:1 | Equal split minimizes complexity in allocation logic |\n| `duration` | 7 days | One full week captures basic cyclicality without long commitment |\n\n- **What you get:** A conclusive answer in one week for effects larger than 10%, with 70% confidence you\'ll detect them if present.\n\n- **Trade-off:** You\'ll miss smaller effects and have higher false positive risk—acceptable for low-stakes decisions, dangerous for revenue-critical changes.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Revenue Test\n\n- **When to use:** Testing pricing changes, checkout flow modifications, or any experiment where incorrect conclusions directly impact business financials.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.01 | Minimize false positives that could lock in revenue-damaging changes |\n| `power` | 0.90 | High probability of detecting true effects worth the extra sample cost |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 2% relative lift | Detect even small revenue shifts that compound at scale |\n| `sample_ratio` | 1:1 | Balanced groups for cleanest variance estimation |\n| `duration` | 21 days | Three full weeks to smooth weekday/weekend and pay-cycle patterns |\n| `sequential_testing` | disabled | Avoid inflated error rates from peeking at results early |\n\n- **What you get:** Highly reliable conclusions for effects as small as 2%, with only 1% false positive risk and 90% detection probability.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Requires 3× the sample size and duration of rapid tests—expensive in time and opportunity cost, but necessary for high-stakes decisions.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Low-Traffic B2B Feature\n\n- **When to use:** Testing features in enterprise software with fewer than 200 weekly active users, where standard sample size calculators return "insufficient traffic."\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Accept higher false positive rate given sample constraints |\n| `power` | 0.65 | Deliberately underpowered but still informative |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 25% relative lift | Only detectable effects are large enough to matter anyway |\n| `sample_ratio` | 4:1 (control:treatment) | Preserve majority on known-good experience |\n| `duration` | 60 days | Extended runtime to accumulate rare conversion events |\n| `metric` | task completion rate | Binary outcome more efficient than continuous metrics in small samples |\n\n- **What you get:** Statistically-informed direction even with severe traffic constraints, focusing on large, unmissable shifts.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Cannot detect subtle improvements; results guide rather than definitively prove.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Novelty Effect Isolation\n\n- **When to use:** Testing UI redesigns, gamification, or notifications where initial user excitement artificially inflates early metrics before regressing to true steady-state impact.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard rigor for strategic decisions |\n| `power` | 0.80 | Standard detection threshold |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 3% relative lift | Modest but meaningful improvement target |\n| `holdback_group` | 10% | Reserve untouched users for long-term comparison |\n| `duration` | 42 days | Six weeks allows novelty decay observation |\n| `analysis_window` | days 29–42 only | Measure steady-state behavior after initial excitement fades |\n\n- **What you get:** True sustained impact measurement isolated from temporary curiosity-driven engagement spikes.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Longer timeline and unused holdback segment increase cost, but prevent false wins from temporary effects.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender struggled with loan application abandonment rates They have 10,000 daily users and plan to run the experiment for two weeks. Which consideration reflects the most fundamental principle of experimental design?\n\nA) Whether to use a larger sample size in the treatment group than the control group to gather more data about the new feature\'s performance\n\nB) Whether the experimental units (users) are independently assigned to conditions so that one user\'s treatment doesn\'t affect another user\'s outcome\n\nC) Whether to randomize users to treatment and control conditions before the experiment starts to ensure groups are comparable on all measured and unmeasured characteristics\n\nD) Whether to segment users by device type and analyze each segment separately to understand where the new checkout flow performs best\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Randomization is the foundational principle that enables **causal inference** in experimental design—it ensures treatment and control groups are probabilistically equivalent on all characteristics (both observed and unobserved) before treatment application, allowing any observed differences in outcomes to be attributed to the treatment itself. Option A reflects a misconception that unequal group sizes improve learning about the treatment (they may reduce power for detecting differences). Option B describes the **Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA)**, which is an important validity condition but secondary to the randomization principle that creates comparable groups. Option D describes subgroup analysis, which is a post-experimental analytical choice rather than a design principle that enables causal inference. The key insight: without randomization, no amount of statistical sophistication can reliably separate treatment effects from pre-existing differences between groups.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. (positive = challenger better)\n    differences = losses_incumbent - losses_challenger\n    n = len(differences)\n    \n    d_bar = np.mean(differences)\n    s_d = np.std(differences, ddof=1)\n    \n    # Test statistic\n    t_stat = d_bar / (s_d / np.sqrt(n))\n    \n    # Two-sided p-value\n    p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat), df=n-1))\n    \n    # Confidence interval\n    t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df=n-1)\n    ci_lower = d_bar - t_crit * s_d / np.sqrt(n)\n    ci_upper = d_bar + t_crit * s_d / np.sqrt(n)\n    \n    return {\n        \'mean_difference\': d_bar,\n        \'std_difference\': s_d,\n        \'t_statistic\': t_stat,\n        \'p_value\': p_value,\n        \'ci_lower\': ci_lower,\n        \'ci_upper\': ci_upper,\n        \'n_observations\': n\n    }\n\n# Calculate per-observation log-loss\n# Note: clip probabilities to avoid log(0)\neps = 1e-15\nloss_incumbent = -(y_eval * np.log(np.clip(y_prob_incumbent, eps, 1-eps)) + \n                   (1-y_eval) * np.log(np.clip(1-y_prob_incumbent, eps, 1-eps)))\nloss_challenger = -(y_eval * np.log(np.clip(y_prob_challenger, eps, 1-eps)) + \n                    (1-y_eval) * np.log(np.clip(1-y_prob_challenger, eps, 1-eps)))\n\nresults = paired_model_test(loss_incumbent, loss_challenger)\n\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint("PAIRED T-TEST: Log-Loss Comparison")\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint(f"Mean incumbent log-loss:   {np.mean(loss_incumbent):.4f}")\nprint(f"Mean challenger log-loss:  {np.mean(loss_challenger):.4f}")\nprint(f"Mean difference:           {results[\'mean_difference\']:.4f}")\nprint(f"Standard deviation:        {results[\'std_difference\']:.4f}")\nprint(f"t-statistic:               {results[\'t_statistic\']:.4f}")\nprint(f"p-value:                   {results[\'p_value\']:.4e}")\nprint(f"95% CI for difference:     [{results[\'ci_lower\']:.4f}, {results[\'ci_upper\']:.4f}]")\nprint(f"Significant at \u03b1=0.05:     {results[\'p_value\'] < 0.05}")\nprint()\n\n# Avoid comparing a model trained on six months of data with one trained on six days.\n\n**Watch for prediction drift, not just accuracy**: If the challenger makes wildly different predictions but similar overall accuracy, investigate why before transitioning. The model might be "right for the wrong reasons."\n\n**Don\'t ignore segment losers**: If your new model crushes it overall but performs worse on your highest-value customer segment, that\'s a red flag worth investigating.\n\n**Build in a grace period**: Set your rollback threshold slightly below your minimum improvement threshold. This gives the new model room to adapt without immediately reverting.\n\n**Document everything**: The node auto-generates a transition log, but add your own notes about *why* you made the decision. Future-you will thank present-you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial assessment of whether a new model architecture is worth pursuing, when Each row represents one decision variable (like "units of Product A to make" or "whether to open Warehouse B").\n\nRequired columns:\n- **Variable Name** (text): Unique identifier for each decision variable\n- **Lower Bound** (numeric): Minimum allowed value (use 0 for non-negative variables)\n- **Upper Bound** (numeric): Maximum allowed value (use a large number like 1000000 for "unlimited")\n- **Objective Coefficient** (numeric): How much each unit contributes to your goal (profit per unit, cost per item, etc.)\n\nOptional columns:\n- **Variable Type** (text): "continuous", "integer", or "binary" (defaults to continuous)\n- **Constraint Coefficients** (numeric): Additional columns defining resource usage per unit\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| Variable Name | Lower Bound | Upper Bound | Objective Coefficient | Labor Hours | Material Kg |\n|---------------|-------------|-------------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|\n| Product_A     | 0           | 500         | 25                    | 2           | 3           |\n| Product_B     | 0           | 300         | 40                    | 3           | 2           |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Objective** | Whether to maximize or minimize | Maximize | Switch to "Minimize" for cost, waste, or risk problems |\n| **Optimization Type** | Linear, mixed-integer, or nonlinear | Linear | Use "Mixed-Integer" when decisions must be whole numbers (people, machines). Use "Nonlinear" for complex relationships |\n| **Constraint Definitions** | Resource limits and business rules | None | Add rows like "Labor Hours \u2264 1000" or "Product_A \u2265 100" to enforce limits |\n| **Solver Time Limit** | Maximum seconds to search for solution | 300 | Increase for complex problems with many variables; decrease for quick estimates |\n| **Optimality Gap** | How close to perfect (0% = exact, 5% = within 5% of optimal) | 0% | Increase to 1-5% for faster solutions on large problems where "close enough" works |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs three things:\n\n**1. Decision Table** — Your input table with a new **Optimal Value** column showing the recommended decision for each variable. This is your action plan.\n\n**2. Solution Summary Card** displaying:\n- **Objective Value**: The best achievable result (total profit, minimum cost, etc.)\n- **Solution Status**: "Optimal" (found best answer), "Feasible" (found good answer), or "Infeasible" (no solution exists within constraints)\n- **Solve Time**: How long the optimization took\n\n**3. Sensitivity Report** (when available) — Shows how much objective coefficients or constraint limits could change before the optimal decision changes. Useful for "what-if" analysis.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n- **Filter** node \u2192 To extract only selected decisions (e.g., where Optimal Value > 0)\n- **Visualise** node \u2192 To create bar charts of recommended decisions or pie charts of resource allocation\n- **Export** node \u2192 To push decisions directly to operational systems or reports\n- **Calculate** node \u2192 To compute secondary metrics like total resource usage or revenue\n\n### Quick Start: Product Mix Optimization\n\n1. **Prepare your data** with one row per product, including profit per unit and resource requirements\n2. **Connect data to Optimise node** and map Variable Name, bounds, and Objective Coefficient columns\n3. **Set Objective to "Maximize"** and Optimization Type to "Linear"\n4. **Add constraints** like "Total_Labor \u2264 available_hours" using your constraint coefficient columns\n5. **Run the node** and check the Solution Status is "Optimal"\n6. **Review Optimal Value column** for how many units of each product to produce\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n- **Start simple**: Test with just 2-3 variables and one constraint before building your full model. Easier to debug.\n- **Check for infeasibility**: If you get "Infeasible", your constraints are too restrictive. Relax bounds or limits one at a time to find the culprit.\n- **Use integer sparingly**: Integer and binary variables slow solving dramatically. Only use them when decimals truly don\'t make sense.\n- **Scale your numbers**: If coefficients vary wildly (0.001 to 1,000,000), divide or multiply columns to bring them into similar ranges. Improves numerical stability.\n- **Save successful models**: Use the Template feature to save constraint definitions you\'ll reuse for monthly production planning or weekly scheduling.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Mode\n\n**When to use:** Initial problem scoping when you need to validate your objective function and constraints are correctly specified before investing in a full solve.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'GLOP\'` or `\'CBC\'` | Fast linear solver with minimal overhead |\n| `time_limit` | `30` | Stop after 30 seconds to get any feasible solution |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.10` | Accept solutions within 10% of optimal |\n| `presolve` | `True` | Let solver simplify problem structure |\n| `threads` | `1` | Avoid thread coordination overhead on small problems |\n\n**What you get:** A feasible solution quickly that confirms your model structure works, typically within seconds for problems under 10,000 variables.\n\n**Trade-off:** Solution quality may be far from optimal; use this only to debug formulation, not for actionable recommendations.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Solve\n\n**When to use:** Final deployment where solution quality directly impacts business outcomes and compute time is acceptable (e.g., weekly production planning, quarterly portfolio allocation).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'SCIP\'` or `\'Gurobi\'` | Industrial-strength solver with advanced techniques |\n| `time_limit` | `3600` | Allow up to 1 hour for convergence |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.001` | Require solutions within 0.1% of proven optimum |\n| `absolute_gap` | `1.0` | Stop if objective improvement drops below 1 unit |\n| `threads` | `-1` | Use all available CPU cores |\n| `emphasis` | `\'optimality\'` | Prioritize solution quality over feasibility speed |\n\n**What you get:** Near-optimal solutions with mathematically proven quality guarantees suitable for high-stakes decision-making.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly longer solve times; may not complete within time limit for very large problems (100,000+ integer variables).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Infeasible Problem Diagnosis\n\n**When to use:** Your model returns "no feasible solution" and you need to identify which constraints are causing conflicts.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'CBC\'` or `\'GLOP\'` | Good diagnostic reporting |\n| `relaxation_mode` | `\'elastic\'` | Allow constraint violations with penalties |\n| `violation_penalty` | `1000000` | High cost makes violations visible in solution |\n| `log_level` | `\'verbose\'` | Show detailed solver progress and conflict detection |\n| `write_model` | `True` | Export model file for external inspection |\n\n**What you get:** A solution showing exactly which constraints cannot be satisfied simultaneously, with violation magnitudes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Not a true optimization—you\'re diagnosing, not solving; requires manual constraint adjustment afterward.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Real-Time Reoptimization\n\n**When to use:** Live systems requiring rapid re-solving as conditions change (e.g., dynamic pricing, ride-sharing dispatch, intraday trading adjustment).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'GLOP\'` | Fastest for LP; use `\'CBC\'` if integer variables needed |\n| `warm_start` | `True` | Initialize from previous solution |\n| `time_limit` | `5` | Hard stop at 5 seconds for responsiveness |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.05` | Accept "good enough" solutions quickly |\n| `presolve` | `False` | Skip when problem structure unchanged from last solve |\n\n**What you get:** Sub-10-second response times enabling continuous re-optimization as new data arrives.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires incremental problem formulation; solutions are approximate but delivered fast enough for operational decisions.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needs to allocate £400M in lending capital across customer segments while managing risk exposure, regulatory capital requirements, and profit targets.
