Need\n\nThe **Discover Causal Structure** node expects a clean tabular dataset where each column represents a variable you want to include in your causal graph. Your data should be continuous (numeric) or categorical variables—mixed types work fine.\n\n**Input requirements:**\n- At least 3 variables (columns)\n- Minimum 100–200 rows recommended for stable results\n- No missing values in the columns you\'re analyzing\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_age | ad_spend | website_visits | purchase_amount |\n|--------------|----------|----------------|-----------------|\n| 34           | 120      | 8              | 450             |\n| 28           | 0        | 2              | 0               |\n| 45           | 200      | 15             | 890             |\n\nThe node will analyze relationships *between* these columns to infer which variables causally influence others.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Algorithm** | Chooses the discovery method (PC, GES, or FCI) | PC | Use GES for smaller datasets with clearer signals; FCI when you suspect hidden confounders |\n| **Significance Level** | Controls how conservative the independence tests are (0–1) | 0.05 | Lower to 0.01 for stricter edges (fewer false positives); raise to 0.10 if graph is too sparse |\n| **Max Parents** | Limits how many direct causes a variable can have | 5 | Increase for complex domains; decrease if results look implausibly dense |\n| **Prior Knowledge** | Optional: specify edges that must/cannot exist | None | Use when domain expertise says "X definitely causes Y" or "A cannot cause B" |\n| **Bootstrap Confidence** | Runs algorithm on resampled data to estimate edge stability | Off | Turn on for robustness checks—adds compute time but shows you which edges are reliable |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\n**Primary output:** A **directed graph visualization** showing variables as nodes and causal relationships as arrows. An edge from `ad_spend \u2192 website_visits` means the algorithm infers that spending causally drives visits.\n\n**Additional outputs:**\n- **Edge list table**: All discovered edges with direction (e.g., `ad_spend \u2192 website_visits`, confidence score if bootstrapping enabled)\n- **Adjacency matrix**: A grid showing which variables connect to which—useful for downstream programming\n- **Fit metrics**: Score measuring how well the discovered structure explains your data (higher = better fit)\n- **Warnings panel**: Flags potential issues like "insufficient data for reliable inference" or "detected possible cycles"\n\nIf bootstrapping is on, you\'ll also see confidence percentages next to each edge (e.g., "appears in 87% of bootstrap samples").\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node pairs naturally with:\n\n- **Estimate Causal Effect**: Feed the discovered DAG to quantify *how much* X affects Y\n- **Counterfactual Simulation**: Use the structure to answer "what if" questions\n- **Feature Selection**: Identify which variables are causes vs. mere correlates of your target\n- **Data Collection Planner**: The graph reveals confounders you should measure in future studies\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Discover Causal Structure node\n2. **Select the columns** you want to include in the analysis (exclude IDs, timestamps, or obvious non-causes)\n3. **Leave defaults** (PC algorithm, 0.05 significance) for your first run\n4. **Execute** and examine the graph visualization\n5. **Interpret arrows**: Follow the direction—arrows point from cause to effect\n6. **Check warnings**: If the node flags issues, consider collecting more data or adding prior knowledge\n7. **Validate**: Does the graph align with domain knowledge? If edges seem backward, review your data quality\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1:** Causal discovery is sample-hungry. If your graph has fewer than 500 rows, treat results as exploratory hypotheses, not firm conclusions.\n\n**Tip 2:** Temporal ordering is your friend. If you *know* variable A was measured before B, add prior knowledge that B cannot cause A—this dramatically improves accuracy.\n\n**Tip 3:** A missing edge is as informative as a present one. If the algorithm doesn\'t connect two variables, it\'s saying "these are independent once we account for everything else."\n\n**Tip 4:** Bootstrap confidence is worth the wait for high-stakes decisions. An edge appearing in only 40% of bootstrap runs deserves skepticism.\n\n**Tip 5:** Combine automated discovery with domain review. Treat the graph as a conversation starter with subject-matter experts, not a final answer.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Hypothesis Screening\n\n**When to use:** Early exploration with 50–200 variables when you need directional insights in minutes, not hours.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"pc"` | Constraint-based; scales well to many variables |\n| `alpha` | `0.05` | Standard significance; conservative enough without being overly strict |\n| `max_cond_vars` | `3` | Limits conditioning sets; drastically reduces compute time |\n| `ci_test` | `"fisherz"` | Fast parametric test for continuous data |\n| `verbose` | `True` | Monitor progress during exploration |\n\n**What you get:** A sparse graph identifying strongest causal candidates with ~70–80% edge precision in 5–15 minutes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Misses weak edges and may include spurious links from limited conditional independence testing.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Discovery\n\n**When to use:** Publishing results, regulatory submission, or when causal claims will drive six-figure decisions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"fges"` | Score-based; Missing values should be handled upstream—consider using an Imputation node first if needed.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Target Variable** | Which column to explain | (none) | Always set this to your outcome of interest |\n| **Driver Variables** | Which columns to analyze as predictors | (all others) | Deselect columns that are IDs, dates, or known non-drivers |\n| **Method** | Algorithm for importance calculation | Shapley | Use "Relative Weights" for faster results on large datasets; stick with Shapley for most accurate attribution |\n| **Normalize Importance** | Whether to scale contributions to sum to 100% | Yes | Turn off if you want to see raw R² contributions instead of percentages |\n| **Min Observations** | Minimum rows required for analysis | 30 | Increase to 100+ for more stable estimates with many drivers |\n| **Confidence Level** | Statistical confidence for importance intervals | 95% | Lower to 90% if you want narrower uncertainty bands |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Main visualization:** A horizontal bar chart showing each driver ranked by importance, with bars representing the percentage of variance explained. Drivers are color-coded from most important (darker) to least important (lighter).\n\n**Data outputs:** The node adds these columns to your dataset and passes it forward:\n- `driver_importance_[variable]` — numeric importance score for each driver\n- `driver_rank_[variable]` — ordinal ranking (1 = most important)\n\n**Summary table:** A sortable table showing:\n- Driver name\n- Importance score (% of R² explained)\n- Confidence interval\n- Cumulative importance (running total)\n\n**Model metrics card:** Displays overall model R², adjusted R², and number of observations analyzed.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter Driver Analysis, you\'ll typically want to:\n\n1. **Filter node** \u2192 Focus on just the top 3-5 drivers for deeper investigation\n2. **Segmentation node** \u2192 Check if driver importance varies across customer segments or regions\n3. **Scenario Analysis node** \u2192 Model what happens if you improve your top drivers by 10%\n4. **Export node** \u2192 Share the importance rankings with stakeholders\n\nThe enriched dataset with importance scores flows through, so you can use those scores in conditional logic or visualizations.\n\n### Quick Start: Finding What Drives Customer Satisfaction\n\n1. **Connect your customer data** to the Driver Analysis node (ensure you have satisfaction scores and potential drivers like price, quality, delivery time)\n2. **Set Target Variable** to your satisfaction metric (e.g., `nps_score` or `csat`)\n3. **Leave Driver Variables** at default to consider all factors, or manually select 5-10 key candidates\n4. **Keep Method as "Shapley"** for balanced accuracy and interpretability\n5. **Run the analysis** and examine the bar chart—your top 3 drivers are your primary action levers\n6. **Connect a Segmentation node** to check if these drivers matter equally for all customer types\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Start broad, then narrow.** Run your first analysis with all plausible drivers included. You can always filter down, but starting too narrow might miss surprises.\n\n**Watch for multicollinearity.** If you see wildly different importance scores across runs, you may have highly correlated drivers (like "price" and "price_tier"). Consider removing redundant variables.\n\n**Context matters more than ranking.** A driver ranked #3 with 18% importance is still highly actionable. Don\'t fixate only on #1.\n\n**Check the cumulative column.** If your top 4 drivers explain 80% of variance, you\'ve found your leverage points. The long tail of small drivers rarely deserves attention.\n\n**Segment before concluding.** Driver importance often varies dramatically across customer types, geographies, or product lines. Your dataset needs three essential columns:\n\n- **Entity ID**: A categorical column identifying each unit (e.g., `company_id`, `country_code`)\n- **Time variable**: A sequential time indicator (e.g., `year`, `quarter`, `date`)\n- **Outcome variable**: The numeric variable you\'re modeling (e.g., `revenue`, `gdp_growth`)\n- **Explanatory variables**: One or more numeric predictors\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| company_id | year | revenue | marketing_spend | employees |\n|------------|------|---------|-----------------|-----------|\n| A          | 2020 | 1.2     | 0.3             | 50        |\n| A          | 2021 | 1.5     | 0.4             | 55        |\n| B          | 2020 | 2.1     | 0.5             | 120       |\n| B          | 2021 | 2.3     | 0.6             | 125       |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Entity Column** | Which column identifies your panel units | — | Required; select your ID variable |\n| **Time Column** | Which column represents time periods | — | Required; must be sequential |\n| **Dependent Variable** | The outcome you\'re modeling | — | Required; what you want to explain |\n| **Independent Variables** | Your predictor variables | — | Select all relevant explanatory factors |\n| **GMM Type** | Difference GMM vs. System GMM | System | Use Difference GMM if your series are non-stationary; System GMM for persistent data |\n| **Lag Depth** | How many lags to use as instruments | 2 | Increase to 3–4 for longer panels; reduce to 1 for short panels to avoid weak instruments |\n| **Collapse Instruments** | Reduces instrument count | False | Enable if you have many time periods (>20) to prevent instrument proliferation |\n| **Two-step Estimation** | Use efficient two-step GMM | True | Keep enabled for better efficiency; disable for simpler one-step if convergence issues arise |\n| **Robust Standard Errors** | Windmeijer finite-sample correction | True | Always keep enabled for reliable inference |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Coefficient Estimates Table**: Shows the effect of each variable, including the lagged dependent variable. The coefficient on your lagged outcome tells you the degree of persistence in your series.\n\n**Diagnostic Statistics Panel**:\n- **AR(1) and AR(2) tests**: You *want* significant AR(1) and *non-significant* AR(2) — this confirms first-differencing removed autocorrelation without introducing second-order issues\n- **Hansen J-test**: Tests instrument validity (p > 0.10 indicates instruments are likely valid)\n- **Instrument count**: Shows number of instruments vs. groups — keep this ratio well below 1\n\n**Residual Plots**: Visualizations showing model fit and helping you spot patterns that suggest misspecification.\n\n### Connecting to Other Nodes\n\nAfter Dynamic Panel estimation, you\'ll typically:\n\n1. **Connect to Prediction node** to forecast future outcomes using your estimated dynamic relationship\n2. **Connect to Sensitivity Analysis** to test how results change under different lag specifications\n3. **Connect to Export node** to save coefficients for reporting or further analysis\n\n### Quick Start: Estimating Revenue Dynamics\n\n1. **Drag your panel dataset** into the canvas and connect it to a Dynamic Panel node\n2. **Set Entity Column** to your company/unit identifier (e.g., `company_id`)\n3. **Set Time Column** to your time variable (e.g., `year`)\n4. **Select Dependent Variable** as your outcome (e.g., `revenue`)\n5. **Choose Independent Variables** (e.g., `marketing_spend`, `employees`)\n6. **Leave GMM Type as System** and **Two-step enabled**\n7. **Click Run** and check diagnostics: AR(2) should be non-significant (p > 0.10)\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Check your instrument count**: A common mistake is having too many instruments relative to panel groups. If your instrument count exceeds your number of entities, enable "Collapse Instruments" immediately.\n\n**Hansen test too perfect?** A p-value of 1.00 on the Hansen test often indicates instrument proliferation. Reduce lag depth or collapse instruments.\n\n**Short panels need care**: With fewer than 5 time periods, reduce lag depth to 1 and consider whether you have enough variation for reliable estimation.\n\n**Persistent variables love System GMM**: If your dependent variable changes slowly (like firm size or country GDP), System GMM dramatically outperforms Difference GMM by adding level equations.\n\n**Always report diagnostics**: Your coefficient estimates mean nothing if the specification tests fail. Include AR(2) and Hansen statistics in any results you share.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial model assessment with medium-sized datasets (N < 5,000, T = 3–7) when you need fast iteration to determine if dynamic structure exists.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `transformation` | `"first_difference"` | Fastest computation, no system matrix construction |\n| `gmm_type` | `"difference"` | Single-step requires no weight matrix iteration |\n| `collapse_instruments` | `True` | Dramatically reduces instrument count, speeds estimation |\n| `max_lags_instruments` | `2` | Limits instrument proliferation while preserving T–2 moments |\n| `robust` | `False` | Skip robust variance calculation for speed |\n\n**What you get:** Results in seconds that reveal whether lagged dependent variable coefficients are significant and whether your data exhibits dynamic properties.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice efficiency gains from system GMM and underestimate standard errors without robust covariance, making this unsuitable for inference.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Inference\n\n**When to use:** Final models for publication, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decisions where statistical validity is paramount.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `transformation` | `"forward_orthogonal"` | Preserves observations in unbalanced panels |\n| `gmm_type` | `"system"` | Combines level and difference equations for efficiency |\n| `collapse_instruments` | `False` | Uses full instrument matrix for optimal efficiency |\n| `max_lags_instruments` | `None` | Exploits all available moment conditions |\n| `robust` | `True` | Windmeijer-corrected standard errors for finite-sample accuracy |\n| `two_step` | `True` | Efficient GMM with optimal weighting matrix |\n\n**What you get:** Asymptotically efficient estimates with valid standard errors suitable for formal hypothesis testing and confidence intervals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computational cost increases substantially, and with T > 10 you risk instrument proliferation leading to bias.\n\n### Recipe 3: Highly Persistent Dependent Variable\n\n**When to use:** When your outcome exhibits near-unit-root behavior (autocorrelation > 0.85) such as firm leverage ratios, GDP levels, or cumulative metrics.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `transformation` | `"forward_orthogonal"` | Better finite-sample properties than first-difference |\n| `gmm_type` | `"system"` | Difference GMM performs poorly with persistent series |\n| `collapse_instruments` | `False` | Need instrument strength with weak identification |\n| `max_lags_instruments` | `4` | Deeper lags provide identifying power for persistent processes |\n| `level_instruments` | `"first_difference"` | Use differences as instruments for levels equation |\n\n**What you get:** Consistent estimates even when the autoregressive parameter approaches unity, where standard difference GMM suffers weak instrument problems.\n\n**Trade-off:** System GMM requires the additional stationarity assumption that may not hold for trending series.\n\n### Recipe 4: Short Panels with Large N\n\n**When to use:** Corporate datasets with thousands of firms but only T = 3–4 years, common in credit risk or short-horizon treatment studies.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `transformation` | `"first_difference"` | Loses only one period—acceptable with short T |\n| `gmm_type` | `"difference"` | System GMM unreliable with insufficient time variation |\n| `collapse_instruments` | `True` | Critical—prevents instruments exceeding cross-sections |\n| `max_lags_instruments` | `1` | Only t–2 available anyway with T = 3–4 |\n| `min_periods` | `3` | Accept absolute minimum for identification |\n\n**What you get:** Valid inference exploiting cross-sectional variation when time dimension barely supports dynamic modeling.\n\n**Trade-off:** Large standard errors from limited moment conditions; power to detect effects is substantially reduced.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA European commercial bank with €50B in assets needs You\'ll need:\n\n- **A date/time column** (daily, weekly, or monthly frequency works best)\n- **An outcome variable** (the metric you\'re measuring — stock returns, website traffic, sales, etc.)\n- **An event date or event indicator** (either a single date or a binary 0/1 column marking when the event occurred)\n\nYour data should look like this:\n\n**Before connecting:**\n| date | daily_revenue | company_id |\n|------------|---------------|------------|\n| 2024-01-15 | 45000 | ACME |\n| 2024-01-16 | 47000 | ACME |\n| 2024-01-17 | 46500 | ACME |\n\n**You\'ll add:** An event indicator showing when your event happened (e.g., a product launch on 2024-01-16).\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Event Date** | The specific date when your event occurred | (required) | Always set this — it\'s your treatment point |\n| **Pre-Event Window** | How many periods before the event to analyze | 30 days | Increase for slow-moving metrics; decrease for volatile ones |\n| **Post-Event Window** | How many periods after the event to track | 30 days | Extend to capture delayed effects (e.g., 90 days for policy changes) |\n| **Outcome Variable** | Which column contains your metric of interest | (required) | Choose your key performance indicator |\n| **Grouping Variable** | Optional: analyze multiple entities separately | None | Use when you have panel data (multiple companies, locations, etc.) |\n| **Counterfactual Method** | How to predict "what would have happened" | Linear trend | Switch to "moving average" for seasonal data or "synthetic control" for complex patterns |\n| **Confidence Level** | Statistical confidence for significance bands | 95% | Use 90% for exploratory analysis, 99% for high-stakes decisions |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs three key components:\n\n**1. Enhanced Dataset** with new columns:\n- `event_time`: Days/periods relative to event (e.g., -5, 0, +3)\n- `counterfactual`: Predicted value had event not occurred\n- `effect`: Difference between observed and counterfactual\n- `cumulative_effect`: Running total of impact over time\n\n**2. Visual Outputs:**\n- **Event study plot**: Shows actual vs. counterfactual with confidence bands — the gap between lines is your effect\n- **Cumulative impact chart**: Tracks total effect accumulation — great for executive summaries\n\n**3. Summary Statistics:**\n- Average treatment effect with p-value\n- Total cumulative impact\n- Time to peak effect\n\n### Quick Start: Measuring a Product Launch Impact\n\n1. **Connect your time series data** to the Event Study node (ensure you have daily metrics and launch date)\n2. **Set Event Date** to your product launch date\n3. **Choose your Outcome Variable** (e.g., `daily_revenue`)\n4. **Set Pre/Post-Event Windows** to 30 days each (adjust if you launched recently)\n5. **Select Counterfactual Method**: start with "Linear trend" — if your visualization shows poor pre-event fit, switch to "Moving average"\n6. **Run the node** and examine the event study plot first — look for a clear separation between actual and counterfactual lines\n7. **Check the p-value** in summary stats — below 0.05 means statistically significant impact\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node pairs naturally with:\n\n- **Statistical Summary** node: to quantify effect sizes and generate report-ready tables\n- **Segmentation** node: to understand which customer groups drove the effect\n- **Export** node: to share visualizations with stakeholders\n- **Time Series Forecast** node: to project the effect forward\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n1. **Always visually inspect the pre-event fit** — if your counterfactual doesn\'t track the actual trend well before the event, your estimate will be biased. Try different counterfactual methods until pre-event lines align closely.\n\n2. **Watch for anticipation effects** — if people knew the event was coming (e.g., announced policy changes), you might see impacts *before* your event date. Extend your pre-window and look carefully.\n\n3. **Multiple events? Use the Grouping Variable** — analyzing five store openings? Group by store_id and you\'ll get both individual and pooled estimates.\n\n4. **Seasonality matters** — if your event happened during holidays or peak season, use "seasonal adjustment" in preprocessing or choose "synthetic control" for your counterfactual.\n\n5. **Document your windows** — your choice of pre/post periods affects results. Screenshot your settings and note why you chose them for reproducibility.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial analysis of a newly identified event when you need rapid feedback on whether any effect exists before investing in rigorous modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `pre_period` | 30 days | Short enough for fast iteration |\n| `post_period` | 30 days | Symmetric window simplifies interpretation |\n| `method` | "synthetic_control" | Handles confounders without manual specification |\n| `inference` | "permutation" | Distribution-free, no assumptions needed |\n| `n_permutations` | 100 | Minimum for p-value stability |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.90 | Less conservative for exploratory work |\n\n**What you get:** A fast pass/fail signal on effect existence with visual diagnostics in under 60 seconds on typical datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** Lower statistical power and wider confidence intervals mean you may miss moderate effects or get false negatives.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Publication-Ready Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for academic publication, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decisions requiring defensible causal claims.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `pre_period` | 365 days | Captures full seasonal cycle |\n| `post_period` | 180 days | Long enough for delayed effects |\n| `method` | "synthetic_control" | Gold standard for causal inference |\n| `inference` | "block_bootstrap" | Preserves autocorrelation structure |\n| `n_bootstrap` | 5000 | Academic standard for CI precision |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.95 | Conventional threshold |\n| `placebo_tests` | True | Validates method assumptions |\n| `covariate_balance_threshold` | 0.1 | Ensures pre-period fit quality |\n\n**What you get:** Fully documented causal estimates with conservative uncertainty quantification that withstands peer review scrutiny.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computational time increases 50-100x and requires substantial pre-event data that may not exist for recent phenomena.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Multiple Events with Spillovers\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing policy rollouts, product launches, or interventions where treatment occurred in waves and early-treated units may affect later controls.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `pre_period` | 90 days | Balance between history and recency |\n| `post_period` | 60 days | Before next wave arrives |\n| `method` | "did_staggered" | Explicitly handles treatment timing heterogeneity |\n| `inference` | "cluster_bootstrap" | Accounts for within-group correlation |\n| `donor_pool_restriction` | "never_treated_only" | Excludes contaminated controls |\n| `anticipation_period` | 14 days | Removes pre-announcement drift |\n\n**What you get:** Unbiased treatment effects even when rollout is sequential and units influence each other geographically or through networks.\n\n**Trade-off:** Smaller donor pool reduces matching quality and increases sensitivity to individual control unit idiosyncrasies.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Detecting Non-Events (Null Hypothesis Testing)\n\n**When to use:** Proving compliance with "no disruption" requirements after system migrations, validating that a policy change had no unintended consequences, or testing market efficiency.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `pre_period` | 180 days | Establishes stable baseline variance |\n| `post_period` | 90 days | Sufficient to detect deviations |\n| `method` | "difference_in_differences" | Simplest model reduces Type I error |\n| `inference` | "equivalence_test" | Tests if effect is within tolerance bounds |\n| `equivalence_margin` | 0.05 * baseline_std | Practically significant threshold |\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | More liberal for safety testing |\n\n**What you get:** Statistical evidence that the event caused no meaningful change, which standard approaches cannot provide (absence of significance \u2260 significance of absence).\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires pre-specifying what "no effect" means quantitatively, which can be contentious in stakeholder negotiations.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Think of this as a "post-experiment" analysis—you need data that includes who received treatment, what happened to them, and characteristics that might explain differences in response.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- **Treatment column** (binary or categorical): Which intervention each unit received\n- **Outcome column** (numeric): The metric you\'re measuring\n- **Covariate columns** (numeric or categorical): Characteristics that might moderate the treatment effect (age, region, prior behavior, etc.)\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | received_discount | purchase_amount | age_group | prior_purchases |\n|-------------|-------------------|-----------------|-----------|-----------------|\n| 1001 | 1 | 142.50 | 25-34 | 3 |\n| 1002 | 0 | 98.20 | 45-54 | 12 |\n| 1003 | 1 | 201.30 | 25-34 | 1 |\n\nConnect your cleaned, merged dataset directly to the Heterogeneous Effects node input port.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Treatment Variable** | Which column indicates treatment assignment | (none) | Always set this first—it\'s your intervention variable |\n| **Outcome Variable** | Which column measures the effect you care about | (none) | The KPI you\'re trying to move (revenue, conversion, retention, etc.) |\n| **Effect Moderators** | Which variables might create different treatment responses | All numeric/categorical | Select theoretically meaningful splits (customer segments, contexts) not every column |\n| **Estimation Method** | Algorithm for discovering heterogeneity (Causal Forest, S-Learner, T-Learner, X-Learner) | Causal Forest | Causal Forest works well generally; try X-Learner with small treatment groups |\n| **Minimum Group Size** | Smallest subgroup to report separately | 30 | Increase to 50+ for noisier data; decrease if you have huge samples and need granularity |\n| **Confidence Level** | Uncertainty intervals for subgroup effects | 95% | Keep at 95% for standard reporting; 90% if you\'re doing exploratory analysis |\n| **Number of Trees** | Complexity of forest-based methods | 2000 | Increase to 4000+ for very large datasets; decrease to 500 for faster iteration |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\nThe node produces several complementary views of treatment effect heterogeneity:\n\n**Subgroup Effects Table**: Shows estimated treatment effects for each meaningful segment, with confidence intervals. You\'ll see which groups benefited most (and least) from treatment.\n\n**Variable Importance Chart**: Ranks which characteristics matter most for explaining effect differences. This tells you *what* drives heterogeneity even before you look at specific subgroups.\n\n**Effect Distribution Plot**: Visualizes the range of individual treatment effects across your population. A wide spread means substantial heterogeneity; a tight cluster means effects are relatively uniform.\n\n**Added data columns**:\n- `predicted_cate`: Estimated individual treatment effect for each unit\n- `subgroup_id`: Assigned segment based on effect patterns\n- `subgroup_effect`: Average effect within each unit\'s subgroup\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Policy Node**: Feed subgroup assignments and effect estimates to design differentiated intervention strategies—give the discount to high-responders, skip it for low-responders.\n\n**Reporting/Dashboard Node**: Visualize which customer segments, regions, or contexts benefit most from your program.\n\n**Uplift Scoring Node**: Use predicted individual effects for rank-ordering future treatment allocation decisions.\n\n### Quick Start: Finding Your Best Responders\n\n1. **Connect your experiment results dataset** to the Heterogeneous Effects node\n2. **Set Treatment Variable** to your intervention indicator (e.g., `received_email`)\n3. **Set Outcome Variable** to your success metric (e.g., `revenue_30d`)\n4. **Select 3-5 Effect Moderators** you think might matter (start with segment, tenure, engagement_score)\n5. **Run the node** and check Variable Importance first—this validates your intuitions\n6. **Review Subgroup Effects Table** to find your most and least responsive segments\n7. **Connect to Policy Node** to operationalize differentiated targeting\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Start with fewer moderators**: Including 20+ potential moderating variables creates noisy, overfit subgroups. Begin with 3-5 theoretically motivated variables, then expand if needed.\n\n**Check the overlap assumption**: If certain subgroups received treatment 95%+ of the time, heterogeneity estimates for them will be unreliable. Filter to subgroups with reasonable treatment/control balance.\n\n**Minimum group size matters more than you think**: A subgroup with huge estimated effects but only 15 people is probably noise. Trust segments with 50+ observations.\n\n**Compare to average treatment effect**: Always contextualize subgroup effects against your overall ATE. A +5% effect in one segment means little if your average is +4.8%.\n\n**Validate on holdout data when possible**: If you\'re making major resource allocation decisions based on discovered heterogeneity, confirm patterns hold in a separate sample before going all-in.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration with Causal Forests\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploratory analysis on datasets with <50,000 observations where you need fast iteration to decide if heterogeneity exists.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_estimators` | 500 | Fast training while maintaining reasonable stability |\n| `min_samples_leaf` | 250 | Prevents overfitting in small subgroups |\n| `max_depth` | 4 | Limits tree complexity for interpretability |\n| `honesty` | True | Essential for valid inference even in exploration |\n| `n_jobs` | -1 | Parallelizes across all cores |\n\n**What you get:** Rough heterogeneity estimates with wide confidence intervals, sufficient to identify major effect variation patterns.\n\n**Trade-off:** Confidence intervals will be too wide for precise targeting decisions; use only for go/no-go on full analysis.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Doubly Robust Estimation\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for deployment when you need defensible estimates with proper uncertainty quantification and model misspecification protection.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_estimators` | 2000 | Ensures asymptotic properties kick in |\n| `min_samples_leaf` | 100 | Conservative splitting for stable estimates |\n| `cv_folds` | 10 | Robust cross-fitting for nuisance parameters |\n| `propensity_clip` | (0.05, 0.95) | Trims extreme propensity scores |\n| `calibration` | True | Ensures coverage of confidence intervals |\n| `honest_fraction` | 0.5 | Half the data held out for estimation |\n\n**What you get:** Asymptotically valid confidence intervals robust to either outcome or propensity model misspecification.\n\n**Trade-off:** 3-5x longer training time and requires minimum 10,000 observations for reliable coverage.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Confounding with Lasso Regularization\n\n**When to use:** Observational data with >100 covariates where many are irrelevant, risking propensity model overfitting.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `propensity_model` | LassoCV | Automatic feature selection for treatment model |\n| `outcome_model` | Ridge | Shrinkage without feature elimination |\n| `cv_lambda` | True | Cross-validates regularization strength |\n| `max_iter` | 10000 | Ensures Lasso convergence with many features |\n| `tol` | 1e-6 | Tight convergence for stable selection |\n\n**What you get:** Sparse propensity models that avoid overfitting while flexibly modeling outcomes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires strong overlap assumption; fails completely if treatment deterministically depends on unselected variables.\n\n### Recipe 4: Continuous Treatment Dosage Effects\n\n**When to use:** Treatment is continuous (ad spend, drug dosage, discount percentage) rather than binary—surprisingly common but often force-binned incorrectly.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `treatment_type` | "continuous" | Enables kernel-based dose-response estimation |\n| `kernel_bandwidth` | 0.1 * std(T) | Local smoothing around treatment values |\n| `derivative_order` | 1 | Estimates marginal effect at each dose |\n| `min_samples_leaf` | 50 | Lower threshold since fewer splits needed |\n| `boundary_trim` | 0.05 | Removes extreme doses with poor support |\n\n**What you get:** Smooth dose-response curves showing marginal returns at each treatment intensity level.\n\n**Trade-off:** Loses ability to interpret effect "of treatment" versus "of no treatment"; gains policy-relevant optimal dosage identification.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was offering the same 0.25% rate discount to all customers who set up automatic payments, costing £8M annually in foregone interest. You need at least 8-10 observations before and after for reliable results—more is better.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Time Column** | Specifies which column contains your dates | First date column | Change if you have multiple date fields |\n| **Outcome Column** | The variable you\'re measuring impact on | (required) | This is your dependent variable |\n| **Intervention Column** | Binary indicator of pre/post periods | (required) | Must be 0 before, 1 after intervention |\n| **Pre-trend Model** | How to fit the baseline (linear, quadratic, auto) | Linear | Use \'quadratic\' if your pre-trend curves; \'auto\' lets the algorithm decide |\n| **Seasonality Adjustment** | Controls for recurring patterns (none, monthly, quarterly, weekly) | None | Enable if you see regular cycles in your data |\n| **Confidence Level** | Sets width of uncertainty bands | 95% | Lower to 90% for tighter bands, raise to 99% for more conservative estimates |\n| **Autocorrelation Correction** | Adjusts standard errors for time dependence | Newey-West | Keep default unless you know your errors are independent (rare) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\nThe node produces **three main outputs**:\n\n**Visualization**: A chart showing your actual data points, the fitted pre-intervention trend line (extended through the post period as a counterfactual), the post-intervention trajectory, and confidence intervals. The vertical line marks your intervention point.\n\n**Summary Metrics Panel**: Key statistics including:\n- **Level change**: The immediate jump (or drop) right after intervention\n- **Slope change**: How the trend\'s steepness changed\n- **P-values**: Statistical significance for both effects\n- **R-squared**: How well the model fits your data\n\n**Enhanced Dataset**: Your original data plus new columns:\n- `predicted_value`: Model\'s fitted values\n- `counterfactual`: What would have happened without intervention\n- `effect_size`: Difference between actual and counterfactual\n- `ci_lower` and `ci_upper`: Confidence interval bounds\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter your ITS analysis, you\'ll typically:\n\n1. **Connect to a Report Builder** to export findings with the visualization and statistics table\n2. **Pipe into a Filter node** to examine specific time windows (e.g., just the first 3 months post-intervention)\n3. **Join with a complementary dataset** to run sensitivity analyses or explore subgroups\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Drag your time series data** into the canvas\n2. **Add the Interrupted Time Series node** and connect your data\n3. **Map your columns**: Select date, outcome, and intervention fields\n4. **Check the auto-generated chart**: Does the pre-trend look reasonable? If it curves significantly, switch Pre-trend Model to "quadratic"\n5. **Review the metrics panel**: Look first at the p-values—if both >0.05, you may not have a significant effect\n6. **Export the enhanced dataset** to explore effect sizes over time\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Time aggregation matters**: If your raw data is daily but noisy, aggregate to weekly or monthly before analysis. ITS works best with ~20-100 time points total.\n\n**Watch for other interventions**: If something else changed during your study period, add it as a control variable or segment your analysis.\n\n**The counterfactual is your friend**: Always visualize it. If the extended pre-trend looks implausible, your model assumptions may be wrong.\n\n**Autocorrelation is almost always present** in time series data—don\'t turn off the correction unless you\'ve specifically tested for independence.\n\n**Check residuals**: Export the predicted values and calculate residuals (actual - predicted). Plot them. They should look random, not patterned.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data inspection when you need to rapidly assess whether an intervention had any visible effect, with minimal computational overhead and before investing in rigorous modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_boot` | 0 | Skip bootstrap inference entirely for speed |\n| `model_type` | "linear" | Simplest functional form assumption |\n| `seasonality` | FALSE | Ignore seasonal patterns initially |\n| `autocorrelation` | FALSE | Ignore serial correlation |\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | More permissive significance threshold |\n\n**What you get:** Near-instant coefficient estimates showing level and slope changes, suitable for deciding whether deeper analysis is warranted.\n\n**Trade-off:** No valid confidence intervals or hypothesis tests; results may be biased if seasonality or autocorrelation are present.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Final causal estimates for publication, regulatory reporting, or high-stakes business decisions where statistical rigor and defensibility are paramount.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_boot` | 10000 | Robust confidence intervals via extensive resampling |\n| `model_type` | "segmented" | Allows flexible trend changes |\n| `seasonality` | TRUE | Control for cyclical patterns |\n| `autocorrelation` | "newey_west" | HAC-robust standard errors |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard significance level |\n| `sensitivity_check` | TRUE | Generate placebo tests at pseudo-intervention points |\n\n**What you get:** Publication-ready estimates with defensible uncertainty quantification and automated robustness checks.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation time increases 50–100× compared to exploration mode; requires sufficient pre-intervention observations (minimum 20).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Monthly Business Metrics with Strong Seasonality\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing monthly or quarterly KPIs (e.g., retail sales, website traffic) where seasonal patterns dominate and could create false positives if ignored.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `seasonality` | TRUE | Essential for monthly/quarterly data |\n| `seasonal_period` | 12 | Match calendar year structure |\n| `detrend_method` | "stl" | Seasonal-trend decomposition using LOESS |\n| `autocorrelation` | "arima_errors" | Model residual dependencies explicitly |\n| `n_boot` | 5000 | Balance precision and runtime |\n\n**What you get:** Intervention effects isolated from predictable seasonal fluctuations, preventing spurious findings during high/low seasons.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires at least 2–3 full seasonal cycles pre-intervention; results harder to interpret for non-technical stakeholders.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Rare Events in Short Time Windows\n\n**When to use:** Evaluating interventions on low-frequency outcomes (e.g., monthly workplace accidents, quarterly fraud incidents) where counts are small and Gaussian assumptions fail.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model_type` | "poisson" | Appropriate for count data |\n| `offset` | log(exposure) | Account for varying population/time at risk |\n| `autocorrelation` | FALSE | Often negligible in rare-event counts |\n| `test_statistic` | "deviance" | Better power for non-normal outcomes |\n| `n_boot` | 2000 | Moderate resampling sufficient for count models |\n\n**What you get:** Valid inference on rate changes even with single-digit monthly counts, properly handling zero-inflation and discrete nature of data.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires exposure denominator data; less familiar to audiences expecting linear regression outputs.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender implemented stricter identity verification rules in March 2020 after a spike in fraud attempts. She has 8 months of pre-intervention data and 6 months post-intervention. She runs a simple before-after comparison and finds a statistically significant decrease (p < 0.01). What is the primary limitation of concluding the protocol caused the reduction?\n\nA) The sample size is too small—ITS requires at least 24 pre-intervention observations to establish a reliable baseline trend\n\nB) Statistical significance doesn't establish causality—the reduction might reflect continuation of a pre-existing downward trend rather than a level or slope change attributable to the intervention\n\nC) Before-after comparisons violate the parallel trends assumption required for difference-in-differences estimation\n\nD) The intervention effect is confounded because she didn't control for seasonal variation in the regression model\n\n**Answer:** B\n\n**Explanation:** The core insight of ITS is that it models the *pre-intervention trend* and tests whether the intervention caused a *change* in level or slope beyond what that trend would predict. Option A reflects a common but false rule (no universal minimum exists, though more data improves power). Option C confuses ITS with difference-in-differences, which is a different method requiring a control group and parallel trends. Option D introduces a real concern (seasonality) but misses the fundamental flaw: without modeling the pre-intervention trend, we can't distinguish intervention effects from existing patterns, regardless of whether we control for covariates.\n" as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. Your data should include:\n\n- **Treatment indicator column**: A binary column (0/1, TRUE/FALSE, or similar) marking which units received treatment\n- **Covariate columns**: Numeric or categorical features you\'ll use to find matches (demographics, pre-treatment measurements, etc.)\n- **Outcome column**: The metric you want to compare between treated and control groups\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | received_coupon | age | past_purchases | region | revenue |\n|-------------|----------------|-----|----------------|--------|---------|\n| 1001 | 1 | 34 | 12 | West | 450 |\n| 1002 | 0 | 35 | 11 | West | 380 |\n| 1003 | 1 | 28 | 3 | East | 220 |\n\nAll units should be in the same table—don\'t split treated and control into separate datasets.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Treatment Column** | Which column identifies treated units | (none—required) | This is always required; select your binary treatment indicator |\n| **Matching Covariates** | Which features to use when finding similar units | (none—required) | Include variables that affect both treatment assignment and outcomes; exclude post-treatment variables |\n| **Matching Method** | Algorithm for finding matches: nearest neighbor, optimal, or exact | Nearest neighbor | Use "exact" for small categorical datasets; "optimal" minimizes total distance but runs slower |\n| **Match Ratio** | How many control units per treated unit | 1:1 | Increase (e.g., 1:3) when you have abundant controls and want tighter confidence intervals |\n| **Caliper** | Maximum allowable distance for a match | 0.25 standard deviations | Tighten (0.1) to enforce stricter similarity; widen if you\'re discarding too many units |\n| **Distance Metric** | How to measure similarity (Mahalanobis, Euclidean, propensity score) | Mahalanobis | Use propensity score for high-dimensional data; Euclidean for scaled numeric features only |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs an **enriched dataset** with these new columns:\n\n- **match_group_id**: Unique identifier linking each treated unit with its matched control(s)\n- **match_weight**: Weight for each unit (controls may be weighted if used in multiple matches)\n- **match_distance**: Similarity score between matched pairs—lower is better\n\nYou\'ll also see a **Balance Diagnostics Panel** showing:\n\n- **Covariate balance table**: Standardized mean differences before and after matching (aim for <0.1)\n- **Love plot**: Visual comparison of covariate balance—dots should cluster near zero after matching\n- **Sample size summary**: How many treated and control units were successfully matched\n\nFinally, the **Treatment Effect Summary** displays your estimated average treatment effect (ATT) with confidence intervals.\n\n### Downstream Connections\n\nConnect Match Groups to:\n\n- **Statistical Test** node to formally test significance of the treatment effect\n- **Data Table** node to inspect individual match groups and verify quality\n- **Visualization** nodes to create custom charts comparing treated vs. control outcomes\n- **Filter** node to remove unmatched units before further analysis\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your data** and select the treatment indicator column\n2. **Choose matching covariates**—include pre-treatment characteristics that predict both treatment and outcome\n3. **Start with defaults** (1:1 nearest neighbor, 0.25 caliper) and click Run\n4. **Check the Love plot**—if any covariates show standardized differences >0.1, consider adding more covariates or tightening the caliper\n5. **Review the ATT estimate** in the treatment effect summary—this is your causal estimate\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Tip 1**: Always examine unmatched units. If you\'re losing >30% of your treated group, your caliper may be too strict or you need better covariates.\n\n**Tip 2**: Categorical variables work best with exact matching. If you have important categories (like region), consider exact matching on those first, then nearest-neighbor on numeric features.\n\n**Tip 3**: Check balance on covariates you *didn\'t* match on. If these also balance, it suggests your matching captured important similarities.\n\n**Tip 4**: When matching with replacement (allowing controls to match multiple treated units), pay attention to match weights in subsequent analyses—some controls matter more than others.\n\n**Tip 5**: Save your match_group_id column. You\'ll need it if you want to perform subgroup analyses or sensitivity checks later.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration Match\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need quick feedback on whether matching is viable for your dataset, or when presenting preliminary findings to stakeholders.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `distance_metric` | `"mahalanobis"` | Fast computation, accounts for covariate correlation |\n| `caliper` | `0.5` | Loose enough to find matches quickly |\n| `max_matches` | `1` | One-to-one matching minimizes computation |\n| `replacement` | `False` | Simpler interpretation for first pass |\n| `exact_match_vars` | `None` | Skip exact matching constraints initially |\n\n**What you get:** Results in seconds to minutes that reveal match feasibility, covariate balance issues, and rough effect size estimates.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice precision and may include poor-quality matches that would fail stricter calipers or balance checks.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Matching\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for publication, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decisions where methodological rigor will be scrutinized.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `distance_metric` | `"propensity"` | Well-understood, defensible choice |\n| `caliper` | `0.01` | Strict threshold ensures high match quality |\n| `max_matches` | `3` | Balance between variance reduction and bias |\n| `replacement` | `True` | Uses control pool efficiently |\n| `exact_match_vars` | Key confounders | Forces balance on critical variables |\n| `balance_check` | `"standardized_diff"` | Standard diagnostic with `threshold=0.1` |\n| `common_support` | `"trim"` | Remove extreme propensity scores |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible matches with documented covariate balance and sensitivity analyses built in.\n\n**Trade-off:** Longer runtime (hours for large datasets) and potentially fewer matched units due to strict quality controls.\n\n### Recipe 3: Time-Varying Treatment Launch\n\n**When to use:** Evaluating product launches, policy rollouts, or interventions that occur at different calendar times across units, where temporal trends could confound effects.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `distance_metric` | `"euclidean"` | Includes time distance in matching space |\n| `caliper` | `0.25` | Moderate threshold |\n| `max_matches` | `5` | Need buffer for time-window constraints |\n| `replacement` | `True` | Limited control pool per time window |\n| `exact_match_vars` | `["month", "year"]` | Force temporal alignment |\n| `time_window` | `30` | Match within ±30 days of treatment |\n\n**What you get:** Matches that control for both unit characteristics and secular trends, preventing time-based confounding.\n\n**Trade-off:** Substantially reduced control pool since each treated unit can only match to contemporaneous controls.\n\n### Recipe 4: Rare Treatment Detection\n\n**When to use:** Evaluating adverse events, fraud detection, or any outcome where treatment/exposure is rare (<5% prevalence) and you have abundant control observations.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `distance_metric` | `"propensity"` | Handles extreme imbalance well |\n| `caliper` | `0.02` | Tight caliper justified by large control pool |\n| `max_matches` | `10` | Leverage abundant controls for precision |\n| `replacement` | `True` | Essential with small treatment group |\n| `exact_match_vars` | High-risk strata | Match within risk categories |\n| `ratio_match` | `"variable"` | Use more matches where propensity overlap is good |\n\n**What you get:** Stable estimates despite rare treatment by maximizing information from the large control reservoir.\n\n**Trade-off:** Asymmetric analysis where some treated units get many matches and others few, complicating variance estimation.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needed to The matched groups are perfectly balanced on these three covariates. Why might the causal estimate still be biased?\n\nA) Matching on multiple covariates simultaneously reduces statistical power, increasing the variance of the treatment effect estimate enough to introduce systematic bias.\n\nB) Perfect balance on observed covariates guarantees unbiased estimates only when the treatment and control groups have equal sample sizes.\n\nC) Units may differ on unobserved characteristics that affect both treatment assignment and outcomes, violating the ignorability assumption required for unbiased causal inference.\n\nD) Matching creates artificial correlation between covariates and treatment status, which propagates measurement error from the covariates into the treatment effect estimate.\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** C is correct because matching only controls for *observed* covariates, but causal inference requires the ignorability (unconfoundedness) assumption: that conditional on measured covariates, treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes. If unobserved confounders exist—such as motivation or social networks that affect both who enrolls in job training and subsequent earnings—the matched estimate remains biased regardless of perfect covariate balance. A misunderstands the bias-variance tradeoff (reduced power increases variance, not bias). B conflates balance with the separate issue of estimation efficiency. D invents a non-existent problem—matching doesn't create spurious correlations that introduce measurement error bias. This question tests whether readers understand that matching addresses *observable* confounding but cannot solve the fundamental problem of unobserved confounders, the critical limitation that separates matching from true experimental randomization.\n" as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. decisions |\n| **Covariates** | Additional variables to control for | None | Add demographic or firmographic factors that might confound results |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Output columns added to your data:**\n- `predicted_counterfactual`: What the outcome would have been without treatment\n- `treatment_effect`: Individual-level impact estimate\n- `propensity_score`: (PSM only) Probability of receiving treatment\n\n**Summary metrics displayed:**\n- **Average Treatment Effect (ATE)**: The headline number — mean impact across all treated units\n- **Standard Error & p-value**: Statistical significance indicators\n- **Confidence Interval**: Range of plausible true effects\n- **Pre-trend test**: Validates parallel trends assumption (DiD only)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Impact over time**: Line chart showing treated vs. control trajectories\n- **Effect distribution**: Histogram of individual treatment effects\n- **Covariate balance**: (PSM) Before/after matching quality\n\n### Quick Start: Measuring Campaign Impact\n\n1. **Connect your data** containing user activity before and after a marketing campaign launch\n2. **Set Method** to "Difference-in-Differences" (the most common starting point)\n3. **Select your Outcome Column** (e.g., weekly_purchases)\n4. **Specify Treatment Column** (e.g., received_campaign)\n5. **Review the pre-trend test** — if p > 0.05, you\'re good to proceed\n6. **Read the ATE** in the summary panel — this is your campaign\'s causal impact\n7. **Export the impact over time chart** for your stakeholder deck\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Typical next nodes:**\n- **Segment Analysis** \u2192 Break down treatment effects by customer segment to find who benefited most\n- **Decision Optimizer** \u2192 Use impact estimates to project ROI of scaling the intervention\n- **Report Builder** \u2192 Package findings with auto-generated narrative\n- **Prediction Model** \u2192 Incorporate treatment effects as features for targeting\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n1. **Check your parallel trends first**: Before trusting DiD results, examine the pre-treatment visualization. If treated and control groups were already diverging, consider PSM or synthetic control instead.\n\n2. **Don\'t confuse statistical significance with business significance**: A p-value < 0.05 with a $0.03 ATE might be "real" but not worth acting on.\n\n3. **Use clustered standard errors by default**: Unless you have genuinely independent observations, clustering (usually by unit ID) prevents overconfident results.\n\n4. **Start simple, then add covariates**: Run the basic model first, then add control variables one at a time to see how estimates stabilize.\n\n5. **Save your counterfactual predictions**: The `predicted_counterfactual` column is gold for storytelling — show stakeholders "here\'s what *would* have happened" vs. what did.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration (Difference-in-Differences Light)\n\n**When to use:** You have panel data with a clear pre/post treatment period and need to quickly assess whether an effect exists before committing to deeper analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"diff_in_diff"` | Simplest causal estimator for before/after comparisons |\n| `n_bootstrap` | `100` | Fast confidence intervals without sacrificing basic validity |\n| `covariates` | `None` | Skip adjustment to reduce computation and model complexity |\n| `parallel_trends_test` | `False` | Defer assumption testing to later stages |\n| `alpha` | `0.10` | More permissive threshold catches signals worth investigating |\n\n**What you get:** Treatment effect estimate with 90% confidence intervals in seconds, suitable for go/no-go decisions on further analysis.\n\n**Trade-off:** You skip covariate adjustment and assumption validation, risking confounding and violating parallel trends without detection.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade RCT Analysis\n\n**When to use:** You\'re analyzing a randomized controlled trial for publication, regulatory review, or high-stakes business decisions requiring defensible causal claims.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"regression_adjustment"` | Incorporates baseline covariates for precision while preserving randomization |\n| `n_bootstrap` | `5000` | Stable, precise confidence intervals for formal reporting |\n| `covariates` | `["baseline_outcome", "segment", "tenure"]` | Pre-specified baseline characteristics improve power |\n| `heterogeneous_effects` | `["segment"]` | Identify differential treatment effects across key subgroups |\n| `balance_test` | `True` | Document randomization success with covariate balance table |\n| `alpha` | `0.05` | Standard threshold for scientific and business reporting |\n| `seed` | `42` | Reproducibility for audits and peer review |\n\n**What you get:** Publication-ready treatment effect with subgroup analyses, balance diagnostics, and reproducible confidence intervals meeting regulatory standards.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation takes 10-50x longer than exploration; requires pre-specifying covariates to avoid p-hacking accusations.\n\n### Recipe 3: Spillover-Robust Network Effects\n\n**When to use:** Measuring impact of a platform feature where treated users interact with control users (e.g., social features, marketplace dynamics, communication tools).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"cluster_randomized"` | Respects network dependencies by randomizing groups, not individuals |\n| `cluster_var` | `"network_component_id"` | Defines boundaries where spillovers are contained |\n| `n_bootstrap` | `1000` | Accounts for reduced effective sample size from clustering |\n| `small_sample_correction` | `True` | Adjusts for limited number of clusters (typically < 50) |\n| `alpha` | `0.05` | Standard threshold |\n\n**What you get:** Valid inference that accounts for intra-cluster correlation, avoiding severe underestimation of standard errors common in networked settings.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires 3-5x more users to achieve equivalent statistical power compared to individual randomization.\n\n### Recipe 4: Negative Control Validation\n\n**When to use:** You\'re suspicious of unobserved confounding in an observational study and want to stress-test your causal design before trusting results.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"doubly_robust"` | Combines propensity scores with outcome modeling for robustness |\n| `outcome` | `"metric_that_should_not_change"` | Test on outcome logically unaffected by treatment |\n| `n_bootstrap` | `2000` | Sufficient precision to detect small confounding signals |\n| `expected_effect` | `0.0` | Explicit null hypothesis for validation |\n| `sensitivity_analysis` | `True` | Quantifies how strong hidden confounding must be to alter conclusions |\n\n**What you get:** A falsification test showing whether your method produces spurious effects on outcomes that shouldn\'t respond, revealing design flaws.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires domain knowledge to identify valid negative controls; null results don\'t guarantee no confounding on your actual outcome.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender introduced a new automated underwriting system All three should be numeric (continuous or properly encoded categorical variables work fine).\n\n**Your input data should look like this:**\n\n| customer_id | purchase_amount | ad_exposure | income_level |\n|-------------|-----------------|-------------|--------------|\n| 1           | 145.20          | 3.5         | 62000        |\n| 2           | 89.50           | 1.2         | 45000        |\n| 3           | 210.30          | 4.8         | 95000        |\n\nYou\'ll specify which column is your dependent variable (Y), independent variable (X), and moderator (M). The node handles the rest—creating interaction terms, centering variables, and running the regression.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Dependent Variable** | Your outcome of interest (Y) | None | Always set this—it\'s what you\'re trying to explain |\n| **Independent Variable** | Your main predictor (X) | None | The variable whose effect you think changes under different conditions |\n| **Moderator Variable** | The "it depends" variable (M) | None | The condition that might strengthen or weaken X\'s effect |\n| **Center Variables** | Subtracts the mean from X and M before creating interactions | Enabled | Keep this on unless you have a meaningful zero point in your raw data |\n| **Include Covariates** | Add control variables to the model | None | Add demographic or confounding variables to isolate the moderation effect |\n| **Confidence Level** | Sets width of confidence intervals | 95% | Increase to 99% for more conservative estimates in high-stakes decisions |\n| **Simple Slopes** | Test effect of X at low/medium/high levels of M | Enabled | Keep on—this is where the "story" lives |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Main Results Table** shows four key coefficients: X\'s main effect, M\'s main effect, the X×M interaction term, and the overall model R². The interaction term is your star—if it\'s significant, you\'ve got moderation.\n\n**Simple Slopes Analysis** breaks down how X affects Y at three levels of the moderator (typically -1 SD, mean, +1 SD). Each slope gets its own significance test. This is what you\'ll reference when you say "ad exposure increases purchases, *but only for high-income customers*."\n\n**Interaction Plot** visualizes the moderation effect with separate regression lines for each moderator level. Diverging lines = moderation; parallel lines = no moderation.\n\n**Model Diagnostics** include residual plots and VIF scores to check your assumptions.\n\n### Quick Start: Testing a Moderation Hypothesis\n\n1. **Connect your cleaned dataset** to the Moderation Analysis node\n2. **Select your dependent variable** (e.g., job_satisfaction)\n3. **Choose your independent variable** (e.g., autonomy_score)\n4. **Pick your moderator** (e.g., manager_support)\n5. **Leave centering enabled** and click Run\n6. **Check the interaction term** in the results table—is it significant (p < .05)?\n7. **Examine the simple slopes table**—where is the effect strongest?\n8. **Review the interaction plot**—do the lines clearly diverge?\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost users flow into **Report Builder** to document findings with auto-generated interpretation text and publication-ready charts. If the interaction is significant, consider connecting to **Subgroup Analysis** to explore additional conditional effects, or to **Prediction** nodes to build models that incorporate the moderating relationships you\'ve discovered.\n\nFor academic work, connect to **LaTeX Export** to generate regression tables formatted for journals.\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Tip 1**: Nonsignificant main effects with significant interactions are perfectly valid—don\'t let reviewers tell you otherwise. The interaction *is* the effect.\n\n**Tip 2**: Always plot your interaction, even if it\'s not significant. Sometimes you\'ll spot nonlinear patterns the linear model missed.\n\n**Tip 3**: If your moderator is categorical (e.g., gender, region), the node automatically dummy-codes it. You\'ll get separate interaction terms for each category.\n\n**Tip 4**: R² changes between the base model and interaction model are often small (2-3%), but theoretically meaningful. Don\'t dismiss substantively important moderation just because the variance explained is modest.\n\n**Tip 5**: Use the covariates parameter liberally—unmodeled confounds can create spurious moderation effects.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration with Continuous Moderator\n\n**When to use:** You\'re in the early stages of analysis and want to quickly check if a continuous moderator (e.g., age, income) meaningfully alters the X\u2192Y relationship before investing in deeper modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Liberal threshold to avoid missing potential effects |\n| `bootstrap_samples` | 0 | Skip resampling to maximize speed |\n| `centering` | `"mean"` | Reduces multicollinearity; aids interpretation |\n| `standardize` | `FALSE` | Keep original units for stakeholder communication |\n| `plot_regions` | 2 | Johnson-Neyman at boundaries only |\n\n**What you get:** A fast pass/fail test on whether moderation exists, with interpretable coefficients in original units.\n\n**Trade-off:** No confidence intervals from bootstrapping; increased Type I error risk due to liberal alpha.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Publication-Ready Rigor\n\n**When to use:** Producing final results for peer review, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decisions where robustness and reproducibility are non-negotiable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard scientific threshold |\n| `bootstrap_samples` | 5000 | Stable CI estimation even with non-normality |\n| `seed` | 42 | Ensures exact reproducibility |\n| `centering` | `"mean"` | Standard practice for interaction terms |\n| `standardize` | `TRUE` | Enables effect size comparison across variables |\n| `heteroskedasticity_robust` | `TRUE` | HC3 standard errors guard against violated assumptions |\n| `plot_regions` | 10 | Fine-grained Johnson-Neyman zones |\n| `simple_slopes_at` | `[-1, 0, 1]` | Mean ± 1 SD per reporting conventions |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible estimates with robust inference, publication-standard visualizations, and full reporting statistics.\n\n**Trade-off:** 10–50× longer runtime; requires larger sample sizes (n > 200 recommended).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Binary Moderator with Small Sample\n\n**When to use:** Testing whether treatment effects differ between two groups (e.g., gender, treatment/control) when n < 100 and normality assumptions are questionable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `bootstrap_samples` | 10000 | Compensates for small n with more resamples |\n| `bootstrap_method` | `"percentile"` | More robust than normal-theory CI with small samples |\n| `centering` | `"none"` | Binary variables lose meaning when centered |\n| `heteroskedasticity_robust` | `TRUE` | Small samples often violate homoscedasticity |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Maintain conventional threshold despite low power |\n\n**What you get:** Conservative inference that doesn\'t over-rely on distributional assumptions.\n\n**Trade-off:** Lower statistical power; may miss true but modest moderating effects.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Probing Hidden Subgroup Effects in "Null" Results\n\n**When to use:** Primary analysis showed no main effect of X on Y, but theory suggests certain subgroups might still respond—this configuration hunts for suppressed interactions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.15 | Deliberately liberal to surface masked effects |\n| `simple_slopes_at` | `[0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9]` | Tests effects across full moderator distribution |\n| `plot_regions` | 20 | Maximum granularity for Johnson-Neyman |\n| `interaction_only` | `TRUE` | Focus solely on XZ term when main effects are theoretically uninteresting |\n| `bootstrap_samples` | 3000 | Balance between precision and exploration speed |\n\n**What you get:** Discovery-oriented analysis that reveals conditional effects invisible in average treatment estimates.\n\n**Trade-off:** High false discovery rate; findings require validation in holdout data or preregistered follow-up.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was puzzled by inconsistent credit score performance across their broker network. Your data should be in "one row per observation" format—typically one row per person, customer, time period, or unit of analysis.\n\n**Required columns:**\n- **Treatment variable** (categorical or binary): The intervention or exposure you\'re investigating\n- **Outcome variable** (numeric): The result you\'re measuring\n- **Covariates** (numeric or categorical): Other variables that might confound the relationship\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | received_email | purchase_amount | age | prior_purchases |\n|-------------|----------------|-----------------|-----|-----------------|\n| 1001        | 1              | 45.20           | 34  | 3               |\n| 1002        | 0              | 0.00            | 28  | 1               |\n| 1003        | 1              | 67.50           | 42  | 5               |\n\n### Quick Start\n\nHere\'s how to run your first causal analysis:\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Prove Causation node\n2. **Select your treatment variable** from the dropdown (e.g., `received_email`)\n3. **Select your outcome variable** (e.g., `purchase_amount`)\n4. **Choose your method**: Start with "Propensity Score Matching" for straightforward experiments\n5. **Add covariates**: Select variables that might influence both treatment and outcome (e.g., `age`, `prior_purchases`)\n6. **Click Run** and review the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) in the results panel\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Method** | The causal inference technique used | Propensity Score Matching | Use IV if you have an instrument; RDD if treatment has a threshold; DiD if you have pre/post periods |\n| **Treatment Variable** | Which column indicates treatment status | (none) | Always required—select your intervention variable |\n| **Outcome Variable** | What you\'re measuring the effect on | (none) | Always required—select your dependent variable |\n| **Covariates** | Control variables for confounding | (none) | Include any variables that might affect both treatment assignment and outcome |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of uncertainty intervals | 95% | Increase to 99% for more conservative estimates |\n| **Matching Method** | manipulation around the cutoff |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs both **enhanced data** and **diagnostic visualizations**:\n\n**Data outputs** (new columns added):\n- `propensity_score`: Estimated probability of receiving treatment\n- `matched_pair`: ID linking treated and control units (PSM only)\n- `counterfactual_prediction`: What the outcome would have been under opposite treatment\n\n**Results panel displays:**\n- **Average Treatment Effect (ATE)**: The causal impact estimate with confidence intervals\n- **Balance diagnostics**: Before/after covariate
