Practical Tips\n\n**Check your overlap.** Before trusting results, verify that treatment and control groups have overlapping propensity scores. If the distributions don\'t overlap, you\'re extrapolating dangerously.\n\n**Start simple, then robustify.** Run basic matching first, then try multiple methods. If estimates agree across approaches, you can be more confident.\n\n**Mind your sample size in subgroups.** The node will estimate effects for any subgroup you specify, but with fewer than ~100 units per group, confidence intervals get very wide.\n\n**Document your assumptions.** The "Assumptions" tab lists what must be true for your estimates to be causal. Screenshot this and include it in your analysis documentation—reviewers will ask.\n\n**Use the covariate balance table.** If standardized differences exceed 0.1 after matching, consider adding more covariates or trying a different method.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Hypothesis Screening\n\n**When to use:** You have 10+ potential treatment variables and need to quickly identify which warrant deeper causal investigation before committing computational resources.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 100 | Faster confidence intervals, acceptable for screening |\n| `propensity_method` | `\'logistic\'` | Simplest model, fastest fitting |\n| `covariate_balance_threshold` | 0.2 | Relaxed SMD tolerance to avoid iterations |\n| `trim_propensity` | `(0.1, 0.9)` | Aggressive trimming removes edge cases quickly |\n| `sensitivity_analysis` | `False` | Skip robustness checks in exploration phase |\n\n**What you get:** Rough effect estimates with wide confidence intervals that flag promising candidates in under 5 minutes per treatment.\n\n**Trade-off:** High false negative risk—you may dismiss true effects with poor covariate balance or violation of unconfoundedness.\n\n### Recipe 2: Publication-Grade Causal Estimate\n\n**When to use:** Finalizing a primary causal claim for peer review, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decision where defensibility matters most.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 2000 | Stable percentile-based CIs for non-normal estimates |\n| `propensity_method` | `\'gbm\'` | Flexible specification captures complex confounding |\n| `covariate_balance_threshold` | 0.05 | Strict SMD ensures exchangeability |\n| `trim_propensity` | `(0.05, 0.95)` | Conservative, retains maximum valid sample |\n| `sensitivity_analysis` | `True` | Required: tests unmeasured confounding impact |\n| `placebo_outcomes` | `[\'pre_treatment_Y\']` | Validates no spurious pre-trends |\n| `cross_fitting_folds` | 5 | Double ML to eliminate regularization bias |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible point estimate with narrow CIs, balance diagnostics, and robustness documentation suitable for appendices.\n\n**Trade-off:** 20–50x slower execution; requires pre-treatment outcome data and domain knowledge for placebo specification.\n\n### Recipe 3: Weak Instrument Recovery\n\n**When to use:** Your instrumental variable barely predicts treatment (F-stat 5–10), but it\'s the only exogenous lever available and you cannot run an RCT.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `iv_method` | `\'liml\'` | Limited-info ML more robust than 2SLS to weak IV |\n| `anderson_rubin_ci` | `True` | Inverts test statistic for valid CIs even when weak |\n| `min_instrument_strength` | 3.0 | Lower threshold acknowledges constraint |\n| `weak_iv_diagnostics` | `True` | Explicitly reports Stock-Yogo critical values |\n| `bootstrapped_se` | `False` | Use analytic SEs; bootstrap unreliable with weak IV |\n\n**What you get:** Conservative but valid inference that honestly reports uncertainty from instrument weakness.\n\n**Trade-off:** Very wide confidence intervals, often crossing zero; may be inconclusive but preserves Type I error control.\n\n### Recipe 4: Natural Experiment in Panel Noise\n\n**When to use:** You observe a policy shock affecting only some units mid-series, but outcomes are highly volatile with autocorrelation and your data has gaps.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'did\'` | Exploits temporal variation from shock |\n| `cluster_se` | `\'unit\'` | Accounts for serial correlation within entities |\n| `allow_unbalanced` | `True` | Uses available observations despite gaps |\n| `pre_trend_test_periods` | 6 | Tests parallel trends over sufficient history |\n| `dynamic_effects` | `range(-6, 12)` | Maps effect evolution, catches anticipation |\n| `bootstrap_clusters` | 999 | Wild cluster bootstrap for few treated units |\n\n**What you get:** Event-study style effect trajectory robust to autocorrelation and missing data patterns.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires at least 6 pre-periods and assumes no composition changes explain gaps.\n\n## Business Think of it as needing everything in one place before you start adjusting.\n\n**Required columns:**\n- **Treatment variable** (categorical or binary) — the intervention or exposure you\'re studying\n- **Outcome variable** (numeric or categorical) — what you\'re trying to measure the effect on\n- **Confounders** (any type) — variables that might influence both treatment and outcome\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| patient_id | received_treatment | recovery_days | age | severity | income_level |\n|------------|-------------------|---------------|-----|----------|--------------|\n| 001 | Yes | 12 | 45 | High | Medium |\n| 002 | No | 18 | 52 | Low | High |\n| 003 | Yes | 9 | 38 | Medium | Low |\n\nAll your variables should be in separate columns, with one row per observation.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Treatment Column** | Which column represents your treatment/exposure | (none) | Always set this to your intervention variable |\n| **Outcome Column** | Which column is your outcome of interest | (none) | Always set this to what you\'re measuring |\n| **Confounder Columns** | Which variables to adjust for | (none) | Select variables you believe cause both treatment and outcome |\n| **Adjustment Method** | Statistical technique used | Regression | Use "IPW" for near-violations of positivity; "Doubly Robust" when unsure |\n| **Treatment Reference Level** | Baseline for comparison (binary/categorical) | First alphabetically | Set to your true control/comparison group |\n| **Propensity Score Model** | Model for treatment probability (IPW/DR methods) | Logistic | Use "GBM" for complex treatment patterns |\n| **Include Interaction Terms** | Allow confounders to interact with treatment | No | Enable when treatment effects vary by subgroup |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of uncertainty intervals | 95% | Rarely change; 90% or 99% for specific reporting needs |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Output columns added to your dataset:**\n- **adjusted_effect** — the estimated causal effect after removing confounding\n- **propensity_score** (if using IPW/DR) — predicted probability of receiving treatment\n- **residual** — difference between observed and expected outcome\n\n**Metrics panel displays:**\n- **Average Treatment Effect (ATE)** — the overall causal impact across your population\n- **Confidence Interval** — statistical uncertainty range\n- **Covariate Balance Statistics** — how well confounders are balanced post-adjustment (SMD values < 0.1 indicate good balance)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Balance Plot** — before/after standardized mean differences for each confounder\n- **Effect Estimate Plot** — treatment effect with confidence intervals\n- **Propensity Score Distribution** (IPW/DR only) — overlap between treatment groups\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically flows into:\n- **Subgroup Analysis** — explore how effects vary across populations\n- **Sensitivity Analysis** — test robustness to unmeasured confounding\n- **Prediction** nodes — use adjusted effects for scenario modeling\n- **Report Builder** — communicate findings with confidence\n\n### Quick Start: Most Common Use Case\n\n1. **Drag your observational dataset** into the canvas and connect it to Remove Confounding\n2. **Select your treatment column** (e.g., "received_training") from the dropdown\n3. **Select your outcome column** (e.g., "productivity_score")\n4. **Add confounder columns** — start with demographics and pre-treatment characteristics\n5. **Leave Adjustment Method as "Regression"** for your first pass\n6. **Click Run** and review the Balance Plot — look for all bars within the ±0.1 zone\n7. **Check the ATE** in the metrics panel — this is your adjusted causal effect\n\n### Practical Tips from Experience\n\n**Start conservative with confounders.** It\'s tempting to throw every variable in, but only include true confounders (common causes). Including mediators or instruments can bias your results.\n\n**Check propensity score overlap** when using IPW or Doubly Robust methods. If treatment and control groups have non-overlapping propensity scores, your estimates will be unstable. Consider trimming extreme values or switching to regression.\n\n**The Balance Plot is your diagnostic friend.** If standardized mean differences remain large (>0.1) after adjustment, you may need interaction terms or a more flexible model.\n\n**Domain knowledge beats algorithms.** No statistical method can fix a missing confounder. Spend time identifying all common causes before running the adjustment—consult subject matter experts.\n\n**Watch for positivity violations.** If some covariate combinations deterministically predict treatment (everyone with X always gets treated), causal effects aren\'t identifiable for those subgroups. The tool will flag this, but you\'ll need to restrict your analysis accordingly.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration with Propensity Score Matching\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploratory analysis when you need fast feedback on whether confounding is substantially biasing your treatment effect estimate, working with datasets under 10,000 observations.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"psm"` | Fastest to compute, intuitive to validate visually |\n| `caliper` | `0.2` | Standard width balances match rate with quality |\n| `matching_ratio` | `1:1` | Minimizes computation while preserving interpretability |\n| `balance_check` | `"standardized_diff"` | Quick diagnostic without bootstrapping |\n| `estimation` | `"att"` | Focuses on treated units only, fewer assumptions |\n\n**What you get:** A point estimate of treatment effect with basic covariate balance diagnostics in under 30 seconds for most datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** You discard unmatched observations (often 20-40%), sacrificing statistical power and potentially external validity.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Doubly Robust Estimation\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for publication, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decisions where robustness to model misspecification is critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"aipw"` | Augmented inverse probability weighting—consistent if either propensity or outcome model is correct |\n| `propensity_model` | `GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.01)` | Flexible enough to capture nonlinear confounding without severe overfitting |\n| `outcome_model` | `GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.01)` | Matches propensity model complexity |\n| `cross_fitting` | `k=5` | Reduces overfitting bias in nuisance parameter estimation |\n| `ci_method` | `"bootstrap"` | Conservative uncertainty quantification |\n| `n_bootstrap` | `1000` | Industry standard for stable confidence intervals |\n| `trim_propensity` | `(0.05, 0.95)` | Excludes extreme weights that destabilize estimates |\n\n**What you get:** A treatment effect estimate robust to model misspecification with reliable 95% confidence intervals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation time increases 50-100x compared to simple methods; requires 5-10x more observations for stable propensity score estimation.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Confounding with Regularization\n\n**When to use:** You have 50+ potential confounders (e.g., claims data with hundreds of diagnosis codes) and suspect only a subset truly matter, but you don\'t know which.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"ipw"` | Separates confounder selection from outcome modeling |\n| `propensity_model` | `LogisticRegressionCV(penalty=\'elasticnet\', l1_ratio=0.7, solver=\'saga\', cv=10)` | L1-dominant penalty performs variable selection automatically |\n| `weight_stabilization` | `True` | Prevents extreme weights in high dimensions |\n| `max_weight` | `10` | Hard cap on any single observation\'s influence |\n\n**What you get:** Automated confounder selection that handles collinearity and identifies the sparse set of true confounders.\n\n**Trade-off:** Less efficient than doubly robust methods when you actually need all covariates; propensity score interpretation becomes harder.\n\n### Recipe 4: Negative Control Outcome for Unmeasured Confounding Detection\n\n**When to use:** You suspect unmeasured confounding but can identify an outcome that treatment should *not* affect (e.g., analyzing drug effects on heart disease using bone fractures as negative control).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"regression"` | Simple enough to run twice (primary + negative control) |\n| `outcome` | `[primary_outcome, negative_control_outcome]` | Parallel estimation |\n| `covariates` | `same_set` | Identical adjustment for valid comparison |\n| `alpha` | `0.10` | Liberal threshold for detecting bias signals |\n\n**What you get:** Evidence of whether residual confounding persists—non-null effect on negative control invalidates your primary estimate.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires domain knowledge to identify valid negative controls; doesn\'t fix the bias, only detects it.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial `spatial_lag_[outcome]`: The weighted average of neighboring values\n- `fitted_values`: Model predictions\n- `residuals`: Prediction errors\n\n**Model diagnostics panel** showing:\n- Spatial autocorrelation coefficient (\u03c1 or \u03bb): tells you how strongly neighbors influence each other\n- Standard regression metrics (R², AIC, BIC)\n- Moran\'s I test on residuals (confirms you\'ve addressed spatial correlation)\n\n**Visualization tab** with:\n- Choropleth map of residuals (check for remaining spatial patterns)\n- Scatter plot of observed vs. fitted values\n- Moran\'s I scatter plot showing spatial correlation structure\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nTypically connect to:\n- **Model Comparison** node to evaluate against non-spatial OLS\n- **Prediction Map** node to visualize fitted values geographically\n- **Report Generator** to document findings with automatic interpretation\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Connect your data** with geographic identifiers and drag in the Spatial Regression node\n2. **Select your outcome variable** from the dependent variable dropdown\n3. **Choose predictors** by checking boxes or dragging fields to the independent variables area\n4. **Set Model Type to "Spatial Lag"** as your starting point\n5. **Click "Auto-Configure Weights"** to let Heuristix determine appropriate neighbors\n6. **Run the model** and check if Moran\'s I test on residuals is non-significant (good!)\n7. **Compare** by connecting a standard Linear Regression node—look for improved AIC/BIC\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n- **Always check residuals spatially**: A good spatial model should show random residuals with no geographic clustering. If you still see patterns, try the Spatial Durbin model.\n\n- **Start simple, then add complexity**: Run OLS first to establish a baseline. Only add spatial structure if Moran\'s I test shows significant autocorrelation in OLS residuals.\n\n- **Distance units matter**: If using lat/long coordinates, the auto-threshold works in decimal degrees. For city-level analysis, consider projecting to meters first using the Transform Coordinates node.\n\n- **Interpretation changes with spatial lag**: When \u03c1 (rho) is significant, a one-unit change in X has both direct effects AND indirect effects through neighboring spillovers. Heuristix calculates both for you in the coefficients table.\n\n- **Edge effects are real**: Regions on boundaries have fewer neighbors, which can bias results. The diagnostics panel flags regions with fewer than 3 neighbors—consider excluding or treating separately.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploratory Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Initial investigation of whether spatial dependence exists in your residuals before committing to full spatial modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model_type` | `"OLS"` | Baseline comparison first |\n| `spatial_test` | `"moran"` | Fast global autocorrelation test |\n| `weights_type` | `"queen"` | Simplest contiguity definition |\n| `n_neighbors` | `8` | Balance between local and computational speed |\n| `permutations` | `99` | Minimum for statistical significance |\n\n**What you get:** Rapid identification of spatial autocorrelation in residuals with Moran\'s I statistic and p-value in under 10 seconds for datasets up to 10,000 observations.\n\n**Trade-off:** No correction for spatial dependence yet; You need:\n\n- **Treatment variable** (categorical or binary): The presumed cause\n- **Outcome variable** (numeric): The effect you\'re measuring\n- **Covariates** (numeric or categorical): Other variables that might confound the relationship\n- **Optional instrumental variable** (any type): A variable that affects treatment but not outcome directly\n\nYour data should be in **one row per observation** format:\n\n| customer_id | received_email | purchase_amount | age | prior_purchases |\n|-------------|----------------|-----------------|-----|-----------------|\n| 1001        | 1              | 45.20           | 34  | 3               |\n| 1002        | 0              | 0.00            | 28  | 1               |\n| 1003        | 1              | 120.50          | 45  | 12              |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Treatment Column** | Which variable represents your causal intervention | (required) | Select the column you believe causes changes in the outcome |\n| **Outcome Column** | What you\'re measuring as the effect | (required) | Choose your key metric of interest |\n| **Covariate Columns** | Variables to control for confounding | (none) | Add any variables that might influence both treatment and outcome |\n| **Instrumental Variable** | Variable for IV-based tests | (none) | Use when you suspect unmeasured confounding and have a valid instrument |\n| **Significance Level** | Threshold for statistical tests | 0.05 | Lower to 0.01 for more conservative tests; raise to 0.10 for exploratory work |\n| **Test Methods** | Which causal tests to run | All | Disable specific tests if you know certain assumptions don\'t hold for your data |\n| **Balance Threshold** | Maximum acceptable covariate imbalance | 0.10 | Tighten to 0.05 for stricter balance requirements |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node produces three types of outputs:\n\n**Diagnostic Metrics Table** shows:\n- **Conditional independence p-values**: Tests whether treatment and outcome remain associated after controlling for covariates (low p-value supports causation)\n- **Covariate balance statistics**: Standardized mean differences showing whether treatment and control groups differ on confounders\n- **IV validity scores**: F-statistics and over-identification tests (when using an instrument)\n\n**Visualization Panel** displays:\n- Balance plots comparing covariate distributions across treatment groups\n- Residual plots showing patterns after removing confounder effects\n- Sensitivity curves indicating how robust findings are to unmeasured confounding\n\n**Enhanced Dataset** (passed downstream) includes:\n- `causal_test_passed`: Boolean flag for whether the relationship survived testing\n- `estimated_effect`: Point estimate of causal effect size\n- `sensitivity_score`: How fragile the finding is (0-1 scale)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect Test Causation to:\n\n- **Treatment Effect Estimator** nodes to quantify causal impacts after validation\n- **Filter** nodes to subset data where causal_test_passed = True for downstream modeling\n- **Report** nodes to document your causal findings with the diagnostic visualizations\n\n### Quick Start: Testing an Email Campaign\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** containing campaign exposure, customer purchases, and demographics\n2. **Set Treatment Column** to your campaign flag (e.g., `received_email`)\n3. **Set Outcome Column** to your conversion metric (e.g., `purchase_amount`)\n4. **Add Covariate Columns** like customer age, tenure, and prior purchase history\n5. **Run the node** and check the conditional independence p-value first\n6. **Review balance plots** to see if treatment/control groups are comparable\n7. **Examine sensitivity score** to understand how robust your conclusion is\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Start with visualization.** Before trusting the p-values, look at the balance plots. If your treatment and control groups are wildly different on covariates, no statistical test will save you.\n\n**The absence of a test failure isn\'t proof of causation.** These tests can rule out obviously spurious relationships, but passing all tests doesn\'t guarantee causality—it just means your data is consistent with it.\n\n**Use domain knowledge to select covariates.** More isn\'t always better. Include variables that plausibly affect both treatment assignment and outcomes, not every column in your dataset.\n\n**Pay attention to sample size warnings.** Many of these tests lose power with small datasets. If you have fewer than 100 observations, interpret results cautiously.\n\n**Chain this with randomization checks.** If your data comes from an experiment, use Test Causation to verify randomization worked. For observational data, use it to stress-test your causal assumptions.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial assessment of potential causal relationships This killed a planned $340K email infrastructure expansion and redirected resources toward in-product interventions that subsequent causal tests validated.\n\n**Public Sector**\n\nA metropolitan transit authority used Test Causation to determine whether new real-time arrival displays actually reduced perceived wait times or merely correlated with recently renovated stations (which independently improved satisfaction). She runs a conditional independence test and finds that tutoring and test scores remain associated even after conditioning on prior GPA. What can she conclude about causation?\n\nA) The association is causal because it persists after controlling for the most obvious confounder\n\nB) The association is causal because the conditional independence test rejected the null hypothesis of no relationship\n\nC) She cannot yet conclude causation because passing one conditional independence test doesn\'t rule out all alternative causal structures\n\nD) The association is non-causal because conditional independence tests can only detect correlation, not causation\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Test Causation requires systematic evaluation through *multiple* falsification procedures and diagnostic tests, not just controlling for one confounder. Option C correctly recognizes that passing a single conditional independence test is insufficient—other unmeasured confounders (motivation, family support, etc.) could still explain the association, and alternative causal structures remain untested. Option A reflects the common misconception that controlling for "obvious" confounders is sufficient for causal claims. Option B misunderstands that rejecting independence doesn\'t imply causation—it only confirms association persists under that specific conditioning set. Option D goes too far in the opposite direction, incorrectly suggesting conditional independence tests have no role in causal inference, when they\'re actually a core component of the Test Causation framework for systematically ruling out non-causal explanations.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '—'. **Trace Effect Over Time** node expects panel data—repeated observations of the same units across time. You\'ll need:\n\n- **Unit identifier** (text or numeric): Individual, customer, region, etc.\n- **Time variable** (date, datetime, or sequential integer): When each observation occurred\n- **Treatment indicator** (binary 0/1): Whether the unit received treatment at that time\n- **Outcome variable** (numeric): The metric you\'re measuring\n- **Covariates** (optional, numeric or categorical): Control variables for adjustment\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | week | treated | revenue | segment |\n|-------------|------|---------|---------|---------|\n| C001 | 1 | 0 | 245 | premium |\n| C001 | 2 | 1 | 290 | premium |\n| C001 | 3 | 1 | 310 | premium |\n\nThe node expects your data in **long format** with one row per unit-time combination. If you have wide data (one row per unit, columns for each time period), use the **Reshape** node first.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Unit ID Column** | Which column identifies your units | — | Required. Choose your entity identifier. |\n| **Time Column** | Which column contains time periods | — | Required. Must be sortable chronologically. |\n| **Treatment Column** | Binary indicator of treatment status | — | Required. Use 1 for treated, 0 for control. |\n| **Outcome Column** | The metric you\'re tracking | — | Required. Should be numeric and continuous. |\n| **Covariates** | Variables to adjust for confounding | None | Add pre-treatment characteristics that affect both treatment and outcome. |\n| **Pre-treatment Periods** | How many periods before treatment to include | 3 | Increase to 5–10 if you want stronger parallel trends validation. |\n| **Post-treatment Periods** | How many periods after treatment to track | 12 | Extend if effects might emerge slowly (e.g., 24 weeks for habit formation). |\n| **Estimation Method** | Statistical approach (DiD, matching, regression) | Difference-in-Differences | Use matching if parallel trends seem questionable; regression for many covariates. |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of confidence intervals | 95% | Lower to 90% for exploratory work; keep at 95% for formal reporting. |\n| **Clustering Variable** | Unit to cluster standard errors by | Unit ID | Change if you have hierarchical structure (e.g., cluster by store, not transaction). |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node produces:\n\n**Output dataset** with new columns:\n- `effect_estimate`: Treatment effect magnitude at each time period\n- `std_error`: Standard error of the estimate\n- `ci_lower` / `ci_upper`: Confidence interval bounds\n- `p_value`: Statistical significance\n- `relative_time`: Periods before/after treatment (negative = pre-treatment)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Effect trajectory plot**: Line chart showing effect size over time with confidence bands—the central deliverable showing when effects appear and how they evolve\n- **Event study plot**: Coefficient plot with pre-treatment placebo tests—validates your causal assumptions\n- **Heatmap** (if multiple treatment groups): Effect magnitude by group and time\n\n**Summary statistics:**\n- Average pre-treatment effect (should be near zero)\n- Peak effect magnitude and timing\n- Cumulative effect over observation window\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nTypical next steps:\n\n- **Filter** \u2192 Subset to statistically significant periods only\n- **Calculate Field** \u2192 Compute cumulative effects or effect decay rates\n- **Segment Analysis** \u2192 Split by customer cohort to find heterogeneous effects\n- **Export** \u2192 Pull the trajectory plot directly into stakeholder presentations\n\n### Quick Start: Standard Implementation\n\n1. **Connect your panel dataset** with at least unit ID, time, treatment, and outcome columns\n2. **Map required fields** in the configuration panel (the four required columns)\n3. **Set your time windows**: 3–5 pre-treatment periods (to test assumptions) and however long you want to track effects\n4. **Start with Difference-in-Differences** as your estimation method—it\'s most interpretable\n5. **Review the event study plot first**—if pre-treatment effects aren\'t near zero, revisit your parallel trends assumption\n6. **Examine the trajectory plot**—note when effects emerge, peak, and potentially fade\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n- **Always inspect pre-treatment estimates**: Non-zero effects before treatment indicate violated assumptions—consider matching or additional covariates\n- **Use relative time, not calendar time**: Effects at "3 weeks post-treatment" are more interpretable than "effect in March" when treatment timing varies\n- **Don\'t over-interpret early noise**: The first 1–2 periods post-treatment often show high variance; look for consistent patterns\n- **Check for balance drift**: If treated and control groups diverge in covariates over time, add time-varying controls\n- **Compare effect stability**: Confidence intervals that widen dramatically over time suggest you\'re losing sample (attrition) or effects are becoming noisier\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** First-pass analysis on a new dataset to check if any temporal effects exist before investing in rigorous modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `time_window` | `"auto"` | Let algorithm detect natural breakpoints |\n| `min_obs_per_period` | `30` | Balance granularity with stability |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | `100` | Adequate for directional confidence intervals |\n| `effect_estimator` | `"difference_in_means"` | Fastest, no model fitting overhead |\n| `multiple_testing_correction` | `None` | Skip initially to see raw patterns |\n| `parallel_backend` | `"threading"` | Reduces setup overhead for quick runs |\n\n**What you get:** Rapid visualization of effect trajectory with approximate confidence bands, sufficient to identify whether effects grow, decay, or stabilize.\n\n**Trade-off:** Confidence intervals are wider and p-values are uncorrected, making this unsuitable for publication or deployment decisions.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Inference\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for regulatory submission, academic publication, or high-stakes business decisions requiring defensible causal claims.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `time_window` | `"calendar_month"` | Reproducible, stakeholder-interpretable periods |\n| `min_obs_per_period` | `100` | Ensures sufficient power per time slice |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | `5000` | Stabilizes confidence interval boundaries |\n| `effect_estimator` | `"doubly_robust"` | Guards against misspecification in either model |\n| `multiple_testing_correction` | `"holm_bonferroni"` | Controls family-wise error rate conservatively |\n| `covariate_balance_threshold` | `0.05` | Fails loudly if pre-treatment balance fails |\n| `parallel_backend` | `"multiprocessing"` | Maximizes throughput for intensive computation |\n\n**What you get:** Publication-ready estimates with conservative inference, complete with diagnostics proving covariate balance at each time point.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime increases 20–50×; requires careful review of all diagnostic outputs before accepting results.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Policy Intervention with Known Lag\n\n**When to use:** Evaluating interventions where domain knowledge suggests effects manifest only after a delay (e.g., training programs, infrastructure projects).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `time_window` | `"week"` | Granular enough to pinpoint onset |\n| `min_time_before_estimation` | `12` | Exclude first 3 months (domain-driven lag) |\n| `effect_estimator` | `"synthetic_control"` | Handles single treated unit with donor pool |\n| `trend_adjustment` | `"linear_detrend"` | Remove secular trends unrelated to treatment |\n| `anticipation_window` | `4` | Account for 4 weeks of potential anticipatory behavior |\n\n**What you get:** Effect trajectory that begins only after the plausible mechanism delay, avoiding premature null findings.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires strong domain priors; misspecifying the lag period can mask or fabricate effects.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Detecting Effect Fadeout in Habit Formation\n\n**When to use:** Testing whether behavioral interventions (nudges, incentives, defaults) create lasting change or only temporary compliance that vanishes post-intervention.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `time_window` | `"day"` | Capture fine-grained behavioral decay |\n| `extend_post_period` | `90` | Observe 3 months beyond intervention end |\n| `effect_estimator` | `"regression_discontinuity_in_time"` | Sharp contrast at intervention boundaries |\n| `test_for_slope_change` | `True` | Distinguish level shifts from trajectory changes |\n| `persistence_metric` | `"half_life"` | Quantify decay rate automatically |\n\n**What you get:** Explicit measurement of how quickly effects dissipate, with half-life estimates for intervention durability.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires extended post-treatment observation; early termination of tracking produces misleading persistence claims.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender introduced a new credit scoring algorithm This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe **Unpack the Pathway** node expects a single dataset with three essential ingredients:\n\n- **Treatment column** (categorical or binary): Your intervention or exposure variable\n- **Outcome column** (numeric): What you\'re trying to explain or predict\n- **Mediator column(s)** (numeric or categorical): The intermediate variables you believe transmit the treatment\'s effect\n\nYour data should be in **row-per-observation** format, with one row per individual, unit, or case. Here\'s what it looks like:\n\n| patient_id | treatment | stress_level | sleep_hours | health_score |\n|------------|-----------|--------------|-------------|--------------|\n| 001 | therapy | 6.2 | 7.1 | 78 |\n| 002 | control | 8.1 | 5.3 | 62 |\n| 003 | therapy | 4.5 | 8.2 | 85 |\n\nIn this example, you\'d analyze whether `therapy` affects `health_score` through the pathway of `stress_level` and `sleep_hours`.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Treatment Variable** | The causal variable whose effect you\'re decomposing | None (required) | Always set this first |\n| **Outcome Variable** | Your dependent variable | None (required) | What you ultimately care about explaining |\n| **Mediator Variables** | Intermediate pathways (select one or more) | None (required) | Choose variables causally between treatment and outcome |\n| **Covariates** | Control variables to adjust for confounding | None | Add pre-treatment variables that affect both mediator and outcome |\n| **Bootstrap Iterations** | Number of resamples for confidence intervals | 1000 | Increase to 5000+ for publication; decrease to 200 for quick exploration |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of uncertainty intervals | 95% | Use 90% for exploratory work, 99% for conservative claims |\n| **Interaction Terms** | Allow treatment effect on outcome to depend on mediator level | Disabled | Enable when you suspect the direct effect varies by mediator values |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\nThe node produces three types of output:\n\n**Decomposition Table**: Shows the total effect split into direct and indirect components. Each row represents a pathway, with effect estimates, standard errors, confidence intervals, and the proportion of total effect mediated.\n\n**Pathway Diagram**: A visual flow chart displaying treatment \u2192 mediator(s) \u2192 outcome with arrows sized by effect magnitude. This makes it immediately clear which mechanisms matter most.\n\n**Sensitivity Analysis**: Charts showing how robust your conclusions are to potential unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically flows into:\n\n- **Report Builder**: To document your mechanistic findings with auto-generated narrative\n- **Scenario Simulator**: To explore "what if we intervened on the mediator directly?"\n- **Segment Analysis**: To check whether pathways differ across subgroups\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your prepared dataset** containing treatment, outcome, and at least one mediator\n2. **Select your treatment variable** from the dropdown (usually your intervention or exposure)\n3. **Select your outcome variable** (what you\'re trying to explain)\n4. **Choose mediator variable(s)** that sit causally between treatment and outcome\n5. **Add any pre-treatment covariates** that might confound mediator-outcome relationships\n6. **Click "Run Analysis"** and examine the decomposition table first\n7. **Review the pathway diagram** to identify your strongest mechanisms\n8. **Check sensitivity analysis** to ensure findings aren\'t fragile\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Draw your causal diagram first**: Before configuring anything, sketch the assumed causal relationships on paper. If you can\'t draw a clear arrow from treatment \u2192 mediator \u2192 outcome, you\'re not ready for mediation analysis.\n\n**Start with one mediator**: Even if you have multiple candidates, analyze them one at a time initially. This helps you understand each mechanism before examining them jointly.\n\n**Check sequential ignorability**: Your results assume no unmeasured confounding of the mediator-outcome relationship. Use the sensitivity analysis output religiously—if small unmeasured confounders could flip your conclusions, report that honestly.\n\n**Proportion mediated isn\'t always between 0-100%**: If you see values above 100% or negative proportions, you likely have inconsistent mediation (suppression effects). This is scientifically interesting, not an error.\n\n**Bootstrap iterations matter more with small samples**: With n < 200, bump bootstrap iterations to 2000+ for stable confidence intervals.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial investigation with a new dataset where you need to quickly assess whether mediation exists before committing to deeper analysis.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 100 | Fast computation while still providing basic uncertainty estimates |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.90 | Lower threshold catches suggestive patterns worth exploring |\n| `estimator` | "linear" | Fastest option; sufficient for initial patterns |\n| `adjust_confounders` | FALSE | Skip initially to see raw associations |\n| `parallel` | TRUE | Use all cores to offset low bootstrap count |\n\n- **What you get:** Quick directional indicators of which mediators show promise, typically completing in under a minute even with moderate sample sizes.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Reduced statistical rigor means you may pursue false leads or miss subtle effects masked by confounding.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Analysis\n\n- **When to use:** Final analysis for publication, regulatory submission, or high-stakes business decision where results will be scrutinized.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 5000 | Stable confidence intervals that withstand sensitivity checks |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.95 | Standard for formal inference |\n| `estimator` | "doubly_robust" | Guards against misspecification in either model |\n| `adjust_confounders` | TRUE | Mandatory for causal claims |\n| `sensitivity_analysis` | TRUE | Document robustness to unmeasured confounding |\n| `preregistered_mediators` | [list] | Prevents p-hacking accusations |\n\n- **What you get:** Defensible causal estimates with documented assumptions and robustness checks suitable for peer review or executive presentation.\n\n- **Trade-off:** 50-100x longer computation time and requires upfront theoretical work to specify confounders and mediators.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Mediator Set\n\n- **When to use:** Analyzing gene expression data, survey batteries, or any scenario with 50+ potential mediators where most are likely null.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `mediator_selection` | "lasso" | Automated sparsity in high dimensions |\n| `alpha_threshold` | 0.01 | Strict correction for multiple testing (Bonferroni/50) |\n| `n_bootstrap` | 1000 | Balance between power and computation with many mediators |\n| `effect_aggregation` | "grouped" | Summarize by mediator families rather than individually |\n| `parallel_mediators` | TRUE | Estimate all mediator models simultaneously to capture interdependence |\n\n- **What you get:** Identification of a sparse set of active mediators while controlling family-wise error rate across the massive testing burden.\n\n- **Trade-off:** May miss weak effects that are causally important when operating in concert but individually fall below detection threshold.\n\n### Recipe 4: Longitudinal Feedback Loops\n\n- **When to use:** Treatment affects mediator which affects outcome which then influences the mediator again (e.g., medication \u2192 symptoms \u2192 exercise \u2192 symptoms).\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `time_varying` | TRUE | Enables sequential mediation tracking |\n| `lag_structure` | [1, 2, 4] | Tests immediate, short-delay, and sustained effects |\n| `cross_lagged` | TRUE | Captures reciprocal causation |\n| `estimator` | "g_computation" | Handles time-dependent confounding |\n| `n_bootstrap` | 2000 | Accounts for added complexity in temporal models |\n\n- **What you get:** Decomposition of effects across time with separate estimates for contemporaneous versus lagged mediation pathways.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Requires panel data with at least 3-4 time points and substantially larger sample sizes to achieve adequate power.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA multinational retail bank struggling with credit card churn deploys a retention programme offering fee waivers, At minimum, you need:\n\n- **Treatment/exposure variable** (categorical or numeric)\n- **Outcome variable** (numeric)\n- **Effect estimates** (numeric, often with confidence intervals)\n- **Optional**: propensity scores, weights, predicted counterfactuals, graph structure data\n\n**Example input structure:**\n\n| treatment | outcome | effect_estimate | ci_lower | ci_upper | covariate_1 |\n|-----------|---------|-----------------|----------|----------|-------------|\n| 0 | 45.2 | 12.3 | 8.1 | 16.5 | 0.42 |\n| 1 | 57.5 | 12.3 | 8.1 | 16.5 | 0.38 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Visualization Type** | Chart format (causal graph, effect plot, distribution plot, sensitivity curve) | Effect plot | Choose "causal graph" for DAGs, "sensitivity curve" for robustness checks |\n| **Treatment Variable** | Which column represents your intervention | Auto-detect | Specify if you have multiple treatment columns |\n| **Outcome Variable** | Which column represents your measured result | Auto-detect | Required when working with raw analysis outputs |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of uncertainty bands (%) | 95% | Lower to 90% for exploratory work; raise to 99% for high-stakes decisions |\n| **Group By** | Stratification variable for subgroup effects | None | Use when examining heterogeneous treatment effects across demographics or segments |\n| **Color Palette** | Visual theme for charts | Default | Switch to "colorblind-safe" for broader accessibility |\n| **Show Null Line** | Display reference line at zero effect | True | Keep on to emphasize statistical significance visually |\n| **Export Format** | Output file type for downloads | PNG | Use SVG for presentations requiring scaling |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\nThe node produces several outputs depending on your visualization type:\n\n**Effect Plots** show your treatment effect estimate as a point with error bars or shaded confidence regions. You\'ll see your outcome variable on the y-axis and treatment conditions on the x-axis, making it immediately clear whether effects are positive, negative, and statistically distinguishable from zero.\n\n**Causal Graphs** render your DAG structure with nodes as variables and directed edges as causal relationships. Confounders, mediators, and colliders appear in distinct visual styles.\n\n**Distribution Plots** display factual versus counterfactual outcome distributions, helping stakeholders understand "what happened" versus "what would have happened" scenarios.\n\n**Sensitivity Curves** plot how your effect estimate changes under different assumptions about unmeasured confounding—critical for assessing robustness.\n\nEach visualization includes an interactive legend, zoom controls, and a download button for exporting to presentations.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nVisualize is typically a terminal node—its purpose is communication, not further computation. However, you might connect it to:\n\n- **Report Builder**: Embed charts into automated stakeholder reports\n- **Dashboard**: Create interactive exploration interfaces for business users\n- **Export Node**: Save publication-ready figures with custom dimensions\n\n### Quick Start: Visualizing Treatment Effects\n\n1. **Connect your Effect Estimation node** output to the Visualize node input\n2. **Select "Effect plot"** as your visualization type\n3. **Verify** treatment and outcome variables are correctly detected\n4. **Set confidence level** to 95% (or your organization\'s standard)\n5. **Toggle on "Show Null Line"** to make statistical significance visually obvious\n6. **Run the node** and review the generated plot\n7. **Export** as PNG for slide decks or SVG for reports\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Tip 1**: Always include uncertainty visualization. Point estimates without confidence intervals mislead stakeholders about effect reliability.\n\n**Tip 2**: When presenting multiple effects, use "Group By" rather than creating separate visualizations—it makes comparisons easier and more honest.\n\n**Tip 3**: For executive audiences, pair effect plots with distribution plots. The latter tells a more intuitive "before/after" story.\n\n**Tip 4**: Before finalizing, check your visualization on a projector or shared screen. Colors and fonts that work on your monitor often fail in presentation contexts.\n\n**Tip 5**: Use sensitivity curves proactively with skeptical stakeholders. Showing robustness analysis builds trust in your causal claims.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploratory DAG Review\n\n- **When to use:** First-pass validation of causal structure with stakeholders in a 30-minute meeting\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `plot_type` | `"networkx"` | Fastest rendering, minimal dependencies |\n| `node_size` | `3000` | Large enough to read on projector/shared screen |\n| `edge_labels` | `False` | Reduces visual clutter for initial review |\n| `layout` | `"spring"` | Automatic positioning, no manual tuning needed |\n| `figsize` | `(12, 8)` | Readable without overwhelming |\n| `dpi` | `72` | Screen-optimized, not print-ready |\n\n- **What you get:** Clean, immediately interpretable graph that renders in under 2 seconds for DAGs up to 50 nodes\n- **Trade-off:** No effect magnitudes shown; purely structural, requiring follow-up visualizations for quantitative claims\n\n### Recipe 2: Publication-Ready Effect Estimates\n\n- **When to use:** Final deliverable for executive report, regulatory submission, or peer-reviewed documentation\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `plot_type` | `"forest"` | Industry standard for effect comparison |\n| `confidence_level` | `0.95` | Conventional statistical threshold |\n| `show_ci` | `True` | Mandatory for uncertainty communication |\n| `dpi` | `300` | Print-quality resolution |\n| `style` | `"seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid"` | Professional, grayscale-friendly |\n| `annotation_precision` | `3` | Sufficient decimal places for reproducibility |\n| `save_format` | `"pdf"` | Vector graphics for scaling |\n\n- **What you get:** Camera-ready visualization with publication-standard uncertainty intervals and typographic clarity\n- **Trade-off:** 5–10× slower rendering; file sizes 500KB+ unsuitable for rapid iteration\n\n### Recipe 3: Sensitivity Analysis for Unmeasured Confounding\n\n- **When to use:** Auditing causal claims when observational data cannot guarantee no hidden confounders\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `plot_type` | `"contour"` | Shows 2D robustness landscape |\n| `confounder_strength_range` | `(0.1, 0.9)` | Realistic partial R² bounds for omitted variables |\n| `resolution` | `50` | Balances smoothness vs. computation time |\n| `breakeven_line` | `True` | Highlights threshold where effect reverses |\n| `alpha_transparency` | `0.7` | Allows overlaying multiple scenarios |\n| `colormap` | `"RdYlGn_r"` | Red = fragile, green = robust (intuitive) |\n\n- **What you get:** Contour map showing how strong an unmeasured confounder must be to nullify your observed effect\n- **Trade-off:** Requires substantive knowledge to interpret axes; often misread as probability statements\n\n### Recipe 4: Counterfactual Distribution Animation\n\n- **When to use:** Explaining policy impact to non-technical audiences when showing "what would have happened" matters more than point estimates\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `plot_type` | `"distribution_shift"` | Comparative density visualization |\n| `animate` | `True` | Shows transition from factual to counterfactual |\n| `frame_rate` | `10` | Smooth without being sluggish |\n| `n_samples` | `10000` | Sufficient for smooth density curves |\n| `kde_bandwidth` | `0.5` | Prevents over-smoothing of bimodal outcomes |\n| `highlight_quantiles` | `[0.1, 0.5, 0.9]` | Shows distributional shift, not just means |\n\n- **What you get:** Animated GIF or interactive HTML showing how outcome distribution morphs under intervention\n- **Trade-off:** 30–60 second generation time; The company had been giving discounts to the wrong people.\n\nThe counterfactual density plot showed two overlapping distributions of predicted retention under treatment and control. Add random variations\n        if np.random.random() > 0.5:\n            base = base.upper() if np.random.random() > 0.5 else base.lower()\n        texts.append(base)\n    return texts\n\n# Create balanced dataset\nn_per_class = 200\npositive_texts = augment_text(positive_templates, n_per_class)\nnegative_texts = augment_text(negative_templates, n_per_class)\n\ntexts = positive_texts + negative_texts\nlabels = [1] * n_per_class + [0] * n_per_class  # 1 = positive, 0 = negative\n\n# Split into train and test sets\nX_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(\n    texts, labels, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=labels\n)\n\n# Vectorize text using TF-IDF\nvectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(\n    max_features=1000,      # Limit vocabulary size\n    ngram_range=(1, 2),     # Include unigrams and bigrams\n    min_df=2,               # Ignore very rare terms\n    stop_words=\'english\'    # Remove common stopwords\n)\n\nX_train_tfidf = vectorizer.fit_transform(X_train)\nX_test_tfidf = vectorizer.transform(X_test)\n\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint("Machine Learning Sentiment Classification")\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint(f"Training samples: {X_train_tfidf.shape[0]}")\nprint(f"Test samples: {X_test_tfidf.shape[0]}")\nprint(f"Vocabulary size: {X_train_tfidf.shape[1]}")\nprint()\n\n# Train Logistic Regression classifier\nlr_model = LogisticRegression(\n    C=1.0,                  # Regularisation strength (inverse)\n    class_weight=\'balanced\', # Handle any class imbalance\n    max_iter=1000,\n    random_state=42\n)\nlr_model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)\n\n# Train Naive Bayes classifier for comparison\nnb_model = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)  # Laplace smoothing\nnb_model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)\n\n# Evaluate both models\nprint("Logistic Regression Results:")\nprint("-" * 40)\nlr_pred = lr_model.predict(X_test_tfidf)\nprint(classification_report(y_test, lr_pred, target_names=[\'Negative\', \'Positive\']))\n\nprint("Naive Bayes Results:")\nprint("-" * 40)\nnb_pred = nb_model.predict(X_test_tfidf)\nprint(classification_report(y_test, nb_pred, target_names=[\'Negative\', \'Positive\']))\n\n# ============================================================\n# Example 3: Interpreting Model Coefficients\n# ============================================================\n\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint("Feature Importance Analysis (Logistic Regression)")\nprint("=" * 60)\n\n# Extract feature names and coefficients\nfeature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/analyze-sentiment_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/analyze-sentiment_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Sentiment Analysis node expects a dataset with at least one text column containing the content you want to analyze. This could be customer reviews, survey responses, social media comments, or any other textual feedback. Your data should have one row per piece of text to analyze.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| review_id | customer_review |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 1 | "This product exceeded my expectations!" |\n| 2 | "Disappointed with the quality." |\n| 3 | "It\'s okay, nothing special." |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Text Column** | Which column contains the text to analyze | (none) | Always set this—it\'s required. Select the column with your review, comment, or feedback text. |\n| **Model** | The sentiment analysis approach | VADER | Use VADER for social media or informal text. Switch to TextBlob for more formal content like business reviews. Try Transformers for the highest accuracy when you have complex, nuanced text. |\n| **Output Column Name** | What to call the new sentiment score column | "sentiment_score" | Change this if you\'re comparing multiple sentiment methods or want a more descriptive name like "review_sentiment". |\n| **Include Confidence** | Whether to add a confidence score alongside the sentiment | Enabled | Keep enabled to understand how certain the model is. Disable if you only need the basic positive/negative/neutral classification. |\n| **Classification Threshold** | Score boundaries for positive/neutral/negative labels | -0.05 to 0.05 (neutral) | Adjust if you\'re seeing too many neutrals. Tightening the range (e.g., -0.1 to 0.1) creates stricter positive/negative classifications. |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node adds several columns to your dataset:\n\n- **sentiment_score**: A numerical value typically ranging from -1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive)\n- **sentiment_label**: A categorical classification—"positive", "negative", or "neutral"\n- **confidence_score**: How certain the model is about its classification (0-1 scale)\n\nYou\'ll also see a **Sentiment Distribution** chart showing the breakdown of positive, negative, and neutral classifications, plus a **Score Histogram** displaying the distribution of raw sentiment scores across your dataset.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter sentiment analysis, you\'ll typically want to:\n\n- **Filter node** \u2192 Isolate negative reviews for customer service follow-up\n- **Group & Aggregate node** \u2192 Calculate average sentiment by product, time period, or customer segment\n- **Correlate node** \u2192 Explore relationships between sentiment and metrics like star ratings or purchase amount\n- **Visualize node** \u2192 Create sentiment trend charts over time\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** containing text reviews or comments to the Sentiment Analysis node\n2. **Select your text column** from the "Text Column" dropdown\n3. **Keep VADER as the model** unless your text is highly formal\n4. **Leave other settings at default** for your first run\n5. **Execute the node** and review the sentiment distribution chart\n6. **Add a Filter node** after sentiment analysis to examine your most negative feedback first\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Watch for short text**. Sentiment analysis struggles with very brief text like "Good" or "Bad". If you see lots of neutral classifications, check if your text is too short to carry meaningful sentiment signals.\n\n**Language matters**. The default models work best with English text. If you\'re analyzing other languages, you\'ll need to switch to the Multilingual Transformer model option.\n\n**Context is king**. A review saying "This isn\'t bad" will often be classified as negative due to the word "bad", even though the customer means something positive. When you spot these inversions in your results, consider switching to the Transformer model, which better handles negation and sarcasm.\n\n**Combine with other data**. Sentiment scores become truly powerful when correlated with structured data—compare sentiment across product categories, customer demographics, or time periods to uncover actionable patterns.\n\n**Validate with spot checks**. Always read a sample of reviews from each sentiment category to ensure the classifications align with your interpretation. This helps you calibrate thresholds and choose the right model for your specific use case.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploratory analysis of a new text dataset when you need rapid feedback on sentiment distribution and don\'t yet know if deeper analysis is warranted.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `"vader"` | Lexicon-based, no training required, instant results |\n| `batch_size` | `1000` | Process large chunks quickly without memory constraints |\n| `output_format` | `"label_only"` | Simplest categorical output (positive/negative/neutral) |\n| `confidence_threshold` | `None` | Accept all predictions to see full distribution |\n\n**What you get:** Fast categorical sentiment labels suitable for quick distribution charts and initial pattern identification.\n\n**Trade-off:** Lower accuracy than ML models; struggles with sarcasm, domain-specific language, and nuanced sentiment.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Classification\n\n**When to use:** Deploying sentiment analysis as part of a customer feedback pipeline, automated monitoring system, or any application where accuracy and reliability are critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `"distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2"` | Transformer-based with strong accuracy across domains |\n| `batch_size` | `16` | Balance GPU memory usage with throughput |\n| `output_format` | `"probabilities"` | Full probability distribution enables confidence filtering |\n| `confidence_threshold` | `0.85` | Flag low-confidence predictions for human review |\n| `max_length` | `512` | Full token capacity for longer reviews/comments |\n| `handle_neutrals` | `True` | Preserve three-class distinction rather than forcing binary |\n\n**What you get:** High-accuracy predictions with confidence scores that enable quality control workflows and exception handling.\n\n**Trade-off:** 10-50x slower than lexicon methods; requires GPU for reasonable performance on large datasets.\n\n### Recipe 3: Financial News Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing market-moving news, earnings call transcripts, or financial social media where domain vocabulary and subtle hedging language are prevalent.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `"finbert"` | Specifically trained on financial text corpus |\n| `negation_scope` | `5` | Capture longer-range negations common in formal language |\n| `aspect_terms` | `["earnings", "guidance", "outlook", "revenue"]` | Focus on market-relevant aspects |\n| `temporal_weight` | `"decay"` | More recent sentences weighted higher in document scoring |\n| `output_format` | `"granular"` | Sentence-level sentiment to catch mixed messages |\n\n**What you get:** Domain-aware sentiment that correctly interprets financial hedging, forward-looking statements, and technical terminology.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires domain-specific model that may underperform on general text; aspect configuration needs market knowledge.\n\n### Recipe 4: Call Center Emotion Escalation Detection\n\n**When to use:** Identifying customer service interactions that are deteriorating emotionally, even when language remains superficially polite—a hidden use case where sentiment trends matter more than absolute values.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_size` | `3` | Rolling sentiment across conversation turns |\n| `metric` | `"sentiment_velocity"` | Rate of sentiment decline, not absolute score |\n| `threshold_delta` | `-0.3` | Flag conversations with rapid negative shifts |\n| `ignore_pleasantries` | `True` | Filter greetings/closings that mask true sentiment |\n| `output_format` | `"time_series"` | Preserve sequential interaction structure |\n\n**What you get:** Early warning system for escalating conversations requiring supervisor intervention, catching frustration before explicit complaints.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires sequential conversation data with turn structure; not applicable to single-instance reviews or posts.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender receives 3,500 customer service emails daily, with 18% containing complaints that regulatory guidelines require be escalated within 24 hours. Clean up naming inconsistencies before appending.\n\n**Use Source Tracking religiously** when combining data from different regions, time periods, or systems. That extra column is a lifesaver when results look unexpected and you need to trace the issue back.\n\n**Watch for hidden schema drift**—a column might be named the same but contain different units (dollars vs. cents) or granularity (daily vs. weekly) across sources. len(grouped))\n    grouped[\'dist_non_events\'] = (grouped[\'non_events\'] + epsilon) / (total_non_events + epsilon * len(grouped))\n    \n    # Calculate WoE and IV\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/bin-features_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/bin-features_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Bin Features node expects a dataset with **at least one continuous numerical column** that you want to discretize. This works best with variables like age, income, transaction amounts, or sensor readings—anything with a wide range of values that might benefit from grouping.\n\n**Before and After Example:**\n\n| customer_id | age | income |\n|-------------|-----|--------|\n| 1 | 23 | 45000 |\n| 2 | 67 | 89000 |\n| 3 | 34 | 52000 |\n\nbecomes:\n\n| customer_id | age | income | age_binned | income_binned |\n|-------------|-----|--------|------------|---------------|\n| 1 | 23 | 45000 | 18-35 | 0-50k |\n| 2 | 67 | 89000 | 65+ | 75k-100k |\n| 3 | 34 | 52000 | 18-35 | 50k-75k |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Columns** | Which numerical columns to bin | None (required) | Select all continuous variables you want to discretize |\n| **Binning Method** | How bins are created: equal width, equal frequency, or custom | Equal Width | Use equal frequency for skewed data; custom when you have domain-specific thresholds |\n| **Number of Bins** | How many intervals to create | 5 | Increase for finer granularity (10+), decrease for simpler groupings (3-4) |\n| **Custom Bin Edges** | Manual breakpoints (e.g., 0, 25, 50, 100) | None | Use when you have meaningful business thresholds like "low/medium/high risk" |\n| **Label Style** | How bins are named: ranges, ordinal numbers, or custom labels | Ranges | Choose ordinal for ML models; custom for business reporting |\n| **Include Boundaries** | Whether intervals are left-closed, right-closed | Right-closed | Rarely needs changing; affects how boundary values are assigned |\n| **Handle Outliers** | Create separate bins for extreme values | Off | Turn on when you have known outliers that shouldn\'t influence bin edges |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\n**Output Columns:** The node adds one new categorical column for each binned variable, with a suffix like `_binned`. The original columns remain unchanged, so you can compare or choose which version to use downstream.\n\n**Visualizations:** You\'ll see a histogram for each variable showing the distribution across bins, with counts and percentages. This helps you verify that bins are meaningful and balanced (or intentionally imbalanced).\n\n**Summary Metrics:** A table displays bin edges, counts per bin, and percentage of total for each variable—essential for understanding how your data was grouped.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect Bin Features to:\n\n- **Feature Selection nodes** — binned variables often perform well in tree-based models\n- **Statistical Summary** — to analyze patterns within each bin\n- **Model Training nodes** — especially logistic regression or decision trees that benefit from categorical inputs\n- **Visualization nodes** — binned data creates cleaner, more interpretable charts\n\n### Quick Start: Most Common Use Case\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Bin Features node input port\n2. **Select your target columns** — start with 1-2 continuous variables (e.g., age, income)\n3. **Choose "Equal Frequency"** as your binning method if your data is skewed\n4. **Set bins to 5** (a sensible starting point for most use cases)\n5. **Run the node** and review the histogram to check distribution\n6. **Adjust bin count** if needed: fewer bins if categories overlap in meaning, more if you\'re losing important detail\n7. **Connect to your modeling node** and compare performance against using the raw continuous variable\n\n### Pro Tips from Experience\n\n**Bin count matters more than you think.** Too few bins (2-3) oversimplify and lose predictive power. Too many (15+) defeat the purpose and approach the original continuous variable. Start with 5-7 and let your validation metrics guide you.\n\n**Check your bin boundaries for business sense.** If "age 35.7-42.3" appears, you might want custom bins like "18-35, 36-50, 51-65, 65+" that stakeholders actually understand and trust.\n\n**Equal frequency handles skewed data beautifully.** If 80% of your income values cluster between 30k-50k, equal width bins waste most bins on sparse regions. Equal frequency ensures each bin has similar sample sizes.\n\n**Keep both versions initially.** Don\'t drop the original continuous variable right away—some models (like random forests) might perform better with the raw data, while others (like logistic regression) prefer bins.\n\n**Watch for data leakage with custom bins.** If you set bin edges based on insights from your test set, you\'re cheating. Always define bins using training data only.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Binning\n\n- **When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need fast insights into variable distributions and want to quickly test if binning improves model performance before investing in optimization.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bins` | 5 | Sufficient granularity without overfitting on small samples |\n| `strategy` | `\'quantile\'` | Ensures equal samples per bin regardless of distribution |\n| `encode` | `\'ordinal\'` | Maintains order while keeping memory footprint minimal |\n| `subsample` | `None` | Dataset small enough during exploration to use all data |\n\n- **What you get:** Fast-to-compute bins with balanced sample sizes that reveal basic non-linear patterns and provide interpretable groupings for stakeholder discussions.\n\n- **Trade-off:** May miss subtle distribution nuances and create arbitrary splits that don\'t align with natural data boundaries or domain logic.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Binning\n\n- **When to use:** Deploying binned features to production where consistency, reproducibility, and robustness to unseen data are critical requirements.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bins` | 10 | Balances granularity with stability across data shifts |\n| `strategy` | `\'quantile\'` | Handles distribution changes better than fixed-width bins |\n| `encode` | `\'onehot\'` | Prevents ordinal assumptions in tree-free models |\n| `subsample` | 100000 | Prevents memory issues with large production datasets |\n| `dtype` | `np.float32` | Reduces memory by 50% vs float64 with negligible precision loss |\n\n- **What you get:** Robust bins that generalize well to new data with explicit handling of edge cases and efficient memory usage for deployment at scale.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Higher computational cost during fit and increased feature dimensionality from one-hot encoding requires more storage and serving infrastructure.\n\n### Recipe 3: Handling Heavy-Tailed Financial Data\n\n- **When to use:** Processing financial metrics (transaction amounts, account balances, claim sizes) where extreme outliers dominate and quantile binning creates uninformative first/last bins.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bins` | 8 | Fewer bins accommodate concentration in tail |\n| `strategy` | `\'kmeans\'` | Clusters similar values, naturally isolating outliers |\n| `encode` | `\'ordinal\'` | Preserves magnitude relationship for credit/risk models |\n| `subsample` | 50000 | K-means computationally expensive on full datasets |\n\n- **What you get:** Bins that capture the dense central distribution with separate bins for meaningful outlier segments, preserving signal in extreme values.\n\n- **Trade-off:** K-means requires iteration and can be unstable across refits if data distribution shifts significantly between training periods.\n\n### Recipe 4: Weakening Feature Leakage\n\n- **When to use:** Suspected target leakage where a continuous feature has suspiciously high importance but domain experts insist it shouldn\'t be removed entirely from the model.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bins` | 3 | Aggressive information loss while retaining directional signal |\n| `strategy` | `\'uniform\'` | Fixed boundaries prevent leakage through training distribution |\n| `encode` | `\'ordinal\'` | Simplest encoding for interpretability audits |\n\n- **What you get:** Coarse categorical representation that preserves only broad patterns, deliberately destroying the granular information that enabled leakage.\n\n- **Trade-off:** May eliminate legitimate predictive signal along with leakage; requires careful validation that model performance remains acceptable after this aggressive dimensionality reduction.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was struggling with credit score models that treated the difference between a 720 and **Profile Data** or **Summary Statistics** to verify improvements\n- **Feature Engineering** for creating analysis-ready variables\n- **Modeling nodes** when cleansing was your final preparation step\n- **Export/Save** to preserve a clean master dataset\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Preserve the original**: Always keep your raw data intact. The Cleansing node\'s `_cleansed` suffix columns let you audit changes—don\'t disable this feature until you\'re certain.\n\n**Iterate on strategy**: Start conservative (Flag Only for missing values) and tighten gradually. Aggressive cleansing can accidentally remove valid edge cases.\n\n**Domain context trumps statistics**: An outlier detection algorithm might flag a $10,000 purchase as anomalous, but in luxury retail, that\'s Tuesday. Use the visual outputs to sanity-check automated decisions.\n\n**Chain multiple Cleansing nodes**: For complex pipelines, use separate nodes for different operations (one for duplicates, another for outliers). This makes troubleshooting easier than one mega-configuration.\n\n**Check the confidence scores**: Rows with low confidence scores might need manual review. Filter and export these for subject matter expert validation before proceeding to analysis.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Cleanse\n\n**When to use:** Initial dataset inspection when you need fast feedback on data quality issues before committing to analysis decisions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `missing_threshold` | 0.50 | Keep columns with <50% missing—aggressive dropping for speed |\n| `outlier_method` | `\'none\'` | Skip outlier detection entirely in exploration phase |\n| `duplicate_subset` | `None` | Check all columns—maximize duplicate detection |\n| `type_inference` | `True` | Auto-detect types to catch obvious mismatches |\n| `standardize_text` | `False` | Skip expensive string operations |\n| `validate_constraints` | `False` | No business rule checking yet |\n\n**What you get:** A rapidly cleaned dataset that exposes major structural problems without computational overhead.\n\n**Trade-off:** You\'ll miss subtle issues like mild outliers and unstandardized categorical values that matter for modeling.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Cleanse\n\n**When to use:** Preparing data for deployed models or critical business reports where data quality directly impacts decisions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `missing_threshold` | 0.95 | Conservative—only drop nearly empty columns |\n| `missing_imputation` | `\'iterative\'` | Use IterativeImputer with max_iter=20 for accuracy |\n| `outlier_method` | `\'isolation_forest\'` | contamination=0.01, robust multivariate detection |\n| `outlier_action` | `\'cap\'` | Winsorize at 1st/99th percentiles—preserve sample size |\n| `duplicate_subset` | Custom business keys | Use domain-specific identifiers |\n| `type_inference` | `True` | With manual validation step |\n| `standardize_text` | `True` | lowercase, strip, unicode normalization |\n| `validate_constraints` | `True` | Enforce all domain rules |\n| `audit_log` | `\'detailed\'` | Track every transformation for compliance |\n\n**What you get:** Maximally cleaned data with full traceability and conservative handling that minimizes information loss.\n\n**Trade-off:** 10-50x slower processing and requires domain expertise to configure business rules correctly.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Cardinality Text Data\n\n**When to use:** Working with customer feedback, product descriptions, or survey responses where text variation creates artificial dimensionality.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `missing_threshold` | 0.80 | Text fields often legitimately sparse |\n| `text_standardize_method` | `\'aggressive\'` | Lowercase, lemmatization, whitespace normalization |\n| `fuzzy_matching` | `True` | dedupe_distance=\'levenshtein\', threshold=0.85 |\n| `rare_category_threshold` | 0.001 | Collapse categories appearing <0.1% into \'Other\' |\n| `encoding_standardization` | `\'utf-8\'` | Force consistent encoding with error=\'replace\' |\n| `special_char_handling` | `\'normalize\'` | Convert smart quotes, dashes, etc. to ASCII |\n\n**What you get:** Dramatically reduced cardinality in categorical text fields while preserving semantic meaning.\n\n**Trade-off:** Loses subtle distinctions that might matter (e.g., merging "5-star" and "5 star" ratings metadata).\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Financial Data\n\n**When to use:** Processing transaction logs, market data, or sensor readings where temporal ordering and forward-looking bias are critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `missing_imputation` | `\'forward_fill\'` | Respect temporal causality—no future information |\n| `outlier_method` | `\'rolling_zscore\'` | window=20, threshold=4.0—context-aware detection |\n| `outlier_action` | `\'flag\'` | Create indicator column, operations |\n\n**What you get:** Cleaned data that maintains temporal integrity and doesn\'t leak future information into historical records.\n\n**Trade-off:** Cannot use more powerful bidirectional imputation methods that might better fill gaps.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was rejecting 18% of loan applications due to address mismatches |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `extract_components` | `[\'year\', \'quarter\', \'dayofyear\']` | Focus on absolute position, not weekly cycles |\n| `cyclical_encoding` | `True,
