observances |\n\n**What you get:** Twenty to thirty features that adapt to each user\'s cultural and geographic context automatically.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires maintaining multiple holiday calendars and adds complexity to feature pipeline versioning.\n\n## Common Misconceptions\n\n**"Adding month and day-of-week features is sufficient for capturing seasonality"**\n\n**Why people believe this:** Most visible business cycles operate on weekly and monthly patterns—weekend sales spikes, month-end purchasing behaviours, quarterly reporting deadlines. These create the illusion that a handful of calendar features can capture all temporal dynamics.\n\n**The truth:** Seasonality operates simultaneously at multiple, interacting timescales. A retail model with only month and day-of-week features cannot distinguish between "the first Monday of December" and "the last Monday of December"—yet consumer behaviour differs dramatically between these periods. True seasonal patterns emerge from the *interaction* of multiple temporal features: week-of-year interacts with day-of-week, day-of-month interacts with month, and hour-of-day varies by day-type. More critically, many seasonal patterns are *not* calendar-aligned—they follow fiscal calendars, school schedules, cultural events, or industry-specific cycles that require custom feature engineering.\n\n**The real-world consequence:** A demand forecasting team at a European retailer added month and weekday features, achieved respectable validation scores, and deployed to production. Their model systematically under-predicted during floating-date events like Easter and Ramadan, which shift within the calendar year. They missed the critical insight that religious holidays follow lunar or computus-based calendars, requiring distance-to-event features rather than fixed calendar positions. The result: three consecutive years of excess inventory write-downs during post-holiday periods.\n\n**"Future dates should use the same feature engineering as historical dates"**\n\n**Why people believe this:** Code reusability is a best practice. If your training pipeline extracts "day of week" from 2023-03-15, the same logic should work for 2024-03-15 during prediction. The feature definition hasn\'t changed.\n\n**The truth:** Certain date features encode information that *doesn\'t exist yet* at prediction time, creating a subtle but catastrophic form of data leakage. Features like "days until next holiday" or "is_last_day_of_month" are valid historical features but become problematic for future dates. More insidiously, features derived from rolling statistics (like "sales in previous 7 days") can silently break if your prediction pipeline doesn\'t perfectly replicate the temporal cutoff logic. The asymmetry runs deeper: training data contains complete weeks/months/quarters, but prediction often occurs mid-period, changing the statistical properties of aggregated features.\n\n**The real-world consequence:** A credit risk model included "days_since_last_payment" as a feature, calculated by subtracting the most recent payment date from the observation date. During training on historical data, this worked perfectly. In production, the feature engineering pipeline inadvertently used the current system date instead of the loan application date, meaning every applicant processed on the same day received identical values for this feature. The model\'s discriminatory power collapsed, and approval rates drifted 40% higher than expected before the team identified the temporal reference point mismatch.\n\n**"Encoding date components as integers preserves their information"**\n\n**Why people believe this:** Month 1 through 12, hour 0 through 23—these are naturally numeric. Converting datetime to integers feels like a lossless transformation that maintains the information while making it algorithm-friendly.\n\n**The truth:** Integer encoding imposes false ordinality and destroys cyclical continuity. Representing December as 12 and January as 1 tells your model that December is "further from" January than it is from November, violating the circular nature of calendars. Linear models learn that hour 23 is maximally distant from hour 0, despite them being adjacent. Tree-based models partially compensate through splits but require exponentially more data to learn patterns that cross the cycle boundary. Cyclical features require cyclical encodings: sine/cosine transformations that preserve the topology of time.\n\n**The real-world consequence:** An energy forecasting model used integer hour-of-day (0-23) and achieved strong daytime performance but systematically failed at the midnight boundary, creating a discontinuous prediction surface between 23:00 and 00:00 that manifested as false demand spikes in operational scheduling.\n\n## How This Connects\n\n### Before This Node\n\n**Data Import** loads raw datetime columns from sources like databases, CSVs, or APIs, establishing the initial timestamp data that Date Features will decompose. Bad upstream data includes timestamps stored as strings in inconsistent formats (mixing "DD/MM/YYYY" and "MM/DD/YYYY") or integers representing Unix epochs without documentation, causing Date Features to misinterpret dates or fail entirely during parsing.\n\n**Missing Data Handling** addresses gaps in temporal sequences through imputation or flagging, ensuring Date Features operates on complete timestamps rather than null values. When missing timestamps aren\'t handled, Date Features propagates nulls through all engineered columns (day-of-week, month, etc.), creating sparse feature matrices that degrade model performance and complicate downstream validation.\n\n**Data Type Conversion** transforms string-formatted dates into proper datetime objects with timezone awareness, providing Date Features with structured temporal data it can reliably extract components from. Without this conversion, Date Features either crashes when attempting mathematical operations on strings or silently treats text timestamps as categorical variables, losing all temporal ordering and cyclical properties.\n\n**Timezone Normalization** standardizes timestamps to a consistent reference frame (typically UTC or local business time), preventing Date Features from extracting incorrect calendar attributes across daylight saving transitions. Bad timezone handling creates features where the same event appears to occur on different days or hours depending on the observer\'s location, introducing systematic errors into time-based pattern detection.\n\n**Outlier Detection** identifies anomalous timestamps like dates in the year 2099 or 1970 (common data entry errors or system defaults), allowing Date Features to operate on realistic temporal ranges. When outliers persist, engineered features like "years since event" produce nonsensical values that dominate scaling operations and cause models to learn spurious relationships between extreme dates and outcomes.\n\n### After This Node\n\n**Feature Scaling** normalizes numeric date features like day-of-year (1–366) and hour (0–23) to comparable ranges, ensuring distance-based algorithms don\'t overweight features with arbitrarily large values. Date Features\' consistently bounded numeric outputs (months always 1–12, weekdays always 0–6) make them ideal candidates for min-max or standard scaling without requiring robust preprocessing.\n\n**Encoding Categorical Variables** transforms Date Features\' categorical outputs like month names or day-of-week labels into numeric representations suitable for model training. The natural ordinality in some date features (Q1 < Q2 < Q3) and pure categorical nature of others (Monday vs. Tuesday) allows downstream encoding to apply both ordinal and one-hot strategies appropriately.\n\n**Feature Selection** identifies which engineered date components (hour, day-of-month, is_weekend) actually correlate with the target variable, reducing dimensionality from the comprehensive set Date Features generates. Date Features often produces 10–20 correlated variables from a single timestamp column, making selection critical to avoid multicollinearity and overfitting.\n\n**Time Series Split** partitions data chronologically for validation using the temporal ordering that Date Features preserves through its "days since" or sequential index features. Date Features\' engineered columns maintain strict time-ordering properties that enable splitters to respect temporal causality and prevent data leakage from future information.\n\n**Model Training** consumes Date Features\' numeric and categorical outputs as predictive variables, leveraging extracted patterns like seasonality and day-of-week effects that algorithms cannot learn from raw timestamps. The interpretable nature of Date Features (e.g., "is_holiday" or "month") allows tree-based models to create human-readable splits and linear models to assign coefficients to specific calendar effects.\n\n### Common Pipeline Patterns\n\n**Retail Demand Forecasting Pipeline**  \nData Import \u2192 Timezone Normalization \u2192 **Date Features** \u2192 Feature Scaling \u2192 Time Series Split \u2192 Model Training  \nPredicts product demand by extracting day-of-week, holiday, and seasonal patterns from transaction timestamps, typically achieving 15–25% improvement over baseline models that ignore calendar effects.\n\n**Customer Churn Prediction Workflow**  \nMissing Data Handling \u2192 Data Type Conversion \u2192 **Date Features** \u2192 Feature Selection \u2192 Encoding Categorical Variables \u2192 Model Training  \nIdentifies at-risk customers by engineering tenure, days-since-last-purchase, and subscription anniversary features from account activity dates, enabling targeted retention campaigns 30–60 days before predicted churn events.\n\n**Fraud Detection System**  \nOutlier Detection \u2192 Timezone Normalization \u2192 **Date Features** \u2192 Feature Scaling \u2192 Model Training \u2192 Real-time Scoring  \nFlags suspicious transactions by detecting unusual hour-of-day or day-of-week patterns compared to user history, with engineered time features contributing 20–40% of model feature importance in production systems.\n\n### What to Have Ready\n\n**Datetime columns properly parsed**: All timestamp fields should be converted to native datetime objects with explicit timezone information, not strings or ambiguous numeric formats—verify with `.dtype` checks showing `datetime64[ns]` or equivalent.\n\n**Temporal scope defined**: Document the meaningful time ranges for your domain (business operating hours, relevant historical lookback period, seasonal cycles), as these boundaries determine which date features matter (quarter-over-quarter growth needs 12+ months of data; hour-of-day patterns require 24-hour operations).\n\n**Target variable temporal alignment**: Confirm that your prediction target corresponds to the same time reference as your date features—predicting next-month churn requires current-month features, not last-month features, preventing off-by-one temporal misalignment.\n\n**Calendar reference data available**: For business-specific date features, have holiday calendars, fiscal year definitions, and promotional period schedules loaded as lookup tables that Date Features can merge against to create domain-relevant boolean flags.\n\n## Try It Yourself\n\n### Recommended Dataset\n\n**Capital Bikeshare Dataset** from `seaborn.load_dataset(\'taxis\')` or generate synthetic bike rental data using You define a 90-day observation window and a 30-day outcome horizon. A customer made their last transaction on March 15th. You need to create a training example with an observation window ending on March 1st. Option D commits the most critical error: using outcome-period information to set the label, which is precisely what Event Target methodology prevents. The key insight is that **temporal boundaries must be strictly enforced**: observation window data predicts outcome horizon labels, and any event in the outcome horizon cannot influence that customer\'s inclusion or label.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. The "Fit on Training Only" toggle handles this automatically.\n\n**Missingness can be a feature**: Before filling, consider whether the *pattern* of missing data tells you something. A customer who didn\'t provide their income might be different from one who did—that\'s why the Indicator Columns option exists.\n\n**Multiple imputation for uncertainty**: For critical analyses, run your pipeline multiple times with different imputation strategies and compare results. You impute them using the median income of the entire dataset, then calculate correlations between income and spending. Which statement best describes what you\'ve done?\n\nA) You\'ve preserved the original correlations while making the dataset complete for analysis\nB) You\'ve introduced bias by not accounting for the missing data mechanism, but preserved the variance of the income distribution\nC) You\'ve artificially weakened the correlation between income and spending by adding values that don\'t reflect the actual relationship\nD) You\'ve improved the reliability of downstream analysis by ensuring no information is lost due to missing data\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Imputing with a single summary statistic (like median) replaces missing values with numbers that have no relationship to the target variable (spending), artificially diluting the true correlation. This is the critical but often-overlooked consequence mentioned in the overview: imputation "fundamentally affects the statistical properties of the resulting dataset—including its mean, variance, and correlations." Option A represents the common misconception that imputation is "neutral"—it\'s not; it changes relationships. Option B is doubly wrong: while it correctly notes that ignoring the missing data mechanism is problematic, median imputation actually *reduces* variance (all imputed values are identical). Option D reflects the dangerous belief that imputation recovers information rather than making educated guesses that introduce their own distortions.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. tabular dataset as input — there are no strict requirements on column types or data shape. You\'ll typically connect it after initial data loading or cleaning steps when you need to create new calculated fields.\n\n**Before:**\n| Product | Price | Quantity |\n|---------|-------|----------|\n| Widget A | 25.00 | 120 |\n| Widget B | 40.00 | 85 |\n\n**After** (with formula `Price * Quantity` creating Revenue):\n| Product | Price | Quantity | Revenue |\n|---------|-------|----------|---------|\n| Widget A | 25.00 | 120 | 3000.00 |\n| Widget B | 40.00 | 85 | 3400.00 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Formula Expression** | The calculation or transformation to apply | (empty) | This is your main workspace — enter any valid expression using column names, math operators (+, -, *, /), functions (SQRT, LOG, ROUND), or text operations (CONCAT, UPPER) |\n| **Output Column Name** | Name of the new column created | "Calculated_Field" | Always change this to something meaningful like "Total_Revenue" or "Price_Per_Unit" |\n| **Data Type** | Expected type of the result (Number, Text, Date, Boolean) | Auto-detect | Override if auto-detection fails, especially for dates or when you need specific numeric precision |\n| **Handle Errors As** | What to do when a calculation fails (null, zero, skip row) | Null | Use "Skip row" when invalid calculations indicate bad data; use "Zero" for additive metrics where missing = zero |\n\n### What You\'ll Get as Output\n\nThe Formula node adds exactly **one new column** to your dataset with the name you specified. The original data passes through unchanged — Formula is non-destructive.\n\n**In the data preview**, you\'ll see your new column appended to the right side of the table. Heuristix highlights it in light blue to show it\'s freshly created.\n\n**In the summary panel**, you\'ll see basic statistics for your new column (min, max, mean for numeric; unique count for text), plus a count of any rows where the formula couldn\'t calculate (errors).\n\n**No charts** are automatically generated, but you can immediately pipe this data to visualization nodes to explore your new metric.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nFormula outputs work seamlessly with any node that accepts tabular data:\n\n- **Filter** — to isolate rows based on your calculated field (e.g., Revenue > 5000)\n- **Aggregate** — to summarize by your new metric (e.g., average Revenue by Region)\n- **Chart nodes** — to visualize distributions or trends using your derived column\n- **Another Formula** — formulas can reference other formula outputs for multi-step calculations\n\n### Quick Start: Calculate Profit Margin\n\n1. **Drag a Formula node** onto your canvas and connect your sales data\n2. **Click the node** to open the configuration panel\n3. **In Formula Expression**, type: `(Revenue - Cost) / Revenue * 100`\n4. **In Output Column Name**, enter: `Profit_Margin_Pct`\n5. **Set Data Type** to Number\n6. **Run the node** and check the preview — your new percentage appears as the last column\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Reference columns exactly as named** — if your column is "Customer Name" (with a space), use quotes in formulas: `CONCAT("Customer Name", " - Premium")`\n\n**Test complex formulas incrementally** — build calculations in stages using multiple Formula nodes rather than one giant expression. It\'s easier to debug and understand.\n\n**Use COALESCE for null-safety** — wrap divisions in null-handling: `COALESCE(Revenue / NULLIF(Quantity, 0), 0)` prevents divide-by-zero errors.\n\n**Formula nodes are cheap** — don\'t overthink combining multiple calculations into one node. Separate formulas with clear names make your workflow self-documenting.\n\n**Check the error count** — after running, always glance at the summary panel\'s error count. If more than 1-2% of rows failed, investigate before proceeding downstream.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping of Business Metrics\n\n**When to use:** You\'re in an exploratory meeting and need to quickly test whether a proposed KPI definition makes sense across your dataset before formalizing it.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `expression` | `revenue / customer_count` | Simple division for average revenue per customer |\n| `output_column` | `avg_revenue_temp` | Temporary naming convention for exploratory work |\n| `error_handling` | `coerce_to_null` | Silently handle division-by-zero without halting execution |\n| `data_type` | `infer` | Let system detect appropriate numeric type |\n| `validate_syntax` | `false` | Skip validation overhead for speed |\n\n**What you get:** Immediate results visible in your data preview with automatic null handling for edge cases.\n\n**Trade-off:** No syntax validation means typos fail silently; unsuitable for any persisted pipeline.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Feature Engineering\n\n**When to use:** Creating features for a machine learning model that will be deployed to production and must handle all edge cases reliably.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `expression` | `log1p(transaction_amount) * is_weekend` | Domain-specific transformation with interaction term |\n| `output_column` | `log_weekend_spend_v2` | Versioned name for model lineage tracking |\n| `error_handling` | `raise_exception` | Fail loudly on any unexpected data quality issues |\n| `data_type` | `float64` | Explicit precision for model consistency |\n| `validate_syntax` | `true` | Catch errors before production deployment |\n| `null_propagation` | `strict` | Any null input produces null output for clean handling |\n| `vectorized` | `true` | Enable NumPy/Pandas vectorization for performance |\n\n**What you get:** Deterministic, auditable transformations with comprehensive error reporting and optimal computational efficiency.\n\n**Trade-off:** Longer initial setup time and pipelines will halt on data quality issues rather than approximating through them.\n\n### Recipe 3: Financial Calculations with Decimal Precision\n\n**When to use:** Computing monetary values, tax calculations, or any finance domain work where floating-point rounding errors are unacceptable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `expression` | `(price * 1.08975).quantize(\'0.01\')` | Sales tax calculation with explicit rounding |\n| `output_column` | `total_with_tax` | Clear business meaning |\n| `data_type` | `decimal(10,2)` | Fixed-point arithmetic prevents rounding errors |\n| `error_handling` | `raise_exception` | Financial calculations must never silently fail |\n| `rounding_mode` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` | Standard accounting rounding rule |\n\n**What you get:** Exact decimal arithmetic matching accounting standards with no floating-point drift.\n\n**Trade-off:** 3-5x slower computation than float64; increased memory usage for large datasets.\n\n### Recipe 4: Text Pattern Flags for Downstream Filtering\n\n**When to use:** Identifying anomalous patterns in text fields to create filter conditions, particularly useful before expensive NLP operations or when debugging data ingestion issues.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `expression` | `len(description) < 10 OR description.str.count(\'[0-9]\') > 20` | Flag suspiciously short or number-heavy text |\n| `output_column` | `is_malformed_text` | Boolean flag for quality control |\n| `data_type` | `boolean` | Explicit flag type for filtering operations |\n| `error_handling` | `coerce_to_false` | Treat evaluation errors as "not malformed" |\n\n**What you get:** Simple boolean flags that enable fast filtering before computationally expensive text processing.\n\n**Trade-off:** Heuristic rules may miss nuanced quality issues that full NLP would catch.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Heuristix\n\n### What Data to Connect\n\nThe Missing Imputation node accepts any structured dataset containing missing values (nulls, NaNs, or empty cells). You can connect it directly after data loading nodes or cleaning steps that have identified missingness in your dataset.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- At least one column with missing values\n- Numeric, categorical, or mixed column types are all supported\n\n**Example before/after:**\n\n| CustomerID | Age | Income | Region |\n|------------|-----|--------|--------|\n| 001 | 34 | 50000 | North |\n| 002 | null | 62000 | South |\n| 003 | 45 | null | North |\n| 004 | 29 | 48000 | null |\n\nAfter imputation (using median for numeric, mode for categorical):\n\n| CustomerID | Age | Income | Region |\n|------------|-----|--------|--------|\n| 001 | 34 | 50000 | North |\n| 002 | 34 | 62000 | South |\n| 003 | 45 | 50000 | North |\n| 004 | 29 | 48000 | North |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Imputation Strategy** | Method used to fill missing values: mean, median, mode, forward-fill, model-based | Median | Use mean for normally distributed data; mode for categorical; model-based when relationships between features matter |\n| **Column Selection** | Which columns to impute | All columns with nulls | Select specific columns when different strategies suit different features |\n| **Missing Threshold** | Maximum % of missing values before dropping column entirely | 50% | Increase to 70-80% if you\'re confident in your imputation method; decrease to 30% for high-stakes applications |\n| **Model Type** (for model-based) | Algorithm for predicting missing values: KNN, Random Forest, Linear | KNN (k=5) | Random Forest for complex relationships; Linear for speed with large datasets |\n| **Create Indicator Columns** | Add binary flags showing which values were imputed | False | Enable when missingness itself is informative (e.g., "declined to answer" patterns) |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\n**Modified Dataset:**\n- Your original columns with missing values replaced\n- Optionally, new binary columns (e.g., `Age_was_missing`) if indicator creation is enabled\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n- Imputation summary showing rows affected per column\n- Before/after missing value counts\n- Distribution comparison charts (histogram overlays showing original vs. imputed values)\n\n**Validation Statistics:**\n- Mean/median preservation metrics\n- Variance change indicators (helps assess if imputation introduced artificial certainty)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node naturally flows into:\n- **Feature Engineering** nodes (now that you have complete data)\n- **Model Training** nodes (most algorithms require complete cases)\n- **Exploratory Data Analysis** nodes (visualizations work better without gaps)\n- **Data Export** nodes (if preparing clean data for external use)\n\nAvoid connecting directly to **Outlier Detection** right after model-based imputation, as imputed values might appear as outliers.\n\n### Quick Start: Most Common Use Case\n\n1. **Connect your data** to the Missing Imputation node after initial loading\n2. **Leave strategy on "Median"** for a quick, robust start with numeric data\n3. **Set "Create Indicator Columns" to True** if you suspect missing patterns matter\n4. **Review the distribution comparison charts** to ensure imputed values look reasonable\n5. **Connect to your modeling node** and proceed with complete data\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Inspect missingness patterns first.** Before imputing, use the Missing Data Analysis node to check if your data is Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) or if there\'s a pattern. This determines which imputation strategy is safest.\n\n**Don\'t impute your target variable.** If your prediction target has missing values, remove those rows instead. Imputing your outcome variable can severely bias your model.\n\n**Try multiple strategies and compare.** Clone your workflow and test different imputation methods on separate branches. Compare model performance downstream to see which approach works best for your specific case.\n\n**Watch for data leakage with model-based imputation.** If using KNN or Random Forest imputation, ensure you\'re only using training data to fit the imputation model, then apply it to test data. Heuristix handles this automatically when used within cross-validation nodes.\n\n**Consider domain knowledge over statistics.** Sometimes a default value (like 0 for "number of previous purchases") makes more business sense than a statistical median.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration for Rapid Prototyping\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need to quickly test model feasibility and don\'t yet know which features matter.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `strategy` | `\'median\'` | Robust to outliers, works for all numeric distributions |\n| `add_indicator` | `True` | Preserves missingness pattern as feature signal |\n| `max_iter` | `1` | Single-pass only, no iterative refinement |\n| `n_neighbors` | Not applicable | Skip KNN methods entirely for speed |\n\n**What you get:** Instant, deterministic imputation that lets you proceed to exploratory visualizations and correlation analysis within seconds, even on datasets with millions of rows.\n\n**Trade-off:** You lose all inter-feature relationships and may introduce mean-shift bias if missingness is informative.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Statistical Rigor\n\n**When to use:** Deploying models to production where audit trails, reproducibility, and statistical validity matter more than training speed.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `strategy` | `\'iterative\'` | Captures multivariate relationships |\n| `estimator` | `BayesianRidge()` | Provides uncertainty estimates, handles collinearity |\n| `max_iter` | `50` | Sufficient convergence for stable estimates |\n| `tol` | `0.001` | Tight tolerance for reproducible convergence |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Ensures identical results across runs |\n| `add_indicator` | `True` | Enables model to learn missingness patterns |\n| `imputation_order` | `\'ascending\'` | Imputes features with least missing data first |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically sound imputations that preserve covariance structure and provide audit-ready reproducibility with quantified uncertainty.\n\n**Trade-off:** Training time increases 10–50× compared to simple imputation; requires sufficient complete cases to train the estimator reliably.\n\n### Recipe 3: Time Series with Forward-Fill Constraints\n\n**When to use:** Sensor data, stock prices, or any temporal dataset where future information cannot leak into past imputations.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'ffill\'` | Forward-fill preserves temporal causality |\n| `limit` | `3` | Prevents propagating stale values too far |\n| `axis` | `0` | Fills down rows (time axis) |\n| Fallback `strategy` | `\'constant\'` | Fills remaining gaps with domain-specific value |\n| `fill_value` | `0` or domain sentinel | Explicit marker for extended gaps |\n\n**What you get:** Temporally valid imputations that respect causal ordering and prevent look-ahead bias in backtesting scenarios.\n\n**Trade-off:** Early observations remain missing unless you accept backward-fill contamination; volatile signals appear artificially smoothed during gaps.\n\n### Recipe 4: Categorical-Heavy Datasets with Rare Levels\n\n**When to use:** Survey data, user behavior logs, or medical records where categorical features dominate and contain many low-frequency categories.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `strategy` | `\'most_frequent\'` for categoricals | Preserves class distribution |\n| Numeric `strategy` | `\'knn\'` | Leverages similar categorical profiles |\n| `n_neighbors` | `15` | Larger pool smooths rare category noise |\n| `weights` | `\'distance\'` | Down-weights less similar donors |\n| Missing category | `\'missing\'` as explicit level | Treats absence as informative signal |\n\n**What you get:** Imputations that leverage categorical clustering structure while treating missingness itself as a meaningful category when appropriate.\n\n**Trade-off:** Rare category combinations may still receive inappropriate imputations; requires careful handling of never-seen-together category pairs.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processing 15,000 applications monthly struggled with incomplete credit You impute missing values using the median income of observed records. What is the primary statistical consequence?\n\nA) The imputation will inflate the variance of the income distribution, making it appear more dispersed than the true population.\n\nB) The imputation will preserve unbiased estimates of mean income since median imputation doesn't favor high or low values.\n\nC) The imputation will underestimate mean income and distort its relationship with other variables, introducing systematic bias.\n\nD) The imputation will create appropriate uncertainty estimates since median is robust to the missing data mechanism.\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** This question tests understanding of how missingness mechanisms interact with imputation methods. The scenario describes **missing not at random (MNAR)** data where high-income individuals are systematically underrepresented in observed data. Simple median imputation will pull missing values toward the center of the *observed* distribution, which is already biased downward, thereby underestimating the true mean and attenuating correlations with predictors of income. Option A represents the misconception that simple imputation inflates variance (it actually *reduces* variance by pulling values toward central tendency). Option B reflects misunderstanding that median imputation produces unbiased estimates regardless of missingness mechanism (it only works reasonably well under MCAR conditions). Option D confuses robustness to outliers with robustness to biased missingness mechanisms—median imputation provides no uncertainty quantification and doesn't address systematic bias in what's missing.\n" as "python" resulted in an error at token: '—'. 2024-01-15 | 45.00           | Electronics      |\n| C001        | 2024-02-03 | 22.50           | Books            |\n| C002        | 2024-01-20 | 100.00          | Electronics      |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Sensible Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|--------------|------------------|----------------|\n| **Prediction Date** | The "as of" moment when you\'re making predictions | Today\'s date | Set to your historical prediction point for backtesting, or your actual prediction date for production |\n| **Window Length** | How far back to look (e.g., 30 days, 90 days, 1 year) | 90 days | Longer windows capture trends but may include stale data; shorter windows are more reactive but potentially noisy |\n| **Entity ID Column** | Which field identifies your subjects | Auto-detected | Change if you have multiple ID columns |\n| **Timestamp Column** | Which date/datetime field to use | Auto-detected | Specify if you have multiple date fields |\n| **Aggregation Type** | How to summarize (sum, count, average, min, max, last) | count | Match to your feature—use sum for amounts, count for frequency, last for most recent status |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\nThe node transforms your event-level data into **one row per entity** with aggregated features calculated over your specified window.\n\n**Output columns include:**\n- Your original entity ID\n- `observation_window_start` and `observation_window_end` (the actual date range used)\n- Aggregated feature columns (named with your chosen aggregation, like `purchase_amount_sum` or `event_count`)\n- `events_in_window` (a helpful diagnostic showing how many records were included)\n\nYou\'ll also see a **summary card** displaying:\n- Total entities processed\n- Date range of the observation window\n- Coverage statistics (what % of entities had at least one event)\n\n### Quick Start: Building Purchase History Features\n\n1. **Connect your transaction data** to the Observation Window node\n2. **Set Prediction Date** to the date you want to make predictions (e.g., 2024-03-01)\n3. **Set Window Length** to 90 days (capturing three months of behavior)\n4. **Select your Entity ID** (customer_id)\n5. **Choose Timestamp Column** (transaction_date)\n6. **Configure aggregations** for each feature (sum for amounts, count for frequency)\n7. **Run the node** and verify the output shows one row per customer\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically flows into:\n- **Feature Engineering** nodes to create ratios or derive additional features\n- **Join** nodes to merge with outcome labels or entity attributes\n- **Train Model** nodes directly if your features are ready for modeling\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Watch for sparse entities.** Some customers may have no events in your window. The node handles this gracefully by creating rows with zero/null values, but you may want to filter these out or treat them specially.\n\n**Mind the window edge.** If your prediction date is too close to your earliest data, you\'ll get incomplete windows. Check the `observation_window_start` output to verify you\'re getting the full period.\n\n**Use multiple windows.** Consider creating 30-day, 90-day, and 365-day windows separately and joining them. This helps your model detect both recent changes and long-term patterns.\n\n**Test your date logic.** Run the node with a known historical prediction date and manually verify a few customers\' aggregations match what you\'d calculate by hand. This catches timezone issues and off-by-one errors early.\n\n**Label your features clearly.** With multiple windows and aggregations, you\'ll quickly accumulate columns like `amount_sum_90d` and `amount_sum_30d`. Establish a naming convention early.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Sprint\n\n- **When to use:** Initial exploration when you need to validate whether temporal features have any predictive signal before investing in infrastructure.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `observation_days` | 30 | Captures one business cycle without computational overhead |\n| `aggregation_level` | Daily | Avoids hourly granularity processing costs |\n| `feature_functions` | `[\'count\', \'sum\']` | Minimal complexity; fastest to compute |\n| `min_history_required` | 7 | Tolerates sparse data; maximizes sample size |\n| `gap_days` | 0 | Skips leakage protection to test upper-bound performance |\n\n- **What you get:** Quick feature matrix in minutes that reveals whether temporal patterns exist worth pursuing.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Zero leakage protection means overly optimistic performance metrics that cannot be deployed.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Deployment\n\n- **When to use:** Building models for live scoring where prediction integrity and regulatory compliance matter.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `observation_days` | 90 | Balances recency with seasonal stability |\n| `aggregation_level` | Hourly | Preserves intraday behavioral patterns |\n| `feature_functions` | `[\'count\', \'sum\', \'mean\', \'std\', \'trend\']` | Comprehensive feature set for robustness |\n| `min_history_required` | 30 | Ensures statistical reliability of computed features |\n| `gap_days` | 2 | Accounts for batch processing delays in real systems |\n| `timezone_handling` | `\'entity_local\'` | Prevents time zone artifacts in user behavior |\n| leakage.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Reduced training sample size due to strict history requirements and prediction gap.\n\n### Recipe 3: Subscription Renewal with Grace Period\n\n- **When to use:** `observation_days` | 60 | Two billing cycles of clean behavioral data |\n| `aggregation_level` | Weekly | Smooths day-of-week noise in subscription actions |\n| `feature_functions` | `[\'count\', with Adversarial Adaptation\n\n- **When to use:** Detecting fraud where attackers rapidly change tactics, making older patterns misleading rather than informative.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `observation_days` | 7 | Short window captures current attack vectors only |\n| `aggregation_level` | Hourly | Attack patterns evolve within days |\n| Think of this as your "anchor" column—the dimension along which you want to ensure complete coverage.\n\n**Before padding:**\n| date       | store_id | revenue |\n|------------|----------|---------|\n| 2024-01-01 | A        | 450     |\n| 2024-01-03 | A        | 520     |\n| 2024-01-01 | B        | 380     |\n\n**After padding (filling missing dates):**\n| date       | store_id | revenue |\n|------------|----------|---------|\n| 2024-01-01 | A        | 450     |\n| 2024-01-02 | A        | *null*  |\n| 2024-01-03 | A        | 520     |\n| 2024-01-01 | B        | 380     |\n| 2024-01-02 | B        | *null*  |\n| 2024-01-03 | B        | *null*  |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Pad Column** | The column that defines your sequence (date, category, index) | *(first column)* | Select your temporal or categorical dimension |\n| **Pad Method** | How to fill: `full_range`, `by_group`, or `explicit_values` | `full_range` | Use `by_group` when different categories need different ranges; `explicit_values` for custom lists |\n| **Group By** | Columns that define separate sequences to pad independently | *(none)* | Essential for multi-entity data (e.g., pad dates *per store*) |\n| **Fill Value** | What to insert in padded rows for other columns | `null` | Change to `0` for counts, `"missing"` for labels, or `forward_fill` to carry forward last known values |\n| **Frequency** | For time series: `day`, `hour`, `month`, etc. | `auto` | Override when auto-detection fails or you need specific intervals |\n| **Min/Max Range** | Explicit boundaries for padding | *(data min/max)* | Set when you need consistent range across multiple datasets |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Output dataset:** Your original data plus new rows inserted at the gaps, with columns populated according to your Fill Value setting. The row count increases—sometimes dramatically if you have sparse data across a wide range.\n\n**Summary panel:** Shows you:\n- Number of rows added\n- Coverage before and after (% of possible values present)\n- Any groups that had significantly more padding than others (useful for spotting data quality issues)\n\n**No charts** are generated directly, but the padded output is now ready for time series visualisation or heatmap nodes that expect complete grids.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Common next steps:**\n\n- **Fill Missing Values** \u2192 Handle those new nulls strategically based on context\n- **Time Series Plot** \u2192 Now displays continuous lines without gaps\n- **Pivot/Heatmap** \u2192 Creates complete grids without missing cells\n- **Aggregation** \u2192 Ensures zero-value periods are counted (not ignored)\n\n### Quick Start: Padding a Time Series\n\n1. **Connect** your time series data to the Padding node\n2. **Set Pad Column** to your date/timestamp field\n3. **Enable Group By** if you have multiple entities (products, locations, users)\n4. **Choose Fill Value**: start with `null`, then chain a Fill Missing Values node, or use `0` directly if missing = zero\n5. **Check the summary** to verify the number of rows added makes sense\n6. **Preview the output** to confirm the new rows appear where expected\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Pad before aggregating.** If you\'re counting events per day, padding ensures days with zero events show as zero (not absent), which matters for averages and trends.\n\n**Watch your row count.** Padding 10 products across 365 days creates 3,650 rows minimum. Preview with filters first if working with large dimensional combinations.\n\n**Group by is your friend.** Different stores opening on different dates? Padding by group prevents creating nonsensical rows before a store existed.\n\n**Consider downstream fill strategy.** Padding with `null` gives you explicit control in the next node; padding with `forward_fill` is faster but less transparent about what was missing.\n\n**Check for duplicates first.** If your source data already has duplicate timestamps per group, padding will add *more* rows at those points. Run a deduplication node upstream if needed.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Time Series Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial exploration of time series data with irregular sampling intervals where you need quick visual inspection of trends without sophisticated interpolation.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'ffill\'` | Forward-fill is computationally trivial and preserves last-known values |\n| `limit` | `5` | Prevents unrealistic propagation of stale values beyond ~5% of typical sampling frequency |\n| `freq` | `\'1D\'` or `\'1H\'` | Match your expected natural cadence; daily for business metrics, hourly for sensor logs |\n| `fill_value` | `None` | Avoid masking genuine data gaps during exploration |\n\n- **What you get:** A uniformly-indexed series that renders cleanly in plots with minimal compute overhead, suitable for stakeholder demos or hypothesis formation.\n- **Trade-off:** Forward-fill introduces bias in statistical summaries (mean, variance) and is unsuitable for predictive modeling or causal inference.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade ML Pipeline Padding\n\n- **When to use:** Preparing training data for production models where padding artifacts must be explicitly flagged and gaps must not leak future information.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `None` | Explicit `NaN` insertion forces downstream imputation strategy rather than silent propagation |\n| `limit` | `None` | Pad all gaps to ensure uniform structure for tensor operations |\n| `freq` | Inferred from `pd.infer_freq()` | Programmatic detection prevents manual drift as data cadence evolves |\n| `fill_value` | `np.nan` | Preserves missingness signal for models that handle nulls natively (XGBoost, LightGBM) |\n| `indicator` | `True` | Adds binary `_padded` column flagging synthetic rows for feature engineering or holdout exclusion |\n\n- **What you get:** A structurally complete dataset where every padded observation is traceable, enabling robust cross-validation without temporal leakage.\n- **Trade-off:** Increases memory footprint by 10–15% due to indicator columns and requires explicit downstream imputation logic.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Panel Data Alignment Across Entities\n\n- **When to use:** Merging sales, inventory, or behavioral data across stores/users/devices with different operational start dates or missing observation windows.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'bfill\'` then `\'ffill\'` | Backward-fill first respects entity lifecycle (no pre-launch data), then forward-fill handles trailing gaps |\n| `limit` | `10` | Aligns with typical reporting lag (e.g., 10 days for retail reconciliation) |\n| `groupby` | `[\'entity_id\']` | Applies padding independently per entity to avoid cross-contamination |\n| `fill_value` | `0` for counts, `np.nan` for rates | Domain-appropriate defaults: zero sales is meaningful, zero conversion rate is not |\n\n- **What you get:** A balanced panel where each entity spans identical time ranges, enabling fixed-effects regression or cohort comparisons.\n- **Trade-off:** Artificially extends entity histories, potentially distorting survival analysis or churn models if not subset appropriately.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Text Sequence Batch Preparation\n\n- **When to use:** Padding variable-length token sequences for mini-batch training in NLP transformers or RNNs where hardware requires fixed dimensions.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `maxlen` | `128` or `512` | Common BERT/GPT context windows; choose based on 95th percentile of sequence lengths in corpus |\n| `padding` | `\'post\'` | Appends padding tokens after real sequence, aligning with causal attention masks |\n| `truncating` | `\'post\'` | Trims end of over-long sequences, preserving critical opening context |\n| `value` | `0` or `tokenizer.pad_token_id` | Model-specific padding token index that attention masks will ignore |\n\n- **What you get:** Uniform-shape arrays enabling efficient batched matrix operations on GPUs without ragged tensor overhead.\n- **Trade-off:** Sequences shorter than `maxlen` waste computation on padding tokens; longer sequences lose tail information.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional Australian credit union processing 18,000 loan applications monthly struggled with fraud detection tabular dataset as input, but works best when your data exceeds approximately 1GB or contains more than a million rows — situations where pandas would struggle or run out of memory. PySpark handles all common data types: strings, integers, floats, dates, booleans, and nested structures like arrays or JSON objects.\n\n**Before (Input):**\n| customer_id | purchase_date | amount | category |\n|-------------|---------------|--------|----------|\n| 101 | 2024-01-15 | 45.99 | electronics |\n| 102 | 2024-01-16 | 23.50 | books |\n| 101 | 2024-01-20 | 89.00 | electronics |\n\n**After (Sample Output with aggregation):**\n| customer_id | total_amount | purchase_count | avg_amount |\n|-------------|--------------|----------------|------------|\n| 101 | 134.99 | 2 | 67.50 |\n| 102 | 23.50 | 1 | 23.50 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Operation Type** | The transformation to perform (filter, aggregate, join, window, pivot) | Select | Choose based on your analysis goal |\n| **Partition Count** | How many parallel chunks to split data across | Auto | Increase for very large datasets (10GB+) or reduce if you have <100MB to avoid overhead |\n| **Cache Result** | Whether to store this transformation in memory for reuse | Disabled | Enable if you\'ll reference this data multiple times downstream |\n| **Shuffle Partitions** | Partitions created during aggregations/joins | 200 | Lower to 20-50 for smaller datasets to reduce task overhead |\n| **Execution Mode** | Local (single machine) vs. Cluster (distributed) | Local | Switch to Cluster when data exceeds available RAM |\n| **Custom Code** | Python/SQL expression for your transformation | Empty | Write PySpark DataFrame operations or Spark SQL queries here |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\n**Transformed Dataset:** The node outputs a new DataFrame with your transformations applied. node accepts any tabular dataset with at least one column you want to transform. It works with text, numerical, and categorical columns—though you\'ll most commonly use it with categorical data or text fields that contain standardised codes or labels.\n\n**Example: Before and After**\n\n| customer_type | status |\n|---------------|--------|\n| b2b | A |\n| B2B | active |\n| business | A |\n| consumer | I |\n\nAfter replacement:\n\n| customer_type | status |\n|---------------|--------|\n| Business | Active |\n| Business | Active |\n| Business | Active |\n| Consumer | Inactive |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | The column where replacements will happen | None (required) | Select the column containing values you want to replace |\n| **Replacement Map** | Key-value pairs defining old\u2192new values | Empty | Add each value you want to replace and what to replace it with |\n| **Match Case** | Whether "Active" and "active" are treated as different | Enabled | Disable for case-insensitive matching when standardizing inconsistent capitalization |\n| **Match Whole Value** | Replace only exact matches vs. partial matches | Enabled | Disable if you want to replace parts of text (e.g., "St" \u2192 "Street" within addresses) |\n| **Handle Unmapped** | What to do with values not in your replacement map | Keep original | Choose "Set to null" or "Set to default" if unlisted values indicate data quality issues |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node outputs your dataset with the target column transformed according to your mapping rules. The original column is replaced—there\'s no separate "new" column created by default.\n\n**In the results panel, you\'ll see:**\n\n- **Replacement Summary**: A count of how many values were changed\n- **Value Distribution**: Before/after frequencies showing which values were replaced and their new distribution\n- **Unmapped Values Alert**: A list of any values in the source data that weren\'t in your replacement map (helpful for catching typos or unexpected values)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter replacing values, you\'ll typically flow into:\n\n- **Group By** or **Pivot**: Now that categories are standardised, aggregations will work correctly\n- **Filter**: To isolate records based on your newly cleaned values\n- **Train Model**: For machine learning nodes that require properly encoded categorical variables\n- **Visualisation nodes**: Charts will now display consistent, readable labels\n\n### Quick Start\n\n**Most common use case: Standardizing inconsistent category labels**\n\n1. Connect your dataset to the Replace Values node\n2. Click the node to open configuration\n3. In **Target Column**, select the column with inconsistent values\n4. Click **Add Replacement** and enter your first old\u2192new pair (e.g., "b2b" \u2192 "Business")\n5. Continue adding pairs until you\'ve mapped all variations\n6. Disable **Match Case** if your data has capitalization inconsistencies\n7. Run the node and check the **Unmapped Values Alert** for any categories you missed\n8. Adjust your mapping and re-run if needed\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Look for patterns before mapping manually.** Run a Value Counts node first to see all unique values in your column. You\'ll often discover variations you didn\'t know existed (extra spaces, typos, different abbreviations).\n\n**Use "Handle Unmapped" strategically.** If you\'re replacing error codes and anything unmapped is definitely an error, set unmapped values to null. But if you\'re only standardizing a subset of values, keep unmapped values as-is.\n\n**Replace in stages for complex transformations.** If you need multiple transformations on the same column, chain multiple Replace Values nodes. It\'s clearer than trying to build a complex single mapping.\n\n**Watch out for whitespace.** "Active" and "Active " (with trailing space) won\'t match. Run a Trim node upstream if you suspect whitespace issues.\n\n**Save your mappings.** If you\'re replacing domain-specific codes (diagnosis codes, product SKUs), document your replacement map in the node notes. Your future self—and your colleagues—will thank you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration Replacement\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need to quickly standardize obvious inconsistencies across multiple columns without validation overhead.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `case_sensitive` | `False` | Catches "YES", "yes", "Yes" variations automatically |\n| `regex` | `False` | Avoids pattern compilation overhead for simple literal matches |\n| `validate_mapping` | `False` | Skips pre-execution checks to maximize speed |\n| `null_handling` | `"ignore"` | Preserves nulls; doesn\'t interrupt batch operations |\n| `partial_match` | `False` | Exact matches only—prevents unintended substitutions |\n\n**What you get:** Near-instantaneous replacements suitable for cleaning exploratory notebooks where speed trumps validation.\n\n**Trade-off:** No safeguards against typos in your mapping dictionary or unexpected data types causing silent failures.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Replacement Pipeline\n\n**When to use:** Deploying replacement logic in automated ETL pipelines where data quality and auditability are critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `case_sensitive` | `True` | Explicit matching prevents ambiguity in audit logs |\n| `validate_mapping` | `True` | Pre-flight check ensures mapping keys exist in data |\n| `null_handling` | `"map_explicit"` | Forces conscious decision on null treatment |\n| `log_replacements` | `True` | Creates audit trail of which values changed |\n| `strict_mode` | `True` | Raises exceptions on unmapped values rather than skipping |\n| `backup_column` | `True` | Retains original values as `{col}_original` |\n\n**What you get:** Enterprise-ready transformations with full traceability and rollback capability.\n\n**Trade-off:** 3–5× slower execution and increased memory footprint from logging and backup columns.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Fuzzy String Normalization\n\n**When to use:** Cleaning user-generated text fields with spelling variations, abbreviations, or extra whitespace that standard replacement misses.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `regex` | `True` | Enables pattern-based matching |\n| `ignore_whitespace` | `True` | Treats "New York" and "NewYork" as identical |\n| `similarity_threshold` | `0.85` | Matches strings with 85%+ Levenshtein similarity |\n| `case_sensitive` | `False` | Handles inconsistent capitalization |\n| `strip_special_chars` | `True` | Removes punctuation before comparison |\n\n**What you get:** Robust standardization that catches "Dept.", "Department", "DEPT" under one mapping rule.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower performance due to distance calculations; risk of false positives at thresholds above 0.90.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Temporal Value Deprecation\n\n**When to use:** Migrating legacy code systems where old values must remain valid during a transition period but need versioning metadata.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `append_suffix` | `True` | Adds `_legacy` to replaced values instead of overwriting |\n| `effective_date` | `"2024-01-01"` | Only replaces values in records after this timestamp |\n| `preserve_unmapped` | `True` | Keeps old codes intact if no new mapping exists |\n| `create_mapping_column` | `True` | Adds boolean flag showing which rows were transformed |\n\n**What you get:** Backward-compatible transformations where historical analysis uses old codes and new reports use updated values.\n\n**Trade-off:** Creates schema changes (additional columns) that downstream systems must accommodate.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processes 8,000 loan applications monthly, each containing credit This could be customer reviews, support tickets, survey responses, social media posts—any unstructured text you want to convert into numerical features for modelling.\n\n**Before:**\n| customer_id | review_text |\n|-------------|-------------|\n| 1001 | "Great product, fast shipping!" |\n| 1002 | "Disappointed with quality" |\n\n**After:**\n| customer_id | review_text | tf_word_great | tf_word_product | ... | text_length |\n|-------------|-------------|---------------|-----------------|-----|-------------|\n| 1001 | "Great product, fast shipping!" | 0.167 | 0.167 | ... | 29 |\n| 1002 | "Disappointed with quality" | 0.000 | 0.000 | ... | 28 |\n\nThe node works with any text column and preserves all your original columns while adding new numerical features.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Text Column** | Which column contains the text to transform | (first text column) | Select the specific column you want to featurize |\n| **Method** | Feature extraction approach: Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, or N-grams | TF-IDF | Use Bag-of-Words for simple counts, TF-IDF for weighted importance, N-grams to capture phrases |\n| **Max Features** | Maximum number of word/phrase features to create | 100 | Increase to 500-1000 for rich vocabularies; decrease to 50 for simpler models or small datasets |\n| **Min Document Frequency** | Ignore words appearing in fewer than N documents | 2 | Increase to 5-10 to remove very rare words; set to 1 if you have limited data |\n| **Max Document Frequency** | Ignore words appearing in more than X% of documents | 0.9 (90%) | Lower to 0.7 to remove common but uninformative words |\n| **N-gram Range** | Word sequence length: (1,1) for single words, (1,2) for words and pairs | (1,1) | Use (1,2) or (1,3) to capture phrases like "not good" or "very satisfied" |\n| **Include Metadata** | Add statistical features: text length, word count, etc. | Yes | Keep enabled—these simple features often prove surprisingly useful |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node adds numerical columns to your dataset, with the exact columns depending on your configuration:\n\n**Feature columns**: One column per word or phrase, named like `tf_word_excellent` or `tfidf_phrase_fast_delivery`. Values represent frequency or weighted importance.\n\n**Metadata columns** (when enabled): `text_length` (character count), `word_count`, `avg_word_length`, `sentence_count`. These capture structural properties of the text.\n\n**Feature importance chart**: A bar chart showing which words or phrases have the highest variance across your dataset—these are likely to be the most useful predictive features.\n\n**Vocabulary summary**: Displays total unique terms extracted and any terms filtered out by your frequency thresholds.\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Drag** the Text Features node onto your canvas and connect your dataset\n2. **Select** the text column you want to transform (e.g., "review_text")\n3. **Choose TF-IDF** as your method—it\'s the most balanced starting point\n4. **Set Max Features to 100** for your first pass\n5. **Run** the node and examine the feature importance chart\n6. **Connect** to a Feature Selection or Classification node downstream\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter text featurization, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Feature Selection**: Narrow down to the most predictive text features before modelling\n- **Classification/Regression nodes**: Use these features to predict outcomes (sentiment, category, churn)\n- **Clustering**: Group documents by textual similarity\n- **Principal Component Analysis**: Reduce dimensionality of high-feature text data\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Start small with Max Features**: Begin with 50-100 features, examine what\'s captured, then increase if needed. Too many features too soon makes results hard to interpret.\n\n**Check the vocabulary**: Look at which words made it through your filters. If you see nonsense or code fragments, you may need text cleaning upstream first.\n\n**N-grams are powerful but expensive**: Switching from (1,1) to (1,3) can explode your feature count. Only add higher n-grams if single words aren\'t capturing meaning (common in sentiment or negation-heavy text).\n\n**Metadata features punch above their weight**: Simple features like text_length often correlate strongly with your target and train faster than vocabulary features.\n\n**Different languages need different settings**: Non-English text may need higher max features to capture the any tabular data with at least one column you want to convert. There are no strict requirements on input data shape—it works with datasets of any size, from a handful of rows to millions.\n\n**Before and after example:**\n\n| user_id | signup_date | is_active | revenue |\n|---------|-------------|-----------|---------|\n| 12345   | 2024-01-15  | 1         | 99.50   |\n| 67890   | 2024-02-20  | 0         | 150.75  |\n\nAfter casting `user_id` to string, `signup_date` to datetime, and `is_active` to boolean:\n\n| user_id | signup_date | is_active | revenue |\n|---------|-------------|-----------|---------|\n| "12345" | 2024-01-15T00:00:00 | True | 99.50 |\n| "67890" | 2024-02-20T00:00:00 | False | 150.75 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Column Selection** | Which column(s) to cast | None (must specify) | Select every column that needs type conversion |\n| **Target Type** | The data type to convert to | String | Choose based on downstream needs: numeric (int, float) for calculations, datetime for time operations, boolean for flags, string for IDs or text |\n| **Error Handling** | What happens when conversion fails | Coerce to null | Use "Raise error" when data quality is critical and you want to catch issues immediately; use "Coerce" for messy real-world data |\n| **Date Format** | Template for parsing datetime strings | Auto-detect | Specify when your dates follow unusual patterns (e.g., "DD/MM/YYYY" or "YYYY.MM.DD") |\n| **Decimal Separator** | Character used for decimals | Period (.) | Change to comma for European-formatted numbers |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output columns:** The node replaces your selected column(s) with the newly cast version(s), preserving column names. Original data isn\'t modified—you can always reconnect to the source if needed.\n\n**Summary panel:** Displays conversion success rate for each column, showing how many values converted successfully versus how many became null due to incompatible values.\n\n**Type indicator:** Each output column shows its new data type in the column header badge, confirming the transformation worked as expected.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nType Cast typically sits early in your pipeline, right after data import. Common next steps:\n\n- **Filter or Pivot nodes**: Now that dates are proper datetime objects, you can filter by date ranges or aggregate by month\n- **Calculate node**: Numeric casts enable mathematical operations\n- **Group By**: Boolean flags become perfect grouping categories\n- **ML nodes**: Most models require specific numeric types; casting ensures compatibility\n\n### Quick Start: Converting Mixed Data Types\n\n1. **Connect your data source** to the Type Cast node\n2. **Click the Column Selection dropdown** and choose `signup_date`\n3. **Set Target Type to "Datetime"**—leave Date Format on Auto-detect unless you see parsing errors\n4. **Add another cast**: Click "+ Add Column" and select `is_active`\n5. **Set Target Type to "Boolean"**—Heuristix automatically recognizes 0/1, true/false, yes/no\n6. **Check the Summary panel**—verify 100% conversion success\n7. **Run the pipeline** and inspect the output preview to confirm your data looks correct\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1:** Always cast ID columns (like `user_id` or `customer_id`) to strings, even if they\'re numbers. This prevents accidental mathematical operations and preserves leading zeros.\n\n**Tip 2:** When converting currencies or prices, cast to float first, then use a Calculate node to round to two decimal places. This prevents floating-point precision issues.\n\n**Tip 3:** If date parsing fails, check the Summary panel to see which values caused problems. Often you\'ll find entries like "N/A" or "Unknown" that need filtering or replacement first.\n\n**Tip 4:** Cast boolean columns as early as possible—downstream nodes like Filter and Group By work much more intuitively with true boolean types than numeric 0/1 values.\n\n**Tip 5:** Use multiple Type Cast nodes for complex workflows rather than one mega-node. This makes debugging easier and lets you verify conversions incrementally.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Cast\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need fast failures.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `infer_objects` | `False` | Requires explicit type declaration |\n| `errors` | `\'raise\'` | Fails immediately on incompatible values |\n| `dtype` | Explicit dict mapping | Enforces exact schema per column |\n| `downcast` | `\'integer\'` / `\'float\'` | Minimizes memory for large-scale processing |\n| `convert_string` | `True` | Uses optimized string dtype |\n| `convert_floating` | `False` | Prevents lossy conversions |\n\n**What you get:** Type-safe transformations with minimal memory usage and guaranteed schema compliance that fails fast on anomalies.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires comprehensive data profiling upfront and rejects edge cases that might be salvageable with coercion.\n\n### Recipe 3: Financial Precision Casting\n\n**When to use:** Processing monetary values, accounting data, or scientific measurements where floating-point rounding errors are unacceptable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dtype` | `\'object\'` then Decimal | Preserves exact precision |\n| `errors` | `\'raise\'` | No tolerance for ambiguous amounts |\n| `decimal_places` | `2` (or domain-specific) | Enforces currency precision |\n| `thousands_separator` | `\',\'` | Handles formatted input strings |\n| `use_nullable_dtypes` | `True` | Distinguishes NULL from zero |\n\n**What you get:** Arbitrary-precision numeric representation that maintains exact values through complex calculations without accumulating rounding errors.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower computation and higher memory usage compared to native float types; incompatible with some NumPy operations.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Aware Text Parsing\n\n**When to use:** Converting free-text timestamp columns from system logs, user inputs, or legacy databases with inconsistent formatting into analysis-ready datetime objects.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dtype` | `\'datetime64[ns]\'` | Standardizes to nanosecond precision |\n| `infer_datetime_format` | `True` | Auto-detects format patterns |\n| `dayfirst` | Locale-dependent | Resolves ambiguous DD/MM vs MM/DD |\n| `utc` | `True` | Normalizes to timezone-aware UTC |\n| `errors` | `\'coerce\'` | Handles malformed entries gracefully |\n| `exact` | `False` | Matches timestamps within longer strings |\n\n**What you get:** Unified temporal index suitable for time-series analysis, resampling, and chronological aggregation with consistent timezone Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/value-mapping_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/value-mapping_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Value Mapping node expects **categorical or discrete data** in one or more columns. You can work with text labels, numeric codes, or any discrete values that need standardising or recoding.\n\n**Before mapping:**\n\n| product_size | status_code | region |\n|--------------|-------------|---------|\n| S | 1 | Northeast |\n| small | 1 | NE |\n| Medium | 2 | South |\n| L | 3 | northeast |\n\n**After mapping:**\n\n| product_size | status_code | region | size_standard |\n|--------------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| S | 1 | Northeast | Small |\n| small | 1 | NE | Small |\n| Medium | 2 | South | Medium |\n| L | 3 | northeast | Large |\n\nThe node works with any data shape—from a few hundred rows to millions. Just make sure your target columns contain discrete values, not continuous numbers.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Source Column** | Which column to transform | (none) | Always set this—it\'s your starting point |\n| **Mapping Dictionary** | The value pairs defining your transformation (old \u2192 new) | {} | Define all conversions you need. Can handle many-to-one mappings (multiple old values \u2192 single new value) |\n| **Output Column Name** | Name for the transformed column | `{source}_mapped` | Use descriptive names like `status_clean` or `category_standard` |\n| **Handle Unmapped Values** | What to do with values not in your mapping | Keep original | Change to "Set to null" if unmapped values signal data quality issues, or "Set to default" with a catch-all label |\n| **Default Value** | Fallback value when "Set to default" is selected | "Other" | Choose something meaningful like "Unknown" or "Uncategorised" |\n| **Case Sensitive** | Whether "Active" and "active" are treated as different | No | Enable if your data legitimately uses case to distinguish meaning |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output columns:** The node adds your newly mapped column alongside the original, so you can verify transformations before dropping the source column.\n\n**Mapping summary panel:** Shows how many values were mapped, unmapped values detected, and the distribution of your new categories. This is invaluable for catching typos in your mapping dictionary.\n\n**Preview table:** Displays before/after rows side-by-side, making it easy to spot-check your transformations.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nValue Mapping typically flows into:\n\n- **Grouping & Aggregation** nodes—once categories are standardised, aggregations become meaningful\n- **Filter** nodes—your clean categories make filtering reliable\n- **Encoding** nodes—for machine learning prep, map to human-readable labels first, then encode to numeric\n- **Visualisation** nodes—charts and dashboards work much better with consistent category labels\n\n### Quick Start: Standardising Status Labels\n\n1. **Drag** the Value Mapping node onto your canvas and connect your dataset\n2. **Select** the messy status column (e.g., containing "active", "Active", "1", "live")\n3. **Define your mapping** in the dictionary: `{"active": "Active", "Active": "Active", "1": "Active", "live": "Active"}`\n4. **Name the output** something clear like `status_clean`\n5. **Set Handle Unmapped** to "Set to null" to flag data quality issues\n6. **Run the node** and check the mapping summary for any unexpected unmapped values\n7. **Review** the preview table to confirm transformations look right\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Build mappings incrementally.** Start with your most common values, run the node, check unmapped values in the summary, then add more mappings. Don\'t try to anticipate every variation upfront.\n\n**Use many-to-one mappings liberally.** They\'re perfect for consolidating variations: `{"cancelled", "canceled", "CANCELLED"}` all map to `"Cancelled"`.\n\n**Keep original columns during development.** Only drop source columns once you\'re confident in your mappings. That preview comparison saves debugging time.\n\n**Export your mapping dictionaries.** Once you\'ve perfected a mapping for customer segments or product categories, save it. You\'ll use it again on next month\'s data.\n\n**Chain multiple Value Mapping nodes** when different columns need different transformations—it\'s clearer than one complex node doing everything.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploratory Standardisation\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need to quickly unify inconsistent categorical labels across imported datasets | Records all mapping failures for monitoring |\n\n**What you get:** Deterministic, auditable transformations that fail loudly on data drift or quality issues.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires comprehensive mapping specification upfront and rejects novel values that might be legitimate.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Multi-Source Geographic Consolidation\n\n**When to use:** Merging datasets from different
