wildly different ranges (e.g., age: 20-80, income: 20000-200000), the node auto-scales them, but you\'ll get better results preprocessing with a Normalize node first.\n\n**Start permissive**: Begin with higher contamination (0.15-0.20) to see more candidates, then tighten the threshold after reviewing what the algorithm considers anomalous in your domain.\n\n**Method selection trick**: Isolation Forest excels at global outliers (transactions from Antarctica when you\'re a local business), while LOF catches local anomalies (a $50 transaction that\'s normal globally but weird for this specific customer).\n\n**Temporal data gotcha**: If your data has time trends, consider detrending or scoring within time windows — otherwise, legitimate seasonal changes get flagged as anomalous.\n\n**Explain your scores**: Always drill into the Feature Contribution plot for flagged items before taking action. A high anomaly score might reveal data quality issues rather than genuine anomalies.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration on New Data\n\n**When to use:** First pass anomaly detection when you\'ve just received a dataset and need quick insight into potential outliers within minutes.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Isolation Forest | Fastest training on medium-to-large datasets |\n| n_estimators | 50 | Minimal trees while maintaining stability |\n| max_samples | 256 | Caps computational cost per tree |\n| contamination | 0.1 | Liberal threshold catches more candidates |\n| n_jobs | -1 | Uses all CPU cores |\n\n**What you get:** A ranked list of the top 10% most anomalous observations with scores computed in seconds to minutes, suitable for interactive exploration.\n\n**Trade-off:** Lower precision than production configurations—expect 30-40% false positive rate in your top-ranked anomalies.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Financial Fraud Detection\n\n**When to use:** Deployed system requiring audit trails, stable scores across retraining, and minimal false positives on transaction data.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Local Outlier Factor | Density-based scores are interpretable to auditors |\n| n_neighbors | 35 | Smooths local density estimates in noisy data |\n| contamination | 0.001 | Reflects realistic fraud base rate (0.1%) |\n| metric | manhattan | Robust to feature scale differences |\n| novelty | True | Enables scoring new transactions against training distribution |\n\n**What you get:** Conservative anomaly scores where flagged transactions have 85%+ precision when manually reviewed, with consistent thresholds across model updates.\n\n**Trade-off:** Training takes 10-50x longer than Isolation Forest; not viable above 100,000 training observations without approximations.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Sensor Data with Correlated Features\n\n**When to use:** Industrial IoT or medical monitoring data with 50+ sensors where many features move together (temperature, pressure, vibration readings).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Autoencoder | Learns manifold structure capturing feature correlations |\n| hidden_layers | [32, 8, 32] | Bottleneck forces compression of redundant information |\n| activation | tanh | Handles negative sensor values unlike ReLU |\n| epochs | 100 | Sufficient convergence without overfitting |\n| threshold_percentile | 95 | Scores via reconstruction error at 95th percentile |\n\n**What you get:** Anomaly scores that detect unusual *combinations* of sensor values missed by univariate or distance-based methods.\n\n**Trade-off:** Black-box scores are difficult to explain; requires GPU for datasets above 10,000 observations; sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.\n\n### Recipe 4: Identifying Novel User Behavior Patterns\n\n**When to use:** Detecting accounts exhibiting genuinely new usage patterns (not just rare)—think emerging bot strategies or novel legitimate user segments before you have labels.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | KNN Distance (mean) | Emphasizes global position over local density |\n| n_neighbors | 3 | Small k detects departure from *any* established pattern |\n| contamination | 0.05 | Balances novelty discovery with actionability |\n| algorithm | ball_tree | Efficient for moderate dimensions (5-20 features) |\n\n**What you get:** Scores highlighting observations unlike *all* existing clusters, useful for discovering emergent segments before clustering or labeling campaigns.\n\n**Trade-off:** Extremely sensitive to feature scaling and irrelevant dimensions—requires careful feature engineering upstream.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA pan-European payment processor handling 450 million transactions monthly needed to identify fraudulent payments without blocking legitimate customers. unsuitable for decisions with material consequences.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Deployment\n\n**When to use:** Forecasts directly inform inventory decisions, financial planning, or resource allocation where forecast errors have measurable business cost.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `max_models` | `12` | Full suite including Prophet, TBATS, ML models |\n| `cv_folds` | `5` | Rolling-origin cross-validation |\n| `ensemble_method` | `"stacked"` | Meta-learner combines multiple models optimally |\n| `seasonality_test` | `True` | Auto-detect multiple seasonal periods |\n| `outlier_treatment` | `"auto"` | Statistical detection with imputation |\n| `prediction_intervals` | `[0.80, 0.95]` | Quantifies forecast uncertainty |\n| `min_train_samples` | `max(100, 3×horizon)` | Ensures statistical validity |\n\n**What you get:** Maximum achievable accuracy with calibrated confidence intervals suitable for risk-adjusted planning.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime 8-15× slower than exploration mode; requires sufficient historical data (typically 2+ seasonal cycles minimum).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Volatility Event Series\n\n**When to use:** Forecasting promotional periods, campaigns with irregular spikes, or any series where anomalies are signal rather than noise.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `outlier_treatment` | `"none"` | Preserves genuine spikes |\n| `model_weights` | `{"gradient_boosting": 0.4, "prophet": 0.3}` | Favor models robust to non-stationarity |\n| `feature_engineering` | `True` | Creates lag features, moving averages |\n| `exogenous_vars` | `[promo_flag, day_of_week]` | External drivers critical for irregular patterns |\n| `trend_flexibility` | `0.8` | High flexibility (0-1 scale) captures regime changes |\n\n**What you get:** Model adapts to structural breaks and promotional patterns rather than smoothing them away.\n\n**Trade-off:** Higher risk of overfitting to random noise; requires domain knowledge to specify relevant exogenous variables.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Sparse Intermittent Demand\n\n**When to use:** Forecasting slow-moving SKUs, rare equipment failures, or any series with many zero values—contexts where traditional methods fail catastrophically.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `zero_inflation_model` | `True` | Two-stage model: probability of demand + quantity |\n| `aggregation_level` | `"weekly"` | Pools sparse data to reduce zero frequency |\n| `model_weights` | `{"croston": 0.5, "tsb": 0.3}` | Specialized intermittent demand methods |\n| `min_nonzero_fraction` | `0.05` | Switches to intermittent mode when <5% nonzero |\n\n**What you get:** Meaningful forecasts for series where 60-90% of periods show zero demand.\n\n**Trade-off:** Aggregation reduces temporal resolution; If you have gaps, use the **Fill Missing Dates** node upstream to interpolate or forward-fill values first.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | The numeric column you want to forecast | (required) | Select your main KPI—sales, demand, signups, etc. |\n| **Date Column** | Your timestamp column | Auto-detected | Change if you have multiple date columns |\n| **Forecast Horizon** | Number of periods to predict forward | 30 | Match your planning cycle: 7 for weekly planning, 90 for quarterly |\n| **Seasonality** | Type of seasonal pattern to detect | Auto | Choose "weekly" for day-of-week patterns, "yearly" for annual cycles, or "none" if your data has no repeating patterns |\n| **Trend Component** | How the trend changes over time | Local linear | Use "constant" for stable metrics, "local linear" for most business metrics, "damped" when growth is slowing |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of prediction intervals | 95% | Lower to 80% for tighter bands; raise to 99% for conservative planning |\n| **Train/Test Split** | Percentage held out for validation | 80/20 | Use 90/10 for short time series, 70/30 when you have years of data |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Forecast Table**: Your original data plus new rows extending into the future, with columns for:\n- `forecast`: The predicted values\n- `lower_bound` and `upper_bound`: Confidence interval edges\n- `is_forecast`: Boolean flag distinguishing predictions from historical data\n\n**Decomposition Chart**: A visual breakdown showing how the model separates your data into trend, seasonal, and residual components—incredibly helpful for understanding what\'s driving your patterns.\n\n**Performance Metrics**: RMSE, MAE, and MAPE calculated on the test set, giving you concrete accuracy measures. Lower is better for all three.\n\n**Forecast Plot**: An interactive chart showing historical actuals, fitted values, and the forecast ribbon extending forward with shaded confidence intervals.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe State Space node outputs forecast data that typically flows to:\n\n- **Filter** node \u2192 isolate just the future predictions (where `is_forecast = true`) for reporting\n- **Export** node \u2192 send forecasts to your data warehouse or Google Sheets for operational use\n- **Chart** node \u2192 create custom visualizations comparing multiple scenarios\n- **Alert** node \u2192 trigger notifications when forecasts exceed thresholds\n\n### Quick Start: Monthly Sales Forecast\n\n1. **Connect your data** containing at least a date column and a sales/revenue column\n2. **Select State Space** from the Forecasting section of the node library\n3. **Choose your target column** (e.g., "monthly_revenue") and confirm the date column is correct\n4. **Set forecast horizon** to 12 for a one-year-ahead forecast\n5. **Click "Run"** and review the decomposition chart to verify seasonality was detected\n6. **Check MAPE** in the metrics panel—under 10% is excellent, under 20% is good for most business applications\n7. **Connect a Filter node** to extract just future predictions for stakeholder reports\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n- **Always inspect the decomposition chart first**. If the seasonal component looks erratic or the trend seems wrong, your data may need preprocessing (check for outliers or structural breaks).\n\n- **Short time series struggle with complex seasonality**. If you have less than 2 full seasonal cycles (e.g., under 24 months of monthly data), consider simplifying by setting seasonality to "none."\n\n- **Confidence intervals widen dramatically** the further you forecast. Don\'t trust precise point estimates 6+ months out—focus on the range instead.\n\n- **Outliers corrupt the state estimates**. Use the **Remove Outliers** node upstream if you had a major one-time event (pandemic, supply chain disruption) that won\'t repeat.\n\n- **Compare multiple models**. Run State Space alongside Prophet or ARIMA nodes and use an **Ensemble** node to combine their forecasts—often more robust than any single model.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid structural changes in a time series before committing to detailed modeling.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'CUSUM\'` | Fastest single-pass algorithm, O(n) complexity |\n| `significance` | `0.10` | Higher \u03b1 catches weaker breaks worth investigating |\n| `min_segment_length` | `10` | Allows detection even in short series |\n| `max_breaks` | `5` | Prevents over-segmentation during exploration |\n| `trimming` | `0.05` | Minimal trimming to maximize detection range |\n\n**What you get:** A rapid overview of potential change-points with high sensitivity, suitable for flagging series that merit deeper investigation.\n\n**Trade-off:** Higher false positive rate means some detected breaks may be spurious noise rather than genuine structural changes.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Detection\n\n**When to use:** Automated monitoring systems where detected breaks trigger business decisions, model retraining, or alerts requiring high confidence.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'Bai-Perron\'` | Rigorous sequential testing with proven asymptotic properties |\n| `significance` | `0.01` | Strict threshold minimizes false positives |\n| `min_segment_length` | `30` | Ensures sufficient data for stable parameter estimation |\n| `max_breaks` | `3` | Conservative limit prevents regime over-fitting |\n| `trimming` | `0.15` | Standard econometric practice for endpoint stability |\n| `information_criterion` | `\'BIC\'` | Penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC |\n| `heteroskedasticity_robust` | `True` | Corrects for variance changes that confound break detection |\n\n**What you get:** Conservative, statistically defensible break-points with low false discovery rate suitable for operational deployment.\n\n**Trade-off:** May miss subtle but genuine regime shifts, particularly near series endpoints or in volatile periods.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Frequency Financial Data\n\n**When to use:** Detecting regime changes in minute-level trading data, sensor streams, or other high-frequency observations where variance breaks dominate mean breaks.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'ICSS\'` | Specifically designed for variance change detection |\n| `test_statistic` | `\'squared_residuals\'` | Targets volatility rather than level shifts |\n| `min_segment_length` | `120` | Two hours of minute data for meaningful volatility estimation |\n| `significance` | `0.05` | Balanced threshold for volatility regimes |\n| `prewhiten` | `True` | Removes autocorrelation that inflates false positives in HF data |\n\n**What you get:** Accurate identification of volatility regime shifts while ignoring level changes that aren\'t structurally meaningful in variance-focused applications.\n\n**Trade-off:** Completely ignores mean-level breaks, which may be important in some financial contexts like overnight gaps or policy announcements.\n\n### Recipe 4: Causal Intervention Detection\n\n**When to use:** Retroactively identifying when policy changes, feature releases, or external shocks impacted your metric, even without prior timestamps.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'Bayesian_changepoint\'` | Provides probability distributions over candidate dates |\n| `prior_breaks` | `\'geometric(0.01)\'` | Assumes interventions are rare events |\n| `min_segment_length` | `14` | Two-week minimum for business metrics |\n| `credible_interval` | `0.95` | Returns date ranges for each probable intervention |\n| `return_probabilities` | `True` | Enables ranking of candidate intervention dates |\n\n**What you get:** Probabilistic break dates with confidence intervals that can be matched against deployment logs or external event calendars for root cause analysis.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computationally expensive (MCMC sampling) and requires careful prior specification to avoid posterior sensitivity.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender experienced unexplained node expects a dataset where each row represents one subject or case, with three essential pieces of information:\n\n- **Duration column** (numeric): How long each subject was observed\n- **Event indicator column** (binary/boolean): Whether the event occurred (1/True) or was censored (0/False)\n- **Feature columns** (any type): Variables that might influence timing\n\nHere\'s what your input data should look like:\n\n| customer_id | days_observed | churned | plan_type | monthly_spend |\n|-------------|---------------|---------|-----------|---------------|\n| C001 | 365 | 1 | premium | 49.99 |\n| C002 | 180 | 0 | basic | 9.99 |\n| C003 | 412 | 1 | premium | 59.99 |\n\nThe node handles the rest—you don\'t need to transform durations or calculate survival probabilities yourself.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Duration Column** | Which field contains the time values | (none) | Always set this—it\'s required |\n| **Event Column** | Which field indicates if event occurred | (none) | Always set this—it\'s required |\n| **Model Type** | Cox Proportional Hazards, Accelerated Failure Time, or Random Survival Forest | Cox PH | Use AFT for parametric assumptions; RSF for complex interactions |\n| **Baseline Hazard** | Shape of underlying risk (Weibull, Exponential, etc.) | Weibull | Only applies to AFT; choose Exponential for constant hazard |\n| **Penalization** | L1/L2 regularization strength | 0.0 | Increase (try 0.1–1.0) when you have many correlated features |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of prediction intervals | 0.95 | Lower to 0.90 for narrower bands; rarely needs changing |\n| **Tie Handling** | How to treat simultaneous events | Efron | Switch to Breslow for very large datasets (it\'s faster) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Survival Curve Chart**: A line graph showing the probability of "surviving" (not experiencing the event) over time. If you\'ve included categorical features, you\'ll see separate curves for each group—perfect for comparing customer segments or treatment groups.\n\n**Coefficients Table**: Shows each feature\'s effect on hazard. Positive coefficients mean the feature *accelerates* the event; negative means it *delays* it. Look for the confidence intervals to assess significance.\n\n**Predictions Dataset**: Your original data plus these new columns:\n- `predicted_hazard`: Relative risk score for each subject\n- `predicted_median_time`: Expected time until event occurs\n- `risk_percentile`: Where this subject ranks (0-100) in terms of risk\n\n**Concordance Index**: Displayed as a single metric (0.5–1.0). Above 0.7 is good; above 0.8 is excellent. It measures how well your model ranks who experiences the event sooner.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe predictions dataset flows naturally into:\n- **Score Banding** node to create risk tiers (high/medium/low)\n- **Model Comparison** to evaluate against other approaches\n- **Business Rule** node to trigger interventions (e.g., "contact customers with predicted_median_time < 30 days")\n- **Visualization** nodes to build stakeholder dashboards showing survival curves by segment\n\n### Quick Start: Customer Churn Prediction\n\n1. **Connect** your customer data containing observation days and churn indicator\n2. **Set** Duration Column to your time field and Event Column to your churn flag\n3. **Select** features like plan type, usage metrics, and demographics\n4. **Leave** Model Type as "Cox Proportional Hazards" for your first run\n5. **Run** the node and examine the survival curves—do they separate by segment?\n6. **Review** coefficients to identify your biggest churn accelerators\n7. **Connect** to Score Banding to create "high churn risk" segments\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Check proportional hazards**: If your survival curves cross each other, the Cox model may not fit well. Switch to Random Survival Forest instead.\n\n**Mind your censoring rate**: If more than 70% of your cases are censored, predictions become unreliable. Consider shortening your observation window or waiting for more events.\n\n**Time units matter**: Express durations in business-relevant units. "Days until churn" is more actionable than "seconds until churn."\n\n**Interpret hazard ratios correctly**: A coefficient of 0.5 doesn\'t mean 50% more risk—exponentiate it first (e^0.5 = 1.65 = 65% increase in hazard).\n\n**Validate with held-out data**: Survival models can overfit. Always check that your concordance index holds up on recent data the model hasn\'t seen.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial dataset assessment when you Option A represents the "complete case" fallacy that throws away information and creates severe bias by systematically excluding longer survivors. List from broadest (Region) to most granular (Store) |\n| **Date Column** | Your time index | Auto-detect | Specify if multiple date columns exist |\n| **Value Column** | Metric to forecast | Auto-detect | Specify if multiple numeric columns exist |\n| **Forecast Horizon** | Number of periods ahead | 12 | Match your planning cycle—52 for weekly annual planning, 12 for monthly |\n| **Reconciliation Method** | How forecasts are made coherent | "optimal" | Use "bottom-up" for stable low-level data, "top-down" for noisy bottom levels |\n| **Minimum History** | Required periods per series | 24 | Reduce for newer products, increase for seasonal patterns (need 2+ cycles) |\n| **Confidence Level** | Prediction interval width | 95% | Lower to 80% for tighter bounds, raise to 99% for conservative planning |\n\n### What You Get Out\n\n**Forecast Table**: Your original data structure extended into the future, with three new columns per level:\n- `forecast_value`: Point prediction\n- `lower_bound`: Bottom of confidence interval  \n- `upper_bound`: Top of confidence interval\n\n**Coherence Report**: Shows how forecasts sum correctly across hierarchy levels—North store forecasts will always add up to the North regional forecast.\n\n**Accuracy Metrics Panel**: Displays MAPE, RMSE, and MAE for each hierarchy level, helping you identify where the model performs best.\n\n**Interactive Chart**: Time series visualization with actual vs. forecast comparison, filterable by any grouping dimension. Hover over any point to see contributing lower-level forecasts.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n- **Scenario Analysis node**: Test "what-if" adjustments that maintain coherence\n- **Export node**: Send forecasts to planning systems or spreadsheets\n- **Monitoring Dashboard**: Track forecast accuracy as actuals arrive\n- **Optimization node**: Use forecasts as inputs for inventory or resource allocation\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your historical data** to the Track Groups node\n2. **Select your grouping columns** in hierarchical order (e.g., Region \u2192 Store \u2192 Product)\n3. **Set forecast horizon** to match your planning needs (typically 12-13 periods)\n4. **Run the node** and check the Accuracy Metrics panel—look for MAPE under 15% as a good baseline\n5. **Inspect the coherence** by filtering the chart to a top-level group and visually confirming child forecasts sum correctly\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Start with fewer hierarchy levels**: Two levels (like Region \u2192 Store) are easier to validate than four. Add complexity once you\'re confident in the basics.\n\n**Watch for sparse series**: If many bottom-level series have intermittent zeros, consider aggregating to a higher level or using "top-down" reconciliation to borrow strength from more stable totals.\n\n**Seasonal patterns need data**: The rule of thumb is at least two complete seasonal cycles—monthly data needs 24+ months, weekly needs 104+ weeks.\n\n**Coherence catches data issues**: If your hierarchical forecasts look wrong, check your grouping structure. expects a **prepared dataset** with your features and target variable. Connect it to nodes like Clean Data, Feature Engineer, or Split Data (use the training split only—never tune on test data).\n\n**Required columns:**\n- One **target column** (numeric for regression, categorical for classification)\n- One or more **feature columns** (numeric or categorical)\n\nYour data should already be cleaned and encoded. Here\'s a simple example:\n\n| customer_age | income | previous_purchases | will_buy (target) |\n|--------------|--------|-------------------|-------------------|\n| 34 | 52000 | 3 | Yes |\n| 45 | 68000 | 7 | Yes |\n| 29 | 41000 | 1 | No |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|----------------|\n| **Algorithm** | Which ML algorithm to tune (Random Forest, XGBoost, etc.) | Random Forest | Based on your problem type and data size |\n| **Metric** | What to optimize for (Accuracy, F1, RMSE, etc.) | Accuracy (classification) or RMSE (regression) | Use F1 for imbalanced classes; use AUC when probability calibration matters |\n| **Search Method** | How to explore hyperparameter space: Grid, Random, or Bayesian | Random Search | Use Grid for small spaces (<50 combinations); Bayesian for expensive models or large spaces |\n| **Number of Iterations** | How many configurations to try | 20 | Increase to 50+ for complex problems; reduce to 10 for quick experiments |\n| **Cross-Validation Folds** | How many folds for validation | 5 | Use 10 for small datasets (<1000 rows); use 3 for very large datasets to save time |\n| **Hyperparameter Ranges** | Min/max values for each hyperparameter | Algorithm-specific defaults | Widen ranges if optimal values hit boundaries; narrow to refine search |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Performance Tab:**\n- **Best Configuration card**: Shows the winning hyperparameters and their cross-validated score\n- **Iteration History chart**: Line plot showing metric improvement across search iterations\n- **Top 10 Configurations table**: All tried configurations ranked by performance\n\n**Model Tab:**\n- **Tuned model object**: Ready to use in downstream nodes\n- **Feature Importance chart** (if supported by algorithm): Which features mattered most\n\n**Console Log:**\n- Real-time progress updates as each configuration is evaluated\n- Warnings if certain configurations failed\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter tuning, connect to:\n- **Train Model** \u2192 Use the best hyperparameters to train on your full training set\n- **Predict** \u2192 Apply the tuned model directly to make predictions\n- **Evaluate Model** \u2192 Test performance on holdout data with your optimized configuration\n\nMost workflows look like: Split Data \u2192 Tune Model (on train) \u2192 Train Model (with best params) \u2192 Predict (on test) \u2192 Evaluate Model.\n\n### Quick Start: Classification with Random Forest\n\n1. **Connect your training data** to Tune Model (after Split Data or Clean Data)\n2. **Select algorithm**: Choose "Random Forest Classifier"\n3. **Pick your metric**: Select "F1 Score" if you have imbalanced classes, otherwise "Accuracy"\n4. **Set iterations**: Start with 20 for your first run\n5. **Run the node** and watch the console—it takes a few minutes\n6. **Review the results**: Check the Best Configuration card for winning parameters\n7. **Connect to Train Model**: Use these parameters to train your final model\n\n### Practical Tips from Experience\n\n**Start small, then scale.** Run 10 iterations with 3-fold CV first to make sure everything works. Once validated, increase to 50 iterations with 5-fold CV for your final tuning run.\n\n**Watch for boundary values.** If the best `max_depth` is at your upper limit (say, 20), widen the range to 30—the true optimum might be higher.\n\n**Tune on subsets for speed.** With datasets over 100K rows, consider random sampling 20-30K rows just for hyperparameter search. The optimal parameters usually transfer well.\n\n**Save your configuration.** Screenshot or export the Best Configuration card—you\'ll want these exact parameters documented for reproducibility.\n\n**Not all hyperparameters matter equally.** Learning rate and regularization usually have bigger impacts than batch size or minor tree parameters. Focus your search ranges there first.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Sweep\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploration phase when you need directional guidance on which Search strategy | Random search | Explores space efficiently without exhaustive evaluation |\n| Number of iterations | 20 | Sufficient to detect major performance gains without overcommitment |\n| CV folds | 3 | Balances variance reduction with speed |\n| Evaluation metric | AUC or R² | Fast to compute, robust to class imbalance |\n| Parallel jobs | 4 | Utilises modern hardware without memory saturation |\n\n**What you get:** A ranked list of configurations showing which hyperparameters drive performance, typically completing in under 30 minutes for moderate datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** Results may miss optimal configurations in narrow performance peaks and provide less stable performance estimates than production-grade tuning.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Optimisation\n\n**When to use:** Final model selection before deployment, when model performance directly impacts business outcomes, or when you need defensible documentation of optimisation rigour.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Search strategy | Bayesian optimisation | Intelligently explores based on previous trials |\n| Number of iterations | 100 | Thorough coverage of promising regions |\n| CV folds | 10 | Low-variance performance estimates |\n| Evaluation metric | F1-score or custom business metric | Aligns directly with deployment objectives |\n| Early stopping | Enabled, patience=15 | Saves time without sacrificing thoroughness |\n\n**What you get:** A stable, well-validated configuration with confidence intervals on expected production performance, typically representing 95–99% of theoretically optimal performance.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires 4–8 hours of compute time and careful monitoring of convergence behaviour.\n\n### Recipe 3: Imbalanced Classification Rescue\n\n**When to use:** Binary classification with class ratios exceeding 20:1, where default configurations produce models that ignore minority classes entirely.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Search strategy | Grid search | Ensures evaluation of critical threshold combinations |\n| Class weight parameter | [1:1, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, \'balanced\'] | Explicitly tests compensation strategies |\n| Threshold tuning | Enabled | Separates discrimination from classification decision |\n| Evaluation metric | Precision-Recall AUC | Ignores irrelevant true negative performance |\n| Stratified sampling | Enforced | Guarantees minority class representation in all folds |\n\n**What you get:** A model that actually detects minority class instances with tuned precision-recall trade-off, often achieving 40–60% recall where defaults yield <5%.\n\n**Trade-off:** Grid search over class weights adds 5× iterations compared to skipping this dimension.\n\n### Recipe 4: Feature Engineering Acceleration\n\n**When to use:** When comparing multiple feature transformation pipelines (polynomial features, iterations | 50 | Explores diverse pipeline architectures |\n| CV folds | 5 | Moderate validation without feature leakage risk |\n| Cache transformations | Enabled | Reuses expensive feature computations across folds |\n\n**What you get:** Discovery that specific feature engineering choices matter more than algorithm selection, often revealing 10–30% performance gains from preprocessing After the tuning process completes, they obtain both the optimal hyperparameters and performance metrics from cross-validation. When they train a final model using these optimal hyperparameters on the full training dataset and evaluate it on a held-out test set, which statement best describes what they should expect?\n\nA) The test set performance should exactly match the cross-validation performance reported by Tune Model, since both use the optimal hyperparameters\n\nB) The test set performance will likely be better than the cross-validation performance, since the final model is trained on more data than each cross-validation fold\n\nC) The test set performance may differ from the cross-validation performance, and could be worse, because cross-validation estimates are subject to variance and the test set represents new unseen data\n\nD) If the test set performance is worse than the cross-validation performance, it indicates that Tune Model selected suboptimal hyperparameters and the tuning process should be repeated\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Cross-validation provides an *estimate* of generalization performance, not a guarantee, and this estimate has inherent variance depending on the specific fold splits and data characteristics. The test set represents truly unseen data that may have different patterns, so discrepancies are natural and expected. Option A reflects the misconception that cross-validation performance is a deterministic predictor of future performance rather than an estimate. Option B misunderstands that while training on more data can help, the cross-validation metric from Tune Model already accounts for this by averaging across folds, and the test set may simply be harder or different. Option D represents the dangerous misconception that any performance gap indicates tuning failure, when in fact some gap is normal and doesn\'t warrant re-tuning, which could lead to indirect test set leakage through repeated optimization.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. You need:\n\n- **Treatment indicator** (binary): 1 for treated, 0 for control\n- **Outcome variable** (binary): 1 for converted/responded, 0 otherwise\n- **Features** (numeric or categorical): individual characteristics used for prediction\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | treatment | purchased | age | previous_purchases | segment |\n|-------------|-----------|-----------|-----|-------------------|---------|\n| 1001 | 1 | 1 | 34 | 2 | premium |\n| 1002 | 0 | 0 | 28 | 0 | basic |\n| 1003 | 1 | 0 | 45 | 5 | premium |\n\nThe node works best with randomized experiment data where treatment was assigned randomly, but it can also work with observational data if you\'re careful about confounding.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Treatment Column** | Which column indicates treatment (1) vs control (0) | - | Always specify this first |\n| **Outcome Column** | Which column contains your target outcome | - | Required—your conversion/response metric |\n| **Model Type** | Algorithm approach (Two-Model, X-Learner, S-Learner) | Two-Model | X-Learner for small treatment groups; S-Learner when treatment effect is uniform |\n| **Cross-Validation Folds** | Number of folds for model validation | 5 | Increase to 10 for small datasets; reduce to 3 for very large ones |\n| **Minimum Uplift Threshold** | Score above which individuals are considered "persuadables" | 0.0 | Set to 0.05 or 0.10 to focus on clearer lift signals |\n| **Feature Selection** | Auto-select relevant features or use all | Auto | Override to "All" when you have domain knowledge about drivers |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\nThe node adds these columns to your dataset:\n\n- **`uplift_score`**: The estimated causal effect—how much more likely this person is to convert *because of* treatment (ranges from -1 to +1)\n- **`segment`**: Automatically assigned group (Persuadables, Sure Things, Lost Causes, Sleeping Dogs)\n- **`treatment_probability`**: Predicted conversion if treated\n- **`control_probability`**: Predicted conversion if not treated\n\n**Visualizations displayed:**\n\n- **Uplift curve**: Shows cumulative gain vs. random targeting—steeper is better\n- **Qini curve**: Alternative performance metric, robust to class imbalance\n- **Segment distribution**: Pie chart showing how your population splits across segments\n- **Feature importance**: Which characteristics drive heterogeneous treatment effects\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your experiment data** to the Uplift Model node input\n2. **Select your treatment column** (the binary indicator of who got the offer/message)\n3. **Select your outcome column** (e.g., "made_purchase" or "clicked")\n4. **Leave Model Type as "Two-Model"** for your first run—it\'s the most interpretable\n5. **Run the node** and examine the segment distribution\n6. **Connect to a Filter node** and filter for `segment = \'Persuadables\'`—these are your high-value targets\n7. **Route that segment** to your campaign execution or export node\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect this node to:\n\n- **Filter node** \u2192 isolate Persuadables or high uplift scores (> 0.1) for targeted campaigns\n- **Model Evaluation node** \u2192 compare uplift model performance against traditional response models\n- **Export node** \u2192 send scored individuals to your marketing automation platform\n- **A/B Test Designer node** \u2192 design a follow-up test focusing on uncertain segments\n\n### Practical Tips from Experience\n\n**Beware of "Sure Things"**: People with high uplift scores are valuable, but don\'t ignore those with *negative* uplift (Sleeping Dogs)—targeting them actively hurts your outcome. Exclude them deliberately.\n\n**Check your balance**: If your treatment/control split is more extreme than 80/20, consider using X-Learner instead of Two-Model—it handles imbalanced groups better.\n\n**Start with a hold-out test**: Before rolling out to your full list, run a small randomized test where you target Persuadables vs. random assignment. This validates your model in production.\n\n**Feature engineering matters here**: Unlike standard prediction models, uplift models benefit enormously from interaction terms and segment indicators that capture *who responds differently* to treatment.\n\n**Don\'t confuse correlation with causation**: The model only estimates causal effects if your original data came from a proper experiment or you\'ve controlled for confounders. Garbage in, garbage out applies doubly here.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** First-pass analysis on a new campaign dataset where you need directional insights within hours, not days.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"two_model"` | Fastest to train; uses standard classifiers |\n| `base_learner` | `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=8)` | Limits tree complexity for speed |\n| `cv_folds` | `3` | Minimum for reasonable validation |\n| `min_samples_treatment` | `100` | Prevents overfitting in small subgroups |\n| `uplift_threshold` | `0` | No filtering; see full distribution |\n\n- **What you get:** Fast segmentation into persuadables, sure things, lost causes, and sleeping dogs with ~70-80% confidence.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Lower precision on individual predictions; may miss subtle heterogeneous effects in complex interactions.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Marketing Deployment\n\n- **When to use:** Deploying uplift targeting for a high-value campaign where false positives cost real money (e.g., retention offers, discount allocation).\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"causal_forest"` or `"x_learner"` | Rigorous causal estimators with theoretical guarantees |\n| `base_learner` | `GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.01, max_depth=5)` | Deep, regularized models for nuanced patterns |\n| `cv_folds` | `10` | Robust standard error estimates |\n| `min_samples_treatment` | `500` | Conservative threshold for targeting |\n| `calibration` | `isotonic` | Ensures uplift scores are interpretable as probabilities |\n| `feature_importance` | `"shap"` | Explainability for auditing and trust |\n\n- **What you get:** Trustworthy uplift scores suitable for automated decisioning, with explainable drivers per segment.\n\n- **Trade-off:** 5-10x longer training time; requires larger sample sizes (minimum ~50K observations recommended).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Imbalanced Treatment Assignment\n\n- **When to use:** Observational data where treatment was given to only 5-15% of population (e.g., proactive customer service outreach logs).\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"s_learner"` | Pools data efficiently when treatment group is small |\n| `propensity_weighting` | `True` | Corrects for selection bias in who received treatment |\n| `propensity_model` | `LogisticRegression(C=0.1, class_weight=\'balanced\')` | Handles class imbalance explicitly |\n| `uplift_normalization` | `"control_group_rate"` | Anchors estimates to realistic baseline |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | `200` | Quantifies uncertainty given small treatment N |\n\n- **What you get:** Unbiased uplift estimates despite skewed treatment assignment, with confidence intervals.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Requires careful propensity modeling; sensitive to unmeasured confounders.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Negative Outcome Prevention\n\n- **When to use:** Identifying whom NOT to contact because intervention causes harm (e.g., survey fatigue, brand perception damage from excessive emails).\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"two_model"` with negative class focus | Explicitly models downside |\n| `cost_matrix` | `[[0, -1], [-5, 0]]` | Heavily penalizes false positives (harmful contacts) |\n| `negative_uplift_threshold` | `-0.02` | Flag anyone with even slight negative effect |\n| `segment_separately` | `"sleeping_dogs"` | Create exclusion list, not targeting list |\n\n- **What you get:** Suppression list of individuals likely harmed by contact, minimizing brand damage.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Conservative approach may exclude neutral cases, slightly reducing reach.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional credit card issuer with 3 million cardholders faced a classic challenge: which inactive customers should receive retention offers? Connect it downstream from any Predict node or model training node.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- A dataset with features (predictor columns) and actual target values\n- A model object from an upstream training node\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | feature_1 | feature_2 | actual_sales | predicted_sales |\n|-------------|-----------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|\n| C001        | 23.5      | 1.2       | 450          | 445             |\n| C002        | 18.9      | 2.1       | 320          | 335             |\n| C003        | 31.2      | 0.8       | 580          | 572             |\n\nThe node works with both regression and classification models. K-Fold for general cases when you want faster computation |\n| **Number of Iterations** | How many times to resample and re-evaluate | 100 | Increase to 500+ for high-stakes decisions; decrease to 50 for quick exploratory analysis |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of reliability intervals (e.g., 95%) | 95% | Use 99% for critical applications like medical or financial models |\n| **Subgroup Analysis** | Column(s) to test for performance consistency across segments | None | Specify demographic or business segments to check for fairness or regional differences |\n| **Performance Metrics** | Which metrics to validate (RMSE, MAE, R², Accuracy, AUC, etc.) | Auto-detected | Select specific metrics aligned with your business KPIs |\n| **Drift Detection Window** | Number of time periods to test temporal stability | None | Enable for production models—tests if performance degrades over time |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n- **Stability Score** (0-100): Overall reliability grade—higher is better\n- **Confidence Intervals**: Upper and lower bounds for each performance metric\n- **Coefficient of Variation**: Shows relative variability (lower = more stable)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Bootstrap Distribution Chart**: Shows spread of metric values across resamples—narrow peaks indicate stable performance\n- **Subgroup Performance Comparison**: Side-by-side bars showing if your model works equally well across segments\n- **Temporal Drift Plot**: Performance trajectory over time periods (if enabled)\n\n**Added Data Columns:**\n- `reliability_flag`: Binary indicator of whether each prediction meets stability thresholds\n- `prediction_interval_lower` and `prediction_interval_upper`: Uncertainty bounds for each row\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Connect your data**: Link the output from your model training/prediction node to Validate Reliability\n2. **Set resampling method**: Choose "Time Series Split" if your data has a date column; otherwise stick with "Bootstrap"\n3. **Specify subgroups**: If you have customer segments, regions, or categories that matter for business fairness, add that column name\n4. **Run the validation**: Click execute and wait 30-60 seconds (depending on data size)\n5. **Check the Stability Score**: If it\'s above 85, you\'re good. Between 70-85, investigate the visualizations. Below 70, your model needs work.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically connects to:\n- **Decision/Deploy nodes**: Use the `reliability_flag` to filter only high-confidence predictions for automated actions\n- **Report Builder**: Include stability metrics in stakeholder documentation\n- **Alert nodes**: Trigger notifications if reliability drops below threshold in production monitoring\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n\U0001f3af **Run this twice**: Once on your test set, once on a recent time slice of production data. Discrepancies reveal deployment issues.\n\n\U0001f3af **Watch the CV coefficient**: If it\'s above 15-20% for your primary metric, your model is too sensitive to data changes.\n\n\U0001f3af **Subgroup analysis is non-negotiable** for customer-facing models—regulatory scrutiny demands proof of fairness.\n\n\U0001f3af **Temporal stability matters more than single-point accuracy**: A model that\'s 95% accurate but unstable month-to-month will break production workflows.\n\n\U0001f3af **Save the validation report**: When stakeholders question model performance six months later, you\'ll have documented proof of what reliability looked like at deployment.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Early-stage model development when you need rapid feedback is a structural zero (0.0 to 1.0)\n- `count_component_mean`: Expected count *if not* a structural zero\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n\n- **Zero Inflation Test**: Chi-square statistic comparing observed vs expected zeros\n- **Vuong Test**: Statistical comparison favoring zero-inflated vs standard count model\n- **RMSE & MAE**: Prediction error on test set\n- **AIC/BIC**: Model comparison metrics (lower is better)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n\n- **Observed vs Expected Zeros**: Bar chart showing if your model captures excess zeros\n- **Residuals Plot**: Actual minus predicted, color-coded by zero/non-zero\n- **Feature Importance**: Which predictors most influence (a) zero probability and (b) count magnitude\n\n### Downstream Connections\n\nConnect the output to:\n\n- **Prediction Writer** to save forecasts with confidence intervals\n- **Model Evaluation** node to compare against standard Poisson or Negative Binomial baselines\n- **Threshold Optimizer** to find the best cutoff for binary decisions (e.g., "will customer purchase anything?")\n- **Segmentation** node using `predicted_zero_probability` to identify "at-risk" zero-count groups\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n1. **Check your zero rate first**: If fewer than 15-20% of your target values are zero, you probably don\'t need zero-inflation—try standard GLM first.\n\n2. **Interpret two stories**: The model tells you *who\'s structurally different* (zero component) and *how much they\'ll do* (count component). A customer might have high purchase counts *if they buy* but also high zero probability.\n\n3. **Feature engineering matters more here**: Create indicators like "days_since_last_purchase > 90" or "has_ever_purchased"—these often strongly predict structural zeros.\n\n4. **Watch for separation warnings**: If a feature perfectly predicts zeros (e.g., all free-tier users have zero purchases), the model may struggle. Consider collapsing categories or removing that feature from inflation predictors.\n\n5. **Validate the inflation assumption**: Use the Vuong test p-value in outputs—if p > 0.05, your excess zeros might be random noise, not a separate process.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data assessment when you suspect excess zeros but haven\'t confirmed the pattern or identified predictors.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dist` | `"poisson"` | Faster convergence than negative binomial |\n| `link` | `"logit"` | Standard link for zero-inflation component |\n| `maxiter` | 50 | Sufficient for exploratory convergence |\n| `method` | `"bfgs"` | Fast gradient-based optimization |\n| `EM_iter` | 0 | Skip EM iterations to speed up fitting |\n\n**What you get:** Fast coefficient estimates revealing whether zero-inflation is present and which predictors matter in each component.\n\n**Trade-off:** May not converge fully; unstable standard errors; unsuitable for inference or deployment.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Model\n\n**When to use:** Deploying to production where model reliability, interpretability, and statistical validity are required.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dist` | `"negbin"` | Handles overdispersion beyond zero-inflation |\n| `link` | `"logit"` | Interpretable probabilities for inflation component |\n| `maxiter` | 500 | Ensures full convergence |\n| `method` | `"newton"` | Most stable for final estimates |\n| `EM_iter` | 20 | Improves starting values for complex models |\n| `disp` | True | Monitor convergence diagnostics |\n| `cov_type` | `"HC1"` | Robust standard errors for inference |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically valid confidence intervals, stable predictions, and defensible parameter estimates for reporting.\n\n**Trade-off:** 5–10× slower fitting time; requires more data to avoid overfitting with negative binomial dispersion parameter.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Survey Data with Structural Zeros\n\n**When to use:** Modeling responses with true structural zeros (e.g., healthcare utilization where some populations have zero access vs. zero usage by choice).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dist` | `"poisson"` | Count component for users with access |\n| `inflation` | `"logit"` | Models probability of structural zero class |\n| `formula_inflate` | Include access barriers only | Separate predictors for structural vs. sampling zeros |\n| `offset` | Population exposure | Accounts for differential observation windows |\n| `weights` | Survey weights | Corrects for sampling design |\n| `maxiter` | 300 | Complex survey structures need more iterations |\n\n**What you get:** Separate interpretable effects for "who has zero access" vs. "how much do those with access use."\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires domain knowledge to specify which predictors belong in inflation vs. count formula.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Rare Event Prediction with Imbalanced Targets\n\n**When to use:** Predicting rare operational events (equipment failures, fraud occurrences) where 85%+ observations are zeros but you need high recall.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dist` | `"poisson"` | Appropriate for count of events in time window |\n| `inflation` | `"probit"` | Better tail behavior for rare probabilities |\n| `pred_type` | `"prob-zero"` | Output probability of zero for threshold optimization |\n| `maxiter` | 200 | Balance between speed and convergence |\n| `method` | `"nm"` | More robust when classes extremely imbalanced |\n| `score_metric` | Custom (1 - P(zero)) | Rank by failure risk rather than expected count |\n\n**What you get:** Probability scores optimized for anomaly detection; better separation of "definitely zero" from "rare but possible."\n\n**Trade-off:** Predicted counts become less accurate; optimized for classification rather than regression performance.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processes thousands of affordability assessments monthly but struggles to predict how many customers will make *zero* additional credit inquiries in the six months post-approval—a key indicator of financial stability. Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe Network Analysis node expects **edge list data** – essentially a table where each row represents a connection between two entities. At minimum, you need two columns identifying the source and target of each relationship.\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| from_user | to_user | interaction_count |\n|-----------|---------|-------------------|\n| alice | bob | 5 |\n| alice | carol | 12 |\n| bob | david | 3 |\n| carol | david | 8 |\n\nThe first two columns define the network structure (who connects to whom), while additional columns can weight those connections or add attributes. After analysis, you\'ll get the same table back with new columns containing calculated network metrics for each node.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Source Column** | The column identifying the starting point of each edge | (none) | Always set this – it\'s your "from" entity |\n| **Target Column** | The column identifying the ending point of each edge | (none) | Always set this – it\'s your "to" entity |\n| **Weight Column** | Optional column to weight edge strength (e.g., transaction amount, frequency) | None | Use when some connections are stronger than others |\n| **Directed Network** | Whether connections have direction (A\u2192B differs from B\u2192A) | True | Set to False for mutual relationships like friendship |\n| **Centrality Metrics** | Which importance measures to calculate (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector) | All | Disable unused metrics to speed up processing on large networks |\n| **Community Detection** | Algorithm for finding clusters (Louvain, Label Propagation, or None) | Louvain | Use Label Propagation for faster results on very large graphs |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node enriches your original dataset with network metrics calculated for each unique node mentioned in your edge list:\n\n**Output columns added:**\n- **degree**: How many connections this node has (in-degree and out-degree for directed networks)\n- **betweenness_centrality**: How often this node sits on the shortest path between others (identifies bridges and gatekeepers)\n- **closeness_centrality**: How quickly this node can reach all others (identifies central, well-connected entities)\n- **eigenvector_centrality**: Importance based on being connected to other important nodes (the "connected to influencers" metric)\n- **community_id**: Which cluster or group this node belongs to\n\n**Visualizations shown:**\n- Network graph with nodes sized by degree centrality\n- Community structure visualization with color-coded clusters\n- Distribution charts for each centrality metric\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter network analysis, you typically want to:\n\n1. **Filter or Rank nodes** \u2192 Use the Filter or Sort nodes to identify your most central/influential entities\n2. **Join back to original data** \u2192 Merge network metrics with your master customer/product/user table to enrich profiles\n3. **Segment by community** \u2192 Use community_id for clustering-based analysis or targeted campaigns\n4. **Visualize in Tableau/PowerBI** \u2192 Export enriched data with centrality scores for custom dashboards\n\n### Quick Start: Analyzing Customer Referral Networks\n\n1. **Connect your edge data** with columns showing who referred whom (referrer \u2192 new_customer)\n2. **Set Source Column** to "referrer" and **Target Column** to "new_customer"\n3. **Set Directed Network** to True (referrals have direction)\n4. **Leave Centrality Metrics** at default (calculate all)\n5. **Run the node** and examine the betweenness_centrality column to find your super-connectors\n6. **Connect a Filter node** to isolate high-centrality customers for VIP outreach\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n- **Start with a sample**: On networks with >100K edges, test your configuration on a filtered subset first – full network calculations can take time\n- **Weight matters**: An unweighted network treats one interaction the same as a hundred. Use the Weight Column when connection strength varies significantly\n- **Community detection is powerful**: The automatically detected communities often reveal natural customer segments, partner ecosystems, or fraud rings you didn\'t know existed\n- **Watch for disconnected components**: If your visualization shows isolated clusters, your network might actually be several separate networks – consider analyzing them independently\n- **Betweenness finds bottlenecks**: In operational networks (supply chains, workflows), high betweenness nodes are your vulnerability points – if they fail, information flow breaks\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial assessment of network topology when you\'ve just loaded a new dataset and need to understand basic structure in under 60 seconds.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `compute_centrality` | `["degree"]` | Degree centrality is O(n) and reveals hubs instantly |\n| `community_detection` | `"label_propagation"` | Near-linear time, good enough for overview |\n| `sample_size` | `10000` | Cap analysis for large networks |\n| `calculate_shortest_paths` | `False` | Expensive computation; skip for exploration |\n| `edge_weight` | `None` | Unweighted analysis is 3-5x faster |\n\n- **What you get:** A structural snapshot showing node importance distribution and rough community boundaries within seconds, even on million-edge networks.\n- **Trade-off:** You miss nuanced centrality measures (betweenness, eigenvector) and may oversimplify weighted relationships in transportation or citation networks.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Analysis\n\n- **When to use:** Publishing results, building production dashboards, or when analysis will inform high-stakes decisions requiring defensible methodology.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `compute_centrality` | `["degree", "betweenness", "closeness", "eigenvector"]` | Comprehensive importance profiling |\n| `community_detection` | `"louvain"` | Modularity-optimizing, peer-reviewed standard |\n| `resolution` | `1.0` | Default modularity; document any deviations |\n| `n_iterations` | `100` | Ensure Louvain convergence stability |\n| `calculate_diameter` | `True` | Report complete topological characteristics |\n| `validate_components` | `True` | Flag disconnected subgraphs explicitly |\n\n- **What you get:** Publication-ready metrics with established theoretical foundations, reproducible results, and comprehensive structural characterization.\n- **Trade-off:** Runtime increases 10-50x compared to exploration mode; may require overnight batch processing for networks exceeding 100K nodes.\n\n### Recipe 3: Temporal Network Drift Detection\n\n- **When to use:** Monitoring evolving networks (social platforms, infrastructure, supply chains) where you need to detect when structure fundamentally changes, not just grows.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `snapshot_interval` | `"daily"` | Match to meaningful change cadence |\n| `compute_centrality` | `["degree", "betweenness"]` | Track hub stability and bridge erosion |\n| `track_metrics` | `["clustering_coefficient", "assortativity", "density"]` | Detect phase transitions in mixing patterns |\n| `comparison_mode` | `"delta"` | Measure relative change, not absolute values |\n| `alert_threshold` | `0.15` | Flag 15%+ shifts in global metrics |\n\n- **What you get:** Time-series of structural indicators that reveal regime changes, degradation, or sudden reorganization invisible in node-count growth alone.\n- **Trade-off:** Requires storing historical network states; false positives occur during planned events (product launches, seasonal patterns).\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomalous Subgraph Detection\n\n- **When to use:** Fraud detection, identifying bot networks, or finding organized coordination in supposedly organic networks where suspicious clusters hide among normal activity.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `community_detection` | `"infomap"` | Optimizes information flow; exposes artificial coordination |\n| `local_clustering` | `True` | High clustering + low external ties signals closed groups |\n| `k_core_decomposition` | `k=3` | Isolate tightly-bound cores from casual periphery |\n| `motif_detection` | `["triangle", "star"]` | Unnatural motif ratios indicate manipulation |\n| `outlier_threshold` | `3.0` | Standard deviations for flagging structural outliers |\n\n- **What you get:** Subgraphs exhibiting coordination patterns statistically inconsistent with organic network formation—bot farms appear as dense, low-diversity clusters.\n- **Trade-off:** High false-positive rate in legitimate tight-knit communities (research collaborations, family networks); requires domain-informed review.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA European investment bank processing 450,000 wire transfers daily needed to detect money laundering networks while maintaining transaction speed. Run a quick visual inspection before committing to a method.\n\n**Don\'t ignore the residuals.** Large residuals indicate your trend model isn\'t capturing important patterns. This often means you need seasonal adjustment or a different trend method.\n\n**Statistical significance \u2260 practical significance.** A p-value of 0.001 means the trend is real, but check the actual magnitude—a "highly significant" daily increase of $2 might not matter for business decisions.\n\n**LOESS is forgiving but dangerous.** It fits almost any shape, which is great for exploration but can overfit. Use it to understand your data, then consider simpler methods for final analysis.\n\n**Polynomial trends extrapolate poorly.** They\'re excellent for capturing historical curves but often produce absurd forecasts. Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Check Fairness node expects a dataset with predictions from your model alongside demographic information. At minimum, you need:\n\n- **Predicted outcomes** (binary or probability scores)\n- **Actual outcomes** (ground truth labels)\n- **Protected attribute(s)** (demographic groups like gender, age bracket, ethnicity)\n\nHere\'s what your input data should look like:\n\n| applicant_id | age_group | predicted_approval | actual_approval | prediction_score |\n|--------------|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|------------------|\n| 1001 | under_30 | 1 | 1 | 0.82 |\n| 1002 | over_50 | 0 | 1 | 0.45 |\n| 1003 | 30-50 | 1 | 1 | 0.91 |\n\nThe node works with binary classification problems—approved/rejected, hired/not hired, flagged/not flagged—where fairness across groups matters.\n\n### Configuring the Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Protected Attributes** | Which demographic columns to analyze for bias | None (required) | Select all attributes where discrimination would be concerning or illegal (age, gender, race, etc.) |\n| **Prediction Column** | The column containing your model\'s predictions (0/1) | Auto-detect | Change if your prediction column has a different name or format |\n| **Actual Outcome Column** | The ground truth labels | Auto-detect | Specify if you have multiple outcome columns |\n| **Score Column** | Probability scores (0-1) from your model | Optional | Include for calibration and threshold analysis; omit if only binary predictions available |\n| **Reference Group** | Which demographic group to compare others against | Largest group | Change to the historically advantaged group for clearer discrimination detection |\n| **Fairness Threshold** | Acceptable disparity ratio (e.g., 0.8 = 80% rule) | 0.8 | Lower for stricter fairness requirements; regulatory guidance often suggests 0.8 |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\nThe node produces three types of outputs:\n\n**Metrics Panel** displays numerical fairness measures for each protected attribute:\n- **Demographic Parity Ratio**: whether groups receive positive outcomes at similar rates\n- **Equalised Odds Difference**: whether true positive and false positive rates are comparable\n- **Calibration Gap**: whether prediction scores mean the same thing across groups\n\n**Visualizations** include:\n- Side-by-side bar charts showing outcome rates by demographic group\n- Confusion matrix breakdowns for each group\n- Calibration curves revealing whether a 70% score means 70% likelihood for all groups\n\n**Flagged Disparities Table** highlights specific group comparisons that fail your fairness threshold, prioritized by severity.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nTypically, Check Fairness connects to:\n\n- **Filter Data** node: to examine specific groups showing bias more closely\n- **Model Tuning** nodes: to adjust decision thresholds per group or retrain with fairness constraints\n- **Report Builder**: to document fairness assessments for compliance or stakeholder communication\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your scored dataset** containing predictions, actuals, and demographic attributes\n2. **Select your protected attributes** from the dropdown (start with one if you\'re exploring)\n3. **Specify prediction and actual columns** (the node usually auto-detects these correctly)\n4. **Run the analysis** and review the metrics panel first\n5. **Check the flagged disparities table** for problematic group comparisons\n6. **Examine visualizations** for groups that failed fairness thresholds\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Start with one protected attribute.** Analyzing five demographic factors simultaneously creates cognitive overload. Check gender first, understand the patterns, then add age or ethnicity.\n\n**Context determines which metrics matter.** For hiring, equalised odds matters most (equal error rates). For loan approvals, calibration is critical (scores should mean the same thing). Don\'t obsess over passing every metric—some are mathematically incompatible.\n\n**Small groups show noisy metrics.** If a demographic group has fewer than 50 members, ratios will fluctuate wildly. Flag these for manual review rather than algorithmic adjustment.\n\n**Fairness isn\'t just a final check.** Run this node during model development, not just before deployment. Early detection lets you fix data issues or feature engineering problems upstream.\n\n**Compare multiple models.** Connect several model outputs to separate Check Fairness nodes. A slightly less accurate model with better fairness properties often wins in production contexts.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Scan\n\n**When to use:** Initial model |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically rigorous, auditable fairness assessment with documented uncertainty bounds suitable for regulatory review.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computational cost increases 50-100x shape: {Z.shape}")\n\n# Step 6: Examine component loadings\nloadings_df = pd.DataFrame(\n    pca_reduced.components_.T,\n    index=feature_names,\n    columns=[f\'PC{i+1}\' for i in range(n_components)]\n)\nprint("\\n--- Component Loadings ---")\nprint(loadings_df.round(3))\n\n# -----------------------------\n# Example 2: Reconstruction error for anomaly detection\n# -----------------------------\n\nprint("\\n\\n--- Anomaly Detection via Reconstruction Error ---")\n\n# Inject anomalies\nX_with_anomalies = X_scaled.copy()\nanomaly_indices = [10, 50, 100]\nX_with_anomalies[anomaly_indices] += np.random.randn(3, n_features) * 5\n\n# Fit PCA on clean data, transform all data\npca_anomaly = PCA(n_components=3)\npca_anomaly.fit(X_scaled)\n\n# Compute reconstruction\nZ_all = pca_anomaly.transform(X_with_anomalies)\nX_reconstructed = pca_anomaly.inverse_transform(Z_all)\n\n# Compute reconstruction error per observation\nreconstruction_error = np.sum((X_with_anomalies - X_reconstructed) ** 2, axis=1)\n\n# Identify anomalies as high reconstruction error\nthreshold = np.percentile(reconstruction_error, 99)\ndetected_anomalies = np.where(reconstruction_error > threshold)[0]\n\nprint(f"Injected anomalies at indices: {anomaly_indices}")\nprint(f"Detected anomalies at indices: {detected_anomalies.tolist()}")\n\n# -----------------------------\n# Example 3: Visualisation\n# -----------------------------\n\n# Reduce to 2D for plotting\npca_2d = PCA(n_components=2)\nZ_2d = pca_2d.fit_transform(X_scaled)\n\nplt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))\nplt.scatter(Z_2d[:, 0], Z_2d[:, 1], alpha=0.6, edgecolors=\'w\', linewidth=0.5)\nplt.xlabel(f\'PC1 ({pca_2d.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%} variance)\')\nplt.ylabel(f\'PC2 ({pca_2d.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.1%\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/compress-features_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/compress-features_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What Data to Connect\n\nThe Compress Features node accepts a dataset with **numeric columns only**. Connect any table where you want to reduce the number of dimensions while keeping the essential patterns intact.\n\n**Before connecting:**\n- Ensure you have at least 2 numeric columns (features)\n- Remove or exclude any text, date, or categorical ID columns\n- Your dataset should have more rows than columns for stable results\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | age | income | spend_food | spend_electronics | spend_clothing |\n|-------------|-----|--------|------------|-------------------|----------------|\n| C001        | 34  | 52000  | 450        | 1200              | 300            |\n| C002        | 45  | 78000  | 680        | 800               | 550            |\n\nOnly the numeric columns (age, income, spend_food, etc.) will be used in the compression.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Number of Components** | How many principal components to extract | 2 | Increase to 3-5 if you need to capture more variance; keep at 2 for visualization purposes |\n| **Variance Threshold** | Minimum percentage of total variance to retain | 80% | Raise to 90-95% when preserving information is critical; lower to 70% when aggressive compression is needed |\n| **Standardize Features** | Whether to scale all features to the same range before PCA | On | Keep on unless your features are already on comparable scales |\n| **Exclude Columns** | Specific columns to ignore during compression | None | Select ID columns, target variables, or any features you want to preserve unchanged |\n\n### What You\'ll Get as Output\n\n**New columns added to your dataset:**\n- `PC1`, `PC2`, `PC3`, etc. — one column per component extracted\n- These contain the transformed values that represent your original features in compressed form\n\n**Metrics displayed:**\n- **Variance Explained**: A table showing what percentage of information each component captures\n- **Cumulative Variance**: Running total to see how many components reach your threshold\n- **Component Loadings**: How much each original feature contributes to each principal component\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Scree Plot**: A line chart showing variance captured by each component — helps you decide how many components to keep\n- **Biplot**: A scatter plot of observations in PC1/PC2 space with arrows showing original feature directions\n- **Loadings Heatmap**: Color-coded grid showing which features matter most for each component\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter compression, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Cluster Analysis** — compressed features make clustering faster and often more accurate by removing noise\n- **Train Model** — use the principal components as inputs for regression or classification\n- **Visualize Data** — plot PC1 vs PC2 to see patterns in high-dimensional data\n- **Detect Anomalies** — unusual patterns become easier to spot in the reduced space\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your numeric dataset** to the Compress Features node input\n2. **Set Number of Components to 2** (good starting point for exploration)\n3. **Leave Standardize Features turned on** (almost always the right choice)\n4. **Run the node** and check the Variance Explained metric\n5. **Review the Scree Plot** — if the first 2 components capture less than 70% variance, increase to 3-4 components\n6. **Connect the output to Visualize Data** and create a scatter plot of PC1 vs PC2 to see your data\'s structure\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Know when you have enough components.** Look for an "elbow" in the Scree Plot where adding more components gives diminishing returns. If the line is still steep after your selected components, you\'re leaving information on the table.\n\n**Interpret loadings to understand what each component means.** PC1 might represent "overall spending level" while PC2 captures "preference for electronics vs. clothing." These interpretations make your analysis actionable.\n\n**Watch for the 70% rule.** If one component alone explains more than 70% of variance, your original features were highly correlated — you\'ve found a natural summary variable.\n\n**Don\'t compress your target variable.** If you\'re building a predictive model, exclude your outcome column from compression and add it back afterward.\n\n**Use compression before clustering high-dimensional data.** Beyond 10-15 features, distance-based algorithms struggle. Compressing to 5-8 components first dramatically improves results.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial data investigation when you need a fast sense of dimensionality and want a 2D/3D visualization within seconds.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_components` | `2` or `3` | Enables immediate plotting; human-interpretable visualization |\n| `scaling` | `standardize` | Equalizes feature scales without assumptions about distributions |\n| `variance_threshold` | `0.01` | Removes near-constant features quickly without overthinking |\n| `missing_strategy` | `drop` | Fastest option; acceptable when <5% missingness |\n\n- **What you get:** A rapid scatter plot showing cluster structure and outliers, with execution time under 1 second for datasets up to 100k rows.\n- **Trade-off:** You discard potentially valuable variance in higher dimensions and lose observations with any missing values.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Compression\n\n- **When to use:** Preprocessing step before modeling in a production pipeline where reproducibility, stability, and information retention are critical.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_components` | `0.95` | Retains 95% cumulative variance; data-driven rather than arbitrary |\n| `scaling` | `robust` | Handles outliers without removal; stable across data refreshes |\n| `variance_threshold` | `0.0` | Lets PCA decide what\'s important; no manual filtering |\n| `missing_strategy` | `iterative_impute` | Most rigorous; preserves all records and relationships |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Ensures reproducibility across runs and deployments |\n\n- **What you get:** A stable transformation that typically reduces dimensions by 40-70% while preserving model-relevant signal and maintaining consistent performance across data updates.\n- **Trade-off:** Longer computation time (5-10x slower than quick exploration) and increased complexity in the preprocessing pipeline.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Correlation Feature Sets\n\n- **When to use:** Datasets with highly collinear features (correlation >0.9) such as sensor arrays, polynomial features, or one-hot encoded sparse categories.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_components` | `0.99` | Aggressive retention needed; redundancy is structural, not noise |\n| `scaling` | `normalize` | L2 normalization for sparse data preserves zero patterns |\n| `variance_threshold` | `0.001` | Very permissive; collinearity creates artificial low-variance features |\n| `correlation_cutoff` | `0.95` | Pre-filter perfectly collinear pairs before PCA to improve stability |\n\n- **What you get:** Dimension reduction of 80-95% typical in multi-collinear datasets while maintaining near-perfect reconstruction capability.\n- **Trade-off:** The first few components become difficult to interpret as they blend many correlated inputs.\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomaly Detection Preprocessing\n\n- **When to use:** When your goal is anomaly detection and you want compressed features that amplify reconstruction error for outliers.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_components` | `0.75` | Intentionally low; normal patterns compress well, anomalies don\'t |\n| `scaling` | `standardize` | Anomalies in any feature should contribute equally |\n| `variance_threshold` | `0.0` | Low-variance features can be anomaly indicators |\n| `whiten` | `True` | Decorrelates components; makes reconstruction error interpretable |\n\n- **What you get:** A feature space where reconstruction error (distance between original and inverse-transformed) becomes a powerful anomaly score.\n- **Trade-off:** This configuration is useless for supervised learning; it\'s purpose-built for unsupervised anomaly detection only.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processing 15,000 loan applications monthly struggled with credit risk models that incorporated 340+ variables from credit bureaus, income verification, and transaction histories.
