A colleague suggests using these 10 components as inputs to train a logistic regression model for customer churn prediction. What is the primary trade-off of this approach?\n\nA) The model will be less accurate because PCA removes 5% of the information, which likely contains the signal most relevant to churn prediction\n\nB) The model will train faster and may generalize better, but you lose the ability to interpret which original features drive churn predictions\n\nC) The compressed features will cause the logistic regression to violate its assumption that predictors should be uncorrelated with each other\n\nD) The dimensionality reduction will introduce non-linear relationships that logistic regression cannot capture, reducing model performance\n\n**Answer:** B\n\n**Explanation:** PCA creates principal components that are linear combinations of all original features, making it impossible to directly interpret which original variables (e.g., "contract length" or "support tickets") drive predictions—you can only see that "PC3 has a strong coefficient." This interpretability loss is the core trade-off when using PCA for preprocessing. Option A reflects the misconception that variance equals predictive signal; the discarded 5% may be noise, and variance doesn\'t necessarily correlate with relevance to the target variable. Option C is backwards—PCA components are orthogonal (uncorrelated) by design, which actually satisfies collinearity concerns better than original features. in Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe **Correct for Trends** node expects time series data with at least two columns: a datetime column and one or more numeric columns you want to detrend. Your data should be sorted by time, though the node will handle sorting if needed.\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| date | sales | temperature |\n|------------|-------|-------------|\n| 2023-01-01 | 245 | 32.1 |\n| 2023-01-02 | 253 | 31.8 |\n| 2023-01-03 | 261 | 33.2 |\n\nThe node works best with regularly spaced time intervals (daily, weekly, monthly), but can handle irregular spacing with appropriate configuration.\n\n### Quick Start\n\nHere\'s the most common workflow to get you started:\n\n1. **Connect your time series data** to the Correct for Trends node input\n2. **Select your datetime column** from the "Time Column" dropdown\n3. **Choose the numeric columns** you want to detrend (sales, revenue, etc.)\n4. **Pick "Linear" as your trend method** — this works well for most business scenarios\n5. **Click Run** and examine the trend visualization to see if the detected trend makes sense\n6. **Connect the output** to downstream analysis nodes like forecasting or anomaly detection\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Time Column** | Which column contains your dates/timestamps | (auto-detect) | Usually auto-detected correctly, but verify it selected the right one |\n| **Value Columns** | Which numeric columns to detrend | All numeric | Deselect columns that shouldn\'t be detrended (like IDs or categories) |\n| **Trend Method** | Algorithm for extracting the trend component | Linear | Use "Polynomial" for curved trends, "Moving Average" for noisy data, "STL" for complex seasonality |\n| **Polynomial Degree** | Curve complexity (only for Polynomial method) | 2 | Increase to 3-4 for more complex curves; higher risks overfitting |\n| **Window Size** | Number of periods to average (Moving Average method) | 7 | Match your data frequency: 7 for weekly patterns in daily data, 12 for yearly in monthly |\n| **Preserve Trend** | Keep the trend column in output instead of removing it | False | Enable when you want both detrended values AND the trend itself |\n| **Handle Missing Values** | How to deal with gaps in your data | Interpolate | Use "Drop" if you have very sparse data; "Forward Fill" for discrete values |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs your original data with new columns added:\n\n- **[column]_detrended**: Your original values with the trend removed — these are stationary and ready for statistical analysis\n- **[column]_trend**: The extracted trend component itself (if "Preserve Trend" is enabled)\n- **Trend visualization**: An interactive chart showing original values, detected trend line, and detrended residuals\n- **Stationarity test results**: Statistical metrics (ADF test) showing whether detrending was successful\n\nThe summary panel displays the trend equation (e.g., "y = 2.3x + 145") and goodness-of-fit metrics to help you assess trend quality.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter detrending, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Forecast** nodes — detrended data produces more accurate predictions\n- **Detect Anomalies** — trends can mask outliers; detrended data reveals them\n- **Statistical Tests** — correlation, regression, and other tests that assume stationarity\n- **Clustering** — groups similar time series by their residual patterns, not their trends\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Visualize before and after.** Always check the trend visualization — if the trend line looks wrong, try a different method. Linear trends shouldn\'t wiggle wildly through your data.\n\n**Seasonality is different from trend.** If your data has repeating patterns (weekly, yearly), you might need seasonal decomposition instead. Try STL method which handles both, or use the Decompose Time Series node first.\n\n**Watch for overfitting with polynomials.** A degree-5 polynomial will fit your data perfectly but won\'t represent a meaningful trend. Stick to degree 2-3 unless you have strong domain reasons.\n\n**Missing data matters.** Large gaps in your time series can create artificial trends. Clean your data first, or use "Drop" for missing values and accept a shorter series.\n\n**Save your trend parameters.** When you deploy models trained on detrended data, you\'ll need to apply the *exact same trend correction* to new data. Document your settings or use the node\'s export feature.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Detrending\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need to quickly assess whether trend is masking underlying patterns in your time series.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'linear\'` | Fastest computation, works for 80% of monotonic trends |\n| `degree` | `1` | Single polynomial degree minimizes overfitting on limited data inspection |\n| `validate` | `False` | Skip stationarity tests to speed up iteration |\n| `preserve_scale` | `False` | Raw residuals easier to interpret during exploration |\n\n**What you get:** A detrended series in milliseconds that reveals cyclical or seasonal patterns if they exist.\n\n**Trade-off:** You miss non-linear trends and get no statistical validation that detrending was actually necessary.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Trend Removal\n\n**When to use:** Deploying detrending as a preprocessing step in automated forecasting pipelines where reliability matters more than speed.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'lowess\'` | Robust to outliers and captures non-linear trends without overfitting |\n| `frac` | `0.1` | 10% smoothing window balances local adaptation with stability |\n| `validate` | `True` | ADF test (p<0.05) confirms stationarity post-detrending |\n| `preserve_scale` | `True` | Maintains interpretability for stakeholder reporting |\n| `handle_missing` | `\'interpolate\'` | Prevents pipeline failures on sparse data |\n\n**What you get:** A statistically validated stationary series with documented trend coefficients for audit trails.\n\n**Trade-off:** 5-10x slower computation and requires sufficient data density for LOWESS smoothing.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Frequency Financial Data\n\n**When to use:** Removing intraday drift from tick data or minute-level price series where polynomial trends create spurious patterns.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'differencing\'` | Eliminates any trend without assuming functional form |\n| `order` | `1` | First-order difference sufficient for price series (second-order adds noise) |\n| `seasonal_diff` | `False` | Intraday data lacks consistent seasonal periods |\n| `stabilize_variance` | `True` | Log-transform before differencing handles volatility clustering |\n\n**What you get:** Returns or price changes ready for mean-reversion strategy testing or volatility modeling.\n\n**Trade-off:** You lose one observation per differencing order and cannot reconstruct original levels without storing initial values.\n\n### Recipe 4: Survey Data with Response Fatigue\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing longitudinal survey responses where participant engagement declines systematically over repeated measurements, creating artificial downward trends.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'polynomial\'` | Fatigue effects often accelerate non-linearly (quadratic decay) |\n| `degree` | `2` | Captures initial stable period followed by declining engagement |\n| `fit_by_group` | `True` | Each participant has unique fatigue trajectory |\n| `preserve_mean` | `True` | Keeps absolute scale meaningful for Likert-type responses |\n| `min_observations` | `5` | Prevents overfitting on participants with few responses |\n\n**What you get:** Response patterns cleaned of engagement decay, revealing true opinion changes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes fatigue follows smooth polynomial rather than sudden dropout effects, potentially oversmoothing genuine attitude shifts.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA pan-European investment bank managing a €40B equity portfolio needs to distinguish genuine alpha signals from broad After detrending, they notice the residuals show increasing variance over time (heteroscedasticity). What does this most likely indicate about their preprocessing choice?\n\nA) The detrending was successful; increasing residual variance is expected after removing trends from growth data\n\nB) They should apply a stronger detrending method like polynomial or Hodrick-Prescott filtering to capture the trend more completely\n\nC) The original series likely has exponential rather than linear growth, requiring log-transformation before linear detrending\n\nD) The heteroscedasticity confirms the series is now stationary and ready for analysis\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** When percentage-based growth (like 5% annually) produces increasing residual variance after linear detrending, this reveals exponential/multiplicative growth in the original series. Linear detrending assumes additive trends (constant absolute increases), but exponential growth creates ever-larger absolute changes over time. Taking the logarithm converts multiplicative growth into additive form, making linear detrending appropriate. Option A misunderstands stationarity requirements (constant variance is essential). Option B reflects the misconception that "stronger" detrending methods can fix functional form mismatches—they cannot transform multiplicative patterns into additive ones. Option D dangerously confuses completing a detrending step with achieving stationarity; heteroscedasticity directly violates the constant variance assumption required for stationary series.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. Need\n\nThe Decompose Cycle node expects time series data with at least two columns: a date/time column and a numeric value column you want to analyze. Your data should be regularly spaced (daily, weekly, monthly, etc.) and ideally span multiple complete cycles—think at least 2-3 years of monthly data or several months of daily data.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| Date | Revenue |\n|------|---------|\n| 2021-01-01 | 45000 |\n| 2021-02-01 | 48500 |\n| 2021-03-01 | 52000 |\n\nThe node works best with data that\'s already been cleaned—no missing dates or gaps in your sequence. If you suspect gaps, run a **Fill Missing Values** node upstream first.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\nHere\'s what you can adjust, and when you\'d want to:\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Value Column** | Which numeric column to decompose | None (required) | Select your metric of interest (sales, inventory, web traffic, etc.) |\n| **Date Column** | Your time index | Auto-detected | Only if auto-detection picks the wrong column |\n| **Cycle Length Range** | Min and max periods to search for cycles | 12-60 periods | Narrow this if you know your cycle length (e.g., 18-24 months for real estate cycles) |\n| **Smoothing Window** | How much to smooth the trend before extracting cycles | 7 periods | Increase for noisy data; if not, adjust the Cycle Length Range\n6. **Export the Cycle column** to use in forecasting or correlation analysis\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe most common next steps:\n\n- **Correlation Analysis**: Feed the Cycle output to see what business factors correlate with cycle peaks (marketing spend, economic indicators, competitor activity)\n- **Forecast Model**: Use decomposed components as features in your predictive model—cycles often improve forecast accuracy\n- **Visualization Dashboard**: Connect to a Line Chart node to create executive-ready cycle reports\n- **Alert Node**: Set thresholds on cycle position to trigger notifications when approaching peaks or troughs\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Start broad, then narrow.** Begin with a wide Cycle Length Range (12-60) to discover what\'s there, then tighten it in a second pass for precision.\n\n**Check your seasonality first.** If you haven\'t already removed seasonal patterns, run **Seasonal Decomposition** upstream—Decompose Cycle works best on deseasonalized data.\n\n**Multiple metrics tell a story.** Run this on revenue, units sold, and customer count separately. When cycles align, you\'ve found something real; when they diverge, you\'ve found something interesting.\n\n**Not all data has cycles.** If your quality score is below 0.3, your data might be purely trending or random. That\'s valuable information too.\n\n**Visual validation matters.** Always eyeball the decomposition chart. If your extracted cycle looks like random noise rather than smooth waves, increase the smoothing window or reconsider whether cyclical patterns exist in this dataset.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need fast feedback on whether cyclical patterns exist before investing in deeper analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"stl"` | Fastest decomposition algorithm with minimal computation |\n| `period` | `None` (auto-detect) | Let the algorithm find cycles without manual specification |\n| `window_length` | `7` | Short window captures cycles quickly without over-smoothing |\n| `smoother` | `"moving_average"` | Simple smoother minimizes processing time |\n| `robust` | `False` | Skip outlier handling to accelerate computation |\n\n**What you get:** A rapid first-pass decomposition that reveals whether cyclical components warrant further investigation, typically processing in seconds even on datasets with thousands of observations.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice robustness to outliers and may miss subtle cycles masked by noise or irregular fluctuations.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Rigor\n\n**When to use:** Final deployment in automated pipelines or executive dashboards where accuracy and stability matter more than speed.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"x13"` | Industry-standard with proven performance on economic data |\n| `period` | `[12, 24, 60]` | Explicitly test multiple cycle lengths relevant to business |\n| `window_length` | `21` | Longer window smooths noise while preserving true cycles |\n| `smoother` | `"loess"` | Non-parametric smoother adapts to non-linear trends |\n| `robust` | `True` | Downweight outliers to prevent distortion |\n| `iterations` | `3` | Multiple passes refine component separation |\n\n**What you get:** Highly stable decomposition with minimal false positives that stands up to audit and supports high-stakes decisions.\n\n**Trade-off:** You incur 5–10x longer processing time and require larger datasets (minimum 3 full cycle periods) for reliable estimation.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Supply Chain Demand Cycles\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing inventory or demand data with known procurement cycles that don\'t align with calendar periods (e.g., 45-day ordering cycles).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"wavelet"` | Handles non-stationary cycles that shift over time |\n| `period` | `45` | Match your actual business cycle, not calendar convenience |\n| `boundary_handling` | `"reflect"` | Prevents edge effects in recent data (critical Use a Group By node first.\n\n**Start conservative**: Begin with a lower contamination rate (5%) and gradually increase. It\'s easier to catch more anomalies than to explain away false positives to stakeholders.\n\n**Domain knowledge beats algorithms**: Always filter your top 20-30 anomalies and ask "why is this flagged?" If the answer is "bad data quality" rather than "interesting outlier," add data cleaning steps upstream.\n\n**Multiple methods tell a story**: Run both Isolation Forest and Z-Score. Records flagged by both methods are highly confident anomalies. Records flagged by only one method deserve closer inspection of what makes them unusual.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Scan\n\n**When to use:** Initial data quality assessment on a new dataset where you need fast feedback on potential issues before investing in deeper analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Z-score | Fastest computation, works on univariate analysis |\n| Threshold | 3.0 | Standard deviation cutoff balances sensitivity and false positives |\n| Features | All numeric | Avoid feature selection overhead |\n| Contamination | 0.05 | Assumes ~5% anomalies, safe default for exploration |\n\n**What you get:** Rapid identification of extreme outliers with clear statistical interpretation, suitable for spot-checking data imports or pipeline failures.\n\n**Trade-off:** Misses multivariate anomalies and assumes normal distribution; will overlook subtle patterns that require interaction effects.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Fraud Detection\n\n**When to use:** Deployed systems requiring reliable anomaly detection with minimal false positives and stable performance across varied data conditions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Isolation Forest + LOF ensemble | Combines tree-based and density approaches for robustness |\n| n_estimators | 500 | Higher tree count improves stability |\n| Contamination | 0.01 | Conservative estimate for fraud scenarios |\n| n_neighbors (LOF) | 50 | Larger neighborhood smooths local density estimates |\n| Max features | 0.8 | Reduces overfitting to specific feature combinations |\n| Random state | Fixed value | Ensures reproducible scoring for audit trails |\n\n**What you get:** Consistent anomaly scoring with quantified confidence intervals, suitable for regulatory review and threshold tuning.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower computation and higher memory requirements; requires periodic retraining as normal behavior drifts.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Customer Behavior Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Customer journey data with 50+ interaction features where standard distance metrics fail due to curse of dimensionality.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Mahalanobis distance | Accounts for feature correlations and scale differences |\n| Feature selection | PCA (retain 95% variance) | Reduces dimensionality while preserving signal |\n| Robust covariance | True | Resistant to existing outliers polluting the baseline |\n| Contamination | 0.10 | Customer behavior naturally more variable |\n\n**What you get:** Anomaly scores that respect feature interdependencies, identifying customers with unusual patterns across multiple correlated dimensions.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires sufficient data for stable covariance estimation (minimum 10× rows per feature); interpretation is less intuitive than univariate methods.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Gap Detection in Sequential Data\n\n**When to use:** Log files, sensor streams, or transactional data where the *absence* of expected events indicates problems, not the presence of extreme values.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Method | Local Outlier Factor | Detects density changes in temporal neighborhoods |\n| Features | Time deltas + rolling statistics | Transforms timestamps into interval patterns |\n| n_neighbors | 20 | Small neighborhood captures local temporal context |\n| Contamination | 0.02 | Gaps are rare in healthy systems |\n| Metric | Manhattan | Less sensitive to single extreme intervals |\n\n**What you get:** Flags unusual silence periods, irregular cadences, or missing heartbeat signals that statistical outlier methods miss entirely.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires careful feature engineering to encode temporal structure; sensitive to seasonality unless detrended first.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional credit union processing 40,000 card transactions daily needs to stop fraud without frustrating legitimate customers. You\'ll Need\n\nThe Change Point Detection node expects **time series data** with at least two columns: a timestamp (or sequence index) and a numeric value you want to analyze for shifts. Your data should be sorted chronologically—the node needs to understand the order of events to identify when changes occur.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| date       | daily_revenue | order_count |\n|------------|---------------|-------------|\n| 2024-01-01 | 45320         | 234         |\n| 2024-01-02 | 46100         | 241         |\n| 2024-01-03 | 44890         | 228         |\n\nYou can analyze multiple metrics simultaneously, but each runs as a separate detection process. The node works best with **at least 50-100 observations**—detecting meaningful change points in very short sequences is statistically unreliable.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Adjust |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Time Column** | Which field contains your sequential ordering (date, timestamp, or index) | First date column | Change if your time field isn\'t auto-detected |\n| **Value Column(s)** | Numeric column(s) to analyze for change points | All numeric columns | Select only the metrics you care about to reduce noise |\n| **Detection Method** | Algorithm used: PELT (fast, penalty-based), Binary Segmentation, or Bayesian | PELT | Binary Segmentation for very long series; Bayesian when you need uncertainty estimates |\n| **Minimum Segment Length** | Smallest number of observations between change points | 10 | Increase to 20-30 to avoid over-segmentation; decrease for high-frequency data |\n| **Penalty/Sensitivity** | How easily the algorithm declares a change point (higher = fewer detections) | Auto-calibrated | Increase if you see too many trivial breaks; decrease if missing obvious shifts |\n| **Change Type** | Detect mean shifts, variance changes, or both | Mean | Switch to "Both" when volatility changes matter (financial data, sensor readings) |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node adds a **change_point** column to your data, marking detected boundaries with sequential labels (0, 1, 2...). Each segment between boundaries gets the same number. You\'ll also see:\n\n**Visualization**: An interactive time series chart with vertical lines marking each detected change point, overlaid on your original data. Segments are color-coded so you can instantly see regime boundaries.\n\n**Summary Table**: Lists each change point\'s location (timestamp), the metric that changed, confidence score, and pre/post statistics (mean before vs. after, variance ratios).\n\n**Segment Statistics**: For each homogeneous region between change points, you get descriptive stats—mean, median, standard deviation—making it easy to characterize "before" and "after" behavior.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll route the output to:\n\n- **Filter** node: Isolate specific segments for deeper analysis ("show me only data after the second change point")\n- **Aggregate** node: Calculate statistics per segment to quantify how dramatically things changed\n- **Visualization** nodes: Create comparative charts showing behavior across regimes\n- **Feature Engineering**: Use segment labels as categorical features in predictive models (e.g., "performance in regime 3 predicts customer churn")\n\n### Quick Start: Detecting Revenue Shifts\n\n1. **Connect your time series data** containing dates and the metric you want to monitor\n2. **Select** your date field as the Time Column and your target metric (e.g., "daily_revenue") as the Value Column\n3. **Leave defaults** for your first run (PELT method, minimum segment length of 10)\n4. **Click Run** and examine the visualization—do the detected points align with known events?\n5. **Adjust Penalty** upward if you see too many minor fluctuations marked as changes, or downward if an obvious shift was missed\n6. **Export the segment labels** and use them to group your analysis ("revenue behavior in Q1 vs. post-change-point period")\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n- **Always validate detected change points** against domain knowledge—a statistical shift might not represent a meaningful business event\n- **Use minimum segment length strategically**: Setting it to ~5% of your total observations prevents spurious micro-segments\n- **Compare multiple methods**: If PELT and Binary Segmentation disagree significantly, your data may have ambiguous boundaries worth investigating manually\n- **Seasonal data needs preprocessing**: Deseasonalize first (using the Seasonal Decomposition node) or you\'ll detect seasonal transitions, not structural breaks\n- **Combine with annotations**: Mark known intervention dates (product launches, policy changes) to see if algorithmic detections align with business reality\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data inspection when you need fast feedback on whether any regime changes exist, particularly useful in exploratory notebooks or during client discovery calls.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"binary_segmentation"` | Single-pass algorithm, fastest runtime |\n| `min_segment_length` | `0.05 * n` | Prevents over-segmentation from noise |\n| `penalty` | `"BIC"` | Automatically balances fit vs. complexity |\n| `max_changepoints` | `5` | Limits search space, speeds computation |\n\n**What you get:** Rapid identification of major structural breaks with completion in seconds even on datasets with 10K+ observations.\n\n**Trade-off:** May miss subtle shifts or closely-spaced changes; not suitable for formal reporting.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Detection\n\n**When to use:** Deployable pipelines requiring defensible change point identification for regulatory reporting, automated alerts, or published research.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"pelt"` | Proven optimal for exact segmentation |\n| `min_segment_length` | `30` | Statistical power for regime confirmation |\n| `penalty` | `"Manual"` with value `log(n) * 4` | Conservative threshold, reduces false positives |\n| `significance_test` | `"permutation"` with `n_permutations=10000` | Non-parametric validation of each change point |\n| `bootstrap_confidence` | `True` with `n_bootstrap=1000` | Quantifies uncertainty in change point locations |\n\n**What you get:** High-confidence detections with statistical validation and uncertainty bounds suitable for audit trails.\n\n**Trade-off:** 10-100x slower than exploratory methods; may require hours for large datasets.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Frequency Financial Data\n\n**When to use:** Detecting regime changes in minute-level or tick-level financial time series where volatility clustering and heavy tails dominate.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `"ar"` with `order=3` | Captures autocorrelation structure |\n| `cost_function` | `"gamma"` | Handles right-skewed distributions |\n| `min_segment_length` | `240` | ~1 trading day prevents intraday noise |\n| `penalty` | `"Manual"` with value `log(n) * 6` | Stricter threshold for autocorrelated data |\n\n**What you get:** Change points aligned with actual market regime shifts rather than spurious volatility spikes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes multiplicative changes; inappropriate for additive shift processes.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Sensor Drift Detection\n\n**When to use:** Identifying calibration degradation or environmental shifts in IoT sensor networks where gradual drift is followed by recalibration jumps—a scenario where change point detection outperforms anomaly detection.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `"clinear"` | Detects changes in trend slope, not just level |\n| `min_segment_length` | `100` | Differentiates drift from calibration events |\n| `jump_penalty` | `0.7` | Favors interpretable jumps over smooth transitions |\n| `edge_buffer` | `0.1 * n` | Ignores startup transients and battery-death endpoints |\n\n**What you get:** Precise timestamps of recalibration events enabling maintenance schedule optimization.\n\n**Trade-off:** Will not flag gradual drift itself, only the corrections—combine with trend analysis for complete monitoring.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional US credit card issuer processing 3 million When would change point detection methods be most appropriately applied to this scenario?\n\nA) Throughout the entire sequence to identify both the gradual growth phases and the sudden drop\nB) Only at the sudden drop, since change point detection requires abrupt shifts rather than gradual trends\nC) At the sudden drop and potentially at the resumption point, after first removing or accounting for the underlying growth trend\nD) Never, because the drop has a known external cause (regulatory change), making statistical detection redundant\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Change point detection identifies locations where **statistical properties** undergo abrupt shifts, which requires examining changes *relative to the local data-generating process*. The gradual growth represents a smooth trend, not a change point; the regulatory shock causes an abrupt shift in level that disrupts this trend. Option C correctly recognizes that trend removal or accounting is necessary first—otherwise, the method might detect spurious changes caused by comparing different points along a slope rather than true structural breaks. Option A misunderstands that gradual changes are not change points (they\'re trends requiring different methods). Option B is partially correct about requiring abrupt shifts but fails to recognize that trend-adjustment may be needed to properly detect those shifts. Option D represents the misconception that knowing the *cause* of a change eliminates the value of *detecting and locating* it statistically; change point methods remain useful for precise timing identification and validation even when causes are suspected.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. A noisy baseline creates constant false alarms.\n\n2. **Monitor drift over sliding windows** — Instead of one reference snapshot, update your baseline monthly so you distinguish genuine shifts from seasonal patterns.\n\n3. **Not all drift is bad** — If your business is expanding to new regions, customer demographics *should* drift. Always ask "is this drift expected given our business changes?"\n\n4. **Check sample sizes** — Tiny current datasets (< 50 rows) will show false drift. Production-Grade Monitoring\n\n**When to use:** Deployed ML models in production where false alarms are costly but missed drift causes business impact.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why Heuristix\n\n### What Data to Connect\n\nThe Ensemble Compete node expects a **prepared dataset** with your features and target variable already defined. Connect it to any node that outputs a clean dataframe—typically a Feature Engineering, Data Cleaning, or Train-Test Split node.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- At least one feature column (numeric or categorical)\n- One target column (for classification or regression)\n- Minimum 100 rows recommended for meaningful comparison\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_age | income | credit_score | previous_purchases | will_churn |\n|--------------|--------|--------------|-------------------|-----------|\n| 34 | 52000 | 680 | 12 | 0 |\n| 45 | 78000 | 720 | 8 | 0 |\n| 29 | 41000 | 590 | 3 | 1 |\n\nThe node automatically detects your target variable type and selects appropriate ensemble methods.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Target Column** | Which column to predict | Last column | Always set this explicitly to your actual target |\n| **Problem Type** | Classification or Regression | Auto-detect | Override if auto-detection fails (rare) |\n| **Ensemble Methods** | Which algorithms to compare | All available | Uncheck methods you want to exclude (e.g., exclude boosting for speed) |\n| **CV Folds** | Number of cross-validation splits | 5 | Increase to 10 for small datasets; decrease to 3 for very large datasets |\n| **Scoring Metric** | How to rank models | Accuracy (classification) / RMSE (regression) | Change to F1-score for imbalanced data, or R² for regression interpretability |\n| **Time Limit** | Maximum training time per model (minutes) | 10 | Reduce for quick exploration; increase for complex datasets |\n| **Random Seed** | Ensures reproducible results | 42 | Change to verify stability across different random states |\n\n### What You\'ll Get as Output\n\n**Performance Comparison Table**: A ranked leaderboard showing each ensemble method with its cross-validated performance metrics. You\'ll see the winning model at the top with scores for accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (classification) or RMSE, MAE, R² (regression).\n\n**Model Comparison Chart**: An interactive bar chart visualizing performance differences across all tested ensembles. This makes it immediately obvious which methods excel for your specific data.\n\n**Best Model Object**: The trained winning ensemble, ready to deploy or connect to downstream prediction nodes.\n\n**Detailed Metrics Report**: Confusion matrices (classification) or residual plots (regression) for the top 3 performers, helping you understand where each model succeeds or struggles.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe most common next steps:\n\n- **Predict Node**: Send the best model object directly here to score new data\n- **Model Explainer**: Connect to understand feature importance and model decisions\n- **Hyperparameter Tuning**: Take the winning ensemble type and fine-tune it further\n- **Model Export**: Save the champion model for production deployment\n\n### Quick Start: Most Common Use Case\n\n1. **Connect your prepared dataset** to the Ensemble Compete node input\n2. **Select your target column** from the dropdown in the configuration panel\n3. **Leave all other settings at default** for your first run\n4. **Click Execute** and wait 5-15 minutes while models train\n5. **Review the leaderboard**—the top model is your winner\n6. **Connect the output** to a Predict node to start scoring new data\n\n### Practical Tips from Experience\n\n**Tip 1: Start broad, then narrow.** Your first run should test all ensemble types. Once you know which family performs best (bagging vs. boosting vs. stacking), run a second iteration with only those methods and longer time limits for better results.\n\n**Tip 2: Watch for tiny performance differences.** If the top three models are within 1-2% of each other, choose the simplest one (usually Random Forest or Gradient Boosting). Complex stacking ensembles rarely justify their overhead for marginal gains.\n\n**Tip 3: Check training time vs. performance.** The output table includes fitting time—a model that\'s 0.5% better but takes 10x longer might not be worth it for your use case.\n\n**Tip 4: For imbalanced datasets**, change the scoring metric to F1-score or AUC-ROC before running. Accuracy alone will mislead you when classes are skewed.\n\n**Tip 5: Save the comparison report.** Export the leaderboard as documentation for stakeholders—it proves you didn\'t just pick your favorite algorithm arbitrarily.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping\n\n**When to use:** Initial dataset exploration when you need directional insights within minutes, not production-grade results.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_folds` | 3 | Minimizes computation while maintaining some cross-validation rigor |\n| `ensemble_methods` | `[\'random_forest\', \'gradient_boosting\', \'logistic_regression\']` | Covers diversity (bagging, boosting, linear) without exhaustive search |\n| `n_estimators` | 50 | Fast training; sufficient to identify patterns |\n| `max_train_size` | 5000 | Caps dataset size to prevent slow iterations |\n| `parallel_jobs` | -1 | Uses all CPU cores available |\n\n**What you get:** A ranked shortlist of viable approaches in under 10 minutes, identifying whether tree methods or linear models dominate.\n\n**Trade-off:** Results may not generalize—model rankings could shift with proper tuning and full data.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Deployment\n\n**When to use:** Final model selection before deploying to production systems where prediction accuracy directly impacts business outcomes.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_folds` | 10 | Maximizes reliability of performance estimates |\n| `ensemble_methods` | `[\'xgboost\', \'lightgbm\', \'catboost\', \'random_forest\', \'extra_trees\', \'stacking\']` | Comprehensive coverage including modern gradient boosting variants |\n| `n_estimators` | 500 | Allows models to reach performance plateau |\n| `hyperparameter_tuning` | `\'bayesian\'` | Optimizes each method thoroughly |\n| `tuning_iterations` | 100 | Exhaustive search of hyperparameter space |\n| `stratified_sampling` | `True` | Preserves class distribution in each fold |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically robust champion model with confidence intervals on expected performance.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation time measured in hours or days; requires significant infrastructure.\n\n### Recipe 3: Severe Class Imbalance\n\n**When to use:** Fraud detection, rare disease prediction, or any scenario where positive class represents <5% of samples and standard accuracy is meaningless.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `scoring_metric` | `\'f1\'` or `\'pr_auc\'` | Focuses on precision-recall balance, not misleading accuracy |\n| `class_weight` | `\'balanced\'` | Forces algorithms to penalize minority class errors heavily |\n| `resampling_strategy` | `\'smote\'` | Synthetically balances training folds |\n| `n_folds` | 5 | Ensures minority class appears sufficiently in each fold |\n| `ensemble_methods` | `[\'xgboost\', \'balanced_random_forest\', \'easy_ensemble\']` | Prioritizes imbalance-aware algorithms |\n\n**What you get:** Rankings based on ability to detect rare events, not just overall correctness.\n\n**Trade-off:** Models may generate more false positives; requires downstream threshold tuning.\n\n### Recipe 4: Interpretability-Constrained Environments\n\n**When to use:** Regulated industries (healthcare, finance) where model decisions require human-auditable explanations or regulatory approval.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `ensemble_methods` | `[\'logistic_regression\', \'decision_tree\', \'rule_ensemble\']` | Excludes black-box methods; all outputs are explainable |\n| `max_depth` | 5 | Limits tree complexity to human-readable size |\n| `feature_selection` | `True` | Reduces model to most impactful predictors |\n| `generate_reports` | `\'verbose\'` | Creates coefficient tables, feature importance, decision paths |\n| `n_estimators` | 10 | Keeps voting ensembles countable and auditable |\n\n**What you get:** A ranked set of transparent models with documented decision logic suitable for regulatory submission.\n\n**Trade-off:** Typically 3-8% lower predictive performance compared to optimized XGBoost or neural approaches.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processes 15,000 loan applications monthly but struggles with false positives in fraud detection—legitimate applications flagged as suspicious cost £340 per manual review. Connect it to a dataset with at least two numeric columns (your clustering dimensions) and enough rows to form meaningful groups (typically 50+ observations work well).\n\n**Input requirements:**\n- **Required**: 2+ numeric columns to cluster on\n- **Optional**: An ID column to track which observation is which\n- **Data shape**: Each row represents one item/customer/event to be grouped\n\nHere\'s a simple example of what goes in:\n\n| customer_id | avg_purchase | visit_frequency | recency_days |\n|-------------|--------------|-----------------|--------------|\n| C001        | 145.50       | 12              | 5            |\n| C002        | 45.20        | 3               | 45           |\n| C003        | 230.00       | 18              | 2            |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Number of Clusters** | How many groups to create | 3 | Increase if you need finer segmentation (5-7 groups). Decrease for simpler, broader categories (2-3 groups). |\n| **Clustering Method** | The algorithm used | K-Means | Switch to Hierarchical for smaller datasets (<1000 rows) or when cluster shapes aren\'t spherical. Use DBSCAN if you suspect outliers. |\n| **Distance Metric** | How "similarity" is measured | Euclidean | Change to Manhattan for data with many dimensions, or Cosine for normalized/scaled features. |\n| **Standardize Features** | Scale all columns to same range | On | Keep on unless your variables are already on comparable scales and those differences matter. |\n| **Random Seed** | Makes results reproducible | 42 | Change only if comparing multiple runs or sharing with collaborators. |\n| **Max Iterations** | How hard the algorithm tries | 300 | Increase if you see a "did not converge" warning (rare with clean data). |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**New Columns Added:**\n- **cluster_id**: The group assignment for each row (0, 1, 2, etc.)\n- **distance_to_centroid**: How "typical" each item is within its cluster (lower = more typical)\n\n**Visualizations Displayed:**\n- **Cluster Scatter Plot**: Your data in 2D/3D space with color-coded groups — instantly see separation quality\n- **Cluster Sizes Bar Chart**: How many items landed in each group\n- **Silhouette Plot**: Quality metric showing how well-defined your clusters are (aim for >0.5)\n- **Feature Importance**: Which input columns most strongly define the clusters\n\n**Summary Metrics Panel:**\n- Overall silhouette score (clustering quality: 0-1 scale)\n- Within-cluster variance (lower is tighter grouping)\n- Between-cluster separation (higher is better)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter clustering, you\'ll typically:\n\n1. **Profile Groups** \u2192 Connect to the **Summarize by Group** node to understand what makes each cluster unique (average purchase, common behaviors, etc.)\n2. **Filter & Export** \u2192 Use **Filter Rows** to isolate specific clusters for targeted action\n3. **Predict Membership** \u2192 Feed into **Train Classifier** to predict which cluster new observations belong to\n4. **Visualize Further** \u2192 Connect to **Custom Chart** for domain-specific cluster visualization\n\n### Quick Start: Customer Segmentation\n\n1. **Connect your customer data** with at least purchase amount, frequency, and recency columns\n2. **Set Number of Clusters to 4** (a good starting point for RFM segmentation)\n3. **Keep Standardize Features ON** (these metrics have different scales)\n4. **Run the node** and check the silhouette score — aim for >0.4\n5. **Connect to Summarize by Group** to profile each segment\'s characteristics\n6. **Adjust cluster count** up or down based on whether segments feel too broad or too granular\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n- **Start with more clusters than you think you need**, then merge similar ones — easier than splitting\n- **The "elbow method"** isn\'t automated here: run multiple times with 2, 3, 4, 5 clusters and watch how the within-cluster variance drops off\n- **Low silhouette scores (<0.3)** suggest your data may not have natural groupings — that\'s useful information too\n- **Check distance_to_centroid** to find your most "typical" examples of each cluster — perfect for personas or representative samples\n- **Exclude purely identifying columns** (names, IDs) from clustering but keep them in your dataset for labeling results later\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial data exploration when you have no idea how many natural groups exist and need rapid feedback to inform next steps.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| algorithm | K-Means | Fastest convergence, lowest computational overhead |\n| k_range | 2-10 | Covers most business scenarios without excessive computation |\n| initialization | k-means++ | Better starting positions than random, minimal time cost |\n| max_iterations | 100 | Sufficient for convergence on well-separated clusters |\n| n_init | 10 | Balance between stability and speed |\n| distance_metric | Euclidean | Computationally cheapest option |\n\n- **What you get:** Rapid cluster assignments across multiple k values with elbow plots and silhouette scores to guide further investigation.\n- **Trade-off:** You sacrifice robustness to outliers and may miss non-spherical cluster shapes that more sophisticated algorithms would detect.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Segmentation\n\n- **When to use:** Deploying customer segmentation or operational groupings where stability, reproducibility, and defensibility matter more than runtime.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| algorithm | HDBSCAN | Robust to noise, discovers variable-density clusters |\n| min_cluster_size | 50 | Ensures segments are actionable (not singletons) |\n| min_samples | 5 | Conservative noise detection |\n| cluster_selection_method | eom (Excess of Mass) | Stable across hierarchical levels |\n| distance_metric | Manhattan | More robust to outliers than Euclidean |\n| validation | Stability analysis with bootstrapping (500 iterations) | Quantifies cluster reliability |\n\n- **What you get:** Hierarchical cluster structure with confidence scores, automatic outlier detection, and stability metrics for each cluster.\n- **Trade-off:** You accept 5-10x longer runtime and require more memory for the dendrogram hierarchy.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Text or Genomic Data\n\n- **When to use:** Clustering datasets with hundreds or thousands of features where distance metrics become unreliable (curse of dimensionality).\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| preprocessing | PCA to 50 components (95% variance) | Dimensionality reduction before clustering |\n| algorithm | Gaussian Mixture Models | Models elliptical clusters in reduced space |\n| n_components | 3-12 | Realistic range for latent topics/groups |\n| covariance_type | full | Captures feature correlations post-PCA |\n| initialization | Multiple random starts (n_init=20) | Critical in high dimensions |\n| distance_metric | Cosine (pre-PCA) | Appropriate for sparse, high-dimensional vectors |\n\n- **What you get:** Probabilistic cluster memberships that respect feature correlations and provide uncertainty quantification for each assignment.\n- **Trade-off:** You lose interpretability of the original feature space and must explain clusters in terms of principal components.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Behavioral Cohorts\n\n- **When to use:** Grouping user journeys, patient disease progressions, or equipment degradation patterns where sequence matters more than snapshot similarity.\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| feature_engineering | Extract: trend slope, variance, autocorrelation, peak count | Captures temporal characteristics |\n| algorithm | Agglomerative Hierarchical | Provides dendrogram for exploring granularity |\n| linkage | Ward | Minimizes within-cluster variance for time patterns |\n| distance_metric | Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) | Handles sequences of different lengths/phases |\n| n_clusters | Cut dendrogram at height=2.5 | Let data dictate grouping via visual inspection |\n\n- **What you get:** Trajectory-based segments that group similar temporal behaviors regardless of exact timing alignment.\n- **Trade-off:** You require substantially more feature engineering upfront and DTW computation scales O(n²) with sequence length.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender with 180,000 customers struggled to identify early warning signs of payment difficulties before Your manager asks: "What causes customers to fall into each spending tier?" What is the most accurate response about what clustering has revealed?\n\nA) The algorithm has identified causal factors—customers with certain characteristics naturally migrate to these spending tiers over time\n\nB) The three tiers represent a natural hierarchy in customer value that can be used to predict which tier new customers will join\n\nC) The algorithm has revealed that three distinct spending patterns exist in the data, but hasn\'t explained why customers exhibit those patterns\n\nD) The clustering has segmented customers based on their underlying propensities to spend, which can now be used to target interventions\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Clustering is fundamentally a *descriptive* technique that reveals structure (natural groupings exist) but does not explain *why* those groupings exist or establish causation. Option C correctly captures that clustering has partitioned observations by similarity without providing explanatory power. Option A misrepresents clustering as revealing causation, a critical misconception. Option B falsely implies clustering provides predictive capability for new observations (it doesn\'t inherently classify unseen data). Option D incorrectly suggests clustering has identified underlying propensities or mechanisms when it has only identified patterns of similarity in observed behavior. This distinction between "finding that groups exist" versus "explaining why they exist" separates practitioners who correctly apply clustering from those who over-interpret its results.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '—'. Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/find-latent-factors_fig1.png)\n![](../../_static/figures/find-latent-factors_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe Find Latent Factors node expects **numeric data** in a table where each row represents an observation and each column represents a variable you want to analyze. Think customer metrics, sensor readings, survey responses, or product features—anything with multiple correlated measurements.\n\n**Required:** At least 3-4 numeric columns (more is better—latent factor methods shine with dozens or hundreds of variables). The node will automatically detect and use all numeric columns unless you specify otherwise.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | purchase_freq | avg_order_value | email_opens | site_visits | support_tickets |\n|-------------|---------------|-----------------|-------------|-------------|-----------------|\n| C001        | 12            | 85.50           | 8           | 24          | 1               |\n| C002        | 3             | 120.00          | 2           | 5           | 0               |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Method** | Algorithm to use: PCA, Factor Analysis, or NMF | PCA | Use FA when you believe measurement error exists; NMF when all values are non-negative and you want interpretable parts-based components |\n| **Number of Factors** | How many latent dimensions to extract | Auto (explained variance) | Set manually if you have a specific dimensionality target—e.g., reducing 50 features to exactly 5 for downstream modeling |\n| **Variance Threshold** | Minimum % of total variance to retain (when auto) | 85% | Lower to 70-75% for aggressive compression; raise to 90-95% when preserving information is critical |\n| **Standardize Inputs** | Whether to scale variables to mean=0, std=1 | On | Turn off only if your variables are already on the same scale and that scale is meaningful |\n| **Rotation** | For Factor Analysis: varimax, promax, or none | varimax | Use promax when factors might be correlated; none when you want raw mathematical factors |\n| **Include Columns** | Which columns to analyze | All numeric | Specify if you want to exclude IDs, dates, or target variables |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**New Columns Added:**\n- `factor_1`, `factor_2`, ... `factor_n`: The factor scores for each observation—these are your new compressed features\n- `reconstruction_error`: How well the factors recreate the original data for each row (lower is better)\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n- Explained variance by factor (bar chart showing what % each factor captures)\n- Cumulative variance plot (helps you see the elbow where adding factors gives diminishing returns)\n- Total variance retained (headline number—aim for 80%+)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Factor loadings heatmap**: Shows which original variables contribute most to each factor—this is where interpretation happens\n- **Scree plot**: Classic elbow diagram for choosing the right number of factors\n- **Biplot** (for PCA): Observations and variables plotted together in the first two factor dimensions\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Most common next steps:**\n\n1. **\u2192 Train Model**: Use the factor scores as features—now you\'re modeling with 5-10 uncorrelated factors instead of 100 noisy variables\n2. **\u2192 Find Clusters**: Cluster in the low-dimensional factor space for more robust segments\n3. **\u2192 Visualize**: Feed factor scores to scatter plots or UMAP nodes for visual exploration\n4. **\u2192 Filter/Score**: Keep only observations with low reconstruction error (high-quality data points)\n\n### Quick Start: Customer Behavior Compression\n\n1. Connect your customer metrics table (purchases, engagement, demographics—10+ columns)\n2. Leave Method as **PCA** and Variance Threshold at **85%**\n3. Ensure **Standardize Inputs** is On (critical when mixing percentages, counts, and dollar amounts)\n4. Run the node and check the **scree plot**—look for where it flattens\n5. Review the **loadings heatmap**: Factor 1 might be "engagement," Factor 2 might be "spending power"—name them based on what loads heavily\n6. Connect to Train Model, using the new factor columns as your feature set\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1:** The loadings heatmap is your interpretation key. If a factor has high loadings (>0.6) on visit frequency, email clicks, and app usage, you\'re looking at an "engagement" dimension—label it accordingly in your documentation.\n\n**Tip 2:** Watch for factors with just one high loading. They often represent unique variance in a single variable (like "number of returns")—consider whether you need them or can drop them.\n\n**Tip 3:** If downstream models aren\'t improving, you may have set the variance threshold too low. Try retaining 90% instead of 80%—that extra 10% sometimes contains signal, not just noise.\n\n**Tip 4:** Reconstruction error helps spot anomalies. Rows with high error don\'t fit the common patterns—they might be data quality issues or genuinely unusual cases worth investigating.\n\n**Tip 5:** Don\'t rotate PCA results (rotation only applies to Factor Analysis). If you accidentally select a rotation method with PCA, the platform will warn you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data inspection when you need to visualize high-dimensional data in minutes and decide if deeper analysis is warranted.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `PCA` | Fastest computation, no iterative fitting |\n| `n_components` | `2` | Enables scatter plot visualization |\n| `svd_solver` | `\'randomized\'` | 3-5× faster than exact for large datasets |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Reproducible results across runs |\n| `whiten` | `False` | Skip unnecessary normalization step |\n\n**What you get:** Two-dimensional projection you can plot immediately to spot clusters, outliers, or confirm data is hopelessly noisy.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice explained variance (typically capturing only 30-60% with two components) and interpretability of the factor loadings.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Feature Extraction\n\n**When to use:** Building a stable preprocessing pipeline for a production ML system where dimensionality reduction must be consistent and auditable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `PCA` | Deterministic, well-tested, no convergence issues |\n| `n_components` | `0.95` | Retain 95% variance while reducing dimensions |\n| `svd_solver` | `\'full\'` | Exact decomposition, no approximation error |\n| `whiten` | `True` | Decorrelates features for downstream models |\n| `copy` | `True` | Prevents accidental modification of input data |\n\n**What you get:** A transformation that balances dimensionality reduction with information preservation, suitable for version control and A/B testing.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower computation (5-10× vs. randomized) and higher memory usage during training, though transform time remains fast.\n\n### Recipe 3: Sparse High-Dimensional Text Data\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing TF-IDF vectors, one-hot encoded categories, or any sparse matrix where most values are zero.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `TruncatedSVD` | Operates directly on sparse matrices without densification |\n| `n_components` | `100` | Sweet spot for typical document collections (1000-100K docs) |\n| `n_iter` | `7` | More iterations than default 5 for better convergence |\n| `algorithm` | `\'randomized\'` | Only option for sparse data, but explicitly set it |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Stabilizes results despite randomized algorithm |\n\n**What you get:** Dense low-dimensional embeddings that preserve document similarity structure while using 100× less memory than original sparse matrices.\n\n**Trade-off:** Cannot compute inverse transform back to original feature space; you lose the ability to interpret "what words define this component."\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomaly-Resistant Dimensionality Reduction\n\n**When to use:** Data with known outliers or corrupted records where standard PCA would be distorted by extreme values.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `FactorAnalysis` | Probabilistic model that down-weights outliers naturally |\n| `n_components` | `10` | Start conservative; FA is sensitive to overparameterization |\n| `max_iter` | `1000` | Allow sufficient convergence for EM algorithm |\n| `tol` | `0.01` | Balance precision vs. runtime (default 0.01 is reasonable) |\n| `svd_method` | `\'lapack\'` | More stable than randomized for noisy data |\n\n**What you get:** Factors representing shared variance while treating measurement noise and outliers as instance-specific rather than systematic patterns.\n\n**Trade-off:** Much slower than PCA (10-50× depending on data size) and requires careful validation that the model has converged properly.\n\n## Business PCA components are linear combinations designed to explain maximal variance, not to align with meaningful constructs like "price sensitivity" or "brand loyalty." This is the key limitation separating competent practitioners (who use latent factors cautiously for interpretation) from novices (who assume high variance-explanation equals meaningful insights). Option A reflects the misconception that unexplained variance invalidates the analysis—82% is typically excellent, and the remaining 18% is often noise. Option C misunderstands that Find Latent Factors is unsupervised by design and perfectly valid for exploratory questions; having a business question doesn\'t require supervised learning. node expects a single dataset with at least two columns: one categorical variable (your groups) and one continuous variable (your outcome). Think of analyzing sales performance across regions, customer satisfaction by product tier, or conversion rates across marketing channels.\n\n**Your input data should look like this:**\n\n| Region | Revenue |\n|--------|---------|\n| North | 45000 |\n| South | 38000 |\n| North | 52000 |\n| West | 41000 |\n\nThe categorical column can have any number of groups (though 2–20 is most practical), and you\'ll need at least a few observations per group for meaningful results.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Group Variable** | The categorical column defining your groups | *(none)* | Select the dimension you want to compare (e.g., Region, Segment, Channel) |\n| **Outcome Variable** | The continuous metric you\'re analyzing | *(none)* | Choose what you\'re measuring (e.g., Revenue, Time, Score) |\n| **Confidence Level** | Sets the certainty threshold for statistical tests | 95% | Use 99% for high-stakes decisions; 90% for exploratory analysis |\n| **Post-hoc Tests** | Enables pairwise group comparisons | On | Turn off if you only need the overall F-test result |\n| **Effect Size Display** | Shows eta-squared and omega-squared metrics | On | Keep on to understand practical significance beyond p-values |\n| **Minimum Group Size** | Excludes groups with fewer observations than this | 5 | Increase to 10+ for more stable estimates with noisy data |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node produces three main outputs:\n\n**Summary Statistics Table**: Shows mean, standard deviation, and count for each group. This gives you the "what\'s happening" view before diving into significance.\n\n**ANOVA Results Panel**: Displays the F-statistic, p-value, and degrees of freedom. A significant p-value (below 0.05 by default) means your groups genuinely differ beyond random chance.\n\n**Effect Size Metrics**: Eta-squared tells you what percentage of total variance your grouping explains. Values above 0.06 indicate meaningful group effects worth acting on.\n\n**Comparison Chart**: A box plot or mean plot showing distributions across groups, making differences visually obvious.\n\n**Post-hoc Comparison Matrix**: When enabled, shows which specific group pairs differ significantly—essential when you have 3+ groups.\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Group Effects node input port\n2. **Select your group variable** from the dropdown (your categorical column)\n3. **Select your outcome variable** (your continuous metric)\n4. **Click Run** and review the ANOVA results panel\n5. **Check the effect size**: if eta-squared > 0.06, examine the comparison chart to see which groups stand out\n6. **Review post-hoc tests** to identify specific pairs driving the differences\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter Group Effects, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Filter nodes** to isolate high-performing or problematic groups for deeper investigation\n- **Visualization nodes** to create presentation-ready charts of group differences\n- **Segment Profile** nodes to understand *why* groups differ by examining their characteristics\n- **Prediction nodes** to build models that treat group membership as a feature\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1**: Don\'t obsess over p-values alone. A tiny effect can be "statistically significant" with large samples but meaningless for business decisions. Always check effect sizes.\n\n**Tip 2**: If you have wildly different group sizes (like 500 in Group A, 12 in Group B), the ANOVA assumptions may be violated. Consider filtering to balanced samples first.\n\n**Tip 3**: The post-hoc comparison matrix gets cluttered fast with many groups. If you have 15+ categories, consider collapsing smaller groups or using a different segmentation.\n\n**Tip 4**: Use the chart export to drop group comparison visuals directly into stakeholder presentations. The visual pattern often tells the story better than statistics.\n\n**Tip 5**: If the overall F-test is non-significant but you *know* groups should differ, check for outliers in your outcome variable—they can mask real patterns.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you have 3-10 groups and want to quickly assess if any meaningful differences exist before investing in deeper analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Higher threshold catches marginal effects worth investigating |\n| `multiple_comparison` | None | Skip adjustment for speed; exploratory context |\n| `effect_size` | eta_squared | Simplest interpretation as proportion of variance |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 0 | Disable resampling to maximize speed |\n| `assumption_checks` | False | Skip diagnostics in exploration phase |\n\n**What you get:** Fast hypothesis screening that identifies which grouping variables warrant detailed investigation, with liberal detection of potential signals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Higher false positive rate means some "significant" results won\'t replicate under rigorous testing.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for stakeholder reporting, publication, or automated decision systems where statistical rigor and defensibility are paramount.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.01 | Conservative threshold reduces false discoveries |\n| `multiple_comparison` | bonferroni | Strict family-wise error control |\n| `effect_size` | omega_squared | Unbiased estimator for population inference |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 10000 | Robust confidence intervals without normality assumptions |\n| `assumption_checks` | True | Document violations that affect interpretation |\n| `welch_correction` | True | Robust to unequal variances across groups |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible results with conservative error control, complete diagnostic documentation, and distribution-free confidence intervals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower computation and reduced statistical power means real effects might not reach significance thresholds.\n\n### Recipe 3: Highly Imbalanced Groups\n\n**When to use:** Comparing groups with extreme size differences (e.g., 5,000 control users vs. 50 in experimental treatment, or rare event categories).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard threshold appropriate |\n| `welch_correction` | True | Essential for unequal group sizes/variances |\n| `effect_size` | cohens_d | Standardized difference unaffected by sample size |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 5000 | Resampling handles small-group instability |\n| `min_group_size` | 30 | Explicit threshold prevents spurious small-sample results |\n| `heteroscedasticity_test` | levene | Verify variance equality assumption |\n\n**What you get:** Valid inference despite group size asymmetry, with automatic safeguards against small-sample artifacts.\n\n**Trade-off:** Conservative filtering may exclude legitimately interesting small segments from analysis entirely.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Regime Detection\n\n**When to use:** Identifying structural breaks in continuous metrics by testing if sequential time windows represent distinct regimes (surprisingly effective alternative to change-point detection).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `grouping_var` | time_window_id | Discrete temporal segments (quarters, product cycles) |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard inference threshold |\n| `post_hoc` | games_howell | Identifies which specific periods differ |\n| `effect_size` | eta_squared | Quantifies regime shift magnitude |\n| `trend_removal` | True | Detrend before grouping to isolate level shifts |\n| `autocorrelation_adjust` | True | Correct standard errors for temporal dependence |\n\n**What you get:** Clear identification of when and how strongly regime changes occurred, with pairwise comparisons revealing transition dynamics.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires pre-specification of candidate breakpoints; won\'t discover unexpected timing of regime changes.\n\n## Business Getting this wrong would mean either underperforming stores or missed revenue opportunities for years.\n\n### The Data\n\nSarah pulled transaction data from the past six months: 847 customer purchases across Northbridge\'s 15 stores, which fell into three format types. She exported a clean table with store format, customer basket size, member status, and purchase date. The data looked straightforward, but she noticed immediately that the "Downtown" category had fewer observations—those flagship stores had lower foot traffic but possibly higher spenders. Here\'s what the first few rows looked like:\n\n| customer_id | store_format | basket_size | member_status | purchase_date |\n|-------------|--------------|-------------|---------------|---------------|\n| C10234      | Suburban     | 127.43      | Premium       | 2024-09-14    |\n| C10411      | Downtown     | 203.18      | Standard      | 2024-09-15    |\n| C10502      | Compact      | 89.75       | Premium       | 2024-09-15    |\n| C10583      | Suburban     | 156.22      | Standard      | 2024-09-16    |\n| C10634      | Downtown     | 278.90      | Premium       | 2024-09-17    |\n\nThe dataset had the usual messiness: a few typos in store_format ("SubUrban" vs "Suburban"), some missing member_status fields, and three outlier transactions above $500 that Sarah flagged for later inspection. She wanted to know two things: first, whether format actually explained meaningful variance in basket size (was this worth arguing about?), and second, which specific formats differed from each other.\n\nShe configured the analysis to compute the F-statistic for overall group differences, calculate eta-squared to measure effect size, and run post-hoc pairwise comparisons. She decided against fancy corrections for multiple comparisons—with only three groups, Bonferroni would be conservative enough without getting too academic for her audience.\n\n```python\nimport pandas as pd\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy import stats\n\n# Sarah\'s Group Effects analysis script\ndf = pd.read_csv(\'northbridge_transactions.csv\')\n\n# Clean format labels\ndf[\'store_format\'] = df[\'store_format\'].str.title().str.strip()\n\n# Group statistics\nformat_groups = df.groupby(\'store_format\')[\'basket_size\']\ngroup_stats = format_groups.agg([\'mean\', \'std\', \'count\'])\nprint("Group Means:\\n", group_stats)\n\n# ANOVA F-test\nformats = [group[\'basket_size\'].values \n           for name, group in df.groupby(\'store_format\')]\nf_stat, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*formats)\n\n# Effect size (eta-squared)\ngrand_mean = df[\'basket_size\'].mean()\nss_between = sum(len(group) * (group.mean() - grand_mean)**2 \n                 for group in formats)\nss_total = sum((df[\'basket_size\'] - grand_mean)**2)\neta_squared = ss_between / ss_total\n\nprint(f"\\nF-statistic: {f_stat:.2f}, p-value: {p_value:.4f}")\nprint(f"Eta-squared: {eta_squared:.3f}")\nprint(f"Format explains {eta_squared*100:.1f}% of basket size variance")\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '!'.
