What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Design Experiment node doesn\'t require historical data to get started—it\'s a planning tool that *generates* your experimental design. However, you can optionally connect existing data to inform your design decisions:\n\n**Optional Input:**\n- **Historical performance data** with outcome metrics (conversion rate, response time, etc.) to estimate variance and effect sizes\n- **Factor lists** containing the variables you want to test and their possible levels\n\nIf starting fresh, you\'ll configure everything directly in the node parameters.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Design Type** | The experimental structure (Full Factorial, Fractional Factorial, Latin Square, etc.) | Full Factorial | Use Fractional when you have 5+ factors to reduce experiment size; use Latin Square when controlling for two blocking variables |\n| **Factors** | Input variables you\'re testing (e.g., email subject line, price point, page layout) | Empty list | Add each variable you want to test with its levels (e.g., "Price: [$9, $14, $19]") |\n| **Response Variable** | The outcome metric you\'re measuring | None (required) | Set to your primary KPI—conversion rate, revenue, engagement time, etc. |\n| **Number of Replicates** | How many times to repeat each treatment combination | 3 | Increase for noisy data or small effect sizes; reduce to save resources when effects are large |\n| **Blocking Variables** | Grouping factors to control for (day of week, user segment, etc.) | None | Add when you know certain variables create systematic variation but aren\'t your focus |\n| **Randomization Seed** | Controls random assignment order | Random | Set a specific number only when you need reproducible assignment sequences |\n| **Power Target** | Minimum statistical power desired (probability of detecting real effects) | 0.80 | Increase to 0.90 for critical decisions; 0.80 is the research standard |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\nThe node generates a complete experimental plan with several components:\n\n**Design Table:** Shows every treatment combination to run, with randomized assignment order. For example, if testing 2 subject lines × 3 prices, you\'ll see 6 unique combinations, each replicated according to your settings.\n\n**Sample Size Calculator:** Displays the total number of experimental units needed and the expected statistical power given your configuration.\n\n**Balance Check Visualization:** A matrix showing how factors are distributed across your design, helping you spot any unintended imbalances.\n\n**Assignment Schedule:** A downloadable CSV ready to implement, with columns for Unit_ID, Treatment_Combination, and any blocking assignments.\n\n### Quick Start: Testing Email Campaign Variables\n\n1. **Drag the Design Experiment node** onto your canvas\n2. **Set Response Variable** to "open_rate" or your success metric\n3. **Add your first factor:** Click "+ Add Factor," name it "Subject_Style," add levels: ["Question", "Statement", "Urgency"]\n4. **Add your second factor:** "Send_Time" with levels: ["9AM", "2PM", "6PM"]\n5. **Choose Design Type:** Keep "Full Factorial" (gives you all 9 combinations)\n6. **Set Replicates:** Start with 3 to ensure statistical validity\n7. **Click Generate Design** and review the assignment table—you\'ll need 27 total sends (9 combinations × 3 replicates)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Experiment Tracker:** Feed your assignment schedule here to monitor incoming results and track which units received which treatments.\n\n**Statistical Test:** Once data is collected, connect to t-test, ANOVA, or Regression nodes to analyze which factors significantly impacted your outcome.\n\n**Decision Matrix:** Compare treatment combinations against business constraints (cost, feasibility) to select the optimal configuration.\n\n### Pro Tips from Experienced Users\n\n**Start smaller than you think.** New users often design experiments with 6+ factors and hundreds of treatment combinations. Start with 2–3 factors you believe have the largest effects. You can always run a follow-up experiment.\n\n**Use blocking strategically.** If you\'re running a week-long test, add "Day" as a blocking variable to account for weekend vs. weekday differences—this increases precision without increasing sample size.\n\n**Check the correlation matrix** in your design output. If two factors are perfectly correlated in your design, you won\'t be able to separate their effects. The tool will warn you, but it\'s worth understanding why.\n\n**Save your design specs.** The node exports a JSON configuration file—keep it! Six months later when someone asks "how did we design that pricing test?" you\'ll be grateful.\n\n**Pilot before full deployment.** Run 10–20% of your planned sample first, check data quality, then complete the full design. This catches implementation bugs early when they\'re cheap to fix.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototype Test\n\n- **When to use:** You need directional evidence quickly with minimal setup—early-stage features, low-traffic pages, or internal tool changes where perfection isn\'t required.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Higher tolerance for false positives speeds decision timeline |\n| `power` | 0.70 | Accept 30% miss rate on true effects to shrink sample size |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 10% relative lift | Only catch large, meaningful changes worth acting on |\n| `sample_ratio` | 1:1 | Equal split minimizes complexity in allocation logic |\n| `duration` | 7 days | One full week captures basic cyclicality without long commitment |\n\n- **What you get:** A conclusive answer in one week for effects larger than 10%, with 70% confidence you\'ll detect them if present.\n\n- **Trade-off:** You\'ll miss smaller effects and have higher false positive risk—acceptable for low-stakes decisions, dangerous for revenue-critical changes.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Revenue Test\n\n- **When to use:** Testing pricing changes, checkout flow modifications, or any experiment where incorrect conclusions directly impact business financials.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.01 | Minimize false positives that could lock in revenue-damaging changes |\n| `power` | 0.90 | High probability of detecting true effects worth the extra sample cost |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 2% relative lift | Detect even small revenue shifts that compound at scale |\n| `sample_ratio` | 1:1 | Balanced groups for cleanest variance estimation |\n| `duration` | 21 days | Three full weeks to smooth weekday/weekend and pay-cycle patterns |\n| `sequential_testing` | disabled | Avoid inflated error rates from peeking at results early |\n\n- **What you get:** Highly reliable conclusions for effects as small as 2%, with only 1% false positive risk and 90% detection probability.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Requires 3× the sample size and duration of rapid tests—expensive in time and opportunity cost, but necessary for high-stakes decisions.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Low-Traffic B2B Feature\n\n- **When to use:** Testing features in enterprise software with fewer than 200 weekly active users, where standard sample size calculators return "insufficient traffic."\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Accept higher false positive rate given sample constraints |\n| `power` | 0.65 | Deliberately underpowered but still informative |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 25% relative lift | Only detectable effects are large enough to matter anyway |\n| `sample_ratio` | 4:1 (control:treatment) | Preserve majority on known-good experience |\n| `duration` | 60 days | Extended runtime to accumulate rare conversion events |\n| `metric` | task completion rate | Binary outcome more efficient than continuous metrics in small samples |\n\n- **What you get:** Statistically-informed direction even with severe traffic constraints, focusing on large, unmissable shifts.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Cannot detect subtle improvements; results guide rather than definitively prove.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Novelty Effect Isolation\n\n- **When to use:** Testing UI redesigns, gamification, or notifications where initial user excitement artificially inflates early metrics before regressing to true steady-state impact.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard rigor for strategic decisions |\n| `power` | 0.80 | Standard detection threshold |\n| `minimum_detectable_effect` | 3% relative lift | Modest but meaningful improvement target |\n| `holdback_group` | 10% | Reserve untouched users for long-term comparison |\n| `duration` | 42 days | Six weeks allows novelty decay observation |\n| `analysis_window` | days 29–42 only | Measure steady-state behavior after initial excitement fades |\n\n- **What you get:** True sustained impact measurement isolated from temporary curiosity-driven engagement spikes.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Longer timeline and unused holdback segment increase cost, but prevent false wins from temporary effects.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender struggled with loan application abandonment rates They have 10,000 daily users and plan to run the experiment for two weeks. Which consideration reflects the most fundamental principle of experimental design?\n\nA) Whether to use a larger sample size in the treatment group than the control group to gather more data about the new feature\'s performance\n\nB) Whether the experimental units (users) are independently assigned to conditions so that one user\'s treatment doesn\'t affect another user\'s outcome\n\nC) Whether to randomize users to treatment and control conditions before the experiment starts to ensure groups are comparable on all measured and unmeasured characteristics\n\nD) Whether to segment users by device type and analyze each segment separately to understand where the new checkout flow performs best\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Randomization is the foundational principle that enables **causal inference** in experimental design—it ensures treatment and control groups are probabilistically equivalent on all characteristics (both observed and unobserved) before treatment application, allowing any observed differences in outcomes to be attributed to the treatment itself. Option A reflects a misconception that unequal group sizes improve learning about the treatment (they may reduce power for detecting differences). Option B describes the **Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA)**, which is an important validity condition but secondary to the randomization principle that creates comparable groups. Option D describes subgroup analysis, which is a post-experimental analytical choice rather than a design principle that enables causal inference. The key insight: without randomization, no amount of statistical sophistication can reliably separate treatment effects from pre-existing differences between groups.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. models.\n    \n    Returns test statistic, p-value, and confidence interval.\n    Positive difference means challenger is better (lower loss).\n    """\n    # Difference: incumbent - challenger (positive = challenger better)\n    differences = losses_incumbent - losses_challenger\n    n = len(differences)\n    \n    d_bar = np.mean(differences)\n    s_d = np.std(differences, ddof=1)\n    \n    # Test statistic\n    t_stat = d_bar / (s_d / np.sqrt(n))\n    \n    # Two-sided p-value\n    p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat), df=n-1))\n    \n    # Confidence interval\n    t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df=n-1)\n    ci_lower = d_bar - t_crit * s_d / np.sqrt(n)\n    ci_upper = d_bar + t_crit * s_d / np.sqrt(n)\n    \n    return {\n        \'mean_difference\': d_bar,\n        \'std_difference\': s_d,\n        \'t_statistic\': t_stat,\n        \'p_value\': p_value,\n        \'ci_lower\': ci_lower,\n        \'ci_upper\': ci_upper,\n        \'n_observations\': n\n    }\n\n# deviation:        {results[\'std_difference\']:.4f}")\nprint(f"t-statistic:               {results[\'t_statistic\']:.4f}")\nprint(f"p-value:                   {results[\'p_value\']:.4e}")\nprint(f"95% Both datasets must contain:\n\n- **Actual outcomes** (your ground truth labels)\n- **Predictions** from each model\n- **A common identifier** to align records (like customer_id or transaction_id)\n- *(Optional)* Segment columns if you want to analyze transitions across business units, regions, or customer types\n\nHere\'s what your input data should look like:\n\n| customer_id | actual_churn | incumbent_pred | challenger_pred | segment |\n|-------------|--------------|----------------|-----------------|---------|\n| C001        | 1            | 0.23           | 0.67            | Premium |\n| C002        | 0            | 0.45           | 0.12            | Standard|\n| C003        | 1            | 0.78           | 0.89            | Premium |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Performance Metric** | How model quality is measured (accuracy, AUC, precision, F1, RMSE, etc.) | AUC | Match this to your business objective—use precision if false positives are costly, recall if false negatives are critical |\n| **Significance Level** | Statistical threshold for declaring improvement (\u03b1) | 0.05 | Lower to 0.01 if you need very high confidence before transitioning; loosen to -10% if you\'re comfortable with experimentation |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node produces three main outputs:\n\n**Transition Recommendation Panel**: A clear go/no-go decision with confidence level, showing whether the challenger outperforms the incumbent with statistical significance. Each row shows the metric name, incumbent value, challenger value, absolute difference, and percentage change.\n\n**Segment Analysis Charts** *(if enabled)*: Heatmaps or bar charts showing where the challenger excels and where it might underperform. This helps you identify whether to do a full transition or a segmented rollout.\n\n**Prediction Shift Distribution**: A histogram showing how much predictions changed between models. Large shifts might indicate the challenger learned genuinely different patterns—or that something\'s wrong.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nConnect this node to:\n\n- **A/B Test Deployment** nodes to implement a controlled rollout if the decision is marginal\n- **Model Registry** to officially promote the challenger to production status\n- **Alert Configuration** to set up monitoring for the new model\'s ongoing performance\n- **Documentation Generator** to automatically record the transition decision and rationale\n\n### Quick Start: Your First Transition Analysis\n\n1. **Connect both model outputs** using the dual-input connectors at the top of the node\n2. **Map your columns**: Select which fields contain actuals, incumbent predictions, and challenger predictions\n3. **Choose your metric**: Pick the performance measure that matters most to your business decision\n4. **Set your standards**: Accept the 2% default minimum improvement or adjust based on your transition costs\n5. **Run the analysis** and review the recommendation panel—look for green lights *and* check the segment breakdown\n6. **Export the decision report** to share with stakeholders before making the switch\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Timing matters**: Run your transition analysis after both models have seen similar data volumes. Avoid comparing a model trained on six months of data with one trained on six days.\n\n**Watch for prediction drift, not just accuracy**: If the challenger makes wildly different predictions but similar overall accuracy, investigate why before transitioning. The model might be "right for the wrong reasons."\n\n**Don\'t ignore segment losers**: If your new model crushes it overall but performs worse on your highest-value customer segment, that\'s a red flag worth investigating.\n\n**Build in a grace period**: Set your rollback threshold slightly below your minimum improvement threshold. This gives the new model room to adapt without immediately reverting.\n\n**Document everything**: The node auto-generates a transition log, but add your own notes about *why* you made the decision. Future-you will thank present-you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial assessment of whether a new model architecture is worth pursuing, when Use "Nonlinear" for complex relationships |\n| **Constraint Definitions** | Resource limits and business rules | None | Add rows like "Labor Hours \u2264 1000" or "Product_A \u2265 100" to enforce limits |\n| **Solver Time Limit** | Maximum seconds to search for solution | 300 | Increase for complex problems with many variables; decrease for quick estimates |\n| **Optimality Gap** | How close to perfect (0% = exact, 5% = within 5% of optimal) | 0% | Increase to 1-5% for faster solutions on large problems where "close enough" works |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node outputs three things:\n\n**1. Decision Table** — Your input table with a new **Optimal Value** column showing the recommended decision for each variable. This is your action plan.\n\n**2. Solution Summary Card** displaying:\n- **Objective Value**: The best achievable result (total profit, minimum cost, etc.)\n- **Solution Status**: "Optimal" (found best answer), "Feasible" (found good answer), or "Infeasible" (no solution exists within constraints)\n- **Solve Time**: How long the optimization took\n\n**3. Sensitivity Report** (when available) — Shows how much objective coefficients or constraint limits could change before the optimal decision changes. Useful for "what-if" analysis.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n- **Filter** node \u2192 To extract only selected decisions (e.g., where Optimal Value > 0)\n- **Visualise** node \u2192 To create bar charts of recommended decisions or pie charts of resource allocation\n- **Export** node \u2192 To push decisions directly to operational systems or reports\n- **Calculate** node \u2192 To compute secondary metrics like total resource usage or revenue\n\n### Quick Start: Product Mix Optimization\n\n1. **Prepare your data** with one row per product, including profit per unit and resource requirements\n2. **Connect data to Optimise node** and map Variable Name, bounds, and Objective Coefficient columns\n3. **Set Objective to "Maximize"** and Optimization Type to "Linear"\n4. **Add constraints** like "Total_Labor \u2264 available_hours" using your constraint coefficient columns\n5. **Run the node** and check the Solution Status is "Optimal"\n6. **Review Optimal Value column** for how many units of each product to produce\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n- **Start simple**: Test with just 2-3 variables and one constraint before building your full model. Easier to debug.\n- **Check for infeasibility**: If you get "Infeasible", your constraints are too restrictive. Relax bounds or limits one at a time to find the culprit.\n- **Use integer sparingly**: Integer and binary variables slow solving dramatically. Only use them when decimals truly don\'t make sense.\n- **Scale your numbers**: If coefficients vary wildly (0.001 to 1,000,000), divide or multiply columns to bring them into similar ranges. Improves numerical stability.\n- **Save successful models**: Use the Template feature to save constraint definitions you\'ll reuse for monthly production planning or weekly scheduling.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Mode\n\n**When to use:** Initial problem scoping when you need to validate your objective function and constraints are correctly specified before investing in a full solve.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'GLOP\'` or `\'CBC\'` | Fast linear solver with minimal overhead |\n| `time_limit` | `30` | Stop after 30 seconds to get any feasible solution |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.10` | Accept solutions within 10% of optimal |\n| `presolve` | `True` | Let solver simplify problem structure |\n| `threads` | `1` | Avoid thread coordination overhead on small problems |\n\n**What you get:** A feasible solution quickly that confirms your model structure works, typically within seconds for problems under 10,000 variables.\n\n**Trade-off:** Solution quality may be far from optimal; use this only to debug formulation, not for actionable recommendations.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Solve\n\n**When to use:** Final deployment where solution quality directly impacts business outcomes and compute time is acceptable (e.g., weekly production planning, quarterly portfolio allocation).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'SCIP\'` or `\'Gurobi\'` | Industrial-strength solver with advanced techniques |\n| `time_limit` | `3600` | Allow up to 1 hour for convergence |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.001` | Require solutions within 0.1% of proven optimum |\n| `absolute_gap` | `1.0` | Stop if objective improvement drops below 1 unit |\n| `threads` | `-1` | Use all available CPU cores |\n| `emphasis` | `\'optimality\'` | Prioritize solution quality over feasibility speed |\n\n**What you get:** Near-optimal solutions with mathematically proven quality guarantees suitable for high-stakes decision-making.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly longer solve times; may not complete within time limit for very large problems (100,000+ integer variables).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Infeasible Problem Diagnosis\n\n**When to use:** Your model returns "no feasible solution" and you need to identify which constraints are causing conflicts.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'CBC\'` or `\'GLOP\'` | Good diagnostic reporting |\n| `relaxation_mode` | `\'elastic\'` | Allow constraint violations with penalties |\n| `violation_penalty` | `1000000` | High cost makes violations visible in solution |\n| `log_level` | `\'verbose\'` | Show detailed solver progress and conflict detection |\n| `write_model` | `True` | Export model file for external inspection |\n\n**What you get:** A solution showing exactly which constraints cannot be satisfied simultaneously, with violation magnitudes.\n\n**Trade-off:** Not a true optimization—you\'re diagnosing, not solving; requires manual constraint adjustment afterward.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Real-Time Reoptimization\n\n**When to use:** Live systems requiring rapid re-solving as conditions change (e.g., dynamic pricing, ride-sharing dispatch, intraday trading adjustment).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'GLOP\'` | Fastest for LP; use `\'CBC\'` if integer variables needed |\n| `warm_start` | `True` | Initialize from previous solution |\n| `time_limit` | `5` | Hard stop at 5 seconds for responsiveness |\n| `relative_gap` | `0.05` | Accept "good enough" solutions quickly |\n| `presolve` | `False` | Skip when problem structure unchanged from last solve |\n\n**What you get:** Sub-10-second response times enabling continuous re-optimization as new data arrives.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires incremental problem formulation; solutions are approximate but delivered fast enough for operational decisions.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needs to allocate £400M in lending capital across customer segments while managing risk exposure, regulatory capital requirements, and profit targets. The question was straightforward but critical: how should they allocate their inventory across the three warehouses to minimize total shipping costs while meeting customer demand? A 10% reduction in logistics costs would add nearly half a million dollars to annual profit.\n\n**The Data**\n\nLena pulled shipment records from the past six months and aggregated them into a cost matrix. The dataset showed the cost per pallet to ship from each warehouse to each customer region, along with warehouse capacity limits and regional demand forecasts:\n\n| From Warehouse | To Region | Cost per Pallet | Warehouse Capacity (pallets) | Region Demand (pallets) |\n|----------------|-----------|-----------------|------------------------------|-------------------------|\n| Chicago        | Midwest   | $45             | 5,000                        | 3,200                   |\n| Chicago        | Southeast | $120            | 5,000                        | 2,800                   |\n| Atlanta        | Midwest   | $95             | 4,200                        | 3,200                   |\n| Atlanta        | Southeast | $50             | 4,200                        | 2,800                   |\n| Denver         | West      | $40             | 3,500                        | 2,400                   |\n\nThe data wasn\'t perfect—some historical routes had incomplete cost records, and she had to estimate a few values based on mileage and average freight rates. Her objective was clear: minimize total shipping cost. She defined decision variables for each warehouse-to-region route—how many pallets to ship on each path. Then she added constraints: no warehouse could ship more than its capacity, and each region had to receive at least its forecasted demand. She chose linear programming as the solver type since all relationships were linear. Atlanta would pick up the remaining Southeast demand. Denver would exclusively serve the West. Under the current ad-hoc system, Chicago had been trying to serve both Midwest and Southeast proportionally, forcing expensive last-minute shipments when Southeast demand spiked. The optimization revealed that Chicago should **max out** its Midwest allocation first, where it had a huge cost advantage, then use remaining capacity for Southeast. Atlanta, despite being slightly farther from some Southeast customers, should absorb overflow because its per-pallet rate was still far better than Chicago\'s expedited pricing. "We\'ve been thinking about this warehouse-by-warehouse," Lena realized. The team agreed to a 90-day pilot using the optimized allocation. By the end of the quarter, logistics costs had dropped by $89,000—slightly under the projection due to some demand volatility, but still a 17% improvement. The savings were reinvested in expanding Denver\'s capacity to better serve the growing West Coast market.\n\n**What Lena Would Do Differently**\n\nLooking back, Lena wished she\'d incorporated uncertainty into the model from the start. Here\'s how to set it up in under two minutes:\n\n1. **Connect your returns data** – drag a connector from a node containing historical asset returns (one column per asset, rows are time periods)\n2. **Open the configuration panel** – the node defaults to mean-variance optimisation with no short-selling\n3. **Set your risk tolerance** – adjust the risk aversion parameter (start with 1.0 for balanced portfolios)\n4. **Run the optimisation** – click execute and review the weights table and efficient frontier chart\n5. **Export or connect downstream** – pipe the optimal weights to a Portfolio Backtest or Report node\n\n### Data Inputs\n\nThis node expects a **returns matrix**: each row represents a time period (daily, weekly, monthly), and each column represents an asset. The node calculates expected returns and covariance internally.\n\n**Example input shape:**\n\n| Date       | AAPL    | MSFT    | GOOGL   |\n|------------|---------|---------|---------|\n| 2023-01-01 | 0.012   | 0.008   | 0.015   |\n| 2023-01-02 | -0.005  | 0.003   | -0.002  |\n| 2023-01-03 | 0.007   | 0.011   | 0.009   |\n\nYou can also optionally connect a **constraints table** for advanced rules (e.g., sector limits, minimum/maximum position sizes).\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Risk Aversion** | How much you penalize variance vs. reward return (higher = more conservative) | 1.0 | Increase to 2–5 for conservative portfolios; decrease to 0.3–0.7 for aggressive growth |\n| **Allow Short Selling** | Permits negative weights (borrowing assets to sell) | Off | Turn on only if your strategy and brokerage support shorting; increases complexity |\n| **Weight Bounds** | Min/max allocation per asset (e.g., 0% to 20%) | 0% to 100% | Set max to 15–20% to avoid concentration risk; set min > 0% to force diversification |\n| **Target Return** | Forces portfolio to achieve this expected return | None | Use when you have a specific return goal (e.g., 8% annually); switches to return-constrained mode |\n| **Regularisation** | Adds L2 penalty to reduce extreme weights | 0 | Set to 0.01–0.1 when weights are too concentrated or unstable across re-optimisations |\n| **Estimation Window** | Number of recent periods to use for calculating returns/covariance | All data | Shorten to 60–120 periods for faster adaptation to market changes; risk overfitting to recent data |\n\n### Outputs\n\n**Optimal Weights Table** – A single-row table showing the fraction of capital to allocate to each asset. Sums to 100% (or your specified total). Export this to execute trades or feed into backtesting.\n\n**Performance Metrics Panel** – Displays expected portfolio return, volatility (standard deviation), and Sharpe ratio for the optimised portfolio.\n\n**Efficient Frontier Chart** – A curve showing the best possible return for each level of risk. Your optimised portfolio is highlighted as a point on this curve. Use this to visually assess trade-offs.\n\n**Contribution Analysis** – Bar chart breaking down which assets contribute most to portfolio risk and return. Helps you understand *why* the optimiser chose these weights.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n- **Portfolio Backtest** – Most common next step. Tests how the optimised weights would have performed historically.\n- **Report Builder** – Compiles weights, metrics, and charts into a client-ready document.\n- **Rebalancing Scheduler** – Automates periodic re-optimisation (e.g., monthly rebalancing).\n- **Risk Dashboard** – Monitors portfolio exposure against limits in real-time.\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n1. **Start with sample data** – Use the built-in "Tech 5" dataset to learn the interface before connecting your own data.\n\n2. **Regularisation prevents instability** – If weights swing wildly when you add one more day of data, add 0.05 regularisation to smooth them out.\n\n3. **Check correlation heatmaps first** – Highly correlated assets (>0.9) can cause numerical issues. Consider dropping redundant assets upstream.\n\n4. **Don\'t over-optimise on short histories** – With fewer than 60 periods, estimates are noisy. Use simpler strategies or increase regularisation.\n\n5. **Combine with scenario analysis** – Clone this node and re-run with stressed covariance matrices (e.g., 2008 crisis correlations) to test robustness.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you want to understand feasible solutions and sensitivity to constraints within seconds, not minutes.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `solver` | `\'OSQP\'` | Fastest general-purpose solver for QP problems |\n| `max_iter` | `1000` | Sufficient for simple problems; col_min)\n            else:  # Cost criterion\n                R[:, j] = (col_max - col) / (col_max - col_min)\n                \n        elif normalisation == "vector":\n            norm = np.sqrt((col ** 2).sum())\n            if d[j] == -1:\n                col = 1 / (col + 1e-10)  # Invert for cost criteria\n                norm = np.sqrt((col ** 2).sum())\n            R[:, j] = col / norm\n            \n        elif normalisation == "sum":\n            if d[j] == -1:\n                col = 1 / (col + 1e-10)\n            R[:, j] = col / col.sum()\n            \n        elif normalisation == "zscore":\n            R[:, j] = zscore(col) * d[j]  # Flip sign for cost criteria\n    \n    # Aggregation step\n    if aggregation == "saw":\n        # Simple Additive Weighting\n        scores = R @ w\n        \n    elif aggregation == "wpm":\n        # Weighted Product Model (requires positive normalised values)\n        R_positive = np.clip(R, 1e-10, None)\n        scores = np.prod(R_positive ** w, axis=1)\n        \n    elif aggregation == "topsis":\n        # TOPSIS method\n        V = R * w  # Weighted normalised matrix\n        \n        # Ideal and anti-ideal solutions\n        A_plus = V.max(axis=0)\n        A_minus = V.min(axis=0)\n        \n        # Euclidean distances\n        D_plus = np.sqrt(((V - A_plus) ** 2).sum(axis=1))\n        D_minus = np.sqrt(((V - A_minus) ** 2).sum(axis=1))\n        \n        # Relative closeness\n        scores = D_minus / (D_plus + D_minus + 1e-10)\n    \n    # Build results dataframe\n    results = decision_matrix.copy()\n    \n    # Add normalised scores\n    for j, criterion in enumerate(criteria):\n        results[f"{criterion}_norm"] = R[:, j]\n    \n    results["priority_score"] = scores\n    results["rank"] = results["priority_score"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)\n    \n    return results.sort_values("rank")\n\n\n# Example: Prioritising IT projects\nnp.random.seed(42)\n\n# Create realistic project data\nn_projects = 15\nprojects = pd.DataFrame({\n    "project_id": [f"PRJ-{i:03d}" for i in range(1, n_projects + 1)],\n    "expected_roi": np.random.uniform(0.05, 0.35, n_projects),  # 5% to 35%\n    "implementation_cost": np.random.uniform(50000, 500000, n_projects),  # £50K to £500K\n    "strategic_alignment": np.random.randint(1, 11, n_projects),  # 1-10 score\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/prioritise_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/prioritise_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You Need to Get Started\n\nThe Prioritise node expects a structured dataset where each row represents an alternative you\'re evaluating (a project, supplier, candidate, location, etc.) and each column represents a criterion you\'re scoring against. quantifying financial or operational risk from historical loss data:\n\n1. **Connect your loss events data** to the Quantify Risk node — you\'ll need at minimum a column with monetary values (losses, costs, or impacts)\n2. **Set your confidence level** to 95% (the standard for most business reporting)\n3. **Choose "Historical Simulation"** as your method if you have 100+ historical observations\n4. **Run the node** and review the Value at Risk (VaR) metric in the summary panel\n5. **Connect to a Decision Tree node** to evaluate risk mitigation options, or to a Report Builder to share findings with stakeholders\n\n### Data Inputs\n\nThis node expects a dataset where each row represents a potential or historical risk event:\n\n| Event_ID | Loss_Amount | Probability | Category calculation (e.g., 95% means "95% of outcomes are better than this") | 95% | Use 99% for conservative estimates in regulated industries; 90% for operational planning |\n| **Time Horizon** | Period over which risk is measured (days, months, quarters) | 1 year | Match to your planning cycle — quarterly for tactical decisions, annual for strategic |\n| **Number of Simulations** | Monte Carlo iterations (more = smoother distribution, slower processing) | 10,000 | Increase to 100,000 for final reports; decrease to 1,000 for exploratory analysis |\n| **Distribution Type** | Shape assumption Risk (VaR)**: "You can expect losses won\'t exceed $X with Y% confidence"\n- **Expected Shortfall (CVaR)**: Average loss in the worst-case scenarios beyond VaR\n- **Expected Loss**: Probability-weighted average across all scenarios\n\n**Generated Visualizations:**\n- **Loss Distribution Chart**: Histogram showing frequency of different loss amounts\n- **Risk Curve**: Cumulative probability plot — quickly see the likelihood of exceeding any threshold\n- **Scenario Breakdown**: If categories provided, shows contribution of each risk type\n\n**Added Data Columns:**\n- `simulated_loss`: Individual scenario outcomes (Monte Carlo only)\n- `percentile_rank`: Where each event falls in the overall distribution\n\n### Downstream Connections\n\n**Decision Tree**: Feed VaR metrics into branches to evaluate whether mitigation investments (insurance, controls) are cost-justified against quantified risk exposure.\n\n**Optimize**: Connect to resource allocation nodes to balance risk reduction across your portfolio of vulnerabilities.\n\n**Report Builder**: Pull summary metrics and visualizations directly into stakeholder dashboards.\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Start with Historical Simulation** even if your data is limited — it\'s more conservative than Monte Carlo and doesn\'t require you to assume a distribution shape that might not fit reality.\n\n**Check your tail**: Look at losses beyond the VaR threshold. If your top 5% of events are dramatically worse than the 95th percentile, Expected Shortfall tells a more complete story than VaR alone.\n\n**Segment your analysis**: Run separate risk quantifications by category, then aggregate. Cyber risks and operational risks rarely follow the same distribution.\n\n**Time-stamp matters**: If using historical data, ensure it\'s relevant. Three-year-old cyber incident data likely understates current risk.\n\n**Sanity-check with domain experts**: A calculated VaR of $2M means nothing if your CFO knows the realistic worst-case is $500K. Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/scenario_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/scenario_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Scenario node expects a **base forecast or model output** as its primary input—typically a table with one row per forecast period or decision point, plus columns for your key metrics (revenue, cost, demand, etc.).\n\n**Required columns:**\n- At least one **date or identifier column** (to define your time horizon or decision points)\n- One or more **metric columns** (numeric values you want to vary across scenarios)\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| Month | Base_Revenue | Base_Cost |\n|-------|-------------|-----------|\n| Jan   | 100000      | 60000     |\n| Feb   | 105000      | 62000     |\n| Mar   | 110000      | 64000     |\n\nThe node will generate multiple scenario variations from this baseline, applying the adjustments you configure.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Scenario Variables** | Select which columns to vary across scenarios | None | Choose the metrics most uncertain or controllable (e.g., price, demand, conversion rate) |\n| **Adjustment Method** | How to modify values: percentage change, absolute shift, or multiplier | Percentage | Use absolute for additive changes (±1000 units); percentage for proportional uncertainty (±15%) |\n| **Optimistic Adjustment** | Upper bound for the optimistic scenario | +20% | Increase for highly volatile markets; decrease for conservative planning |\n| **Pessimistic Adjustment** | Lower bound for the pessimistic scenario | -20% | Mirror your optimistic setting, or make asymmetric if downside risk is greater |\n| **Number of Scenarios** | Generate base + N additional scenarios | 3 (base, optimistic, pessimistic) | Add 5–7 scenarios for Monte Carlo-style analysis with mid-range variations |\n| **Scenario Names** | Custom labels for each scenario | "Base", "Optimistic", "Pessimistic" | Use business-meaningful names like "Economic Downturn" or "Competitor Entry" |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\nThe Scenario node outputs an **expanded table** with all your original rows duplicated for each scenario, plus:\n\n**Added columns:**\n- **Scenario_Name**: Text label identifying which scenario each row belongs to\n- **[Metric]_Adjusted**: New columns for each variable you chose to vary, showing the scenario-specific values\n- **Scenario_ID**: Numeric identifier for filtering and grouping\n\n**Visualizations displayed:**\n- **Scenario Comparison Chart**: Line or bar chart showing how your key metric evolves across all scenarios\n- **Sensitivity Tornado**: Horizontal bar chart ranking which variables create the biggest swings in outcomes\n- **Range Fan Chart**: Visual envelope showing the spread between best and worst cases over time\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter scenario analysis, you\'ll typically route to:\n\n- **Decision Tree** or **Optimization** nodes to identify which strategy performs best across scenarios\n- **Aggregation** nodes to calculate summary statistics (average outcome, worst-case, probability-weighted expected value)\n- **Filter** nodes to isolate specific scenarios for detailed drill-down\n- **Visualization** nodes to create executive dashboards comparing scenario outcomes side-by-side\n\n### Quick Start: Three-Scenario Revenue Forecast\n\n1. **Connect your forecast table** to the Scenario node (must include date and revenue columns)\n2. **Select "Revenue" as your Scenario Variable** in the configuration panel\n3. **Set Adjustment Method to "Percentage"** and enter +30% optimistic, -30% pessimistic\n4. **Leave Number of Scenarios at 3** (base, high, low)\n5. **Run the node** and examine the Scenario Comparison Chart to see your revenue range\n6. **Connect to an Aggregation node** to calculate total revenue by scenario for decision-making\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Start with asymmetric scenarios.** Real business risks are rarely symmetric—a 20% upside might be possible, but a 40% downside could be catastrophic. Reflect this in your adjustment parameters.\n\n**Use scenario names that tell a story.** "Scenario_2" is forgettable; "Supply Chain Disruption" instantly communicates what assumptions changed and helps stakeholders engage with the analysis.\n\n**Don\'t vary everything at once.** Begin with 1–2 key drivers, validate the output makes business sense, then layer in additional variables. This builds intuition and prevents "scenario explosion."\n\n**Chain scenarios with filters for contingency planning.** Create a separate analysis branch for each scenario to develop scenario-specific action plans, rather than trying to find one "optimal" strategy.\n\n**Remember correlation matters.** If price goes up, volume usually goes down. The Scenario node varies each input independently by default—you may need to encode relationships in upstream formula nodes first.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial scoping when you have 3–5 uncertain variables and need directional insights within minutes, not publication-ready results.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_scenarios` | 8–12 | Covers basic factorial combinations without computational overhead |\n| `sampling_method` | `\'grid\'` | Ensures corner cases are included; transparent logic |\n| `monte_carlo_samples` | 0 | Skip probabilistic simulation entirely |\n| `confidence_interval` | `None` | No uncertainty quantification needed yet |\n| `parallel` | `False` | Overhead exceeds benefit at this scale |\n\n**What you get:** Clear best-case/worst-case boundaries and intuition about which variables dominate outcomes.\n\n**Trade-off:** No statistical rigor or probability-weighted expectations—purely deterministic corner exploration.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Decision Support\n\n**When to use:** Board presentations, regulatory submissions, or capital allocation decisions requiring defensible probabilistic forecasts.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_scenarios` | 1000 | Smooth probability distributions across outcome space |\n| `sampling_method` | `\'sobol\'` | Low-discrepancy quasi-random coverage; better than pure Monte Carlo |\n| `monte_carlo_samples` | 10000 | Stable percentile estimates (95% CI within ±0.5%) |\n| `confidence_interval` | `0.95` | Standard for executive reporting |\n| `parallel` | `True` | Cuts runtime from hours to minutes |\n| `seed` | `42` | Reproducibility for audits |\n| `output_format` | `\'pdf_report\'` | Includes tornado charts, CDFs, scenario trees |\n\n**What you get:** Publication-ready probabilistic forecasts with variance decomposition showing each input\'s contribution to outcome uncertainty.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires 50–200× more compute than exploration; overkill if assumptions are still unstable.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Correlated Risk Modeling\n\n**When to use:** Financial portfolios, supply chain disruptions, or any domain where inputs move together (interest rates + exchange rates, or demand + commodity prices).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_scenarios` | 500 | Balance between correlation accuracy and speed |\n| `sampling_method` | `\'latin_hypercube\'` | Better stratification than Sobol for correlated inputs |\n| `correlation_matrix` | Custom (e.g., `[[1, 0.7], [0.7, 1]]`) | Encode historical or expert-estimated dependencies |\n| `copula` | `\'gaussian\'` | Preserves marginal distributions while enforcing correlation |\n| `tail_dependence` | `0.3` | Captures joint extreme events (both inputs hit worst-case together) |\n\n**What you get:** Scenarios that reflect realistic co-movement patterns, avoiding the independence fallacy that understates risk.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires estimating correlation structure—garbage-in-garbage-out if correlations are guessed poorly.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Reverse Stress Testing\n\n**When to use:** Identifying "what would have to go wrong" for a strategy to fail catastrophically—required by many financial regulators, useful for resilience planning.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `target_outcome` | Critical threshold (e.g., `\'NPV < 0\'`) | Define failure explicitly |\n| `sampling_method` | `\'targeted\'` | Concentrates samples near the failure boundary |\n| `n_scenarios` | 200 | Enough to map the failure surface |\n| `sensitivity_analysis` | `True` | Shows which input combinations lead to failure |\n| `visualize_boundary` | `True` | 2D/3D plots of the "failure zone" |\n\n**What you get:** A map of dangerous input combinations and early warning indicators (e.g., "if variable X exceeds 1.2 *and* Y drops below 0.8, abort").\n\n**Trade-off:** Only explores failure region—tells you nothing about upside scenarios or typical performance.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needs to maintain adequate capital buffers under Basel III while Their analyst creates three scenarios: "Optimistic" (high demand, low competition), "Pessimistic" (low demand, high competition), and "Most Likely" (moderate demand and competition). What is the primary limitation of this approach to scenario analysis?\n\nA) The scenarios should include at least five different outcome levels to properly capture the range of uncertainty\n\nB) The scenarios treat independent variables (demand and competition) as if they always move together in predictable patterns\n\nC) The scenarios are defined by outcome desirability rather than by coherent sets of driving assumptions about the future business environment\n\nD) The analysis lacks quantitative modeling and relies too heavily on qualitative assessments\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Effective scenario analysis constructs scenarios around coherent sets of *assumptions about uncertain driving forces* (e.g., "Economic boom + regulatory liberalization" versus "Recession + trade restrictions"), not around outcome attractiveness. Option C correctly identifies that labeling scenarios by desirability ("Optimistic"/"Pessimistic") confuses outputs with inputs and prevents genuine exploration of different plausible futures. Option B represents a real concern but misdiagnoses the problem—the issue isn\'t correlation between variables but rather starting from outcomes instead of drivers. Option A reflects a misconception that more scenarios always improve analysis, when quality and coherence matter more than quantity. Option D mistakes scenario analysis for simulation; scenarios can be qualitative or quantitative, and the method\'s value lies in structured exploration of multiple futures, not in mathematical sophistication.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. stakeholders.\n\n3. **Check for dominated strategies early** — if a decision loses in every scenario, remove it to simplify your analysis.\n\n4. **Export the regret chart for presentations** — executives immediately grasp "how wrong could we be" better than abstract robustness scores.\n\n5. **Use the scenario weighting thoughtfully** — equal weights often reveal more than Initial investment: Triangular(8M, 10M, 15M)\n    - Annual revenue: Lognormal(\u03bc=2.5M, \u03c3=0.3M)\n    - Operating costs: Normal(\u03bc=1.2M, \u03c3=0.2M)\n    - Discount rate: Normal(\u03bc=0.10, \u03c3=0.02)\n    - operating_costs[sim, year-1]\n            discount_factor = (1 + discount_rate[sim]) ** year\n            npv[sim] += cash_flow / discount_factor\n    \n    return npv, investment, annual_revenue, operating_costs, discount_rate\n\n\ndef calculate_risk_metrics(outcomes, confidence_levels=[0.05, 0.10, 0.25]):\n    """\n    Calculate comprehensive risk metrics from simulation outcomes.\n    """\n    losses = -outcomes  # Convert to loss perspective\n    \n    metrics = {\n        \'mean\': np.mean(outcomes),\n        \'std\': np.std(outcomes),\n        \'median\': np.median(outcomes),\n        \'skewness\': stats.skew(outcomes),\n        \'kurtosis\': stats.kurtosis(outcomes),\n        \'prob_positive\': np.mean(outcomes > 0),\n        \'prob_loss_gt_5m\': np.mean(outcomes < -5)\n    }\n    \n    # Value at Risk and CVaR at various confidence levels\n    for alpha in confidence_levels:\n        var = np.percentile(losses, 100 * (1 - alpha))\n        cvar = losses[losses >= var].mean() if np.any(losses >= var) else var\n        metrics[f\'VaR_{int((1-alpha)*100)}\'] = var\n        metrics[f\'CVaR_{int((1-alpha)*100)}\'] = cvar\n    \n    return metrics\n\n\n# Run basic simulation\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint("Example 1: Capital Project NPV Risk Simulation")\nprint("=" * 60)\n\nnpv_results, inv, rev, costs, rates = simulate_project_npv(n_simulations=50000)\nmetrics = calculate_risk_metrics(npv_results)\n\nprint(f"\\nSimulation Results (n=50,000):")\nprint(f"  Expected NPV:           £{metrics[\'mean\']:.2f}M")\nprint(f"  Standard Deviation:\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/simulate-risk_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/simulate-risk_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Simulate Risk node expects a dataset with at least one **numeric column** representing the uncertain variable you want to simulate (revenue, cost, demand, etc.). risk exceeds acceptable levels\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Start with fewer simulations during setup.** Run 1,000 iterations while you\'re experimenting with distributions and parameters, then scale to 10,000+ for final analysis. Your iterations will be 10× faster.\n\n**The distribution matters more than you think.** A Normal distribution assumes outcomes can go negative; use Log-Normal or Gamma for strictly positive variables like revenue or time durations.\n\n**Check the histogram before trusting the numbers.** If you see a weird shape (multiple peaks, hard cutoffs), your distribution assumptions may not match reality.\n\n**Use triangular distributions when stakeholders think in min/likely/max.** It\'s easier to elicit three-point estimates from business partners than to explain standard deviations.\n\n**Correlation is where beginners get burned.** If you\'re simulating multiple variables independently but they actually move together (like material costs and shipping costs), your total risk will be understated. Add correlation when variables share common drivers.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial feasibility check on a new business case when you need directional insight within minutes, not publication-ready precision.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_simulations` | 1,000 | Minimum for stable percentile estimation |\n| `random_seed` | 42 | Reproducibility during iterative exploration |\n| `sampling_method` | "latin_hypercube" | Better coverage than pure random at low N |\n| `output_percentiles` | [10, 50, 90] | Focus on median and plausible range only |\n| `correlation_method` | "none" | Skip unless you know dependencies exist |\n\n**What you get:** Rough probability bounds in under 30 seconds; sufficient to decide whether to invest in detailed modeling.\n\n**Trade-off:** Tail estimates (P5, P95) will be noisy; unsuitable for regulatory reporting or capital reserving.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Risk Reporting\n\n**When to use:** Quarterly enterprise risk assessments, regulatory filings, or any output where audit trail and statistical rigor are mandatory.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_simulations` | 50,000 | Stable estimates to P1/P99 with <2% variance |\n| `random_seed` | System timestamp | Defensible non-cherry-picking; log separately |\n| `sampling_method` | "sobol" | Quasi-random for deterministic coverage |\n| `output_percentiles` | [1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 95, 99] | Full distribution characterization |\n| `correlation_method` | "copula" | Preserve tail dependencies between risk factors |\n| `convergence_check` | True | Halt if running variance exceeds tolerance |\n| `antithetic_variates` | True | Variance reduction without added compute |\n\n**What you get:** Publication-grade distributions with documented convergence; defendable in board meetings or audits.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime typically 20–50× slower than exploration mode; requires validated correlation matrices.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Fat-Tailed Event Modeling\n\n**When to use:** Insurance reserves, cybersecurity loss estimation, or any domain where rare catastrophic outcomes dominate expected value.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_simulations` | 100,000 | Need dense sampling in extreme tails |\n| `input_distributions` | Student\'s t (df=3) or Pareto | Heavy-tailed, not normal assumptions |\n| `sampling_method` | "importance" | Oversample tail regions explicitly |\n| `importance_threshold` | 95th percentile | Focus compute where losses hurt most |\n| `output_percentiles` | [90, 95, 99, 99.5, 99.9] | Standard percentiles mislead here |\n\n**What you get:** Reliable estimates of 1-in-100 and 1-in-1000 events that normal distributions severely underestimate.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires subject-matter expertise to specify appropriate heavy-tailed distributions; standard datasets rarely inform these tails.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Portfolio Rebalancing Under Constraints\n\n**When to use:** Optimizing asset allocations, supply chain node weights, or resource distribution when constraints (budget caps, minimum thresholds) interact with uncertainty.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_simulations` | 10,000 | Sufficient for constraint violation rates |\n| `constraint_check` | "per_scenario" | Test feasibility in each future, not just average |\n| `objective_function` | "conditional_value_at_risk" | Optimize worst 5% outcomes, not mean |\n| `resampling_method` | "bootstrap" | Assess solution stability across sample variation |\n\n**What you get:** Allocations that remain feasible across scenarios, with quantified probability of constraint violation.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computationally expensive; may require convex solver integration for each simulation iteration.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needs to set capital reserves to meet regulatory requirements while remaining competitive on loan pricing. You\'ll need:\n\n- **Date column**: Your time dimension (Date type)\n- **Outcome column**: The metric you\'re trying to explain—revenue, conversions, signups (Numeric)\n- **Marketing spend columns**: One column per channel with spend amounts (Numeric)\n- **Control variables** (optional): Seasonality indicators, promotions, external factors (Numeric or Categorical)\n\n**Example input shape:**\n\n| |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Outcome Variable** | The metric you\'re modeling (dependent variable) | First numeric column | Set to your KPI—revenue, conversions, etc. |\n| **Date Column** | Time dimension for the model | Auto-detected | Change if multiple date fields exist |\n| **Marketing Channels** | Which columns represent marketing spend | All numeric columns | Deselect non-marketing columns like revenue |\n| **Adstock Type** | How advertising effects issues.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `adstock_max_lag` | 4 | Limits computational load while capturing immediate effects |\n| `model_type` | `ridge` Production-Grade Attribution Model\n\n**When to use:** Building a model for quarterly budget planning where stakeholders will redistribute 6–7 figure budgets based on your ROI estimates.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `adstock_max_lag` | 13 | Captures full quarterly carry-over effects |\n| `model_type` | `bayesian_ridge` | Provides uncertainty intervals for ROI confidence bounds |\n| `n_iterations` | 10000 | Ensures posterior convergence and stable coefficient estimates |\n| `saturation_function` | `hill` | Models diminishing returns with flexible inflection points |\n| `control_variables` | `[seasonality, trend, events, macroeconomic]` | Isolates marketing effects from confounders |\n| `holdout_validation` | `time_series_cv` with 4 folds | Protects against overfitting to recent volatility |\n| `prior_strength` | 0.3 | Weakly informative—respects domain knowledge without overriding data |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible, uncertainty-quantified ROI estimates suitable for executive presentation and financial commitment.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime of 2-6 hours and requires careful prior elicitation for each channel—not viable for rapid iteration.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Multicollinearity Environments\n\n**When to use:** Your channels are highly correlated (e.g., paid search, shopping, and brand campaigns all spike during promotions), causing unstable coefficient estimates.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model_type` | `elastic_net` | L1 penalty handles feature selection when channels are redundant |\n| `alpha` | 0.5 | Balances L1 (sparsity) and L2 (stability) |\n| `channel_grouping` | `enabled` | Combines correlated channels into meta-channels pre-modeling |\n| `vif_threshold` | 5 | Flags problematic collinearity before fitting |\n\n**What you get:** Sparse, interpretable coefficients that don\'t flip signs between model runs.\n\n**Trade-off:** You lose granular channel attribution—grouped channels share credit collectively.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Product Launch Attribution\n\n**When to use:** Measuring marketing effectiveness during a new product launch where no baseline exists and marketing drives 100% of initial awareness.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `baseline_estimation` | `disabled` | No organic demand exists yet—all volume is marketing-attributed |\n| `time_window` | First 90 days only | Avoids mixing launch dynamics with steady-state behavior |\n| `adstock_priors` | Channel-specific decay from comparable launches | Borrows strength from historical patterns |\n\n**What you get:** Full credit assignment to marketing without incorrectly marketing channel, feature, or intervention\n- **Conversion Flag** (binary: 0/1): Indicates whether this event resulted in the desired outcome\n- **Optional: Conversion Value** (numeric): Revenue or | 0 | 0 |\n| U001 | 2024-01-07 | Social | 0 | 0 |\n| U001 | 2024-01-10 | Search | 1 | 150 |\n| U002 | 2024-01-06 | Display | 0 | 0 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Attribution Model** | How credit is distributed across touchpoints | Last-touch | Use "Linear" for equal credit, "Time Decay" when recency matters, "Shapley" for game-theoretic fairness |\n| **Lookback Window** | Maximum days between first touch and conversion | 30 days | Extend to 60-90 days for long sales cycles (B2B, high-ticket items); shorten to 7-14 days for fast purchases |\n| **Conversion Window** | Hours after last touchpoint to count as conversion | 24 hours | Reduce to 1-2 hours for immediate actions (app installs); extend to 7 days for considered purchases |\n| **Minimum Touchpoints** | Exclude journeys with fewer interactions | 2 | Set to 1 to include direct conversions; increase to 3+ to focus on complex multi-touch journeys |\n| **Position Weighting** | Emphasis on first/last touch (for position-based models) | 40-20-40 | Adjust middle percentage if you want to credit assisting touches more heavily |\n\n### What You\'ll See as Output\n\nThe node generates three main outputs:\n\n**Attribution Table** (new columns added to your data):\n- `attribution_credit`: Fractional credit assigned to each touchpoint (sums to 1.0 per journey)\n- `attributed_value`: Monetary value allocated based on credit and conversion value\n- `position_in_journey`: Numeric position (1 = first touch, etc.)\n- `journey_length`: Total touchpoints in this user\'s conversion path\n\n**Summary Metrics Panel:**\n- Total attributed conversions by channel\n- Average journey length to conversion\n- Most common conversion paths (top 10)\n- Channel efficiency scores (attributed value per touchpoint)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- Sankey diagram showing flow between touchpoints\n- Bar Optimizer** to reallocate spend based on true contribution (most common next step)\n- **Segmentation** to identify high-value customer journey patterns\n- **What-If Scenario** to model impact of user interactions with marketing channels\n2. **Map columns**: user_id \u2192 Customer ID, timestamp \u2192 Event Time, channel \u2192 Touchpoint, purchase_flag \u2192 Conversion\n3. **Select "Time Decay"** as your attribution model (weights recent touches more heavily)\n4. **Set lookback window to 30 days** (typical for e-commerce)\n5. **Run the node** and examine the attribution table\n6. Tips from Experienced Users\n\n1. **Always run multiple models side-by-side** — Compare linear, time decay, and Shapley results. If they roughly agree, you can be confident in the findings. Large discrepancies mean your choice matters significantly.\n\n2. **Check for data leakage** — If your conversion rate is suspiciously high, you may have included post-purchase touchpoints. Filter to only pre-conversion events.\n\n3. **Segment before attributing** — Run separate attribution analyses for new vs. returning customers. Their journeys differ dramatically, and blending them obscures insights.\n\n4. **Watch for the "long tail"** — 80% of conversions often come from 5-7 common paths. Use the minimum touchpoints filter to reduce noise from rare journey patterns.\n\n5. **Validate with holdout tests** — After reallocating budget based on attribution, run controlled experiments to confirm the model\'s predictions match real-world lift.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Channel Triage\n\n**When to use:** You have 2–4 weeks of clickstream data and need to decide tomorrow which marketing channels deserve further investigation.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `first_touch` | Fastest computation, no convergence issues |\n| `lookback_window` | `7 days` | Captures recency without diluting signal in sparse data |\n| `min_events_per_path` | `3` | Filters noise while retaining 80%+ of conversion paths |\n| `attribution_window` | `24 hours` | Focuses on direct-response channels only |\n\n**What you get:** A rough rank-ordering of channels by conversion contribution, computed in minutes even on 100K+ sessions.\n\n**Trade-off:** You completely ignore lagged effects and cross-channel synergies—fine for initial filtering, dangerous for budget allocation.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Multi-Touch Attribution\n\n**When to use:** You\'re building a recurring report that CFO will use to justify quarterly marketing spend across 8+ channels.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `shapley_value` | Game-theoretic fairness; defensible in exec meetings |\n| `lookback_window` | `30 days` | Industry standard for considered purchases |\n| `min_paths_per_channel` | `100` | Ensures statistically stable estimates |\n| `attribution_window` | `90 days` | Captures full customer journey for B2B/high-ticket |\n| `convergence_threshold` | `0.001` | Tight tolerance for consistent month-over-month comparisons |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | `1000` | Generates confidence intervals for budget decisions |\n\n**What you get:** Auditable attribution scores with uncertainty bounds, stable across reporting periods.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation takes 10–50× longer than heuristic models; requires dedicated pipeline infrastructure.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Post-iOS14 Mobile Attribution\n\n**When to use:** Your mobile app conversion tracking broke after ATT framework implementation and deterministic matching dropped below 40%.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `markov_chain` | Handles probabilistic state transitions when identifiers fragment |\n| `matching_strategy` | `probabilistic` | Accepts fuzzy joins on device fingerprints |\n| `lookback_window` | `3 days` | Shorter window where probabilistic matching stays accurate |\n| `removal_effect_threshold` | `0.15` | Aggressive pruning of low-signal channels in noisy data |\n| `aggregate_by` | `campaign_type` | Groups granular sources to recover statistical power |\n\n**What you get:** Attribution estimates despite 60% user-level tracking loss, trading individual precision for aggregate accuracy.\n\n**Trade-off:** Cannot attribute individual conversions; Each row represented one touchpoint in a customer\'s path to purchase:\n\n| customer_id | touchpoint_date | channel       | conversion | revenue |\n|-------------|----------------|---------------|------------|---------|\n| C10423      | 2024-01-12     | Instagram     | 0          | 0       |\n| C10423      | 2024-01-14     | Google Search | 0          | 0       |\n| C10423      | 2024-01-18     | Email         | 1          | 287     |\n| C10891      | 2024-01-15     | Podcast       | 0          | 0       |\n| C10891      | 2024-01-16     | Email         | 1          | 412     |\n\nThe dataset had 340,000 rows spanning 89,000 customers. Shapley values, borrowed from game theory, would calculate each channel\'s marginal contribution by considering all possible orderings of touchpoints—mathematically fair, if computationally expensive.\n\nShe configured her analysis to:\n- Group journeys by `customer_id`\n- Order by `touchpoint_date`\n- Attribute based on `conversion` as the outcome\n- Weight contributions by `revenue` to understand value, not just volume\n\nShe also set a 30-day attribution window—touchpoints older than that were excluded. "If someone saw an Instagram ad two months ago," she reasoned, "it\'s probably not causing today\'s purchase."\n\n## The Results\n\nThe Shapley attribution model ran for six minutes, iterating through journey permutations. The output reshaped everything:\n\n| channel       | Shapley_credit | pct_of_revenue | last_click_pct |\n|---------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|\n| Instagram     | 0.28           | 28%            | 8%             |\n| Google Search | 0.24           | 24%            | 19%            |\n| Email         | 0.22           | 22%            | 61%            |\n| Podcast       | 0.18           | 18%            | 7%             |\n| Affiliate     | 0.08           | 8%             | 5%             |\n\nInstagram, which received only 8% credit under last-click, was actually contributing 28% of revenue when its assistive role was properly valued. Email was still important, but less dominant than it appeared. Podcast sponsorships—nearly canceled the previous quarter—were driving 18% of attributed value, primarily by initiating journeys that converted later through other channels.\n\n## The Insight\n\nThe "aha moment" came when Sarah overlaid budget allocation. Instagram was getting 12% of spend but driving 28% of attributed revenue. Podcast was getting 8% of spend but contributing 18%. Email, meanwhile, was receiving 35% of budget but only contributing 22%. \n\n"Email isn\'t performing badly," Sarah explained in the follow-up meeting. "It\'s just overinvested. It\'s a great closer, but we\'re starving the channels that start customer journeys. We\'re optimizing for the last step and wondering why the funnel is shrinking."\n\n## The Decision\n\nSarah presented to the executive team the following Wednesday. The CMO initially pushed back—"Shapley values sound academic"—but the CFO loved the game-theoretic fairness angle. They agreed to a three-month reallocation test: shift 8% of budget from email to Instagram and podcast, particularly targeting lookalike audiences that matched converter profiles.\n\nBy Q4, the test showed a 14% increase in new customer acquisition and a 6% increase in overall revenue with the same total spend. Email performance barely declined—the team had been over-sending anyway. The reallocation became permanent.\n\n## What Sarah Would Do Differently\n\nReflecting later, Sarah noted two limitations. First, Shapley values treat all orderings as equally likely, but customer journeys have patterns—people rarely see an email *before* an Instagram ad. A Markov chain model might better capture sequential dependencies. Columns are units, rows are time periods.\n    treated_unit : int\n        Column index of the treated unit (0-indexed).\n    pre_periods : int\n        Number of pre-treatment periods (T_0).\n    covariates : np.ndarray, optional\n        Shape (K, J+1) matrix of additional covariates.\n    v_weights : np.ndarray, optional\n        Diagonal weights for predictor importance. If None, optimised.\n    \n    Returns\n    -------\n    dict\n        Contains weights, synthetic control series, treatment effects, and fit statistics.\n    """\n    T, n_units = outcome_matrix.shape\n    donor_indices = [j for j in range(n_units) if j != treated_unit]\n    n_donors = len(donor_indices)\n    \n    # Extract treated and donor outcomes\n    Y_treated = outcome_matrix[:, treated_unit]\n    Y_donors = outcome_matrix[:, donor_indices]\n    \n    # Build predictor matrix (pre-treatment outcomes + covariates)\n    X_treated = Y_treated[:pre_periods].copy()\n    X_donors = Y_donors[:pre_periods, :].copy()\n    \n    if covariates is not None:\n        X_treated = np.concatenate([X_treated, covariates[:, treated_unit]])\n        X_donors = np.vstack([X_donors, covariates[:, donor_indices]])\n    \n    k = len(X_treated)  # Number of predictors\n    \n    def compute_weights(v_diag: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:\n        """Inner optimisation: find W given V."""\n        V = np.diag(v_diag)\n        \n        def loss_w(w):\n            diff = X_treated - X_donors @ w\n            return diff @ V @ diff\n        \n        # Constraints: weights sum to 1, all non-negative\n        constraints = {\'type\': \'eq\', \'fun\': lambda w: np.sum(w) - 1}\n        bounds = [(0, 1) for _ in range(n_donors)]\n        w0 = np.ones(n_donors) / n_donors\n        \n        result = minimize(loss_w, w0, method=\'SLSQP\', bounds=bounds, \n                         constraints=constraints, options={\'maxiter\': 1000})\n        return result.x\n    \n    def outer_loss(v_diag: np.ndarray) -> float:\n        """Outer optimisation: find V to minimise pre-treatment MSPE."""\n        w = compute_weights(v_diag)\n        Y_synth_pre = Y_donors[:pre_periods, :] @ w\n        mspe = np.mean((Y_treated[:pre_periods] - Y_synth_pre) ** 2)\n        return mspe\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/build-synthetic-control_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/build-synthetic-control_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### Quick Start\n\nHere\'s the fastest path to your first synthetic control analysis:\n\n1. **Prepare your panel data** with three key columns: unit identifier (like country or state), time period (dates or years), and your outcome variable (the metric you\'re measuring).\n2. **Drag the Synthetic Control node** onto your canvas and connect your data.\n3. **Specify your treated unit** (e.g., "California") and the intervention date (e.g., "2010-01-01").\n4. **Select your donor pool** — the comparison units that could form your synthetic control.\n5. **Run the analysis** and examine the fit plot to see how well your synthetic control matches the treated unit before intervention.\n\n### Required Data Inputs\n\nYour dataset should be in **long panel format** with these columns:\n\n| Column Type | Description | Example |\n|-------------|-------------|---------|\n| Unit ID | Identifier for each unit | "California", "Texas", "Florida" |\n| Time | Date or period | 2000, 2001, 2002... or actual dates |\n| Outcome | Variable you\'re analyzing | GDP, crime rate, sales |\n| Predictors (optional) | Additional matching variables | population, income, temperature |\n\n**Example data shape:**\n\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '!'. Look for dots clustered near zero (good balance) rather than spread far apart.\n\n**Distribution Comparison** — Side-by-side histograms of outcomes for treated vs. control groups, helping you see if effects are driven by the whole distribution or outliers.\n\nThe node adds these columns to your dataset for downstream use:\n- `propensity_score` — estimated probability of treatment\n- `matched_pair_id` — which control unit each treated unit matched to (if using matching)\n- `weight` — observation weight for weighted analyses\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter Compare, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Segment** node — to explore effect heterogeneity ("Does the treatment work differently for different customer types?")\n- **Report** node — to communicate findings with formatted tables and charts\n- **Model** node — to build predictive models using your causally-identified features\n\n### Quick Start: Email Campaign Analysis\n\n1. **Connect your data** containing email recipients, purchase behavior, and customer characteristics\n2. **Set Treatment Column** to your email indicator (sent/not sent)\n3. **Set Outcome Column** to purchase amount or conversion\n4. **Add Covariates**: past purchase history, customer tenure, demographics\n5. **Choose "Propensity Score Matching"** as your method\n6. **Run the node** and check balance diagnostics first — if groups aren\'t well-balanced, add more relevant covariates\n7. **Interpret the ATE** — this is your best estimate of email campaign impact\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Start simple, then add complexity.** Run with no covariates first to see the raw difference, then add controls one at a time to watch how your estimate changes.\n\n**Balance diagnostics matter more than you think.** A statistically significant effect with poor balance is less trustworthy than a null result with excellent balance.\n\n**Watch your sample size.** Common support trimming can drop substantial observations. `covariate_adjustment` | `False` | Skip preprocessing to maximize speed |\n\n**What you get:** Immediate directional signal with approximate uncertainty bounds in seconds, even on large datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** Vulnerable to confounding and selection bias; estimates may be substantially wrong if treatment assignment isn\'t random.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Causal Inference\n\n**When to use:** High-stakes decisions requiring defensible causal estimates with maximum bias reduction and robust uncertainty quantification.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"doubly_robust"` | Protected if either outcome or propensity model is correct |\n| `propensity_model` | `GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=500, review.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower runtime (minutes to hours) and requires sufficient sample size in both treatment groups.\n\n### Recipe 3: Rare Treatment with Extreme Imbalance\n\n**When
