node accepts any tabular dataset with at least one column you want to transform. It works with text, numerical, and categorical columns—though you\'ll most commonly use it with categorical data or text fields that contain standardised codes or labels.\n\n**Example: Before and After**\n\n| customer_type | status |\n|---------------|--------|\n| b2b | A |\n| B2B | active |\n| business | A |\n| consumer | I |\n\nAfter replacement:\n\n| customer_type | status |\n|---------------|--------|\n| Business | Active |\n| Business | Active |\n| Business | Active |\n| Consumer | Inactive |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | The column where replacements will happen | None (required) | Select the column containing values you want to replace |\n| **Replacement Map** | Key-value pairs defining old\u2192new values | Empty | Add each value you want to replace and what to replace it with |\n| **Match Case** | Whether "Active" and "active" are treated as different | Enabled | Disable for case-insensitive matching when standardizing inconsistent capitalization |\n| **Match Whole Value** | Replace only exact matches vs. partial matches | Enabled | Disable if you want to replace parts of text (e.g., "St" \u2192 "Street" within addresses) |\n| **Handle Unmapped** | What to do with values not in your replacement map | Keep original | Choose "Set to null" or "Set to default" if unlisted values indicate data quality issues |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node outputs your dataset with the target column transformed according to your mapping rules. The original column is replaced—there\'s no separate "new" column created by default.\n\n**In the results panel, you\'ll see:**\n\n- **Replacement Summary**: A count of how many values were changed\n- **Value Distribution**: Before/after frequencies showing which values were replaced and their new distribution\n- **Unmapped Values Alert**: A list of any values in the source data that weren\'t in your replacement map (helpful for catching typos or unexpected values)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter replacing values, you\'ll typically flow into:\n\n- **Group By** or **Pivot**: Now that categories are standardised, aggregations will work correctly\n- **Filter**: To isolate records based on your newly cleaned values\n- **Train Model**: For machine learning nodes that require properly encoded categorical variables\n- **Visualisation nodes**: Charts will now display consistent, readable labels\n\n### Quick Start\n\n**Most common use case: Standardizing inconsistent category labels**\n\n1. Connect your dataset to the Replace Values node\n2. Click the node to open configuration\n3. In **Target Column**, select the column with inconsistent values\n4. Click **Add Replacement** and enter your first old\u2192new pair (e.g., "b2b" \u2192 "Business")\n5. Continue adding pairs until you\'ve mapped all variations\n6. Disable **Match Case** if your data has capitalization inconsistencies\n7. Run the node and check the **Unmapped Values Alert** for any categories you missed\n8. Adjust your mapping and re-run if needed\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Look for patterns before mapping manually.** Run a Value Counts node first to see all unique values in your column. You\'ll often discover variations you didn\'t know existed (extra spaces, typos, different abbreviations).\n\n**Use "Handle Unmapped" strategically.** If you\'re replacing error codes and anything unmapped is definitely an error, set unmapped values to null. But if you\'re only standardizing a subset of values, keep unmapped values as-is.\n\n**Replace in stages for complex transformations.** If you need multiple transformations on the same column, chain multiple Replace Values nodes. It\'s clearer than trying to build a complex single mapping.\n\n**Watch out for whitespace.** "Active" and "Active " (with trailing space) won\'t match. Run a Trim node upstream if you suspect whitespace issues.\n\n**Save your mappings.** If you\'re replacing domain-specific codes (diagnosis codes, product SKUs), document your replacement map in the node notes. Your future self—and your colleagues—will thank you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration Replacement\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need to quickly standardize obvious inconsistencies across multiple columns without validation overhead.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `case_sensitive` | `False` | Catches "YES", "yes", "Yes" variations automatically |\n| `regex` | `False` | Avoids pattern compilation overhead for simple literal matches |\n| `validate_mapping` | `False` | Skips pre-execution checks to maximize speed |\n| `null_handling` | `"ignore"` | Preserves nulls; doesn\'t interrupt batch operations |\n| `partial_match` | `False` | Exact matches only—prevents unintended substitutions |\n\n**What you get:** Near-instantaneous replacements suitable for cleaning exploratory notebooks where speed trumps validation.\n\n**Trade-off:** No safeguards against typos in your mapping dictionary or unexpected data types causing silent failures.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Replacement Pipeline\n\n**When to use:** Deploying replacement logic in automated ETL pipelines where data quality and auditability are critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `case_sensitive` | `True` | Explicit matching prevents ambiguity in audit logs |\n| `validate_mapping` | `True` | Pre-flight check ensures mapping keys exist in data |\n| `null_handling` | `"map_explicit"` | Forces conscious decision on null treatment |\n| `log_replacements` | `True` | Creates audit trail of which values changed |\n| `strict_mode` | `True` | Raises exceptions on unmapped values rather than skipping |\n| `backup_column` | `True` | Retains original values as `{col}_original` |\n\n**What you get:** Enterprise-ready transformations with full traceability and rollback capability.\n\n**Trade-off:** 3–5× slower execution and increased memory footprint from logging and backup columns.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Fuzzy String Normalization\n\n**When to use:** Cleaning user-generated text fields with spelling variations, abbreviations, or extra whitespace that standard replacement misses.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `regex` | `True` | Enables pattern-based matching |\n| `ignore_whitespace` | `True` | Treats "New York" and "NewYork" as identical |\n| `similarity_threshold` | `0.85` | Matches strings with 85%+ Levenshtein similarity |\n| `case_sensitive` | `False` | Handles inconsistent capitalization |\n| `strip_special_chars` | `True` | Removes punctuation before comparison |\n\n**What you get:** Robust standardization that catches "Dept.", "Department", "DEPT" under one mapping rule.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower performance due to distance calculations; risk of false positives at thresholds above 0.90.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Temporal Value Deprecation\n\n**When to use:** Migrating legacy code systems where old values must remain valid during a transition period but need versioning metadata.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `append_suffix` | `True` | Adds `_legacy` to replaced values instead of overwriting |\n| `effective_date` | `"2024-01-01"` | Only replaces values in records after this timestamp |\n| `preserve_unmapped` | `True` | Keeps old codes intact if no new mapping exists |\n| `create_mapping_column` | `True` | Adds boolean flag showing which rows were transformed |\n\n**What you get:** Backward-compatible transformations where historical analysis uses old codes and new reports use updated values.\n\n**Trade-off:** Creates schema changes (additional columns) that downstream systems must accommodate.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processes 8,000 loan applications monthly, each containing credit This could be customer reviews, support tickets, survey responses, social media posts—any unstructured text you want to convert into numerical features for modelling.\n\n**Before:**\n| customer_id | review_text |\n|-------------|-------------|\n| 1001 | "Great product, fast shipping!" |\n| 1002 | "Disappointed with quality" |\n\n**After:**\n| customer_id | review_text | tf_word_great | tf_word_product | ... | text_length |\n|-------------|-------------|---------------|-----------------|-----|-------------|\n| 1001 | "Great product, fast shipping!" | 0.167 | 0.167 | ... | 29 |\n| 1002 | "Disappointed with quality" | 0.000 | 0.000 | ... | 28 |\n\nThe node works with any text column and preserves all your original columns while adding new numerical features.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Text Column** | Which column contains the text to transform | (first text column) | Select the specific column you want to featurize |\n| **Method** | Feature extraction approach: Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, or N-grams | TF-IDF | Use Bag-of-Words for simple counts, TF-IDF for weighted importance, N-grams to capture phrases |\n| **Max Features** | Maximum number of word/phrase features to create | 100 | Increase to 500-1000 for rich vocabularies; decrease to 50 for simpler models or small datasets |\n| **Min Document Frequency** | Ignore words appearing in fewer than N documents | 2 | Increase to 5-10 to remove very rare words; set to 1 if you have limited data |\n| **Max Document Frequency** | Ignore words appearing in more than X% of documents | 0.9 (90%) | Lower to 0.7 to remove common but uninformative words |\n| **N-gram Range** | Word sequence length: (1,1) for single words, (1,2) for words and pairs | (1,1) | Use (1,2) or (1,3) to capture phrases like "not good" or "very satisfied" |\n| **Include Metadata** | Add statistical features: text length, word count, etc. | Yes | Keep enabled—these simple features often prove surprisingly useful |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node adds numerical columns to your dataset, with the exact columns depending on your configuration:\n\n**Feature columns**: One column per word or phrase, named like `tf_word_excellent` or `tfidf_phrase_fast_delivery`. Values represent frequency or weighted importance.\n\n**Metadata columns** (when enabled): `text_length` (character count), `word_count`, `avg_word_length`, `sentence_count`. These capture structural properties of the text.\n\n**Feature importance chart**: A bar chart showing which words or phrases have the highest variance across your dataset—these are likely to be the most useful predictive features.\n\n**Vocabulary summary**: Displays total unique terms extracted and any terms filtered out by your frequency thresholds.\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Drag** the Text Features node onto your canvas and connect your dataset\n2. **Select** the text column you want to transform (e.g., "review_text")\n3. **Choose TF-IDF** as your method—it\'s the most balanced starting point\n4. **Set Max Features to 100** for your first pass\n5. **Run** the node and examine the feature importance chart\n6. **Connect** to a Feature Selection or Classification node downstream\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter text featurization, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Feature Selection**: Narrow down to the most predictive text features before modelling\n- **Classification/Regression nodes**: Use these features to predict outcomes (sentiment, category, churn)\n- **Clustering**: Group documents by textual similarity\n- **Principal Component Analysis**: Reduce dimensionality of high-feature text data\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Start small with Max Features**: Begin with 50-100 features, examine what\'s captured, then increase if needed. Too many features too soon makes results hard to interpret.\n\n**Check the vocabulary**: Look at which words made it through your filters. If you see nonsense or code fragments, you may need text cleaning upstream first.\n\n**N-grams are powerful but expensive**: Switching from (1,1) to (1,3) can explode your feature count. Only add higher n-grams if single words aren\'t capturing meaning (common in sentiment or negation-heavy text).\n\n**Metadata features punch above their weight**: Simple features like text_length often correlate strongly with your target and train faster than vocabulary features.\n\n**Different languages need different settings**: Non-English text may need higher max features to capture the any tabular data with at least one column you want to convert. There are no strict requirements on input data shape—it works with datasets of any size, from a handful of rows to millions.\n\n**Before and after example:**\n\n| user_id | signup_date | is_active | revenue |\n|---------|-------------|-----------|---------|\n| 12345   | 2024-01-15  | 1         | 99.50   |\n| 67890   | 2024-02-20  | 0         | 150.75  |\n\nAfter casting `user_id` to string, `signup_date` to datetime, and `is_active` to boolean:\n\n| user_id | signup_date | is_active | revenue |\n|---------|-------------|-----------|---------|\n| "12345" | 2024-01-15T00:00:00 | True | 99.50 |\n| "67890" | 2024-02-20T00:00:00 | False | 150.75 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Column Selection** | Which column(s) to cast | None (must specify) | Select every column that needs type conversion |\n| **Target Type** | The data type to convert to | String | Choose based on downstream needs: numeric (int, float) for calculations, datetime for time operations, boolean for flags, string for IDs or text |\n| **Error Handling** | What happens when conversion fails | Coerce to null | Use "Raise error" when data quality is critical and you want to catch issues immediately; use "Coerce" for messy real-world data |\n| **Date Format** | Template for parsing datetime strings | Auto-detect | Specify when your dates follow unusual patterns (e.g., "DD/MM/YYYY" or "YYYY.MM.DD") |\n| **Decimal Separator** | Character used for decimals | Period (.) | Change to comma for European-formatted numbers |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output columns:** The node replaces your selected column(s) with the newly cast version(s), preserving column names. Original data isn\'t modified—you can always reconnect to the source if needed.\n\n**Summary panel:** Displays conversion success rate for each column, showing how many values converted successfully versus how many became null due to incompatible values.\n\n**Type indicator:** Each output column shows its new data type in the column header badge, confirming the transformation worked as expected.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nType Cast typically sits early in your pipeline, right after data import. Common next steps:\n\n- **Filter or Pivot nodes**: Now that dates are proper datetime objects, you can filter by date ranges or aggregate by month\n- **Calculate node**: Numeric casts enable mathematical operations\n- **Group By**: Boolean flags become perfect grouping categories\n- **ML nodes**: Most models require specific numeric types; casting ensures compatibility\n\n### Quick Start: Converting Mixed Data Types\n\n1. **Connect your data source** to the Type Cast node\n2. **Click the Column Selection dropdown** and choose `signup_date`\n3. **Set Target Type to "Datetime"**—leave Date Format on Auto-detect unless you see parsing errors\n4. **Add another cast**: Click "+ Add Column" and select `is_active`\n5. **Set Target Type to "Boolean"**—Heuristix automatically recognizes 0/1, true/false, yes/no\n6. **Check the Summary panel**—verify 100% conversion success\n7. **Run the pipeline** and inspect the output preview to confirm your data looks correct\n\n### Pro Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1:** Always cast ID columns (like `user_id` or `customer_id`) to strings, even if they\'re numbers. This prevents accidental mathematical operations and preserves leading zeros.\n\n**Tip 2:** When converting currencies or prices, cast to float first, then use a Calculate node to round to two decimal places. This prevents floating-point precision issues.\n\n**Tip 3:** If date parsing fails, check the Summary panel to see which values caused problems. Often you\'ll find entries like "N/A" or "Unknown" that need filtering or replacement first.\n\n**Tip 4:** Cast boolean columns as early as possible—downstream nodes like Filter and Group By work much more intuitively with true boolean types than numeric 0/1 values.\n\n**Tip 5:** Use multiple Type Cast nodes for complex workflows rather than one mega-node. This makes debugging easier and lets you verify conversions incrementally.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Cast\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need fast failures.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `infer_objects` | `False` | Requires explicit type declaration |\n| `errors` | `\'raise\'` | Fails immediately on incompatible values |\n| `dtype` | Explicit dict mapping | Enforces exact schema per column |\n| `downcast` | `\'integer\'` / `\'float\'` | Minimizes memory for large-scale processing |\n| `convert_string` | `True` | Uses optimized string dtype |\n| `convert_floating` | `False` | Prevents lossy conversions |\n\n**What you get:** Type-safe transformations with minimal memory usage and guaranteed schema compliance that fails fast on anomalies.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires comprehensive data profiling upfront and rejects edge cases that might be salvageable with coercion.\n\n### Recipe 3: Financial Precision Casting\n\n**When to use:** Processing monetary values, accounting data, or scientific measurements where floating-point rounding errors are unacceptable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dtype` | `\'object\'` then Decimal | Preserves exact precision |\n| `errors` | `\'raise\'` | No tolerance for ambiguous amounts |\n| `decimal_places` | `2` (or domain-specific) | Enforces currency precision |\n| `thousands_separator` | `\',\'` | Handles formatted input strings |\n| `use_nullable_dtypes` | `True` | Distinguishes NULL from zero |\n\n**What you get:** Arbitrary-precision numeric representation that maintains exact values through complex calculations without accumulating rounding errors.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower computation and higher memory usage compared to native float types; incompatible with some NumPy operations.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Aware Text Parsing\n\n**When to use:** Converting free-text timestamp columns from system logs, user inputs, or legacy databases with inconsistent formatting into analysis-ready datetime objects.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `dtype` | `\'datetime64[ns]\'` | Standardizes to nanosecond precision |\n| `infer_datetime_format` | `True` | Auto-detects format patterns |\n| `dayfirst` | Locale-dependent | Resolves ambiguous DD/MM vs MM/DD |\n| `utc` | `True` | Normalizes to timezone-aware UTC |\n| `errors` | `\'coerce\'` | Handles malformed entries gracefully |\n| `exact` | `False` | Matches timestamps within longer strings |\n\n**What you get:** Unified temporal index suitable for time-series analysis, resampling, and chronological aggregation with consistent timezone Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/value-mapping_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/value-mapping_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Value Mapping node expects **categorical or discrete data** in one or more columns. You can work with text labels, numeric codes, or any discrete values that need standardising or recoding.\n\n**Before mapping:**\n\n| product_size | status_code | region |\n|--------------|-------------|---------|\n| S | 1 | Northeast |\n| small | 1 | NE |\n| Medium | 2 | South |\n| L | 3 | northeast |\n\n**After mapping:**\n\n| product_size | status_code | region | size_standard |\n|--------------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| S | 1 | Northeast | Small |\n| small | 1 | NE | Small |\n| Medium | 2 | South | Medium |\n| L | 3 | northeast | Large |\n\nThe node works with any data shape—from a few hundred rows to millions. Just make sure your target columns contain discrete values, not continuous numbers.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Source Column** | Which column to transform | (none) | Always set this—it\'s your starting point |\n| **Mapping Dictionary** | The value pairs defining your transformation (old \u2192 new) | {} | Define all conversions you need. Can handle many-to-one mappings (multiple old values \u2192 single new value) |\n| **Output Column Name** | Name for the transformed column | `{source}_mapped` | Use descriptive names like `status_clean` or `category_standard` |\n| **Handle Unmapped Values** | What to do with values not in your mapping | Keep original | Change to "Set to null" if unmapped values signal data quality issues, or "Set to default" with a catch-all label |\n| **Default Value** | Fallback value when "Set to default" is selected | "Other" | Choose something meaningful like "Unknown" or "Uncategorised" |\n| **Case Sensitive** | Whether "Active" and "active" are treated as different | No | Enable if your data legitimately uses case to distinguish meaning |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output columns:** The node adds your newly mapped column alongside the original, so you can verify transformations before dropping the source column.\n\n**Mapping summary panel:** Shows how many values were mapped, unmapped values detected, and the distribution of your new categories. This is invaluable for catching typos in your mapping dictionary.\n\n**Preview table:** Displays before/after rows side-by-side, making it easy to spot-check your transformations.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nValue Mapping typically flows into:\n\n- **Grouping & Aggregation** nodes—once categories are standardised, aggregations become meaningful\n- **Filter** nodes—your clean categories make filtering reliable\n- **Encoding** nodes—for machine learning prep, map to human-readable labels first, then encode to numeric\n- **Visualisation** nodes—charts and dashboards work much better with consistent category labels\n\n### Quick Start: Standardising Status Labels\n\n1. **Drag** the Value Mapping node onto your canvas and connect your dataset\n2. **Select** the messy status column (e.g., containing "active", "Active", "1", "live")\n3. **Define your mapping** in the dictionary: `{"active": "Active", "Active": "Active", "1": "Active", "live": "Active"}`\n4. **Name the output** something clear like `status_clean`\n5. **Set Handle Unmapped** to "Set to null" to flag data quality issues\n6. **Run the node** and check the mapping summary for any unexpected unmapped values\n7. **Review** the preview table to confirm transformations look right\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Build mappings incrementally.** Start with your most common values, run the node, check unmapped values in the summary, then add more mappings. Don\'t try to anticipate every variation upfront.\n\n**Use many-to-one mappings liberally.** They\'re perfect for consolidating variations: `{"cancelled", "canceled", "CANCELLED"}` all map to `"Cancelled"`.\n\n**Keep original columns during development.** Only drop source columns once you\'re confident in your mappings. That preview comparison saves debugging time.\n\n**Export your mapping dictionaries.** Once you\'ve perfected a mapping for customer segments or product categories, save it. You\'ll use it again on next month\'s data.\n\n**Chain multiple Value Mapping nodes** when different columns need different transformations—it\'s clearer than one complex node doing everything.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploratory Standardisation\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need to quickly unify inconsistent categorical labels across imported datasets | Records all mapping failures for monitoring |\n\n**What you get:** Deterministic, auditable transformations that fail loudly on data drift or quality issues.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires comprehensive mapping specification upfront and rejects novel values that might be legitimate.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Multi-Source Geographic Consolidation\n\n**When to use:** Merging datasets from different Need\n\nThe Window Features node expects a **time series or sequentially ordered dataset** with at least one numeric column you want to aggregate. You\'ll typically connect this after a Sort node to ensure your data is properly ordered by date or sequence.\n\n**Before Window Features:**\n\n| date       | product_id | sales |\n|------------|------------|-------|\n| 2024-01-01 | A          | 100   |\n| 2024-01-02 | A          | 120   |\n| 2024-01-03 | A          | 115   |\n\n**After Window Features (with 2-day rolling mean):**\n\n| date       | product_id | sales | sales_rolling_mean_2 |\n|------------|------------|-------|----------------------|\n| 2024-01-01 | A          | 100   | NaN                  |\n| 2024-01-02 | A          | 120   | 110.0                |\n| 2024-01-03 | A          | 115   | 117.5                |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column(s)** | Which numeric column(s) to compute windows over | None (required) | Select the metrics you want to track over time — sales, temperature, stock price, etc. |\n| **Window Size** | How many rows to include in each calculation | 7 | Use smaller windows (3-5) for rapidly changing data; larger windows (30-90) for smoother, long-term trends |\n| **Aggregation Function** | The statistic to compute (mean, sum, min, max, std, median) | mean | Use `sum` for cumulative totals, `std` for volatility detection, `min/max` for range tracking |\n| **Group By Column(s)** | Compute separate windows per category | None (optional) | Essential when working with multiple products, stores, or customers — keeps their trends separate |\n| **Min Periods** | Minimum observations required to compute a value | 1 | Set equal to window size to avoid partial calculations at the start of your series |\n| **Center Window** | Whether to center the window on the current row | False | Enable for retrospective analysis where you want context from both sides of each point |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\n**New Columns:** The node adds one column per aggregation function, named using the pattern `{original_column}_{function}_{window_size}`. If you compute a 7-day rolling mean on `sales`, you\'ll get `sales_mean_7`.\n\n**Summary Statistics:** The output panel displays how many features were created, the number of NaN values generated (expected at the start of the series), and warnings if any group has insufficient data.\n\n**Preview Chart:** A line plot overlays your original column with the computed window feature, making it easy to visually confirm the smoothing or aggregation pattern looks correct.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Most common next steps:**\n\n- **Model Training nodes** — Window features are often your most predictive inputs for forecasting tasks\n- **Feature Selection** — Test which window sizes and aggregations actually improve model performance\n- **Transform nodes** — Create interaction features or ratios between different window sizes (e.g., short-term vs long-term averages)\n- **Filter or Drop NaN** — Remove incomplete rows at the start of your dataset if your model can\'t handle missing values\n\n### Quick Start: 7-Day Sales Trend\n\n1. **Sort your data** by date within each product/store using a Sort node first\n2. **Connect to Window Features** and select your `sales` column as the target\n3. **Set window size to 7** and choose `mean` as the aggregation function\n4. **Add `product_id` to Group By** if you have multiple products\n5. **Run the node** and inspect the preview chart — your new rolling average should smooth out daily noise\n6. **Connect to a Model Training node** and include both the original `sales` column and your new rolling feature as predictors\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n\U0001f3af **Always sort first** — Window features are order-dependent. If your data isn\'t properly sorted by time and grouped by category, your windows will mix unrelated observations.\n\n\U0001f3af **Try multiple window sizes together** — Create 3-day, 7-day, and 30-day rolling means simultaneously. Short windows capture recent changes; long windows show overall trends. Models often benefit from both.\n\n\U0001f3af **Watch out for data leakage** — Never include future data in your window when building predictive models. The default backward-looking window is safe; centered windows are not.\n\n\U0001f3af **Handle leading NaNs thoughtfully** — The first N-1 rows will have NaN values. Either drop them, set `min_periods=1` to compute partial windows, or use forward-fill if you need complete data.\n\n\U0001f3af **Combine window features with lag features** — A rolling 7-day average from last week (lagged by 7 days) can be more predictive than just yesterday\'s rolling average alone.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping on Small Time Series\n\n**When to use:** You\'re exploring a new dataset with <10,000 observations and want quick feedback on whether temporal patterns exist before investing in feature engineering.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_sizes` | `[3, 7]` | Two windows capture immediate and weekly patterns without computation overhead |\n| `functions` | `[\'mean\', \'std\']` | Mean shows trend, std shows volatility—minimal but informative |\n| `min_periods` | `1` | Avoid NaN losses at sequence starts in small datasets |\n| `center` | `False` | Keep causal structure for later modeling |\n| `step` | `1` | No skipping—preserve all temporal resolution |\n\n**What you get:** Light feature set (4 columns per input variable) computable in seconds, sufficient to identify if rolling statistics correlate with your target.\n\n**Trade-off:** You miss complex patterns like skewness or percentile shifts that might matter in production.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Financial Forecasting\n\n**When to use:** Deploying a trading signal or financial risk model where look-ahead bias would be catastrophic and regulatory audit requires defensible methodology.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_sizes` | `[5, 21, 63, 252]` | Standard trading windows (week, month, quarter, year in business days) |\n| `functions` | `[\'mean\', \'std\', \'min\', \'max\', \'quantile_25\', \'quantile_75\']` | Comprehensive statistics covering central tendency, dispersion, and tail behavior |\n| `min_periods` | Equal to window size | Strict: only output when full window available—no partial calculations |\n| `center` | `False` | Absolutely causal—zero look-ahead |\n| `closed` | `\'left\'` | Exclude current observation to prevent target leakage |\n| `step` | `1` | Every observation matters in financial applications |\n\n**What you get:** 24 features per variable (4 windows × 6 functions) with guaranteed temporal integrity, suitable for regulatory scrutiny.\n\n**Trade-off:** First 252 observations yield incomplete features; requires substantial warm-up data period.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Sensor Data with Irregular Sampling\n\n**When to use:** IoT or medical device data where measurements arrive at inconsistent intervals (e.g., event-triggered readings, not fixed-frequency logs).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_sizes` | `\'30min\', \'2h\', \'24h\'` | Time-based windows instead of observation counts |\n| `functions` | `[\'mean\', \'count\', \'std\']` | Count reveals sampling density; mean/std capture signal behavior |\n| `min_periods` | `3` | Require minimum observations for statistical validity but tolerate sparsity |\n| `center` | `False` | Maintain causal ordering |\n| `closed` | `\'both\'` | Include boundaries—don\'t lose sparse measurements |\n\n**What you get:** Features robust to sampling irregularity, where a 2-hour window always spans 2 hours of clock time regardless of measurement density.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires datetime index and resampling logic; computationally heavier than integer-position windows.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomaly Context in Stable Processes\n\n**When to use:** Manufacturing quality control or infrastructure monitoring where the goal is detecting deviations from local norms, not long-term forecasting.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_sizes` | `[50]` | Single, large window establishes "recent normal" baseline |\n| `functions` | `[\'median\', \'mad\']` | Median and median absolute deviation are robust to outliers you\'re trying to detect |\n| `min_periods` | `50` | Full window required for stable baseline |\n| `center` | `True` | Centered windows give best local context for anomaly scoring |\n| `step` | `10` | Downsample features—baseline changes slowly in stable processes |\n\n**What you get:** Robust local baseline per variable; compute `(value - rolling_median) / rolling_mad` to get standardized anomaly scores.\n\n**Trade-off:** Centered windows make this unsuitable for real-time prediction; offline analysis only.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional US credit card issuer with 3.2 million active accounts was losing approximately You create a 7-day rolling mean of sales as a feature and split your data chronologically: weeks 1-8 for training, weeks 9-10 for validation. During feature engineering, when should you compute the rolling mean for your validation set?\n\nA) Compute it independently on the validation set only, using just the validation set\'s own observations\n\nB) Compute it on the entire dataset before splitting, so both training and validation sets have complete rolling features\n\nC) Compute it on the training set, then extend the calculation into the validation set using the trained window that crosses the split boundary\n\nD) Compute it separately for each set, but initialize the validation set\'s first window with the training set\'s final values\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** The correct approach computes the rolling mean on training data first, then continues the rolling calculation into validation data, allowing the window to legitimately span across the chronological boundary. This mimics real-world deployment where new predictions use historical context from actual past observations. Option A creates data leakage by computing validation statistics in isolation—those statistics wouldn\'t be available at prediction time in production. Option B is the most dangerous error: it allows future validation data to contaminate training features through the rolling window, creating severe leakage. Option D represents a common confusion about statefulness; while the window needs historical context, you don\'t "initialize" with summary statistics—you use the actual raw observations that naturally precede the validation period in time. This question tests understanding of temporal integrity and the production-deployment perspective that separates novice from competent window feature engineering.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '—'. Connect it after your data cleaning and feature engineering steps, but before model training.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- A dataset with at least one **categorical target column** (your class labels)\n- One or more **feature columns** (numeric or categorical)\n\n**Example before/after:**\n\n| customer_id | credit_score | income | defaulted |\n|-------------|--------------|--------|-----------|\n| 1001 | 720 | 65000 | No |\n| 1002 | 580 | 42000 | Yes |\n| 1003 | 690 | 58000 | No |\n\nAfter balancing (with SMOTE), you\'ll see the same columns but with adjusted row counts to balance the "defaulted" classes.\n\n### Quick Start\n\nHere\'s the most common workflow for handling imbalanced classification:\n\n1. **Connect your preprocessed dataset** to the Balance Classes node\n2. **Select your target column** from the dropdown (e.g., "defaulted", "churned", "converted")\n3. **Choose "SMOTE" as your balancing method** (works well for most cases)\n4. **Set target ratio to 0.5** to create a 1:1 balance between classes\n5. **Enable stratified split** if you\'re planning to split data afterward\n6. **Run the node** and check the class distribution chart in the output\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Sensible Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | Which column contains your class labels | None (required) | Must select your dependent variable |\n| **Balancing Method** | Technique used to balance classes | SMOTE | Use "Random Oversample" for small datasets; "Random Undersample" if you have millions of rows; "ADASYN" for noisy boundaries |\n| **Target Ratio** | Desired ratio of minority to majority class | 0.5 (balanced) | Use 0.3-0.4 for slight imbalance if full balance feels artificial; keep 0.5 for highly skewed data |\n| **Sampling Strategy** | Which classes to resample | Auto (minority only) | Select "all" to set specific ratios for multi-class problems |\n| **Random State** | Seed for reproducible results | 42 | Change to any integer for different randomization; keep consistent for reproducibility |\n| **K Neighbors** | Number of nearest neighbors (SMOTE/ADASYN only) | 5 | Reduce to 2-3 for very small minority classes; increase to 7-10 for smoother synthetic samples |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output dataset:** Your original columns with adjusted row counts. Check the info panel to verify the new class distribution.\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Class distribution chart (before/after):** Bar chart showing original vs. balanced class counts—this is your validation that balancing worked\n- **Sample distribution plot:** Scatter plot showing how synthetic samples (if using SMOTE) are positioned relative to original data\n\n**Metrics displayed:**\n- Original class counts and percentages\n- New class counts and percentages\n- Number of samples added/removed per class\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe Balance Classes node outputs a dataset ready for model training. **Always connect it before your train-test split** if possible, or use stratified splitting to maintain balance in both sets.\n\n**Typical next steps:**\n- \u2192 **Split Data node** (with stratification enabled)\n- \u2192 **Random Forest** or **XGBoost** classification nodes\n- \u2192 **Cross-Validation** node to verify model performance on balanced data\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Timing matters:** Apply balancing *after* splitting your data into train/test sets, and *only* to the training set. Balancing your test set would give you an unrealistic evaluation.\n\n**Don\'t oversample tiny classes blindly:** If you have 5 fraud cases and 10,000 normal transactions, SMOTE will create many very similar synthetic examples. Consider collecting more data or using anomaly detection instead.\n\n**Check your model\'s confusion matrix afterward:** Even with balancing, examine whether your model is actually performing well on minority classes—balancing helps but doesn\'t guarantee success.\n\n**Cost-sensitive learning is an alternative:** If you\'re using tree-based models, try adjusting class weights in the model parameters instead of resampling—it\'s often faster and equally effective.\n\n**Preserve your original data:** Always keep an unbalanced version of your dataset connected to a separate branch—you\'ll need it for realistic model evaluation and deployment testing.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration with SMOTE\n\n**When to use:** Initial model prototyping with small-to-medium imbalanced datasets (1:10 to 1:100 ratio) when you need fast iteration to validate if the minority class contains learnable signal.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `sampling_strategy` | `\'auto\'` | Resamples minority to match majority size |\n| `k_neighbors` | `5` | Default—fast computation, reasonable diversity |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Reproducibility during exploration |\n| `n_jobs` | `-1` | Use all CPU cores for speed |\n\n**What you get:** Balanced training set in seconds with synthetic minority samples that preserve feature relationships.\n\n**Trade-off:** May introduce synthetic noise that inflates validation performance versus real-world deployment.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Class Weighting\n\n**When to use:** High-stakes production systems (fraud detection, medical diagnosis) where you cannot risk data leakage from synthetic samples and need audit-transparent preprocessing.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `class_weight` | `\'balanced\'` | Algorithmically penalizes majority errors |\n| `stratify` | `y` | Maintains class ratio in train/test split |\n| `cv` | `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True)` | Robust validation with class preservation |\n| `scoring` | `\'f1\'` or `\'balanced_accuracy\'` | Metrics that don\'t reward majority bias |\n\n**What you get:** Models that optimize directly on imbalanced data using cost-sensitive learning without data manipulation.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires classifier support for sample weights (not compatible with all algorithms like standard KNN).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Extreme Imbalance with Hybrid Sampling\n\n**When to use:** Rare event prediction with 1:1000+ imbalance (network intrusion, manufacturing defects) where pure oversampling creates unwieldy datasets and undersampling discards too much information.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `over_sampling` | `SMOTE(sampling_strategy=0.1)` | Increase minority to 10% of majority |\n| `under_sampling` | `RandomUnderSampler(sampling_strategy=0.5)` | Reduce majority to 2× minority count |\n| Pipeline order | Oversample \u2192 Undersample | Prevents removing synthetic samples |\n| `k_neighbors` | `3` | Fewer neighbors for sparse minority regions |\n\n**What you get:** 1:2 final ratio that\'s computationally tractable while retaining majority class diversity.\n\n**Trade-off:** Two-stage randomness increases sensitivity to `random_state` selection—requires multiple seed testing.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Anomaly Detection\n\n**When to use:** Sequential data (server logs, sensor readings) where temporal ordering matters and standard resampling would destroy autocorrelation structure.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Resampling | **None** | Preserve time dependencies |\n| `class_weight` | `{0: 1, 1: 50}` | Manual weight for ~2% anomaly rate |\n| `threshold` | `0.3` | Lower classification boundary from default 0.5 |\n| Validation | `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)` | Respects temporal order in CV |\n\n**What you get:** Models that detect anomalies without compromising time-based feature engineering or creating look-ahead bias.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires manual threshold tuning per dataset—no universal weighting formula exists.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage You need at least two columns:\n\n- **Predicted probabilities**: continuous values between 0 and 1 (typically from a Predict or Train Model node)\n- **Actual outcomes**: binary labels (0/1, True/False, or similar) representing what actually happened\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | predicted_churn_prob | actual_churn |\n|-------------|---------------------|--------------|\n| 1001        | 0.73                | 1            |\n| 1002        | 0.28                | 0            |\n| 1003        | 0.91                | 1            |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|--------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Probability Column** | Which column contains your model\'s predicted probabilities | (auto-detect) | Select the column with values between 0-1 from your classifier |\n| **Actual Outcome Column** | Which column has the true labels | (auto-detect) | Point to your ground truth binary outcome |\n| **Calibration Method** | Algorithm used to adjust probabilities | Platt Scaling | Use Isotonic Regression for larger datasets (1000+ samples) or when probabilities show non-sigmoid miscalibration |\n| **Number of Bins** | How many groups to divide predictions into for reliability diagrams | 10 | Increase to 15-20 for large datasets; decrease to 5-7 for smaller ones (fewer than 500 samples) |\n| **Cross-validation Folds** | Splits for fitting calibration to avoid overfitting | 5 | Increase to 10 for very small datasets where you want more robust estimates |\n\n**Calibration methods explained:**\n- **Platt Scaling**: Fits a logistic regression on your predictions. Fast, works well when your model is roughly sigmoid-shaped but shifted.\n- **Isotonic Regression**: More flexible, learns any monotonic transformation. Better for complex miscalibration patterns but needs more data.\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node adds a new column to your dataset:\n\n- **calibrated_probability**: Adjusted probability values that better reflect true frequencies\n\nYou\'ll also see two key visualizations:\n\n**Reliability Diagram (Calibration Curve)**: Shows predicted probability bins on the x-axis against actual observed frequency on the y-axis. A perfectly calibrated model hugs the diagonal line. If your original predictions fall above the line, your model is under-confident; below means over-confident.\n\n**Calibration Metrics Panel**: Displays before/after comparison including Brier Score (lower is better, measures probability accuracy) and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Aim for ECE under 0.05 for well-calibrated predictions.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter calibration, connect to:\n\n- **Threshold Optimizer**: Now that probabilities are calibrated, you can meaningfully set decision thresholds based on business costs\n- **Deploy Model**: Push calibrated predictions to production scoring pipelines\n- **Calculate Metrics**: Compare calibrated vs. uncalibrated model performance on probability-sensitive metrics\n- **Export Data**: Send calibrated probabilities to dashboards or decision systems\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your prediction output** from a Train Model or Predict node to the Calibrate Predictions input\n2. **Select your probability column** (e.g., "pred_prob_class_1") and outcome column (e.g., "actual_label")\n3. **Keep Platt Scaling as your method** unless you have 1000+ samples and suspect complex miscalibration\n4. **Run the node** and examine the reliability diagram—look for how far your original curve deviates from the diagonal\n5. **Check the ECE metric**—if it dropped by more than 0.02, calibration meaningfully improved your probabilities\n\n### Tips from the Pros\n\n**Always calibrate on held-out data.** If you trained your model on a dataset, calibrate using validation or test data that the model hasn\'t seen—otherwise you\'re just fitting to noise.\n\n**Watch your sample size per bin.** If bins have fewer than 20 samples each, reduce the number of bins or expect noisy calibration curves.\n\n**Calibration doesn\'t improve ranking.** Your ROC-AUC won\'t change—calibration adjusts the probability scale, not which predictions are higher or lower than others.\n\n**Check calibration separately for subgroups.** A model might be well-calibrated overall but poorly calibrated for specific segments (new customers, rare product categories). Filter your data and run separate calibration analyses.\n\n**Recalibrate periodically in production.** As your data distribution shifts over time, previously calibrated probabilities can drift. Plan to refresh calibration quarterly or when you retrain models.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Validation Check\n\n**When to use:** You\'ve just trained a model and want to quickly assess whether calibration is needed before investing time in tuning.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'isotonic\'` | Fast, non-parametric, works for any miscalibration pattern |\n| `cv` | `3` | Minimal cross-validation to avoid data leakage while staying fast |\n| `n_bins` | `10` | Standard binning for reliability diagrams without over-segmentation |\n| `ensemble` | `False` | Single calibrator keeps computation minimal |\n\n**What you get:** A calibration curve and calibrated probabilities in under a minute that reveal whether your model needs adjustment.\n\n**Trade-off:** Not production-ready; isotonic can overfit on small validation sets and 3-fold CV provides limited reliability assessment.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Financial Model\n\n**When to use:** Deploying a credit risk, fraud detection, or medical diagnosis model where probability accuracy has regulatory or life-critical implications.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'beta\'` | Smooth, bounded [0,1], well-behaved at extremes |\n| `cv` | `10` | Robust variance reduction for calibration map estimation |\n| `n_bins` | `20` | Fine-grained reliability assessment |\n| `ensemble` | `True` | Average calibrators from all folds for stability |\n| `strategy` | `\'stratified\'` | Preserve class distribution in each fold |\n\n**What you get:** Reliable, stable probabilities with smooth calibration maps that generalize well to new data and withstand audit scrutiny.\n\n**Trade-off:** 5-10× longer training time and requires sufficient data in each probability bin (minimum ~1000 samples recommended).\n\n### Recipe 3: Imbalanced Binary Classification (1% Positive Rate)\n\n**When to use:** Rare event prediction where uncalibrated models systematically overpredict the minority class probability.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'platt\'` | Parametric sigmoid handles sparse regions better than isotonic |\n| `cv` | `5` | Balance between robustness and preserving rare positive samples |\n| `sample_weight` | `\'balanced\'` | Prevent calibrator from ignoring minority class |\n| `pos_prior` | `0.01` | Explicitly encode true base rate |\n\n**What you get:** Calibrated probabilities that respect the true 1% base rate instead of clustering around 10-20%.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes sigmoid-shaped miscalibration; won\'t fix models with irregular calibration errors.\n\n### Recipe 4: Multi-Model Ensemble Reconciliation\n\n**When to use:** You\'re averaging predictions from multiple models (random forest, XGBoost, neural net) and the ensemble probabilities are poorly calibrated despite good discrimination.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'isotonic\'` | Flexible enough to correct complex non-monotonic distortions from averaging |\n| `cv` | `\'prefit\'` | Use held-out calibration set since models already trained separately |\n| `increasing` | `True` | Enforce monotonicity constraint |\n| `out_of_bounds` | `\'clip\'` | Handle edge cases where ensemble averaging creates extreme values |\n\n**What you get:** Well-calibrated ensemble probabilities that preserve rank-ordering while fixing probability scale distortions.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires dedicated calibration set separate from model training and validation data (typically 20% of available data).\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender uses credit scoring models to decide which applicants require manual underwriting review. Predictors node takes **multiple prediction outputs** from upstream models and merges them into a single, stronger prediction. You\'ll need:\n\n- **2 or more prediction columns** from different models (regression outputs or class probabilities)\n- **The actual target column** for training the combiner (if using weighted or stacked methods)\n- **Optional**: An ID column to track observations\n\nYour input data should look like this:\n\n| order_id | actual_sales | model_1_pred | model_2_pred | model_3_pred |\n|----------|--------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|\n| 1001 | 450 | 425 | 460 | 440 |\n| 1002 | 780 | 800 | 770 | 795 |\n\nAfter combining, you\'ll see:\n\n| order_id | actual_sales | model_1_pred | model_2_pred | model_3_pred | combined_pred |\n|----------|--------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|---------------|\n| 1001 | 450 | 425 | 460 | 440 | 442 |\n| 1002 | 780 | 800 | 770 | 795 | 788 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Combination Method** | How predictions are merged (Simple Average, Weighted Average, Stacking) | Simple Average | Use Weighted or Stacking when models have very different accuracy levels |\n| **Base Models** | Which prediction columns to combine | All available | Deselect underperforming models that hurt overall accuracy |\n| **Meta-learner** | Algorithm for stacking method (Linear, Ridge, Lasso) | Ridge | Use Lasso if you want automatic model selection; Linear for interpretability |\n| **Validation Split** | Percentage held out for meta-learner training | 30% | Increase to 40% if you have lots of data; decrease to 20% for smaller datasets |\n| **Weights** | Manual weights for Weighted Average method | Equal (e.g., 0.33 each) | Set based on individual model performance from validation metrics |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\n**Output Columns:**\n- `combined_pred`: The final ensemble prediction\n- `combination_method`: Records which method was used (useful for experiment tracking)\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n- **Ensemble Performance**: RMSE, MAE, or accuracy (depending on problem type)\n- **Improvement over Best Base**: Shows percentage gain versus your strongest individual model\n- **Model Contribution**: Bar chart showing each model\'s influence on final predictions\n\n**Charts:**\n- **Prediction Comparison**: Line plot comparing ensemble predictions to actuals and base models\n- **Residuals Distribution**: Histogram showing prediction errors\n- **Weights Visualization** (for weighted/stacking methods): Shows learned importance of each base model\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node typically flows into:\n\n- **Evaluate Model** \u2192 Compare ensemble performance against individual models\n- **Deploy Prediction** \u2192 Push the combined predictions to production\n- **Export Data** \u2192 Save predictions for external reporting\n- **Feature Importance** \u2192 Understand which base models drive decisions (for stacking method)\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your prediction outputs**: Link 2–5 model nodes (Random Forest, XGBoost, Linear Regression, etc.) to Combine Predictors\n2. **Select Simple Average** as your first attempt—it\'s robust and requires no training\n3. **Review the improvement metric**: Check if the ensemble beats your best individual model\n4. **If improvement is modest**, switch to Stacking with Ridge meta-learner\n5. **Examine model contribution chart** to identify and remove any models with negative weights\n6. **Connect to Evaluate Model** to generate final performance reports\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Start simple, then optimize**: Simple averaging often performs 80% as well as complex stacking with 5% of the setup time. Only move to stacking if you need that extra edge.\n\n**Diversity matters more than accuracy**: Combining three very different models (tree-based, linear, neural) typically outperforms combining five similar tree models, even if those tree models individually score higher.\n\n**Watch for data leakage**: When using stacking, ensure your meta-learner trains on out-of-fold predictions. Heuristix handles this automatically, but if you\'re manually setting weights, never use the same data for base model predictions and weight optimization.\n\n**Monitor model contributions**: If a model receives near-zero weight in stacking, it\'s redundant—remove it to simplify your pipeline.\n\n**Test odd-numbered ensembles for classification**: When combining probability predictions, 3 or 5 models can break ties more naturally than 2 or 4.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping Ensemble\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploration phase when you need quick feedback on whether ensembling will help your problem, working with datasets under 50,000 rows.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_models` | 3 | Minimum for meaningful diversity without overhead |\n| `base_estimators` | `[\'RandomForest\', \'GradientBoosting\', \'LinearRegression\']` | Maximum algorithmic diversity with fast training |\n| `combination_method` | `\'simple_average\'` | No hyperparameter tuning required |\n| `cv_folds` | 3 | Fastest cross-validation that still validates |\n| `max_training_time` | 300 seconds | Hard stop to keep iteration cycles short |\n\n**What you get:** A baseline ensemble performance metric within 5 minutes that tells you if the effort is worthwhile.\n\n**Trade-off:** Potentially 5-15% lower accuracy than optimised ensembles; may miss optimal model weights.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Stacked Ensemble\n\n**When to use:** Deploying to production where model performance directly impacts business metrics and retraining happens weekly or less frequently.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_models` | 7-10 | Optimal bias-variance reduction without diminishing returns |\n| `base_estimators` | `[\'XGBoost\', \'LightGBM\', \'CatBoost\', \'RandomForest\', \'ExtraTrees\', \'Ridge\', \'ElasticNet\']` | Diverse algorithms covering tree-based, linear, and regularised approaches |\n| `combination_method` | `\'stacking\'` | Learns optimal weights from data |\n| `meta_learner` | `\'Ridge\'` with `alpha=1.0` | Regularised to prevent overfitting on base predictions |\n| `cv_folds` | 10 | Robust out-of-fold predictions for meta-learner |\n| `use_feature_stacking` | `True` | Includes original features alongside predictions |\n\n**What you get:** Maximum predictive performance with robust generalisation and stable predictions across deployment cycles.\n\n**Trade-off:** Training time 10-20x longer; requires significant computational resources and maintenance complexity.\n\n### Recipe 3: Imbalanced Classification Ensemble\n\n**When to use:** Binary classification with class imbalance ratios exceeding 1:10 (fraud detection, rare disease diagnosis, equipment failure prediction).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_models` | 5 | Balance between diversity and training on limited minority samples |\n| `base_estimators` | All with `class_weight=\'balanced\'` | Prevents majority class dominance |\n| `combination_method` | `\'weighted_average\'` | Weights based on minority class F1-score, not accuracy |\n| `optimization_metric` | `\'f1_minority\'` or `\'pr_auc\'` | Accuracy is misleading with imbalance |\n| `prediction_threshold` | `0.3` | Lower than default 0.5 to increase recall |\n\n**What you get:** Substantially improved minority class detection without flooding predictions with false positives.\n\n**Trade-off:** Overall accuracy will appear lower; requires careful threshold tuning for your cost matrix.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Regime Detection Ensemble\n\n**When to use:** Forecasting problems where underlying data patterns shift over time (market conditions, seasonal demand with trend breaks, user behaviour evolution).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_models` | 4-6 | Different models capture different regimes |\n| `base_estimators` | Mix of `[\'ARIMA\', \'Prophet\', \'XGBoost\', \'LSTM\']` | Statistical, algorithmic, and deep learning perspectives |\n| `combination_method` | `\'dynamic_weighting\'` | Weights shift based on recent performance window |\n| `recency_window` | 30 days | Adapts to regime changes within a month |\n| `retrain_frequency` | Weekly | Keeps models current without excessive overhead |\n\n**What you get:** Ensemble automatically adapts to regime shifts, maintaining accuracy through structural breaks that break individual models.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires streaming infrastructure to track and update model weights; more complex deployment than static ensembles.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional credit union with 150,000 members struggled with credit default prediction—conservative models rejected too many viable borrowers, while aggressive models increased charge-offs. Think of it as wrapping your existing predictions with statistical guarantees.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- A model node (any regression or classification model you\'ve already trained)\n- A calibration dataset with the same features as your training data, plus true labels/values\n- Optionally, new data to generate prediction intervals for\n\nHere\'s what your calibration data should look like:\n\n| customer_id | feature_1 | feature_2 | actual_churn |\n|-------------|-----------|-----------|--------------|\n| 1001        | 0.45      | 23        | 0            |\n| 1002        | 0.78      | 31        | 1            |\n\nThe key requirement: your calibration set must be **separate from training data**. At \u03b1=0.1, you get 90% coverage. | 0.1 | Lower for more conservative intervals (\u03b1=0.05 \u2192 95% coverage). "conditional" when you have important feature-based patterns. |\n| **Calibration Split** | Auto-split your data into calibration/test if you haven\'t already | 0.2 | Increase to 0.3 if you have abundant data; decrease to 0.1 if data is scarce. |\n| **Symmetric Intervals** | (Regression only) Force symmetric prediction bands | True | Set False for asymmetric uncertainty (e.g., housing prices with upper tail). |\n| **Class-Conditional** | (Classification only) Compute separate thresholds per class | False | Enable for imbalanced datasets where error costs differ by class. |\n\n### What You\'ll See\n\n**Output columns added to your dataset:**\n\n- `prediction_lower` / `prediction_upper`: The interval bounds for each prediction (regression)\n- `prediction_set`: A list of plausible You can always relax it after validating the intervals make sense for your use case.\n\n**Watch for violated coverage.** If empirical coverage drops below your target, your calibration set may not represent production data well—this is an early warning signal.\n\n**Interval width is your canary.** Suddenly widening intervals in production suggest data drift or concept shift, even if point predictions look okay.\n\n**Classification prediction sets can be multi-label.** When uncertain, conformal methods might return {Class A, Class B} rather than forcing a single choice—this is a feature, not a bug.\n\n**Calibration data is sacred.** Never reuse training data for calibration. The mathematical guarantees completely break down. Always use fresh, unseen data.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** You\'re exploring a new dataset and want to rapidly assess if conformal prediction can add local coverage |\n\n**What you get:** Valid coverage even when test distribution differs, with tighter intervals than non-adaptive methods.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires access to unlabeled samples from deployment distribution and assumes labels shift only through covariates.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Online Calibration for Streaming Data\n\n**When to use:** Predictions arrive sequentially (e.g., True parameters\n    means = [0.05, -0.02]  # Monthly returns: 5% vs -2%\n    stds = [0.02, 0.06]    # Volatility: 2% vs 6%\n    \n    # Transition matrix: regimes are persistent\n    # P(stay in regime 1) = 0.95, P(stay in regime 2) = 0.90\n    transition_matrix = np.array([[0.95, 0.05],\n                                   [0.10, 0.90]])\n    \n    # Generate regime sequence\n    regimes = np.zeros(n_obs, dtype=int)\n    regimes[0] = 0  # Start in regime 1\n    \n    for t in range(1, n_obs):\n        regimes[t] = np.random.choice(\n            [0, 1], \n            p=transition_matrix[regimes[t-1], :]\n        )\n    \n    # Generate observations\n    observations = np.zeros(n_obs)\n    for t in range(n_obs):\n        observations[t] = np.random.normal(\n            means[regimes[t]], \n            stds[regimes[t]]\n        )\n    \n    # Create datetime index (monthly data)\n    dates = pd.date_range(start=\'1980-01-01\', periods=n_obs, freq=\'M\')\n    \n    return pd.Series(observations, index=dates, name=\'returns\'), regimes\n\n# Generate data\nreturns, true_regimes = generate_regime_switching_data(n_obs=500)\n\nprint("Data Summary:")\nprint(returns.describe())\nprint(f"\\nTrue regime distribution: {np.bincount(true_regimes)}")\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 1: Basic Markov-Switching Mean Model\n# =============================================================================\n\nprint("\\n" + "="*60)\nprint("Example 1: Markov-Switching Mean Model")\nprint("="*60)\n\n# Fit a 2-regime switching model for the mean\nmodel_mean = MarkovRegression(\n    returns,\n    k_regimes=2,           # Number of regimes\n    switching_variance=True # Allow variance to switch between regimes\n)\n\n# Fit the model using EM algorithm\nresults_mean = model_mean.fit(search_reps=20)  # Multiple starts to avoid local optima\n\nprint("\\nModel Summary:")\nprint(results_mean.summary())\n\n# Extract regime-specific parameters\nprint("\\nRegime-Specific Parameters:")\nfor regime in range(2):\n    print(f"\\nRegime {regime + 1}:")\n    print(f"  Mean: {results_mean.params[f\'const[{regime}]\']:.4f}")\n    print(f"  Std Dev: {np.sqrt(results_mean.params[f\'sigma2[{regime}]\']):.4f}")\n\n# Extract transition matrix\nprint("\\nEstimated Transition Matrix:")\ntrans_matrix = results_mean.regime_transition\nprint(trans_matrix)\n\n# Get smoothed regime probabilities\nsmoothed_probs = results_mean.smoothed_marginal_probabilities\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 2: Markov-Switching Autoregressive Model\n# =============================================================================\n\nprint("\\n" + "="*60)\nprint("Example 2: Markov-Switching AR(1) Model")\nprint("="*60)\n\n# Fit a 2-regime switching AR(1) model\nmodel_ar = MarkovAutoregression(\n    returns,\n    k_regimes=2,\n    order=1,                  # AR(1)\n    switching_ar=True,        # AR coefficients switch\n    switching_variance=True   # Variance switches\n)\n\nresults_ar = model_ar.fit(search_reps=20)\n\nprint("\\nAR Model Summary:")\nprint(results_ar.summary())\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 3: Model Selection - Choosing Number of Regimes\n# =============================================================================\n\nprint("\\n" + "="*60)\nprint("Example 3: Model Selection")\nprint("="*60)\n\n# Compare models with different numbers of regimes\nmodel_results = {}\ncriteria = {\'AIC\': [], \'BIC\': [], \'LogLik\': []}\n\nfor k in [1, 2, 3]:\n    if k == 1:\n        # Single regime is just a standard model\n        from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg\n        model = AutoReg(returns, lags=0)\n        res = model.fit()\n        criteria[\'AIC\'].append(res.aic)\n        criteria[\'BIC\'].append(res.bic)\n        criteria[\'LogLik\'].append(res.llf)\n    else:\n        model = MarkovRegression(\n            returns, \n            k_regimes=k, \n            switching_variance=True\n        )\n        res = model.fit(search_reps=10)\n        criteria[\'AIC\'].append(res.aic)\n        criteria[\'BIC\'].append(res.bic)\n        criteria[\'LogLik\'].append(res.llf)\n    model_results[k] = res\n\nprint\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/detect-regimes_fig1.png)\n![](../../_static/figures/detect-regimes_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Detect Regimes node expects **time series data** with at least one numeric column you want to analyze for regime changes. If the colored regions don\'t align with your domain intuition, your features may need transformation (log returns instead of raw prices, for example).\n\n**Tip 3:** The regime probability column is gold for risk management. Low probability values indicate transitional periods—often the riskiest times to make predictions.\n\n**Tip 4:** If you\'re seeing regimes that change every few periods, increase the minimum regime duration and smoothing window together. Real structural shifts rarely happen daily.\n\n**Tip 5:** Use the transition matrix to understand regime stability. A diagonal-heavy matrix means sticky regimes (good); a uniform matrix suggests your features aren\'t discriminative enough.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to The algorithm often catches rhythms you didn\'t expect.\n\n**Small datasets struggle here.** You need at least 2-3 cycles of your seasonality pattern (e.g., 3 weeks of data for weekly patterns) for reliable detection.\n\n**Not all anomalies are bad.** A positive sales spike might be anomalous but wonderful—use the anomaly_score to prioritize investigation, not to automatically trigger alarms.\n\n**Group By is powerful for heterogeneous data.** If you\'re monitoring multiple products or regions with different scales, always group rather than detecting on the combined series.\n\n**Check your expected_range values** when sensitivity feels off. If ranges seem too wide or narrow, adjust your lookback window before tweaking sensitivity.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Scan\n\n**When to use:** Initial data quality checks You\'ll typically connect this after a regression or classification model node.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- Your original feature columns (same ones used for training)\n- Actual target values (for calibration)\n- Model predictions (from your upstream model)\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | income | age | credit_score | actual_churn | predicted_churn |\n|-------------|--------|-----|--------------|--------------|-----------------|\n| 1001 | 65000 | 34 | 720 | 0 | 0.23 |\n| 1002 | 48000 | 45 | 680 | 1 | 0.78 |\n\nThe node works with both regression tasks (predicting continuous values) and classification tasks (predicting probabilities).\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|------------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Uncertainty Method** | The technique used: Quantile Regression, Conformal Prediction, or Bootstrap Ensemble | Conformal Prediction | Use Bootstrap for smaller datasets (<5,000 rows); Quantile Regression for very large datasets where speed matters |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of prediction intervals (e.g., 90%, 95%, 99%) | 95% | Increase to 99% for high-stakes decisions; decrease to 90% for faster experimentation |\n| **Calibration Split** | Percentage of data reserved for uncertainty calibration | 20% | Increase to 30% if you have many data points; never go below 15% |\n| **Bootstrap Samples** | Number of resampled models (Bootstrap method only) | 100 | Increase to 500+ for more stable intervals, but expect longer runtime |\n| **Return Full Distribution** | Whether to output entire predictive distribution or just intervals | Off | Turn on when you need custom percentiles or want to visualize the full uncertainty shape |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**New columns added to your dataset:**\n\n- `prediction_lower`: Lower bound of prediction interval\n- `prediction_upper`: Upper bound of prediction interval\n- `prediction_width`: How wide the uncertainty interval is (upper - lower)\n- `uncertainty_score`: Normalized confidence metric (0-1, where 1 = most certain)\n\n**Visualizations displayed:**\n\n- **Calibration Plot**: Shows if your uncertainty intervals are honest (should hit the diagonal line)\n- **Uncertainty Distribution**: Histogram showing how confidence varies across predictions\n- **Prediction Interval Chart**: Sample of predictions with their error bars\n\n**Summary metrics:**\n\n- Coverage rate (what % of actuals fall within intervals)\n- Average interval width\n- Sharpness score (narrower is better, if properly calibrated)\n\n### Quick Start: Most Common Use Case\n\n1. **Connect your trained model** output to the Estimate Uncertainty node\n2. **Select "Conformal Prediction"** as your uncertainty method (best all-around choice)\n3. **Keep 95% confidence** unless you have a specific risk tolerance requirement\n4. **Run the node** and check the calibration plot first—you want to see points near the diagonal\n5. **Filter by `uncertainty_score`** to identify predictions you can trust most (score > 0.7)\n6. **Connect to a Filter node** downstream to split high-confidence vs. low-confidence predictions\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Typical next nodes:**\n\n- **Filter Node**: Separate high-confidence predictions for automated action vs. low-confidence for human review\n- **Dashboard Node**: Display uncertainty metrics to stakeholders\n- **Decision Node**: Route predictions based on uncertainty thresholds (e.g., only auto-approve loans with uncertainty_score > 0.8)\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Tip 1:** If your calibration plot shows points consistently above the diagonal, your intervals are too narrow—increase the calibration split percentage or switch to Bootstrap method.\n\n**Tip 2:** The `prediction_width` column is gold for operational planning. Wide intervals = you need more data or better features in those regions.\n\n**Tip 3:** For time series, always use a time-based split for calibration data (not random sampling) or your coverage rates will be misleading.\n\n**Tip 4:** Don\'t obsess over perfect 95% coverage. Anywhere between 93-97% is excellent in practice. Below 90% means something\'s wrong.\n\n**Tip 5:** When presenting to non-technical stakeholders, show them the uncertainty distribution histogram—it\'s the easiest way to communicate "we\'re more confident about some predictions than others."\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Fast Prototyping with Quantile Regression\n\n**When to use:** Initial model exploration when you need quick uncertainty bounds on tabular data with minimal computational overhead.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `quantile_regression` | Single-pass training, no ensembling overhead |\n| `quantiles` | `[0.1, 0.9]` | 80% interval balances coverage with interpretability |\n| `loss` | `pinball` | Native quantile loss, no post-processing needed |\n| `max_depth` | `5` | Shallow trees train fast, prevent overfitting to noise |\n| `n_estimators` | `100` | Minimum for stable quantile estimates |\n\n**What you get:** Point predictions plus lower/upper bounds in <30 seconds for datasets under 100K rows.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes quantiles are independent; won\'t capture full distributional shape or multimodal uncertainty.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Conformal Prediction\n\n**When to use:** Deployed models requiring statistically valid coverage guarantees with heterogeneous data distributions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `adaptive_conformal` | Adjusts interval width per prediction difficulty |\n| `calibration_split` | `0.25` | Reserve sufficient data for valid calibration |\n| `coverage_level` | `0.90` | Standard for business-critical decisions |\n| `symmetry` | `False` | Allow asymmetric intervals for skewed distributions |\n| `batch_recalibration` | `True` | Maintain coverage under distribution drift |\n| `min_calibration_samples` | `1000` | Ensure statistical validity of quantiles |\n\n**What you get:** Mathematically guaranteed 90% coverage on exchangeable test data with minimal assumptions on base model.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires holdout calibration set, reducing training data; intervals can be conservative for rare inputs.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Cardinality Time Series Forecasting\n\n**When to use:** Predicting thousands of SKUs/sensors where individual model training is prohibitive but tail risk matters.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `quantile_loss_global` | Single model learns uncertainty across all series |\n| `quantiles` | `[0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95]` | Captures full distribution for inventory decisions |\n| `scaling` | `per_series_standard` | Prevents large series from dominating loss |\n| `embedding_dim` | `32` | Encodes series identity for learned patterns |\n| `lookback_window` | `12` | Match seasonal cycle length |\n| `quantile_regularization` | `0.01` | Prevents quantile crossing without sorting overhead |\n\n**What you get:** Simultaneous probabilistic forecasts across entire portfolio with shared pattern learning.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes series share structural similarity; unusual series get less tailored uncertainty estimates than individual models.\n\n### Recipe 4: Causal Inference Treatment Effect Bounds\n\n**When to use:** A/B tests or observational studies where treatment effect heterogeneity drives decisions, not just average effects.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `cqr_double_ml` | Combines causal doubly-robust estimation with conformal intervals |\n| `target_estimand` | `cate` | Estimate conditional average treatment effect |\n| `nuisance_folds` | `5` | Cross-fitting prevents overfitting propensity/outcome models |\n| `coverage_level` | `0.95` | Conservative for policy decisions |\n| `trimming_threshold` | `0.05` | Drop extreme propensity scores for stability |\n\n**What you get:** Per-individual treatment effect estimates with valid uncertainty, revealing *who* benefits most.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires randomization or strong unconfoundedness; complex pipeline with multiple modeling stages.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender struggled with loan approval decisions that were either too conservative (losing good customers) or too risky (accepting defaults). Option B is correct because SHAP values (and other prediction explanation methods) decompose *individual predictions* and show feature contributions for *that specific instance*—a high SHAP value for one prediction does not indicate that feature is globally important across the model. Option A represents the most common misconception: conflating local explanations with global feature importance.
