Your data should be clean, with missing values handled and categorical variables encoded if necessary.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- At least one feature column (predictor variable)\n- Exactly one target column (what you\'re trying to predict)\n- Minimum 50 rows recommended for reliable cross-validation\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_age | income | credit_score | purchased |\n|--------------|--------|--------------|-----------|\n| 34 | 52000 | 680 | 1 |\n| 45 | 78000 | 720 | 0 |\n| 29 | 43000 | 650 | 1 |\n\nThe node automatically detects whether you\'re solving a classification or regression problem based on your target column type.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Target Column** | The variable you want to predict | None (required) | Always set this first |\n| **Feature Columns** | Variables used for prediction | All except target | Exclude irrelevant columns or IDs |\n| **Problem Type** | Classification or Regression | Auto-detect | Override if auto-detection is wrong |\n| **CV Folds** | Number of cross-validation splits | 5 | Use 10 for small datasets (<500 rows); use 3 for large datasets (>100k rows) to save time |\n| **Models to Try** | Which algorithms to evaluate | All available | Deselect slow algorithms (e.g., SVM) for very large datasets |\n| **Time Limit** | Maximum search duration in minutes | 30 | Increase for complex problems; decrease for quick experiments |\n| **Optimization Metric** | What to maximize/minimize | Accuracy (classification) or RMSE (regression) | Use F1 for imbalanced classes; use MAE if outliers matter less |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Primary output:** A trained model object you can use for predictions, plus a detailed comparison table.\n\n**Results table** shows for each candidate model:\n- Model name (e.g., "Random Forest", "XGBoost")\n- Cross-validation score (mean and standard deviation)\n- Training time\n- Rank (1 = best)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Model comparison chart**: Horizontal bar chart showing each model\'s performance with confidence intervals\n- **Best model details**: Feature importance plot showing which variables matter most\n- **Confusion matrix** (classification) or **residual plot** (regression) for the winning model\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe Find Best Model node outputs a trained model object. Connect it to:\n\n- **Predict** node: Apply the best model to new data for scoring\n- **Model Explainer** node: Generate SHAP values or other interpretability reports\n- **Deploy Model** node: Push to production as an API endpoint\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect to **Predict** first to score a holdout test set, then evaluate those predictions with a **Model Performance** node.\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Connect your prepared dataset** to the Find Best Model node\n2. **Set the Target Column** in the configuration panel\n3. **Review the Feature Columns** and deselect any ID or date columns that shouldn\'t be used for prediction\n4. **Choose your Optimization Metric** based on your business goal (e.g., F1-score if false negatives are costly)\n5. **Run the node** and wait for the search to complete\n6. **Examine the results table** to see how different algorithms performed\n7. **Connect a Predict node** to apply your winning model to test data\n\n### Practical Tips from the Trenches\n\n**Start with the defaults.** The auto-detected settings work well for 80% of problems. Don\'t over-optimize your first run.\n\n**Watch your metric choice carefully.** Accuracy is misleading for imbalanced classes (e.g., fraud detection with 1% fraud rate). Switch to F1-score, precision, or recall depending on which errors are costlier.\n\n**Time limits prevent runaway experiments.** If the search hits your time limit, the node returns the best model found so far—you still get a working result.\n\n**Feature importance is gold.** After finding your best model, spend time understanding which features drive predictions. This often reveals data quality issues or business insights.\n\n**Stratified CV happens automatically** for classification, ensuring each fold has balanced classes. For time-series problems, use a dedicated time-series validation node instead.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Prototyping\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploration on a new dataset when you need directional insights within minutes, not production-ready models.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `cv_folds` | 3 | Minimum for variance estimate without time overhead |\n| `max_time_minutes` | 5 | Hard stop for initial runs |\n| `algorithms` | `[\'logistic\', \'decision_tree\', \'random_forest\']` | Fast-training linear and tree baselines only |\n| `metric` | `\'accuracy\'` or `\'rmse\'` | Simple, interpretable default metrics |\n| `n_jobs` | -1 | Use all cores to maximise speed |\n| `verbose` | 1 | Monitor progress without log spam |\n\n**What you get:** A rough performance ceiling and algorithm type indication (linear vs. nonlinear) in under 10 minutes on most datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice 2–5% final performance and miss algorithms that require longer training (gradient boosting, neural nets).\n\n### Recipe 2: Production Deployment\n\n**When to use:** Final model selection before deployment where performance, reliability, and audit trails matter more than compute cost.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `cv_folds` | 10 | Robust variance estimates for confidence intervals |\n| `cv_strategy` | `\'stratified\'` or `\'timeseries\'` | Match validation to production data structure |\n| `algorithms` | Full suite including `\'xgboost\'`, `\'lightgbm\'`, `\'catboost\'` | Don\'t exclude potential winners |\n| `metric` | Business metric (e.g., `\'f1\'`, `\'mae\'`) | Align with actual success criteria |\n| `random_state` | Fixed integer (e.g., 42) | Ensure reproducibility for audits |\n| `score_full_data` | `True` | Report performance on entire dataset post-selection |\n| `return_models` | `True` | Preserve all fitted models for inspection |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically defensible model choice with complete provenance and performance documentation suitable for regulated environments.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime increases 5–10× compared to rapid prototyping; requires proportionally more compute resources.\n\n### Recipe 3: Severe Class Imbalance (1:100+ ratio)\n\n**When to use:** Fraud detection, rare disease diagnosis, or any binary classification where positive class represents <1% of samples.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `metric` | `\'pr_auc\'` or `\'f1\'` | Accuracy is meaningless at 99:1 ratios |\n| `cv_strategy` | `\'stratified\'` | Preserve class ratios in every fold |\n| `algorithms` | `[\'logistic\', \'random_forest\', \'xgboost\']` with `class_weight=\'balanced\'` | Tree methods handle imbalance; avoid distance-based algorithms |\n| `cv_folds` | 5 | Balance between minority class samples per fold and variance |\n| `threshold_tuning` | `True` | Optimize decision boundary post-training |\n\n**What you get:** Models optimized for minority class detection rather than overall accuracy.\n\n**Trade-off:** Higher false positive rates in exchange for catching rare events; requires domain expertise to set acceptable precision/recall trade-off.\n\n### Recipe 4: Feature Engineering Validation\n\n**When to use:** Testing whether engineered features (lags, interactions, embeddings) actually improve predictive power over raw features.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithms` | `[\'linear_regression\', \'ridge\']` or `[\'logistic\', \'lasso\']` | Simple models isolate feature quality from algorithm complexity |\n| `cv_folds` | 5 | Standard statistical power |\n| `feature_sets` | `[raw_features, engineered_features, combined]` | Run three separate searches for comparison |\n| `return_feature_importance` | `True` | Identify which engineered features matter |\n| `metric` | Same across all runs | Enable apples-to-apples comparison |\n\n**What you get:** Quantitative evidence of feature engineering ROI; identifies which transformations justify pipeline complexity.\n\n**Trade-off:** Deliberately uses simpler algorithms, so absolute performance will be lower than ensemble methods would achieve.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Which statement best reflects the fundamental assumption that makes this a forecasting problem rather than a general prediction problem?\n\nA) The forecast will be more accurate if we include external variables like marketing spend and competitor pricing as features\nB) The historical decomposition into trend and seasonality components will continue to manifest in similar patterns during the forecast horizon\nC) The prediction intervals will narrow as we move further into the future because we accumulate more information about the pattern\nD) The residual noise component must be normally distributed for the forecast to produce valid point estimates\n\n**Answer:** B\n\n**Explanation:** B is correct because forecasting fundamentally assumes that historical patterns (trend, seasonality) identified through decomposition will persist into the future—this continuity assumption distinguishes forecasting from general prediction. A represents a misconception that forecasting is primarily about adding more features; while covariates can improve forecasts, the core mechanism relies on temporal pattern projection, not feature engineering. C reverses the actual behavior—prediction intervals *widen* with longer horizons due to compounding uncertainty, a critical property novices often misunderstand. D confuses model assumptions with problem definition; while some forecasting methods assume normally distributed residuals for interval construction, non-normal residuals don't invalidate the forecast's point estimates or the fundamental nature of the forecasting problem itself.\n" as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. Need\n\nThe Forecast with Drivers node expects a time series dataset with at least three components: a date column, your target variable (what you want to forecast), and one or more driver columns | winter |\n| 2024-01-03 | 11800 | 7500            | 30.99            | winter |\n\n**Required columns:**\n- **Date/time column**: Any standard date or datetime format\n- **Target variable**: Numeric grain (daily, weekly, monthly) without gaps. If you have missing dates, use a Fill Missing Values node upstream first.\n\n### Quick Start\n\nThe fastest path to your first forecast:\n\n1. **Connect your time series data** to the Forecast with forecast plot** and accuracy metrics in the output panel\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Date Field** | Which column contains your timestamps | None | Always set this first |\n| **Target Field** | The variable you\'re forecasting | None | Your key metric (sales, demand, etc.) |\n| **Driver Fields** | External variables that influence your target | None | Include all relevant drivers, but avoid highly correlated ones |\n| **Forecast Horizon** | How many time periods ahead to predict | 30 | Match your business planning cycle |\n| **Algorithm** | Model type (Auto, Gradient Boosting, Neural Network, Linear) | Auto | Use Auto unless you have specific requirements; try Gradient Boosting for complex patterns |\n| **Train/Test Split** | Percentage of historical data reserved for validation | 80/20 | Use 70/30 if you have limited history; 90/10 for very long series |\n| **Include Trend** | Whether to model long-term directional movement | True | Disable for stationary series that oscillate around a constant level |\n| **Include Seasonality** | Automatically detect and model repeating patterns | True | Keep enabled for most business metrics |\n| **Confidence Interval** | Width of uncertainty bands around forecast | 95% | Use 80% for narrower bands, 99% for more conservative planning |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nAfter running, the node outputs:\n\n**Enhanced dataset** with these new columns:\n- future periods, False for historical)\n\n**Visualizations displayed:**\n- **Forecast plot**: Time series showing historical actuals, fitted values, and future predictions with confidence bands\n- Here\'s how to get started:\n\n1. **Connect your training data** with at least one feature column and one target column (both numeric)\n2. **Drag the Gaussian Process node** onto your canvas and connect your data\n3. **Set your target column** in the node configuration panel\n4. **Leave kernel at "RBF"** (Radial Basis Function) for your first run—it works well for most smooth relationships\n5. **Click Run** and examine the prediction intervals in the output visualization\n\nYou\'ll immediately see predictions with confidence bands, showing not just what the model predicts, but how certain it is.\n\n### Input Data Requirements\n\nYour input dataset needs:\n\n- **Feature columns**: One or more numeric columns (continuous or discrete)\n- **Target column**: One numeric column you want to predict\n- **Minimum rows**: At least 10 observations (ideally 50+)\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| temperature | humidity | pressure | yield |\n|-------------|----------|----------|-------|\n| 23.5        | 65.2     | 1013.2   | 87.3  |\n| 25.1        | 58.9     | 1015.8   | 92.1  |\n\nThe `yield` column would be your target; Beyond ~2,000 points, computation slows significantly—consider switching to other methods or using a sparse GP approximation.\n\n2. **Check prediction uncertainty, not just accuracy**: A GP telling you "I\'m uncertain here" (wide intervals) is valuable information. If most predictions have huge uncertainty, you may need more data or different features.\n\n3. **Kernel choice matters more than you think**: The default RBF assumes smooth functions. What does this covariance matrix fundamentally represent?\n\nA) Computational inefficiency that can be eliminated by using independent predictions at each test point\n\nB) Overfitting in the model that occurs when the number of test points exceeds the number of training points\n\nC) Joint uncertainty across all predictions, capturing how learning about the true function value at one test location informs our beliefs at nearby locations\n\nD) The kernel matrix that needs to be inverted to compute the posterior mean predictions\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** The 1000×1000 covariance matrix represents the joint posterior distribution over all test predictions simultaneously, which is fundamental to GPs defining a distribution over *functions* rather than making independent point predictions. Your dataset needs:\n\n- **A cluster identifier column** (categorical/text) — groups your correlated observations\n- **An outcome variable** (numeric or binary) — what you\'re predicting\n- **One or more predictor columns** (numeric or categorical)\n- **Optional: a time/sequence column** if observations have a natural order within clusters\n\nHere\'s what your data might look like:\n\n| patient_id | visit_week | treated | symptom_score |\n|------------|-----------|---------|---------------|\n| P001       | 0         | 1       | 7.2           |\n| P001       | 4         | 1       | 5.1           |\n| P001       | 8         | 1       | 3.8           |\n| P002       | 0         | 0       | 6.9           |\n| P002       | 4         | 0       | 6.5           |\n\nEach patient has multiple visits — observations within a patient are correlated, but between patients they\'re independent.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Cluster Variable** | Column identifying your groups | (none) | **Always set this** — it\'s how GEE knows which observations are correlated |\n| **Outcome Variable** | What you\'re predicting | (none) | Your target/response variable |\n| **Outcome Distribution** | Statistical family for your outcome | Gaussian | Use "Binomial" for binary outcomes, "Poisson" for counts, "Gamma" for positive continuous values |\n| **Predictors** | Independent variables in your model | (none) | Select all features you want to include |\n| **Working Correlation** | Assumed correlation pattern within clusters | Exchangeable | Use "Exchangeable" when all pairs equally correlated; "AR-1" for time series; "Independent" as baseline; "Unstructured" when you have small clusters and want flexibility |\n| **Time Variable** | Orders observations within clusters | (none) | Set this when using AR-1 or other time-based correlation structures |\n| **Link Function** | Transforms the linear predictor | Identity (Gaussian) | Usually auto-selected based on distribution; change only if you have specific modeling needs |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Coefficient Table**: Shows the population-averaged effect of each predictor with confidence intervals and p-values. Unlike mixed models, these represent average effects across all clusters, not cluster-specific effects.\n\n**Model Diagnostics**: \n- QIC (quasi-likelihood information criterion) for comparing models with different correlation structures\n- Working correlation matrix showing the assumed pattern\n- Residual plots to check model fit\n\n**Predictions**: The node adds a new column with fitted values for each observation, useful for downstream evaluation.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe GEE node outputs work beautifully with:\n\n- **Model Evaluation** nodes — feed predictions to calculate RMSE, MAE, or classification metrics\n- **Visualization** nodes — plot actual vs. predicted by cluster to spot patterns\n- **Comparison** nodes — run the same data through Mixed Effects to see if cluster-specific vs. population-averaged effects differ meaningfully\n\n### Quick Start: Clinical Trial Analysis\n\n1. **Connect your longitudinal patient data** with columns for patient ID, treatment group, time point, and outcome measure\n2. **Set Cluster Variable** to your patient identifier\n3. **Choose Outcome Distribution** (Gaussian for continuous symptoms, Binomial for yes/no events)\n4. **Select Working Correlation**: start with "Exchangeable" for equal correlation between time points\n5. **Add your predictors**: treatment, baseline covariates, time effects\n6. **Run the node** and examine coefficient confidence intervals — these tell you population-level treatment effects\n7. **Compare QIC values** if you try different correlation structures to see which fits best\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Don\'t obsess over correlation structure**: GEE gives you consistent estimates even if you guess wrong. Start simple with exchangeable, only get fancy if you have strong domain knowledge.\n\n**Cluster size matters**: GEE works best with many clusters (30+) rather than few large ones. If you only have 5 schools with 200 students each, consider alternatives.\n\n**Watch for convergence warnings**: If the algorithm struggles, you might have too many predictors for your cluster count, or perfect separation in binary outcomes.\n\n**Population-averaged \u2260 cluster-specific**: A GEE coefficient of 2.0 means "on average across the population," not "each cluster increases by 2.0." If you need the latter, use Mixed Effects instead.\n\n**Time-varying covariates are fine**: Unlike some methods, GEE handles predictors that change within clusters gracefully — treatment changes, age, disease progression, etc.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploratory Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration with clustered data when you need fast parameter estimates and aren\'t yet concerned about optimal efficiency.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | `Gaussian()` | Start with continuous outcomes; simplest link function |\n| `corstr` | `\'independence\'` | Fastest computation; still gives consistent estimates |\n| `maxiter` | `50` | Sufficient for initial convergence on well-behaved data |\n| `scale` | `\'X2\'` | Pearson chi-square for quick dispersion estimation |\n\n**What you get:** Fast, consistent coefficient estimates with conservative standard errors that allow quick assessment of predictor relationships.\n\n**Trade-off:** Ignoring correlation structure inflates standard errors, reducing statistical power and potentially missing significant effects.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Longitudinal Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Final models for longitudinal studies where subjects are measured repeatedly over time and efficiency matters.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | Match outcome distribution | Use `Binomial()`, `Poisson()`, or `Gaussian()` as appropriate |\n| `corstr` | `\'ar1\'` | Accounts for temporal decay in correlation |\n| `maxiter` | `100` | Ensures convergence for complex correlation patterns |\n| `scale` | `\'X2\'` | Robust dispersion estimation |\n| `cov_type` | `\'robust\'` | Sandwich estimator protects against misspecification |\n| `missing` | `\'drop_rowwise\'` | Conservative handling of incomplete observations |\n\n**What you get:** Efficient estimates with valid inference even if correlation structure is imperfect, suitable for publication and decision-making.\n\n**Trade-off:** Longer computation time and requires sufficient cluster size (minimum 10-15) for correlation estimation.\n\n### Recipe 3: Small Cluster Count with Large Cluster Sizes\n\n**When to use:** Studies with few clusters (5-20) but many observations per cluster, like multi-site clinical trials with extensive patient data per site.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | Match outcome | As required by data |\n| `corstr` | `\'exchangeable\'` | Simple structure when cluster count limits estimation |\n| `maxiter` | `100` | Standard convergence threshold |\n| `cov_type` | `\'bias_reduced\'` | Corrects for finite-cluster bias |\n| `df_adjust` | `True` | Uses cluster count minus parameters for degrees of freedom |\n| `scale_inv_sqrt` | `True` | Stabilizes variance estimation with few clusters |\n\n**What you get:** Conservative inference that accounts for limited cluster-level replication, avoiding anti-conservative Type I error rates.\n\n**Trade-off:** Wider confidence intervals and reduced power compared to methods that ignore the small-cluster problem.\n\n### Recipe 4: Survey Data with Complex Sampling\n\n**When to use:** Survey data with unequal sampling probabilities and geographic clustering, where weights are essential and clusters represent sampling units rather than scientific units.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | Typically `Gaussian()` or `Binomial()` | Survey outcomes usually continuous or binary |\n| `corstr` | `\'independence\'` | Sampling-induced correlation handled via weights |\n| `weights` | Inverse probability weights | Accounts for unequal selection probabilities |\n| `cov_type` | `\'cluster\'` | Clusters variance by primary sampling unit |\n| `scale` | `1.0` | Fixed scale when using sampling weights |\n| `df_adjust` | `True` | Conservative inference for complex designs |\n\n**What you get:** Population-representative estimates that properly account for survey design, matching standard survey analysis practices.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires accurate sampling weights and knowledge of survey design structure; cannot estimate within-cluster effects.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial pure aggregation |\n| `forecast_horizon` | `12` | Short enough for quick iteration |\n| `base_model` | `"naive_seasonal"` | Zero training time; establishes baseline |\n| `cv_folds` | `1` | Single train-test split only |\n| `parallel` | `True` | Use all available cores |\n\n**What you get:** Fast baseline showing whether lower-level forecasts naturally aggregate well or need reconciliation.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice accuracy for speed—bottom-up ignores top-level patterns and naive methods miss complex dynamics.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Reconciliation\n\n**When to use:** Deploying forecasts where consistency is contractually required (budget allocation, SLA planning, inventory systems).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"mint_shrink"` | Optimal reconciliation with robust covariance estimation |\n| `forecast_horizon` | `horizon + 4` | Forecast beyond needed range to assess stability |\n| `base_model` | `"auto_arima"` or `"lightgbm"` | Production-quality base forecasts |\n| `cv_folds` | `5` | Rolling-origin validation for realistic errors |\n| `shrinkage_target` | `"identity"` | Regularizes reconciliation when series are noisy |\n| `residual_length` | `min(500, train_length * 0.8)` | Sufficient sample for covariance without overfitting |\n| `store_insample` | `True` | Keep for monitoring and diagnostics |\n\n**What you get:** Statistically optimal reconciliation that minimizes forecast error variance while guaranteeing coherence.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computational cost is 5–10× the exploration recipe; use 12–24 periods |\n| `handle_negatives` | `"truncate_zero"` | Croston can produce negatives; force non-negative |\n| `cv_folds` | `3` | Balance between validation rigor and sparse data |\n\n**What you get:** Stable forecasts that distribute top-level signal proportionally, reducing zero-inflation issues.\n\n**Trade-off:** You lose bottom-up information and assume historical proportions persist—dangerous if mix is shifting.\n\n### Recipe 4: Multi-Seasonal Event Calendar\n\n**When to use:** Hierarchies with multiple seasonalities and irregular events (e.g., tourism by region-accommodation type with holidays, festivals, school breaks).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `"mint_sample"` | Sample covariance better captures event correlations |\n| `base_model` | `"prophet"` or `"tbats"` | Native multi-seasonality and regressor support |\n| `external_regressors` | Holiday indicators, event dummies | Critical for event-driven series |\n| `seasonality_modes` | `["weekly", "yearly"]` | Explicit multiple seasonal periods |\n| `cv_folds` | `3` with event-aware splits | Ensure each fold contains event examples |\n| `aggregation_levels` | Include temporal aggregation (daily\u2192weekly) | Events impact different time scales |\n\n**What you get:** Coherent forecasts that respect both hierarchical structure and complex calendar effects across levels.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires careful feature engineering for events; Prophet can be slow on hundreds of series.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Retail: Multi-channel inventory optimisation**\n\nA European fashion retailer operating 400 stores and an e-commerce platform needs to forecast demand for 50,000 SKUs across brand, category, size, colour, and location hierarchies. You\'ll Need\n\nThe Linear Regression node expects a single dataset with both your predictor variables and the target variable you want to predict. Your target must be numeric and continuous (like sales revenue, temperature, or price). Predictor variables can be numeric or categorical—the node will automatically create dummy variables for any categorical columns you select.\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | age | region | previous_purchases | revenue |\n|-------------|-----|--------|-------------------|---------|\n| C001 | 34 | North | 5 | 450.20 |\n| C002 | 45 | South | 2 | 230.15 |\n| C003 | 28 | North | 8 | 620.50 |\n\nIn this example, you\'d select `revenue` as your target variable and `age`, `region`, and `previous_purchases` as predictors.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Variable** | The column you want to predict | None (required) | Always set this first—it\'s what your model will learn to predict |\n| **Predictor Variables** | Features used to make predictions | None (required) | Select columns you believe influence the target. Start with 2-5 predictors. |\n| **Train/Test Split** | Percentage of data held back for validation | 80/20 | Use 70/30 if you have limited data; 90/10 if you have abundant data |\n| **Include Intercept** | Whether to fit a y-intercept term | True | Keep True almost always. Only disable if you know your relationship passes through zero. |\n| **Standardize Predictors** | Scale predictors to mean=0, std=1 | False | Enable when predictors have very different scales (e.g., age vs. income) to interpret coefficients fairly |\n| **Remove Outliers** | Automatically flag and exclude extreme values | False | Enable if you see unusual predictions. Uses IQR method on residuals. |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Model Metrics Panel:**\n- **R² Score**: How much variance your model explains (0-1 scale; higher is better)\n- **RMSE**: Average prediction error in your target\'s units\n- **MAE**: Average absolute error (more robust to outliers than RMSE)\n- **Coefficients Table**: Shows the effect size of each predictor with p-values for statistical significance\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Actual vs. Predicted scatter plot**: Points should cluster along the diagonal\n- **Residuals plot**: Should look randomly scattered (no patterns)\n- **Feature Importance bar chart**: Shows which predictors matter most\n\n**Output Dataset:**\nThe node adds three columns to your input data:\n- `predicted_[target]`: Model\'s prediction for each row\n- `residual`: Actual minus predicted value\n- `train_test_flag`: Indicates which split each row belonged to\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nMost commonly, you\'ll connect the Linear Regression node to:\n- **Filter node** \u2192 Examine rows with the largest residuals to understand prediction failures\n- **Evaluate Model node** \u2192 Compare performance against other regression methods\n- **Apply Model node** \u2192 Score new data without target values using your trained model\n- **Feature Importance node** \u2192 Deep dive into which variables drive predictions\n\n### Quick Start: Predict Customer Revenue\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** containing customer features and a revenue column\n2. **Open the Linear Regression node** and select your revenue column as the Target Variable\n3. **Choose 3-5 predictor columns** that you think influence revenue\n4. **Keep default settings** (80/20 split, include intercept) for your first run\n5. **Run the node** and check the R² score—above 0.7 is strong; 0.3-0.7 is moderate\n6. **Review the coefficients table** to see which predictors have p-values below 0.05 (statistically significant)\n7. **Examine the residuals plot**—look for random scatter, not patterns\n\n### Pro Tips from Experienced Users\n\n**Start simple, then add complexity.** Begin with just 2-3 predictors you\'re confident matter. Check the model performance, then add more variables one at a time. This helps you understand each predictor\'s contribution.\n\n**Watch for multicollinearity.** If two predictors are highly correlated (like "house size" and "number of rooms"), their coefficients become unstable. Remove one or use the Standardize option.\n\n**The residuals plot is your best diagnostic.** If you see a funnel shape, your errors grow with prediction size—consider log-transforming your target. If you see a U-shape, you might need polynomial features.\n\n**Don\'t confuse statistical significance with practical importance.** A predictor can have p < 0.05 but a tiny coefficient that barely moves predictions. coefficients may be unstable if predictors are correlated.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Inference\n\n**When to use:** Deploying a model where stakeholders will make decisions based on coefficient interpretations and confidence intervals.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `fit_intercept` | `True` | Proper baseline for interpretation |\n| Feature scaling | Standardize all predictors | Comparable coefficient magnitudes |\n| Cross-validation | 10-fold | Stable performance estimates |\n| `alpha` (Ridge) | `1.0` | Mild regularization for coefficient stability |\n| Bootstrap iterations | `1000` | Robust confidence intervals |\n| VIF threshold | `< 5` | Remove multicollinear features pre-fit |\n\n**What you get:** Stable, defensible coefficient estimates with valid confidence intervals and reliable out-of-sample performance metrics.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower training and slightly biased coefficients due to regularization; may sacrifice minor predictive accuracy for interpretability.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Data (p > n)\n\n**When to use:** More predictors than observations, such as genomics data, text features, or sensor arrays where traditional OLS fails.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| Regularization | Elastic Net | Handles correlated features and sparsity |\n| `alpha` | `0.1` to `10.0` | Grid search across magnitudes |\n| `l1_ratio` | `0.5` | Balance between Ridge and Lasso |\n| Cross-validation | Leave-one-out | Maximizes training data usage |\n| Feature scaling | Standardize | Required for fair penalization |\n| `max_iter` | `10000` | Ensure convergence with many features |\n\n**What you get:** A sparse model automatically selecting the most important features while remaining estimable despite p > n.\n\n**Trade-off:** Heavily biased coefficients that underestimate true effects; prediction-focused rather than inference-focused.\n\n### Recipe 4: Extrapolation with Physical Constraints\n\n**When to use:** Forecasting scenarios where predictions must respect known physical limits (e.g., efficiency percentages, concentration rates, thermodynamic bounds).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `fit_intercept` | `False` | Force zero-origin when theoretically required |\n| `positive` | `True` | Constrain coefficients to non-negative |\n| Feature engineering | Polynomial degree 2 | Capture curvature within constraints |\n| Regularization | Ridge with `alpha=0.1` | Smooth predictions near boundaries |\n| Sample weights | Distance from boundary | Prioritize fitting constraint regions |\n\n**What you get:** Predictions that never violate domain constraints, maintaining scientific validity even outside the training range.\n\n**Trade-off:** Reduced in-sample fit quality; model may underperform black-box methods on purely predictive metrics but remains scientifically defensible.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender uses linear regression to predict property valuations across different postcodes, combining historical sale prices with variables like square footage, number of bedrooms, local school ratings, and proximity to transport links. features. longer training than LightGBM on purely numerical data.\n\n### Recipe 4: Extrapolation Beyond Training Range\n\n**When to use:** Predicting values outside historical ranges—forecasting during market shifts, estimating performance of new product configurations, or modeling under novel conditions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `Ridge` | Linear extrapolation behavior |\n| `alpha` | `10.0` | Heavy regularization to prevent wild extrapolations |\n| `polynomial_features` | `degree=2, interaction_only=True` | Capture non-linear patterns while maintaining monotonic extrapolation |\n| `feature_engineering` | `log_transform` on skewed features | Compress extreme values |\n| `clip_predictions` | `True, quantiles=[0.01, 0.99]` | Hard bounds on plausible range |\n\n**What you get:** Predictions that trend sensibly beyond training data rather than exploding to implausible values.\n\n**Trade-off:** Conservative predictions sacrifice accuracy within the training range for safety outside it; Switch to zero-inflated variants when you see excessive zeros (>60% of values). |\n| **Target Column** | Which column contains your count data | (none) | Select your event count variable—must be non-negative integers. |\n| **Feature Columns** | Predictor variables to include | (none) | Include variables you believe influence event frequency. The node handles categorical encoding automatically. |\n| **Train/Test Split** | Percentage of data held out for validation | 80/20 | Increase test size (e.g., 70/30) for smaller datasets; decrease (e.g., 90/10) for very large ones. |\n| **Include Intercept** | Whether to fit a baseline rate | True | Leave enabled unless you have a theoretical reason to force predictions through zero. |\n| **Max Iterations** | Convergence limit for model fitting | 100 | Increase to 500 if you see convergence warnings, especially with many features. |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Out\n\n**Predictions table**: Your original data plus these new columns:\n- `predicted_count`: Expected number of events\n- `prediction_lower` / `prediction_upper`: Confidence interval bounds\n- `residual`: Actual minus predicted count\n\n**Model diagnostics panel**:\n- **Dispersion ratio**: If >1.5, your data is overdispersed (variance exceeds mean)—consider Negative Binomial over Poisson\n- **AIC/BIC scores**: Lower is better; use these to compare model variants\n- **Pseudo R²**: Rough measure of explanatory power (0–1 scale)\n- **Rootogram chart**: Visual check for model fit—bars should hover near zero line\n\n**Feature importance chart**: Shows which predictors most strongly influence event rates\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Typical next steps:**\n\n1. **Evaluate Model** node \u2192 Compare performance metrics across different model types\n2. **Apply Model** node \u2192 Generate predictions on new, unseen data\n3. **Explain Predictions** node \u2192 Understand why specific counts were predicted for individual observations\n4. **Business Rules** node \u2192 Flag high-risk predictions (e.g., predicted claims > 5) for intervention\n\n### Quick Start: Predicting Customer Support Tickets\n\n1. **Connect your data** containing customer attributes and ticket counts to the Model Event Counts node\n2. **Select target**: Choose your count column (e.g., "monthly_tickets")\n3. **Select features**: Add predictors like account_age, plan_type, previous_issues\n4. **Set model type** to "Negative Binomial" (handles real-world count data well)\n5. **Run the node** and check the dispersion ratio—if it\'s near 1.0, you could simplify to Poisson\n6. **Review the rootogram**—if you see a tall bar at zero, try a zero-inflated variant\n7. **Connect to Apply Model** to score new customers\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Watch for zero-inflation**: If more than 60% of your counts are zero, standard models will underperform. Switch to zero-inflated variants and check if the "excess zeros" component improves fit.\n\n**Feature scaling doesn\'t matter here**: Unlike some ML algorithms, count regression models don\'t require normalized inputs—use your raw numeric values.\n\n**Check exposure carefully**: If observation windows vary (some customers tracked 30 days, others 60), create an exposure variable (like "days_observed") and include it as a feature—or better yet, normalize your counts to rates first.\n\n**Interpret coefficients exponentially**: A coefficient of 0.5 doesn\'t mean "0.5 more events"—it means exp(0.5) \u2248 1.65× the event rate. The feature importance chart handles this translation for you.\n\n**Start simple, add complexity**: Begin with standard Negative Binomial. Only move to zero-inflated models if diagnostics clearly indicate poor fit at zero.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration with Poisson Baseline\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need quick coefficient estimates and don\'t yet know if overdispersion or zero-inflation exists.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | `poisson` | Fastest GLM fit, no extra dispersion parameter |\n| `solver` | `lbfgs` | Efficient for moderate feature sets (<100 vars) |\n| `max_iter` | `100` | Balance speed vs. convergence |\n| `alpha` | `0` | No regularization to see raw relationships |\n| `fit_intercept` | `True` | Capture baseline rate |\n\n**What you get:** Coefficient signs and significance within seconds, suitable for 10K–1M observations with clean predictors.\n\n**Trade-off:** Ignores overdispersion entirely—standard errors will be underestimated if variance exceeds mean.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Negative Binomial\n\n**When to use:** Deployment pipeline for count outcomes where variance exceeds mean (most real-world cases) and you need robust uncertainty estimates.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | `negative_binomial` | Accounts for overdispersion via extra parameter |\n| `solver` | `newton-cg` | Most stable for production convergence |\n| `max_iter` | `500` | Ensure convergence on difficult data |\n| `alpha` | `0.01` | Light L2 penalty prevents overfitting |\n| `cross_validation` | `5-fold` | Tune alpha if features >50 |\n| `offset` | `log(exposure)` | Normalize by time window or population |\n\n**What you get:** Reliable prediction intervals and properly calibrated standard errors for statistical inference.\n\n**Trade-off:** 3–5× slower than Poisson; requires sufficient variance in counts (avoid if >40% zeros).\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: Zero-Inflated for Behavioral Data\n\n**When to use:** Modelling user actions (clicks, purchases, support tickets) where structural zeros exist—users who will *never* perform the action regardless of predictors.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `model` | `ZeroInflatedPoisson` or `ZeroInflatedNegBin` | Separate process for excess zeros |\n| `inflation` | `logit` | Model zero-inflation probability explicitly |\n| `zi_predictors` | Subset of main predictors | Often demographic/eligibility features |\n| `count_predictors` | Full feature set | Models intensity given non-zero |\n| `max_iter` | `1000` | EM algorithm needs more iterations |\n\n**What you get:** Separate insights into "who never engages" vs. "engagement intensity when active."\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires >200 observations and >15% zeros to identify; prone to convergence issues below this threshold.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Rare Disease Surveillance with Offset\n\n**When to use:** Epidemiological monitoring where event counts depend heavily on variable population sizes or observation periods across units.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `family` | `poisson` | Rare events often not overdispersed |\n| `offset` | `log(person_years)` or `log(population)` | Models *rate* not raw count |\n| `solver` | `lbfgs` | Handles offset efficiently |\n| `alpha` | `0.001` | Minimal regularization preserves interpretability |\n| `link` | `log` | Natural scale for multiplicative effects on rates |\n\n**What you get:** Coefficients as rate ratios (exponentiated \u03b2) directly comparable across jurisdictions with different denominators.\n\n**Trade-off:** Assumes offset coefficient exactly equals 1.0—misspecified exposure measure biases all other coefficients.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender needs to predict the number of missed payments each customer will experience over the next 12 months to inform forbearance strategies and capital reserve requirements. The sample mean is 3.2 complaints and the sample variance is 3.4 complaints. A colleague suggests using a Poisson regression model. What is the most statistically sound reasoning for whether this is appropriate?\n\nA) Poisson regression is inappropriate because the variance exceeds the mean, indicating underdispersion that violates the Poisson equidispersion assumption\n\nB) Poisson regression is appropriate because the variance-to-mean ratio of approximately 1.06 is close enough to 1.0 to satisfy the equidispersion assumption\n\nC) While Poisson regression could be attempted as a baseline, the variance exceeding the mean suggests potential overdispersion, which should be tested formally and may warrant negative binomial regression instead\n\nD) Poisson regression is inappropriate because count data with means above 3.0 automatically require zero-inflated models to handle the excess of zero values\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** The correct answer recognizes that when variance exceeds the mean (even slightly), this signals potential *overdispersion*—a key phenomenon in count modelling where the Poisson assumption of variance equaling the mean may be violated. Option C appropriately suggests using Poisson as a baseline while acknowledging that negative binomial regression, which includes an additional parameter to model overdispersion, may be more appropriate. Option A incorrectly identifies this as "underdispersion" (which occurs when variance is *less than* the mean). Option B dismisses a potential distributional problem too readily—even modest overdispersion can lead to underestimated standard errors and incorrect inference. Option D confuses overdispersion with zero-inflation; zero-inflated models address *excess zeros* beyond what the base distribution predicts, not simply data with higher means, and there\'s no indication here of a zero-inflation problem.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '?'. This often signals redundancy or data leakage elsewhere.\n\n**Compare MRC shape to domain expectations.** If you expect "age" to have a U-shaped relationship with customer churn but the MRC is flat, your model may be missing crucial interaction effects or the feature needs transformation.\n\n**Use categorical grouping strategically.** When plotting categorical features with many levels, group rare categories into "Other" beforehand—otherwise your MRC becomes unreadable.\n\n**Export MRCs for model documentation.** Regulators and stakeholders love these charts—they\'re far more intuitive than coefficient tables or tree diagrams for explaining *how* your model actually works.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial model assessment during EDA or debugging a feature\'s influence on predictions\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `grid_resolution` | 20 | Fast computation while capturing basic shape |\n| `percentile_range` | (5, 95) | Avoids sparse regions, focuses on data-dense areas |\n| `ice_curves` | False | Skip individual curves for speed |\n| `center_curves` | False | Raw predictions are easier to interpret quickly |\n| `n_jobs` | -1 | Use all cores for maximum speed |\n\n- **What you get:** A rough but informative curve showing the feature\'s directional influence in under 30 seconds for most datasets.\n- **Trade-off:** May miss fine-grained inflection points or interactions; requires more interpretation effort.\n\n### Recipe 3: Categorical Feature with Many Levels\n\n- **When to use:** Analyzing high-cardinality categoricals (e.g., ZIP codes, product IDs) where default alphabetical ordering obscures patterns\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `grid_values` | `sorted_by=\'prediction\'` | Orders categories by predicted value, revealing monotonic patterns |\n| `min_count` | 50 | Excludes rare categories with unstable estimates |\n| `aggregate_tail` | True | Groups low-frequency levels into "Other" |\n| `ice_curves` | False | Individual curves are meaningless for categoricals |\n| `error_bars` | True | Shows prediction variance per category |\n\n- **What you get:** A clear ranking of category effects with statistical reliability indicators.\n- **Trade-off:** Lose the original category ordering; may obscure domain-meaningful groupings.\n\n### Recipe 4: Interaction Detection\n\n- **When to use:** Suspecting a feature\'s effect varies across subpopulations (e.g., age\'s impact differs by gender)\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `ice_curves` | True | Individual curves reveal when averaging hides heterogeneity |\n| `sample_ice` | 1000 | Need sufficient samples to detect clustering |\n| `cluster_ice` | True | Groups similar response patterns |\n| `n_clusters` | 3–5 | Detects 2–4 distinct subpopulations |\n| `color_by` | `<suspected_interaction_feature>` | Visually validates if clusters align with another variable |\n| `grid_resolution` | 50 | Fine enough to see cluster divergence points |\n\n- **What you get:** Visual confirmation of interactions; clustered ICE curves suggest a two-way interaction worth modeling.\n- **Trade-off:** Requires follow-up with 2D PDPs or SHAP interaction values for quantification; visual inspection can be ambiguous.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender struggles to explain to regulators *why* their credit scoring model declines applicants with debt-to-income ratios above 42% but approves those at 41%, especially when other factors vary. She generates a Model Response Curve for square footage and observes a strong positive relationship. She concludes that "square footage is the most important predictor in my model." What is the primary issue with this interpretation?\n\nA) Model Response Curves cannot be generated for random forest models because they are ensemble methods that combine multiple decision trees\n\nB) The curve shows correlation, not causation, so she cannot claim square footage causes higher prices without a controlled experiment\n\nC) Model Response Curves show how a model uses a feature, not the feature\'s importance; a feature can have a strong marginal relationship but low predictive importance if other features capture the same information\n\nD) She should have standardized square footage before creating the curve, since features on different scales cannot be meaningfully compared in response curves\n\n**Answer:** C\n\n**Explanation:** Model Response Curves visualize the *functional form* of the relationship between a predictor and the model\'s output, holding other features constant—they reveal *how* the model uses that feature, not *how much* it contributes to predictive performance. A feature can exhibit a strong marginal relationship in an MRC while contributing little to overall model accuracy if its information is redundant with other predictors. Option A is wrong because MRCs are model-agnostic and work with any supervised model. Option B confuses interpretation methods with causal inference—MRCs describe model behavior, not causal claims (which the scientist didn\'t actually make). Option D is incorrect because MRCs plot the relationship on the feature\'s natural scale and don\'t require standardization; the strength of the visual relationship has no bearing on cross-feature importance comparisons.\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '#'. If even hold-out data shows high volatility, you have a model stability problem, not a generalization problem.\n\n**Time-based data needs special handling**: For time series, ensure your run_id represents models trained on different time windows, not just different seeds—otherwise you\'re measuring random noise, not genuine volatility.\n\n**Don\'t ignore clustered volatility**: If high-volatility records share common features (like being from a specific region or product line), that\'s actionable insight—you may need a specialized model for that segment.\n\n**Volatility \u2260 error**: A prediction can be consistently wrong (low volatility, high error) or inconsistently right (high volatility, low average error). Look at both together.\n\n**Use this for model selection**: When comparing architectures, choose models with lower median volatility, especially for high-stakes predictions where consistency matters as much as accuracy.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial model selection when comparing 3–5 candidate algorithms before committing computational Think of these indicators as your high-frequency signals—things like daily web traffic, weekly sales reports, or monthly survey results that arrive before official quarterly GDP numbers.\n\n**Example input structure:**\n\n| date       | weekly_sales | web_traffic | consumer_sentiment |\n|------------|--------------|-------------|-------------------|\n| 2024-01-07 | 125000       | 45000       | 102.3             |\n| 2024-01-14 | 128500       | 47200       | 103.1             |\n| 2024-01-21 | 131200       | 46800       | 101.8             |\n\nYour target variable (the thing you\'re nowcasting) can be missing for recent periods—that\'s the whole point. You\'re using available data to estimate what\'s happening right now.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Variable** | The economic/business variable you\'re estimating | None (required) | Select the column containing your lagging official statistic |\n| **Indicator Variables** | High-frequency predictors | All numeric columns | Choose variables that logically lead or correlate with your target |\n| **Forecast Horizon** | How many periods ahead to nowcast | 1 | Increase if you need estimates for the next 2-3 periods before data arrives |\n| **Model Type** | Algorithm used (Dynamic Factor Model, Bridge Equation, or MIDAS) | Dynamic Factor Model | Try Bridge Equation for simpler relationships; MIDAS when mixing frequencies (daily + monthly) |\n| **Confidence Level** | Width of prediction intervals | 95% | Lower to 80% for tighter bands; raise to 99% for critical decisions |\n| **Include Seasonal Adjustment** | Pre-processes data to remove seasonal patterns | Yes | Turn off if your data is already seasonally adjusted |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe Nowcast node outputs an **enriched time series** with several new columns:\n\n- **`nowcast_value`**: The point estimate for your target variable\n- **`nowcast_lower`** and **`nowcast_upper`**: Confidence interval boundaries\n- **`contribution_[indicator]`**: How much each input variable contributed to the nowcast (one column per indicator)\n\nYou\'ll also see a **visualization panel** showing:\n- A line chart overlaying historical actuals with nowcast estimates and confidence bands\n- A contribution breakdown chart showing which indicators drove the current estimate\n- A model performance summary displaying RMSE and MAE on historical validation periods\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe Nowcast node pairs naturally with:\n\n- **Alert Node**: Trigger notifications when the nowcast crosses critical thresholds\n- **Report Builder**: Create executive dashboards showing current state estimates\n- **Scenario Analysis Node**: Test "what-if" questions by adjusting indicator values\n- **Compare Models Node**: Benchmark the nowcast against simpler forecasting methods\n\n### Quick Start: Nowcasting Monthly Revenue\n\n1. **Connect your data** containing a date column, monthly revenue (your target), and weekly leading indicators like web sessions and email signups\n2. **Set Target Variable** to your visualization\n6. **Check contribution charts** to understand which signals matter most\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Handle missing indicators gracefully**: Unlike traditional forecasting, nowcasting works even when some indicators haven\'t updated yet. The model adjusts confidence intervals accordingly—wider bands when data is sparse.\n\n**Update frequently**: The magic of nowcasting emerges when you refresh estimates as new indicator data arrives. Set up a daily or weekly refresh schedule rather than running it once.\n\n**Watch for structural breaks**: If your business model changes significantly (new product launch, market expansion), retrain the model. The relationships between indicators and your target may have shifted.\n\n**Start simple**: Begin with 2-3 obvious leading indicators before adding more. More isn\'t always better—irrelevant variables add noise without improving accuracy.\n\n**Compare to naive forecasts**: Always benchmark against a simple "last known value" baseline. Nowcasting should demonstrably beat just carrying forward the previous period\'s number.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial assessment of whether Outcome node expects a dataset with:\n\n- **One target column** containing your ordered categories (like "Low", "Medium", "High" or 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)\n- **Predictor columns** that can be numeric or categorical features\n\nYour target variable must have a natural order—think satisfaction ratings, risk levels, or education degrees. The node will automatically detect the ordering from your data (numerically or alphabetically), but you can override this if needed.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| CustomerID | MonthlySpend | SupportCalls | Region | SatisfactionLevel |\n|------------|--------------|--------------|---------|-------------------|\n| 1001 | 450 | 2 | West | Medium |\n| 1002 | 890 | 0 | East | High |\n| 1003 | 120 | 5 | South | Low |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | Which column contains your ordered outcome | None (required) | Select your ordinal response variable |\n| **Feature Columns** | Predictors to include in the model | All non-target columns | Exclude ID fields or columns with data leakage |\n| **Category Order** | Explicit ordering of your outcome levels | Auto-detected | Override when alphabetical/numeric order doesn\'t match natural order (e.g., "Poor", "Fair", "Good" would sort incorrectly) |\n| **Link Function** | Mathematical function connecting predictors to probabilities | Logit (proportional odds) | Try probit for normally-distributed latent variables; complementary log-log for time-to-event ordered outcomes |\n| **Test Split** | Percentage of data held out for validation | 20% | Increase to 30% for smaller datasets; decrease to 10% for very large ones |\n| **Cross-Validation Folds** | Number of CV folds for model assessment | 5 | Use 10 for more robust estimates on smaller datasets |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Columns Added to Your Data:**\n\n- **Predicted_Category**: The most likely category for each observation\n- **Probability_[Category]**: One column per category showing the predicted probability (e.g., Probability_Low, Probability_Medium, Probability_High)\n- **Cumulative_Probability_[Category]**: Probability of being at or below each threshold\n\n**Model Performance Metrics:**\n\n- **Proportional Odds Test**: Statistical test checking if the proportional odds assumption holds (p > 0.05 suggests the assumption is reasonable)\n- **Ordinal Accuracy**: Percentage of exact matches\n- **Mean Absolute Error**: Average distance between predicted and actual categories (treating them as numeric)\n- **Confusion Matrix**: Heatmap showing how predictions align with actual categories\n\n**Visualizations:**\n\n- **Coefficient Plot**: Shows which features push predictions toward higher vs. lower categories\n- **Predicted Probability Distribution**: Stacked bar charts showing probability distributions across categories\n- **Threshold Diagram**: Illustrates the estimated cut-points between categories\n\n### Quick Start: Rating Prediction in 5 Steps\n\n1. **Connect your data** to the Ordinal Outcome node—ensure your rating/level column is clearly named\n2. **Select your target** from the Target Column dropdown (e.g., "CustomerSatisfaction")\n3. **Review the auto-detected category order** and adjust if necessary (satisfaction typically goes Low \u2192 Medium \u2192 High)\n4. **Click "Train Model"** and wait for the proportional odds test result\n5. **Examine the coefficient plot** to identify which features most strongly influence your outcome\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThe predictions flow naturally into:\n\n- **Score New Data** node: Apply your trained model to fresh records\n- **Business Rules** node: Create automated actions based on predicted categories (e.g., flag predicted "High Risk" customers)\n- **Model Comparison** node: Benchmark against regular multinomial logistic regression to confirm ordinal structure adds value\n- **Feature Importance** node: Deep-dive into which predictors matter most\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Check the proportional odds assumption first.** If the test fails (p < 0.05), your categories might not follow the parallel slopes assumption. Consider collapsing similar categories or using partial proportional odds models.\n\n**Don\'t confuse ordinal with interval scales.** Just because you have 1-5 ratings doesn\'t mean the difference between 1 and 2 equals the difference between 4 and 5. That\'s exactly why you\'re using this node instead of linear regression.\n\n**Watch for class imbalance.** If 90% of your observations are "Medium," the model will struggle. Consider collecting more diverse data or using resampling techniques upstream.\n\n**Interpret coefficients directionally.** A positive coefficient means higher values of that predictor increase the probability of being in higher categories—but the exact magnitude is less intuitive than in linear models.\n\n**Use predicted probabilities, not just categories.** A prediction of "Medium" with 51% confidence is very different from one with 95% confidence. Feed those probability columns downstream for richer decision-making.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data analysis when you need fast iteration to understand if ordinal structure exists in your outcome and which predictors matter.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `link` | `\'logit\'` | Fastest convergence, most interpretable odds ratios |\n| `solver` | `\'newton\'` | Fewer iterations than gradient descent |\n| `fit_intercept` | `True` | Essential for threshold estimation |\n| `max_iter` | `100` | Sufficient for convergence on clean data |\n| `alpha` | `0.0` | No regularization to see raw relationships |\n| `n_folds` | `3` | Minimum for cross-validation without excessive runtime |\n\n**What you get:** Rapid coefficient estimates with standard errors that reveal predictor importance and direction without optimization overhead.\n\n**Trade-off:** No regularization means potential overfitting on noisy features; unsuitable for production deployment.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Deployment\n\n**When to use:** Building a model for live scoring systems where prediction accuracy, stability, and regulatory defensibility are required.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `link` | `\'logit\'` | Industry-standard, auditable interpretation |\n| `solver` | `\'lbfgs\'` | Robust convergence for production stability |\n| `alpha` | `0.1` | Moderate L2 regularization prevents coefficient drift |\n| `max_iter` | `1000` | Ensures convergence on difficult surfaces |\n| `tol` | `1e-6` | Tight tolerance for consistent predictions |\n| `n_folds` | `10` | Rigorous cross-validation for reliable performance estimates |\n| `parallel` | `True` | Reduces scoring latency in production |\n\n**What you get:** Stable, well-calibrated predictions with reproducible performance metrics suitable for monitoring and governance.\n\n**Trade-off:** Longer training time and slightly lower training-set accuracy due to regularization penalty.\n\n### Recipe 3: Imbalanced Ordinal Categories\n\n**When to use:** Survey data or rare-event scenarios where extreme categories (e.g., "strongly disagree" or "critical failure") contain <5% of observations.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `link` | `\'cloglog\'` | Asymmetric link handles rare upper categories better |\n| `alpha` | `0.01` | Light regularization preserves signal in sparse categories |\n| `class_weight` | `\'balanced\'` | Prevents model from ignoring minority categories |\n| `threshold_method` | `\'fixed\'` | Maintains category boundaries despite imbalance |\n| `max_iter` | `500` | Extra iterations for harder optimization landscape |\n\n**What you get:** Improved sensitivity to rare ordinal levels without collapsing categories or losing ordered structure.\n\n**Trade-off:** May sacrifice overall accuracy for better representation of tail categories; coefficients less stable.\n\n### Recipe 4: Non-Proportional Odds Detection\n\n**When to use:** Exploratory phase when you suspect predictor effects vary across category thresholds (e.g., price sensitivity differs between "dissatisfied\u2192neutral" vs. "satisfied\u2192very satisfied").\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `link` | `\'logit\'` | Standard baseline for comparison |\n| `alpha` | `0.05` | Slight regularization stabilizes threshold-specific effects |\n| `partial_proportional` | `True` | Allows selected predictors to violate proportional odds |\n| `threshold_specific_params` | `[\'price\', \'age\']` | Test suspected non-proportional predictors |\n| `aic_selection` | `True` | Automatically compares proportional vs. non-proportional fit |\n\n**What you get:** Diagnostic insight into whether standard ordinal regression assumptions hold; identifies predictors needing separate threshold coefficients.\n\n**Trade-off:** Exponentially increases parameters and complexity; should inform model choice rather than serve as final model.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processes 15,000 applications monthly, historically relying on binary approve/reject decisions that left profitable middle-tier applicants unserved. Cross-validation score\n    cv_scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring=\'neg_mean_squared_error\')\n    cv_mse = -cv_scores.mean()\n    \n    # Plot\n    axes[idx].scatter(X, y, alpha=0.5, label=\'Data\')\n    axes[idx].plot(X_plot, y_pred_plot, \'r-\', linewidth=2, label=f\'Degree {degree}\')\n    axes[idx].set_xlabel(\'Marketing Spend (£000s)\')\n    axes[idx].set_ylabel(\'Sales Uplift (%)\')\n    axes[idx].set_title(f\'Degree {degree}: R² = {r2:.3f}, CV-MSE = {cv_mse:.2f}\')\n    axes[idx].legend()\n    axes[idx].grid(True, alpha=0.3)\n    \n    print(f"Degree {degree}:")\n    print(f"  Training MSE: {mse:.3f}")\n    print(f"  Training R²:  {r2:.3f}")\n    print(f"  CV MSE:       {cv_mse:.3f}")\n    print(f"  Coefficients: {model.named_steps[\'linear\'].coef_}")\n    print(f"  Intercept:    {model.named_steps[\'linear\'].intercept_:.3f}")\n    print()\n\nplt.tight_layout()\nplt.savefig(\'polynomial_comparison.png\', dpi=150)\nplt.show()\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 2: Statistical inference with statsmodels\n# =============================================================================\nprint("=== Example 2: Statistical Inference with statsmodels ===\\n")\n\n# Create polynomial features manually for statsmodels\nX_poly = np.column_stack([x, x**2])\nX_poly_with_const = sm.add_constant(X_poly)\n\n# Fit OLS model\nols_model = sm.OLS(y, X_poly_with_const).fit()\n\nprint\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/polynomial-regression_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/polynomial-regression_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe Polynomial Regression node expects a dataset with at least one numeric predictor column and one numeric target column. Your data should be in tabular format where each row represents an observation.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| Temperature | Sales |\n|------------|-------|\n| 15.2 | 245 |\n| 22.8 | 412 |\n| 18.5 | 318 |\n\nThe node will work with any numeric columns, though it performs best when your predictor variable shows a curved relationship with your target (think U-shapes, diminishing returns, or accelerating growth patterns).\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Predictor Column** | The input variable (x) used to predict | None (required) | Select the variable you believe influences your target in a nonlinear way |\n| **Target Column** | The outcome variable (y) you want to predict | None (required) | Choose the metric you\'re trying to forecast or explain |\n| **Polynomial Degree** | How many curves the model can fit (2 = quadratic, 3 = cubic, etc.) | 2 | Increase to 3-4 for more complex curves; keep low to avoid overfitting |\n| **Train/Test Split** | Percentage of data held back for validation | 80/20 | Use 70/30 for smaller datasets (<500 rows) |\n| **Include Intercept** | Whether to fit a y-intercept term | True | Rarely change; turn off only if your relationship must pass through zero |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**New Columns Added:**\n- `predicted_[target]`: The model\'s prediction for each row\n- `residual`: The difference between actual and predicted values (actual - predicted)\n\n**Metrics Displayed:**\n- **R² Score**: How much variance your polynomial explains (0-1 scale; higher is better)\n- **RMSE**: Average prediction error in your target\'s units\n- **Train vs. Test Performance**: Side-by-side comparison to spot overfitting\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Fitted Curve Plot**: Your original data points with the polynomial curve overlaid—this is where you\'ll visually confirm if the curve makes sense\n- **Residuals Plot**: Shows if errors are randomly scattered (good) or show patterns (problems)\n- **Actual vs. Predicted**: Diagonal scatter plot showing prediction accuracy\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter fitting your polynomial model, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Predict Node**: Apply your trained model to new data for forecasting\n- **Model Comparison Node**: Stack against linear regression or other models to justify the added complexity\n- **Feature Engineering Node**: Use the polynomial features as inputs to more complex models\n- **Export Node**: Save predictions or the model itself for production use\n\n### Quick Start: Fitting Your First Polynomial Model\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Polynomial Regression node input port\n2. **Select your predictor and target columns** from the dropdowns—start with variables where you suspect a curved relationship\n3. **Set polynomial degree to 2** for your first attempt (classic quadratic fit)\n4. **Run the node** and examine the fitted curve plot—does the curve follow your data\'s natural shape?\n5. **Check the R² score** on both train and test sets—if they\'re similar, you\'re good; if test is much lower, reduce the polynomial degree\n6. **Connect to a Predict node** to score new data once satisfied\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1: Start simple, add complexity only if needed.** Degree 2 captures most real-world curves. Only move to degree 3-4 if your residuals plot shows clear patterns and domain knowledge supports it.\n\n**Tip 2: Watch for edge explosions.** Polynomials can swing wildly beyond your data range. If predicting outside your training range, inspect predictions carefully—they may be unrealistic.\n\n**Tip 3: Standardize for high-degree polynomials.** If using degree 3+, consider standardizing your predictor first (using the Standardize node upstream) to prevent numerical instability.\n\n**Tip 4: Compare against linear.** Always run a simple linear regression alongside your polynomial. If R² improvement is under 5%, the simpler model is usually the better choice.\n\n**Tip 5: Multiple predictors? Use this differently.** This node focuses on one predictor. For multiple variables with polynomial terms, connect to the Feature Engineering node first to create interaction terms, then use Multiple Regression.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need to rapidly assess whether nonlinear patterns exist worth modeling further.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `degree` | 2 | Captures basic curvature without overfitting noise |\n| `fit_intercept` | True | Standard for most real-world data |\n| `interaction_only` | False | Include all polynomial terms for full flexibility |\n| Train/test split | 70/30 | Quick split, no cross-validation needed |\n| Feature scaling | None | Skip preprocessing to minimize setup time |\n\n**What you get:** A fast initial fit that reveals whether quadratic relationships exist, typically completing in seconds even on moderately large datasets.\n\n**Trade-off:** Without feature scaling, coefficients may be numerically unstable and difficult to interpret; no validation of generalization performance.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Deployment\n\n**When to use:** Building a polynomial model for deployment in production systems where reliability and validated performance are critical.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `degree` | 2-3 (via grid search) | Systematically determine optimal complexity |\n| `fit_intercept` | True | Standard unless domain knowledge dictates otherwise |\n| Feature scaling | StandardScaler | Prevents numerical instability in polynomial terms |\n| Cross-validation | 10-fold CV | Robust estimate of generalization error |\n| Regularization | Ridge with \u03b1=1.0, 0.1, 0.01 (grid search) | Control overfitting from high-degree terms |\n| Train/validation/test | 60/20/20 | Separate holdout test set never touched during tuning |\n\n**What you get:** A rigorously validated model with documented performance metrics and numerical stability guarantees.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly longer training time due to nested cross-validation; increased implementation complexity.\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Feature Space\n\n**When to use:** Working with 10+ original features where polynomial expansion creates hundreds or thousands of terms.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `degree` | 2 only | Higher degrees create unmanageable feature explosion |\n| `interaction_only` | True | Include x\u2081×x\u2082 but exclude x\u2081², reducing features by ~50% |\n| Feature scaling | StandardScaler | Essential for regularization effectiveness |\n| Regularization | Lasso with \u03b1=0.01 | Automatic feature selection to handle sparsity |\n| `max_iter` | 5000 | Lasso may need more iterations with many features |\n\n**What you get:** A sparse model that automatically identifies which polynomial terms matter, keeping only 10-30% of generated features.\n\n**Trade-off:** May miss important pure quadratic terms (x²) by excluding non-interaction polynomials.\n\n### Recipe 4: Periodic Business Metrics\n\n**When to use:** Modeling business metrics with seasonal patterns (monthly sales, quarterly earnings) where you suspect non-sinusoidal periodicity.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `degree` | 3-4 | Captures asymmetric peaks/valleys in seasonal data |\n| Feature engineering | Add `month_of_year` as categorical (one-hot encoded) | Combines periodic structure with polynomial trends |\n| `fit_intercept` | True | Represents baseline level |\n| Feature scaling | MinMaxScaler (0,1) | Preserves interpretability of time-based features |\n| Regularization | Ridge with \u03b1=0.1 | Light regularization to smooth seasonal curves |\n\n**What you get:** A model that captures both long-term polynomial trends and seasonal variations without requiring Fourier transforms.\n\n**Trade-off:** Less interpretable than pure time series methods; assumes seasonal patterns remain stable.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA regional credit union serving 150,000 members struggled with pricing home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) competitively while managing default risk.
