Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/find-latent-factors_fig1.png)\n![](../../_static/figures/find-latent-factors_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe Find Latent Factors node expects **numeric data** in a table where each row represents an observation and each column represents a variable you want to analyze. Think customer metrics, sensor readings, survey responses, or product features—anything with multiple correlated measurements.\n\n**Required:** At least 3-4 numeric columns (more is better—latent factor methods shine with dozens or hundreds of variables). The node will automatically detect and use all numeric columns unless you specify otherwise.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | purchase_freq | avg_order_value | email_opens | site_visits | support_tickets |\n|-------------|---------------|-----------------|-------------|-------------|-----------------|\n| C001        | 12            | 85.50           | 8           | 24          | 1               |\n| C002        | 3             | 120.00          | 2           | 5           | 0               |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Method** | Algorithm to use: PCA, Factor Analysis, or NMF | PCA | Use FA when you believe measurement error exists; NMF when all values are non-negative and you want interpretable parts-based components |\n| **Number of Factors** | How many latent dimensions to extract | Auto (explained variance) | Set manually if you have a specific dimensionality target—e.g., reducing 50 features to exactly 5 for downstream modeling |\n| **Variance Threshold** | Minimum % of total variance to retain (when auto) | 85% | Lower to 70-75% for aggressive compression; raise to 90-95% when preserving information is critical |\n| **Standardize Inputs** | Whether to scale variables to mean=0, std=1 | On | Turn off only if your variables are already on the same scale and that scale is meaningful |\n| **Rotation** | For Factor Analysis: varimax, promax, or none | varimax | Use promax when factors might be correlated; none when you want raw mathematical factors |\n| **Include Columns** | Which columns to analyze | All numeric | Specify if you want to exclude IDs, dates, or target variables |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**New Columns Added:**\n- `factor_1`, `factor_2`, ... `factor_n`: The factor scores for each observation—these are your new compressed features\n- `reconstruction_error`: How well the factors recreate the original data for each row (lower is better)\n\n**Metrics Panel:**\n- Explained variance by factor (bar chart showing what % each factor captures)\n- Cumulative variance plot (helps you see the elbow where adding factors gives diminishing returns)\n- Total variance retained (headline number—aim for 80%+)\n\n**Visualizations:**\n- **Factor loadings heatmap**: Shows which original variables contribute most to each factor—this is where interpretation happens\n- **Scree plot**: Classic elbow diagram for choosing the right number of factors\n- **Biplot** (for PCA): Observations and variables plotted together in the first two factor dimensions\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Most common next steps:**\n\n1. **\u2192 Train Model**: Use the factor scores as features—now you\'re modeling with 5-10 uncorrelated factors instead of 100 noisy variables\n2. **\u2192 Find Clusters**: Cluster in the low-dimensional factor space for more robust segments\n3. **\u2192 Visualize**: Feed factor scores to scatter plots or UMAP nodes for visual exploration\n4. **\u2192 Filter/Score**: Keep only observations with low reconstruction error (high-quality data points)\n\n### Quick Start: Customer Behavior Compression\n\n1. Connect your customer metrics table (purchases, engagement, demographics—10+ columns)\n2. Leave Method as **PCA** and Variance Threshold at **85%**\n3. Ensure **Standardize Inputs** is On (critical when mixing percentages, counts, and dollar amounts)\n4. Run the node and check the **scree plot**—look for where it flattens\n5. Review the **loadings heatmap**: Factor 1 might be "engagement," Factor 2 might be "spending power"—name them based on what loads heavily\n6. Connect to Train Model, using the new factor columns as your feature set\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1:** The loadings heatmap is your interpretation key. If a factor has high loadings (>0.6) on visit frequency, email clicks, and app usage, you\'re looking at an "engagement" dimension—label it accordingly in your documentation.\n\n**Tip 2:** Watch for factors with just one high loading. They often represent unique variance in a single variable (like "number of returns")—consider whether you need them or can drop them.\n\n**Tip 3:** If downstream models aren\'t improving, you may have set the variance threshold too low. Try retaining 90% instead of 80%—that extra 10% sometimes contains signal, not just noise.\n\n**Tip 4:** Reconstruction error helps spot anomalies. Rows with high error don\'t fit the common patterns—they might be data quality issues or genuinely unusual cases worth investigating.\n\n**Tip 5:** Don\'t rotate PCA results (rotation only applies to Factor Analysis). If you accidentally select a rotation method with PCA, the platform will warn you.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data inspection when you need to visualize high-dimensional data in minutes and decide if deeper analysis is warranted.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `PCA` | Fastest computation, no iterative fitting |\n| `n_components` | `2` | Enables scatter plot visualization |\n| `svd_solver` | `\'randomized\'` | 3-5× faster than exact for large datasets |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Reproducible results across runs |\n| `whiten` | `False` | Skip unnecessary normalization step |\n\n**What you get:** Two-dimensional projection you can plot immediately to spot clusters, outliers, or confirm data is hopelessly noisy.\n\n**Trade-off:** You sacrifice explained variance (typically capturing only 30-60% with two components) and interpretability of the factor loadings.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Feature Extraction\n\n**When to use:** Building a stable preprocessing pipeline for a production ML system where dimensionality reduction must be consistent and auditable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `PCA` | Deterministic, well-tested, no convergence issues |\n| `n_components` | `0.95` | Retain 95% variance while reducing dimensions |\n| `svd_solver` | `\'full\'` | Exact decomposition, no approximation error |\n| `whiten` | `True` | Decorrelates features for downstream models |\n| `copy` | `True` | Prevents accidental modification of input data |\n\n**What you get:** A transformation that balances dimensionality reduction with information preservation, suitable for version control and A/B testing.\n\n**Trade-off:** Slower computation (5-10× vs. randomized) and higher memory usage during training, though transform time remains fast.\n\n### Recipe 3: Sparse High-Dimensional Text Data\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing TF-IDF vectors, one-hot encoded categories, or any sparse matrix where most values are zero.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `TruncatedSVD` | Operates directly on sparse matrices without densification |\n| `n_components` | `100` | Sweet spot for typical document collections (1000-100K docs) |\n| `n_iter` | `7` | More iterations than default 5 for better convergence |\n| `algorithm` | `\'randomized\'` | Only option for sparse data, but explicitly set it |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Stabilizes results despite randomized algorithm |\n\n**What you get:** Dense low-dimensional embeddings that preserve document similarity structure while using 100× less memory than original sparse matrices.\n\n**Trade-off:** Cannot compute inverse transform back to original feature space; you lose the ability to interpret "what words define this component."\n\n### Recipe 4: Anomaly-Resistant Dimensionality Reduction\n\n**When to use:** Data with known outliers or corrupted records where standard PCA would be distorted by extreme values.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `FactorAnalysis` | Probabilistic model that down-weights outliers naturally |\n| `n_components` | `10` | Start conservative; FA is sensitive to overparameterization |\n| `max_iter` | `1000` | Allow sufficient convergence for EM algorithm |\n| `tol` | `0.01` | Balance precision vs. runtime (default 0.01 is reasonable) |\n| `svd_method` | `\'lapack\'` | More stable than randomized for noisy data |\n\n**What you get:** Factors representing shared variance while treating measurement noise and outliers as instance-specific rather than systematic patterns.\n\n**Trade-off:** Much slower than PCA (10-50× depending on data size) and requires careful validation that the model has converged properly.\n\n## Business PCA components are linear combinations designed to explain maximal variance, not to align with meaningful constructs like "price sensitivity" or "brand loyalty." This is the key limitation separating competent practitioners (who use latent factors cautiously for interpretation) from novices (who assume high variance-explanation equals meaningful insights). Option A reflects the misconception that unexplained variance invalidates the analysis—82% is typically excellent, and the remaining 18% is often noise. Option C misunderstands that Find Latent Factors is unsupervised by design and perfectly valid for exploratory questions; having a business question doesn\'t require supervised learning. node expects a single dataset with at least two columns: one categorical variable (your groups) and one continuous variable (your outcome). Think of analyzing sales performance across regions, customer satisfaction by product tier, or conversion rates across marketing channels.\n\n**Your input data should look like this:**\n\n| Region | Revenue |\n|--------|---------|\n| North | 45000 |\n| South | 38000 |\n| North | 52000 |\n| West | 41000 |\n\nThe categorical column can have any number of groups (though 2–20 is most practical), and you\'ll need at least a few observations per group for meaningful results.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Group Variable** | The categorical column defining your groups | *(none)* | Select the dimension you want to compare (e.g., Region, Segment, Channel) |\n| **Outcome Variable** | The continuous metric you\'re analyzing | *(none)* | Choose what you\'re measuring (e.g., Revenue, Time, Score) |\n| **Confidence Level** | Sets the certainty threshold for statistical tests | 95% | Use 99% for high-stakes decisions; 90% for exploratory analysis |\n| **Post-hoc Tests** | Enables pairwise group comparisons | On | Turn off if you only need the overall F-test result |\n| **Effect Size Display** | Shows eta-squared and omega-squared metrics | On | Keep on to understand practical significance beyond p-values |\n| **Minimum Group Size** | Excludes groups with fewer observations than this | 5 | Increase to 10+ for more stable estimates with noisy data |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node produces three main outputs:\n\n**Summary Statistics Table**: Shows mean, standard deviation, and count for each group. This gives you the "what\'s happening" view before diving into significance.\n\n**ANOVA Results Panel**: Displays the F-statistic, p-value, and degrees of freedom. A significant p-value (below 0.05 by default) means your groups genuinely differ beyond random chance.\n\n**Effect Size Metrics**: Eta-squared tells you what percentage of total variance your grouping explains. Values above 0.06 indicate meaningful group effects worth acting on.\n\n**Comparison Chart**: A box plot or mean plot showing distributions across groups, making differences visually obvious.\n\n**Post-hoc Comparison Matrix**: When enabled, shows which specific group pairs differ significantly—essential when you have 3+ groups.\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Group Effects node input port\n2. **Select your group variable** from the dropdown (your categorical column)\n3. **Select your outcome variable** (your continuous metric)\n4. **Click Run** and review the ANOVA results panel\n5. **Check the effect size**: if eta-squared > 0.06, examine the comparison chart to see which groups stand out\n6. **Review post-hoc tests** to identify specific pairs driving the differences\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter Group Effects, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Filter nodes** to isolate high-performing or problematic groups for deeper investigation\n- **Visualization nodes** to create presentation-ready charts of group differences\n- **Segment Profile** nodes to understand *why* groups differ by examining their characteristics\n- **Prediction nodes** to build models that treat group membership as a feature\n\n### Practical Tips from the Field\n\n**Tip 1**: Don\'t obsess over p-values alone. A tiny effect can be "statistically significant" with large samples but meaningless for business decisions. Always check effect sizes.\n\n**Tip 2**: If you have wildly different group sizes (like 500 in Group A, 12 in Group B), the ANOVA assumptions may be violated. Consider filtering to balanced samples first.\n\n**Tip 3**: The post-hoc comparison matrix gets cluttered fast with many groups. If you have 15+ categories, consider collapsing smaller groups or using a different segmentation.\n\n**Tip 4**: Use the chart export to drop group comparison visuals directly into stakeholder presentations. The visual pattern often tells the story better than statistics.\n\n**Tip 5**: If the overall F-test is non-significant but you *know* groups should differ, check for outliers in your outcome variable—they can mask real patterns.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you have 3-10 groups and want to quickly assess if any meaningful differences exist before investing in deeper analysis.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.10 | Higher threshold catches marginal effects worth investigating |\n| `multiple_comparison` | None | Skip adjustment for speed; exploratory context |\n| `effect_size` | eta_squared | Simplest interpretation as proportion of variance |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 0 | Disable resampling to maximize speed |\n| `assumption_checks` | False | Skip diagnostics in exploration phase |\n\n**What you get:** Fast hypothesis screening that identifies which grouping variables warrant detailed investigation, with liberal detection of potential signals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Higher false positive rate means some "significant" results won\'t replicate under rigorous testing.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Analysis\n\n**When to use:** Final analysis for stakeholder reporting, publication, or automated decision systems where statistical rigor and defensibility are paramount.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.01 | Conservative threshold reduces false discoveries |\n| `multiple_comparison` | bonferroni | Strict family-wise error control |\n| `effect_size` | omega_squared | Unbiased estimator for population inference |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 10000 | Robust confidence intervals without normality assumptions |\n| `assumption_checks` | True | Document violations that affect interpretation |\n| `welch_correction` | True | Robust to unequal variances across groups |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible results with conservative error control, complete diagnostic documentation, and distribution-free confidence intervals.\n\n**Trade-off:** Significantly slower computation and reduced statistical power means real effects might not reach significance thresholds.\n\n### Recipe 3: Highly Imbalanced Groups\n\n**When to use:** Comparing groups with extreme size differences (e.g., 5,000 control users vs. 50 in experimental treatment, or rare event categories).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard threshold appropriate |\n| `welch_correction` | True | Essential for unequal group sizes/variances |\n| `effect_size` | cohens_d | Standardized difference unaffected by sample size |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | 5000 | Resampling handles small-group instability |\n| `min_group_size` | 30 | Explicit threshold prevents spurious small-sample results |\n| `heteroscedasticity_test` | levene | Verify variance equality assumption |\n\n**What you get:** Valid inference despite group size asymmetry, with automatic safeguards against small-sample artifacts.\n\n**Trade-off:** Conservative filtering may exclude legitimately interesting small segments from analysis entirely.\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Regime Detection\n\n**When to use:** Identifying structural breaks in continuous metrics by testing if sequential time windows represent distinct regimes (surprisingly effective alternative to change-point detection).\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `grouping_var` | time_window_id | Discrete temporal segments (quarters, product cycles) |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard inference threshold |\n| `post_hoc` | games_howell | Identifies which specific periods differ |\n| `effect_size` | eta_squared | Quantifies regime shift magnitude |\n| `trend_removal` | True | Detrend before grouping to isolate level shifts |\n| `autocorrelation_adjust` | True | Correct standard errors for temporal dependence |\n\n**What you get:** Clear identification of when and how strongly regime changes occurred, with pairwise comparisons revealing transition dynamics.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires pre-specification of candidate breakpoints; won\'t discover unexpected timing of regime changes.\n\n## Business Getting this wrong would mean either underperforming stores or missed revenue opportunities for years.\n\n### The Data\n\nSarah pulled transaction data from the past six months: 847 customer purchases across Northbridge\'s 15 stores, which fell into three format types. She exported a clean table with store format, customer basket size, member status, and purchase date. The data looked straightforward, but she noticed immediately that the "Downtown" category had fewer observations—those flagship stores had lower foot traffic but possibly higher spenders. Here\'s what the first few rows looked like:\n\n| customer_id | store_format | basket_size | member_status | purchase_date |\n|-------------|--------------|-------------|---------------|---------------|\n| C10234      | Suburban     | 127.43      | Premium       | 2024-09-14    |\n| C10411      | Downtown     | 203.18      | Standard      | 2024-09-15    |\n| C10502      | Compact      | 89.75       | Premium       | 2024-09-15    |\n| C10583      | Suburban     | 156.22      | Standard      | 2024-09-16    |\n| C10634      | Downtown     | 278.90      | Premium       | 2024-09-17    |\n\nThe dataset had the usual messiness: a few typos in store_format ("SubUrban" vs "Suburban"), some missing member_status fields, and three outlier transactions above $500 that Sarah flagged for later inspection. She wanted to know two things: first, whether format actually explained meaningful variance in basket size (was this worth arguing about?), and second, which specific formats differed from each other.\n\nShe configured the analysis to compute the F-statistic for overall group differences, calculate eta-squared to measure effect size, and run post-hoc pairwise comparisons. She decided against fancy corrections for multiple comparisons—with only three groups, Bonferroni would be conservative enough without getting too academic for her audience.\n\n```python\nimport pandas as pd\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy import stats\n\n# Sarah\'s Group Effects analysis script\ndf = pd.read_csv(\'northbridge_transactions.csv\')\n\n# Clean format labels\ndf[\'store_format\'] = df[\'store_format\'].str.title().str.strip()\n\n# Group statistics\nformat_groups = df.groupby(\'store_format\')[\'basket_size\']\ngroup_stats = format_groups.agg([\'mean\', \'std\', \'count\'])\nprint("Group Means:\\n", group_stats)\n\n# ANOVA F-test\nformats = [group[\'basket_size\'].values \n           for name, group in df.groupby(\'store_format\')]\nf_stat, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*formats)\n\n# Effect size (eta-squared)\ngrand_mean = df[\'basket_size\'].mean()\nss_between = sum(len(group) * (group.mean() - grand_mean)**2 \n                 for group in formats)\nss_total = sum((df[\'basket_size\'] - grand_mean)**2)\neta_squared = ss_between / ss_total\n\nprint(f"\\nF-statistic: {f_stat:.2f}, p-value: {p_value:.4f}")\nprint(f"Eta-squared: {eta_squared:.3f}")\nprint(f"Format explains {eta_squared*100:.1f}% of basket size variance")\n' as "python" resulted in an error at token: '!'. Use the Elbow Chart output to guide this decision. |\n| **Features to Include** | Which columns drive the clustering | All numerical columns | Exclude ID fields and irrelevant metrics. Include only variables that define meaningful similarity. |\n| **Clustering Method** | Algorithm used (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN) | k-means | Use k-means for speed and simplicity. Try hierarchical when you want to see nested relationships. DBSCAN when you expect unusual cluster shapes or outliers. |\n| **Standardize Features** | Whether to normalize data to same scale | On (recommended) | Keep ON unless all features already share the same scale and range—otherwise features with larger numbers will dominate. |\n| **Random Seed** | Makes results reproducible | 42 | Change if you want to test stability across different initializations. Same seed = same results. |\n\n### What You\'ll Get as Output\n\n**New columns added to your data:**\n- `segment_id`: A categorical label (1, 2, 3, etc.) indicating which cluster each row belongs to\n- `distance_to_center`: How far each observation is from its assigned cluster center (useful for finding outliers within segments)\n\n**Visualizations displayed:**\n- **Segment Distribution Chart**: Bar chart showing how many observations fall into each segment\n- **Elbow Chart**: Helps you choose the right number of clusters by showing where adding more clusters stops improving fit\n- **Feature Comparison Chart**: Side-by-side comparison of average feature values for each segment (this is gold for profiling!)\n- **2D Cluster Map**: If you have many features, this shows a dimensionality-reduced view so you can visually see cluster separation\n\n**Summary statistics:**\n- Silhouette score (0-1 scale; higher = better-defined clusters)\n- Cluster centers (the "average profile" of each segment)\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nAfter segmentation, you\'ll typically connect to:\n\n- **Filter Data** node: To isolate one segment for deeper analysis\n- **Profile Statistics** node: To generate detailed descriptive statistics for each segment\n- **Build Classifier** node: To create a model that predicts segment membership for new data\n- **Visualize Distribution** node: To explore how other variables differ across segments\n\n### Quick Start Recipe\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** containing the customer or entity features you want to segment by\n2. **Select 3-5 meaningful features** (e.g., purchase frequency, average order value, recency)\n3. **Keep standardization ON** and start with **k=3 clusters**\n4. **Run the node** and examine the Elbow Chart—look for the "bend" where the line levels off\n5. **Adjust k** if needed based on the elbow point and your business need for granularity\n6. **Review the Feature Comparison Chart** to name and interpret each segment\n7. **Connect to Profile Statistics** to build detailed segment personas\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n**Start simple, then refine.** Your first pass should use just 3-4 of your most important features. Add complexity only after you understand the basic patterns.\n\n**Name your segments immediately.** As soon as you see the feature profiles, give them business-friendly names like "Frequent Big Spenders" or "At-Risk Dormant" rather than "Cluster 2."\n\n**Watch for unbalanced segments.** If one cluster contains 95% of your data, you\'ve probably got too many clusters or need to remove an outlier-heavy feature.\n\n**Use distance_to_center to find edge cases.** Observations with high distance scores are unusual members of their segment—worth investigating individually.\n\n**Clustering is exploratory.** Don\'t expect perfect, clean groups. The goal is insight, not precision. If segments make intuitive business sense, they\'re useful even if the statistics aren\'t perfect.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n- **When to use:** Initial data exploration when you don\'t know how many natural groups exist and need rapid iteration across multiple k values.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"k-means"` | Fastest for initial scans |\n| `k_range` | `range(2, 11)` | Tests 2–10 clusters without overwhelming choice |\n| `n_init` | `3` | Reduces computation while maintaining stability |\n| `max_iter` | `100` | Sufficient for convergence on clean data |\n| `random_state` | `42` | Ensures reproducibility |\n| `standardize` | `True` | Prevents scale dominance |\n\n- **What you get:** Fast silhouette scores and elbow plots across multiple k values, identifying promising cluster counts within minutes.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Lower n_init means less protection against poor centroid initialization; may miss optimal solutions on complex data.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Segmentation\n\n- **When to use:** Final customer segmentation model for automated targeting, pricing tiers, or personalization engines where stability and reproducibility are critical.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"k-means++"` | Smart initialization reduces variance |\n| `k` | `[determined from exploration]` | Fixed value from validated analysis |\n| `n_init` | `50` | High runs ensure global optimum |\n| `max_iter` | `500` | Guarantees convergence |\n| `tol` | `1e-6` | Tight tolerance for stability |\n| `random_state` | `[fixed seed]` | Exact reproducibility |\n| `validation_split` | `0.2` | Holdout set for stability testing |\n\n- **What you get:** Highly stable cluster assignments with minimal variation across runs; assignments robust to small data changes.\n\n- **Trade-off:** 10–15× slower than exploration settings; requires predetermined k value from prior analysis.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 3: High-Dimensional Sparse Data\n\n- **When to use:** Text embeddings, one-hot encoded categorical variables, or genomic data where Euclidean distance breaks down and most features are zero.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"MiniBatchKMeans"` | Handles large sparse matrices efficiently |\n| `distance_metric` | `"cosine"` | Better than Euclidean for sparse/directional data |\n| `n_init` | `10` | Balance between speed and quality |\n| `batch_size` | `1024` | Efficient memory use for large datasets |\n| `dimensionality_reduction` | `"TruncatedSVD"` | PCA alternative for sparse matrices |\n| `n_components` | `50` | Captures variance while reducing noise |\n\n- **What you get:** Clusters based on directional similarity rather than absolute distance; scalable to millions of observations.\n\n- **Trade-off:** MiniBatch approximation introduces slight randomness; results less deterministic than standard k-means even with fixed seed.\n\n---\n\n### Recipe 4: Time-Series Pattern Discovery\n\n- **When to use:** Grouping customer purchase rhythms, sensor patterns, or usage sequences where shape matters more than absolute values—surprisingly effective for behavioral fingerprinting.\n\n- **Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `algorithm` | `"KMeans"` on transformed features | Applies to engineered time features |\n| `feature_engineering` | `["FFT_coefficients", "autocorrelation", "trend_slope"]` | Captures temporal structure |\n| `k` | `5–8` | Time patterns typically have fewer natural groups |\n| `distance_metric` | `"euclidean"` post-transform | Valid after feature engineering |\n| `standardize` | `"per_series"` | Normalizes each sequence independently |\n\n- **What you get:** Clusters representing distinct temporal behaviors (e.g., "weekend spiker," "steady user," "declining engagement") rather than magnitude differences.\n\n- **Trade-off:** Requires domain-specific feature engineering upfront; raw time-series values would produce meaningless clusters.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender with 150,000 customers struggled to differentiate its retention strategy across a diverse portfolio. The company had run campaigns before, but they\'d always used crude splits—age brackets, membership tier—and the results were mediocre. This time, she needed to let the data reveal the natural groupings.\n\nShe pulled together a behavioral dataset spanning the previous six months. Each row represented a member; each column captured how they actually used the gym. Here\'s what a slice looked like:\n\n| member_id | visits_per_month | avg_session_mins | class_attendance | personal_training_hrs | monthly_spend |\n|-----------|------------------|------------------|------------------|----------------------|---------------|\n| M10234    | 12.3             | 65               | 8                | 2.0                  | 89            |\n| M10891    | 2.1              | 22               | 0                | 0.0                  | 49            |\n| M11203    | 18.7             | 45               | 15               | 0.0                  | 49            |\n| M11456    | 8.5              | 90               | 2                | 4.5                  | 189           |\n\nThe data was messy in the ways real data always is. t-test for correlation significance\n            r = corr_matrix.loc[col1, col2]\n            t_stat = r * np.sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r**2))\n            p_values.loc[col1, col2] = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat), n - 2))\n        else:\n            p_values.loc[col1, col2] = 0.0\n\nprint("\\n=== P-values for Correlations ===")\nprint(p_values.round(4))\n\n# Apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction\n# Extract upper triangle of p-values (excluding diagonal)\nupper_tri_indices = np.triu_indices(len(df.columns), k=1)\np_vals_flat = p_values.values[upper_tri_indices]\n\n# Perform FDR correction\nrejected, p_adjusted, _, _ = multipletests(p_vals_flat, alpha=0.05, method=\'fdr_bh\')\n\nprint(f"\\n=== FDR Correction Results ===")\nprint(f"Number of significant correlations (FDR < 0.05): {sum(rejected)} out of {len(p_vals_flat)}")\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 2: Building and Analysing the Dependency Graph\n# =============================================================================\n\ndef build_dependency_graph(corr_matrix, threshold=0.3, p_value_matrix=None, alpha=0.05):\n    """\n    Construct a NetworkX graph from a correlation matrix.\n    \n    Parameters:\n    -----------\n    corr_matrix : pd.DataFrame\n        Symmetric correlation matrix\n    threshold : float\n        Minimum absolute correlation to include edge\n    p_value_matrix : pd.DataFrame, optional\n        Matrix of p-values for significance filtering\n    alpha : float\n        Significance level for p-value filtering\n        \n    Returns:\n    --------\n    G : networkx.Graph\n        Dependency graph with correlation weights\n    """\n    G = nx.Graph()\n    \n    # Add all variables as nodes\n    for var in corr_matrix.columns:\n        G.add_node(var)\n    \n    # Add edges for significant correlations above threshold\n    for i, var1 in enumerate(corr_matrix.columns):\n        for j, var2 in enumerate(corr_matrix.columns):\n            if i < j:  # Upper triangle only\n                corr = corr_matrix.loc[var1, var2]\n                \n                # Check threshold\n                if abs(corr) >= threshold:\n                    # Check significance if p-values provided\n                    if p_value_matrix is not None:\n                        if p_value_matrix.loc[var1, var2] >= alpha:\n                            continue\n                    \n                    G.add_edge(var1, var2, \n                              weight=abs(corr),\n                              correlation=corr,\n                              sign=\'positive\' if corr > 0 else \'negative\')\n    \n    return G\n\n# Build the dependency graph\nG = build_dependency_graph(corr_matrix, threshold=0.3, p_value_matrix=p_values)\n\nprint("\\n=== Dependency Graph Statistics ===")\nprint(f"Number of nodes: {G.number_of_nodes()}")\nprint(f"Number of edges: {G.number_of_edges()}")\nprint(f"Graph density: {nx.density(G):.4f}")\n\n# Calculate node-level metrics\ndegree_dict = dict(G.degree())\nstrength_dict = dict(G.degree(weight=\'weight\'))\n\n# Clustering coefficients\nclustering_dict = nx.clustering(G, weight=\'weight\')\n\nprint("\\n=== Node Metrics ===")\nmetrics_df = pd.DataFrame({\n    \'Degree\': degree_dict,\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/map-dependencies_fig1.png)\n![](../../_static/figures/map-dependencies_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What You\'ll Need\n\nThe Map Dependencies node works with any tabular dataset containing multiple variables you want to analyze together. Connect it to a data node or any upstream transformation that outputs a table.\n\n**Required inputs:**\n- At least two columns (numeric, categorical, or mixed)\n- No minimum row count, though 30+ rows gives more reliable associations\n\nThe node intelligently handles different column types, calculating Pearson correlations for numeric pairs, Cramér\'s V for categorical pairs, and correlation ratios for mixed types.\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| customer_id | age | income | region | purchase_count |\n|-------------|-----|--------|--------|----------------|\n| 1001 | 34 | 65000 | North | 12 |\n| 1002 | 28 | 48000 | South | 5 |\n| 1003 | 45 | 92000 | North | 23 |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Correlation Method** | Which coefficient to use for numeric pairs | Pearson | Use Spearman for monotonic non-linear relationships or when data has outliers |\n| **Minimum Strength** | Threshold for displaying edges in the graph | 0.3 | Lower to 0.1-0.2 to see weaker relationships; raise to 0.5+ to focus only on strong dependencies |\n| **Include Self-Loops** | Whether to show variables\' correlation with themselves | Off | Turn on for sanity-checking (should always be 1.0) |\n| **Significance Level** | P-value threshold for statistical significance | 0.05 | Tighten to 0.01 for conservative analysis with large datasets |\n| **Cluster Variables** | Group strongly connected variables visually | On | Keep on for datasets with 10+ variables; turn off for simpler datasets where clustering creates clutter |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\n**Dependency Graph Visualization:** An interactive network diagram where each variable appears as a node. Edge thickness represents association strength—thicker lines mean stronger relationships. Hover over any edge to see the exact correlation coefficient and p-value.\n\n**Correlation Matrix:** A heatmap showing all pairwise associations. Color intensity indicates strength, with a diverging palette (typically red for positive, blue for negative). This gives you a complete numerical view complementing the graph.\n\n**Top Dependencies Table:** Lists the strongest relationships in descending order with columns for Variable 1, Variable 2, Coefficient, and P-value. Perfect for quickly identifying your most important relationships.\n\n**Summary Statistics:** Shows total variables analyzed, number of significant relationships found, and average association strength across the dataset.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Feature Selection nodes** are natural next steps—use the dependency map to identify and remove redundant features showing correlation above 0.8-0.9.\n\n**Regression or Classification models** benefit from seeing potential confounders beforehand. If two predictors are highly correlated, you might choose to include only one.\n\n**PCA or Dimensionality Reduction** works well after mapping dependencies—the correlation matrix output can flow directly into these nodes.\n\n### Quick Start: First-Time Setup\n\n1. Drag your prepared dataset onto the canvas and connect it to a Map Dependencies node\n2. Leave all parameters at defaults initially and run the node\n3. Examine the dependency graph—look for clusters of highly connected variables\n4. Check the Top Dependencies table for correlations above 0.7 (potentially redundant features)\n5. Adjust the Minimum Strength slider to filter the visualization to your key relationships\n\n### Practical Tips from Experience\n\n**Watch for spurious correlations in small datasets.** With fewer than 50 rows, you\'ll often see significant p-values that don\'t replicate. Focus on effect size (correlation strength) rather than just significance.\n\n**Color-code your graph by variable type** (if your platform allows). This helps you quickly spot cross-type relationships that might need special handling in models.\n\n**Save the correlation matrix as a separate output.** You\'ll reference it repeatedly during feature engineering, and it\'s invaluable documentation for understanding your final model\'s behavior.\n\n**Look for "bridge" variables** that connect otherwise separate clusters—these often represent important conceptual links in your domain.\n\n**Don\'t obsess over removing all correlated features.** A correlation of 0.6 might seem high, but both variables could still contribute unique information to your model. Use this map to inform decisions, not dictate them.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender processing 12,000 applications monthly struggled with a credit risk model containing 247 variables sourced from credit bureaus, internal transaction history, and property valuations. You can feed it data straight from a file import, a database query, or any transformation node. The node will automatically identify all numeric columns and calculate correlations between them.\n\n**Example input data:**\n\n| customer_id | age | income | spending | days_since_purchase |\n|-------------|-----|--------|----------|---------------------|\n| 1001 | 34 | 65000 | 2400 | 12 |\n| 1002 | 45 | 82000 | 3100 | 8 |\n| 1003 | 29 | 48000 | 1800 | 45 |\n\nThe node will analyze correlations between age, income, spending, and days_since_purchase (customer_id is typically excluded as an identifier).\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Method** | The correlation coefficient formula used | Pearson | Use **Spearman** for ranked or non-linear relationships; **Kendall** for small datasets or when you need robustness against outliers |\n| **Minimum Threshold** | Only shows correlations above this absolute value | 0.0 | Set to 0.3 or 0.5 to filter out weak correlations and focus on meaningful relationships |\n| **Include Missing** | How to handle rows with null values | Pairwise | Choose **Listwise** to use only complete rows across all variables; keep **Pairwise** to maximize data usage |\n| **Columns to Include** | Which numeric columns to analyze | All numeric | Exclude identifier columns (IDs, keys) or columns you know aren\'t relevant |\n| **Sort Results By** | Order of the correlation pairs | Strength | Keep as **Strength** to see the strongest relationships first; change to **Alphabetical** for easier lookup |\n\n### What You\'ll Get\n\nThe node produces three key outputs:\n\n**Correlation Matrix Table**: A grid showing every pairwise correlation coefficient. Age and income might correlate, but there are many confounding factors.\n\n**Try different methods**: If Pearson correlations look weak but you suspect a relationship exists, switch to Spearman. It can catch monotonic relationships that aren\'t strictly linear.\n\n**Watch your sample size**: Correlations become more reliable with larger datasets. With fewer than 30 rows, take coefficients with a grain of salt.\n\n**Use this before feature engineering**: Understanding natural correlations helps you create better derived variables and avoid creating features that duplicate existing information.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration Scan\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you have 20+ variables and need to identify the strongest relationships within minutes, prioritizing speed over precision.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'pearson\'` | Fastest computation, sufficient for initial screening |\n| `min_periods` | `30` | Balance between robustness and inclusivity with missing data |\n| `significance_threshold` | `0.05` | Standard without imputation overhead |\n\n**What you get:** A rapid heatmap highlighting relationships worth investigating further, computed in seconds even with hundreds of variables.\n\n**Trade-off:** You matrices for regulatory reporting, academic publication, or decision-critical dashboards where accuracy and reproducibility are non-negotiable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'spearman\'` | Robust to outliers and captures monotonic non-linear patterns |\n| `min_periods` | `100` | Ensures stable coefficient estimates |\n| `significance_threshold` | `0.001` | Conservative threshold after Bonferroni correction |\n| `bootstrap_iterations` | `1000` | Generate confidence intervals for each coefficient |\n| correlation estimates with confidence intervals and rigorously controlled false discovery rates.\n\n**Trade-off:** Computation time increases 50-100x, and listwise deletion may exclude substantial data if missingness is scattered.\n\n### Recipe 3: Time Series with Lag Dependencies\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing operational metrics, sensor data, or financial time series where correlation between a variable and past values of another variable matters more than contemporaneous correlation.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'pearson\'` | Appropriate for stationary series after differencing |\n| `max_lag` | `7` | Test relationships up to one week of daily data |\n| `detrend` | `True` | Remove spurious correlation from shared trends |\n| `min_periods` | `50` | Sufficient observations after lag adjustment |\n| `autocorrelation_adjust` | `True` | Correct standard errors for serial dependence |\n\n**What you get:** A lag-correlation matrix revealing leading/lagging indicators that contemporaneous analysis would miss entirely.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires stationary data and interpretation becomes complex when multiple lags show significance.\n\n### Recipe 4: High-Dimensional Sparse Feature Selection\n\n**When to use:** Pre-filtering 500+ candidate features (genomics, text embeddings, sensor arrays) before machine learning, where most variables are irrelevant.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `method` | `\'kendall\'` | More efficient than Spearman for large n, similar robustness |\n| `target_only` | `True` | Compute correlation only with outcome variable, not between predictors |\n| `significance_threshold` | `0.001` | Control false discovery with high-dimensional correction |\n| `absolute_threshold` | `0.15` | Retain weak effects that may interact with other features |\n| `parallel` | `True` | Distribute computation across cores |\n\n**What you get:** Reduced feature space (often 90%+ reduction) for downstream modeling while retaining non-linear relationships.\n\n**Trade-off:** Misses feature combinations that are jointly predictive but individually uncorrelated with the target.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender was experiencing rising default rates but couldn\'t pinpoint the leading Distribution node expects **a single numeric column** from your dataset. Think of it as analyzing one variable at a time—your response times, transaction amounts, sensor readings, or customer ages.\n\n**Input requirements:**\n- One numeric column (continuous or discrete)\n- At least 30 observations (more is better; 100+ gives reliable results)\n- Data should be cleaned (no nulls, infinities, or obvious errors)\n\n**Example input:**\n\n| response_time_ms |\n|-----------------|\n| 245 |\n| 198 |\n| 312 |\n| 276 |\n| ... |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Does | Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|\n| **Target Column** | The numeric field you want to analyze | None (required) | Select the variable you\'re investigating |\n| **Distributions to Test** | Which theoretical distributions to fit | Auto (common set) | Add specialized ones (Weibull, Pareto) if you know your domain; remove unlikely candidates to speed analysis |\n| **Significance Level** | Threshold for goodness-of-fit tests (\u03b1) | 0.05 | Use 0.01 for stricter testing in high-stakes applications; 0.10 if you\'re exploring |\n| **Number of Bins** | Histogram granularity for visual fit assessment | Auto (Sturges) | Increase for large datasets (1000+); decrease for small/noisy data |\n| **Show Q-Q Plots** | Display quantile-quantile diagnostic plots | Yes | Disable to reduce clutter if you only need summary statistics |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\n**Distribution Rankings Table:** The node ranks every tested distribution by fit quality, showing:\n- Distribution name (Normal, Lognormal, Gamma, etc.)\n- Fitted parameters (\u03bc, \u03c3, shape, scale—whatever that distribution needs)\n- Goodness-of-fit statistics (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, Chi-squared)\n- P-values for each test\n- Overall rank score\n\n**Visual Outputs:**\n- **Overlay histogram:** Your actual data with the best-fit distribution curves superimposed in different colors\n- **Q-Q plots:** For the top 3 distributions, showing how well theoretical quantiles match your data\n- **P-P plots:** Probability-probability comparisons for additional validation\n\n**Added Columns** (appended to your dataset):\n- `fitted_[distribution]_pdf`: Probability density at each point\n- `fitted_[distribution]_cdf`: Cumulative probability\n- `is_outlier_[distribution]`: Flag for values in extreme tails (beyond 99th percentile)\n\n### Quick Start: Common Use Case\n\n**Goal:** Determine which distribution best describes your sales transaction amounts.\n\n1. **Connect your data source** to a Model Distribution node\n2. **Select `transaction_amount`** as your Target Column\n3. **Leave Distributions to Test** on Auto—it\'ll try Normal, Lognormal, Gamma, Exponential, and Weibull\n4. **Run the analysis** (click Execute)\n5. **Check the rankings table**—look for p-values > 0.05 (distribution isn\'t rejected)\n6. **Review the overlay histogram**—does the top-ranked curve visually track your data?\n7. **Inspect the Q-Q plot**—points should hug the diagonal line for a good fit\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**Typical next nodes:**\n- **Synthetic Data Generator:** Use the fitted distribution parameters to create realistic test data\n- **Anomaly Detection:** Flag transactions that fall in extreme tails (already computed as outlier columns)\n- **Risk Simulator:** Feed parameters into Monte Carlo simulations\n- **Report Builder:** Document your findings with auto-generated distribution cards\n\n### Pro Tips\n\n\U0001f3af **Multiple peaks?** If your histogram is bimodal or multimodal, standard distributions won\'t fit well. Try splitting your data by a categorical variable first (morning vs. evening traffic, product categories) and fit distributions separately.\n\n\U0001f4ca **Don\'t trust rankings blindly.** Always look at the visual fits. A distribution can win on statistics but have poor tail behavior where you care most.\n\n\u26a1 **Start narrow, then expand.** Begin testing 3–4 likely candidates based on domain knowledge. Only run the full suite if nothing fits—saves time and reduces false positives.\n\n\U0001f50d **Transform stubborn data.** If nothing fits your raw data, try log-transform or square-root transform first, then fit. Many real-world phenomena are lognormal rather than normal.\n\n\U0001f4c8 **Sample size matters for tails.** If you need accurate extreme-value modeling (99th+ percentile), you need thousands of observations. Small datasets only give reliable fits in the central range.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Rapid Exploration Scan\n\n**When to use:** Initial data profiling when you need quick distributional insights across dozens of variables with minimal compute overhead.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `candidate_distributions` | `[\'norm\', \'expon\', \'uniform\']` | Limit to three simple, fast-to-fit families |\n| `method` | `\'mle\'` | Maximum likelihood converges faster than method-of-moments |\n| `n_bins` | `30` | Sufficient resolution without overfitting histograms |\n| `goodness_of_fit_test` | `\'ks\'` | Kolmogorov-Smirnov is computationally cheaper than chi-square |\n| `alpha` | `0.10` | Relaxed significance threshold for exploratory phase |\n\n**What you get:** Fast classification into broad distribution families with ~80% confidence, sufficient for dashboard visualizations and triage decisions.\n\n**Trade-off:** You\'ll miss complex distributions (mixtures, heavy-tailed) and may incorrectly accept poor fits due to the relaxed alpha.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Validation\n\n**When to use:** Pre-deployment model validation where distributional assumptions directly impact financial, safety, or regulatory outcomes.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `candidate_distributions` | `[\'norm\', \'lognorm\', \'gamma\', \'weibull_min\', \'beta\', \'t\', \'gumbel_r\', \'pareto\']` | Comprehensive coverage of common real-world patterns |\n| `method` | `\'mle\'` | Asymptotically efficient and stable |\n| `n_bins` | `\'sturges\'` | Data-adaptive binning prevents arbitrary choices |\n| `goodness_of_fit_test` | `[\'ks\', \'anderson\', \'chi2\']` | Triple validation reduces Type I/II errors |\n| `alpha` | `0.01` | Stringent threshold for high-stakes decisions |\n| `bootstrap_samples` | `1000` | Confidence intervals on parameter estimates |\n\n**What you get:** Rigorous, defensible distribution selection with quantified uncertainty suitable for audit trails and documentation.\n\n**Trade-off:** 10–50× slower than exploration mode; requires larger sample sizes (n > 500) for bootstrap stability.\n\n### Recipe 3: Heavy-Tailed Financial Returns\n\n**When to use:** Modeling asset returns, insurance claims, or any domain where extreme events dominate risk profiles and normal distributions catastrophically underestimate tail probability.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `candidate_distributions` | `[\'t\', \'cauchy\', \'levy_stable\', \'pareto\', \'genhyperbolic\']` | Focus exclusively on heavy-tailed families |\n| `fit_method` | `\'mle\'` with `floc=0` constraint | Stabilize location parameter for symmetric returns |\n| `tail_focus_percentile` | `0.05` | Weight fitting toward outer 5% of data |\n| `goodness_of_fit_test` | `\'anderson\'` | More sensitive to tail deviations than KS |\n\n**What you get:** Accurate extreme quantile estimates (VaR\u2089\u2089, CVaR) that don\'t systematically underestimate risk.\n\n**Trade-off:** Poor fits in the distribution\'s center; inappropriate for datasets without genuine extreme events.\n\n### Recipe 4: Change Point Detection via Distribution Shift\n\n**When to use:** Time-series monitoring where the data-generating process subtly changes regimes (e.g., sensor drift, market regime shifts) but means/variances remain deceptively stable.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `window_size` | `250` | Rolling window for sequential re-fitting |\n| `candidate_distributions` | `[\'gamma\', \'weibull_min\', \'lognorm\']` | Shape-parameter families sensitive to process changes |\n| `track_parameter` | `\'shape\'` | Monitor shape parameter trajectory, not location/scale |\n| `alert_threshold` | `2.5 * rolling_std` | Flag when shape parameter exceeds 2.5\u03c3 band |\n\n**What you get:** Early warning of distributional regime changes invisible to mean-based control charts.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires stationary periods for baseline; high false-positive rate in non-stationary environments.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA pan-European investment bank managing a €40B derivatives portfolio needs to estimate tail risk exposure under predicts "no fraud" for everyone gets 99% accuracy when fraud is 1%, but it\'s useless. Focus on precision, recall, and F1-score instead.\n\n**Tip 2**: The optimized threshold is rarely 0.5. Your model might predict best at 0.15 or 0.73—let the node find this for you based on your cost sensitivity.\n\n**Tip 3**: If you have time-ordered data (fraud over months, equipment failures over years), always use time_series validation. Standard cross-validation will leak future information and give falsely optimistic results.\n\n**Tip 4**: Start with fewer features rather than more. With rare events, complex models easily overfit to noise. Try 5-10 strong predictors before adding everything.\n\n**Tip 5**: Save the probability scores, not just the binary predictions. Downstream teams can create different rules (flag top 2% for manual review, auto-block top 0.1%) using the same model.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration with Severe Imbalance\n\n**When to use:** Initial exploration of datasets with extreme imbalance (< 1% positive class) where you need fast feedback on whether signal exists before investing in elaborate pipelines.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `sampling_strategy` | 0.1 | Undersample majority to 10:1 ratio—fast while preserving some context |\n| `model` | `LogisticRegression(max_iter=100)` | Simplest baseline; terminates quickly |\n| `cv` | 3 | Minimal cross-validation for speed |\n| `scoring` | `\'average_precision\'` | Robust to imbalance without threshold dependence |\n| `class_weight` | `None` | Resampling handles imbalance; no double-correction |\n\n**What you get:** A 5-minute runtime checkpoint revealing whether predictive signal exists and which features show promise in initial coefficients.\n\n**Trade-off:** Aggressive undersampling discards majority-class information that might contain critical boundary cases.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Grade Fraud Detection\n\n**When to use:** Deploying a rare event model (0.1–2% fraud rate) in production where false positives have quantifiable costs and regulatory audit is likely.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `sampling_strategy` | `\'auto\'` with SMOTE | Synthetic oversampling preserves all real cases |\n| `model` | `LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_depth=6, scale_pos_weight=50)` | Gradient boosting with explicit class weighting for double protection |\n| `cv` | `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10)` | Maximum stability for confidence intervals |\n| `scoring` | Custom F-beta (\u03b2=2) | Prioritizes recall over precision per business requirements |\n| `calibration` | `CalibratedClassifierCV(method=\'isotonic\', cv=5)` | Produces interpretable probabilities for threshold tuning |\n| `threshold` | Business-optimized | Set via cost matrix, not default 0.5 |\n\n**What you get:** Calibrated probabilities enabling cost-based decision rules with documented performance across multiple validation folds.\n\n**Trade-off:** Training time increases 10–15× compared to exploration recipe; requires careful SMOTE parameter tuning to avoid overfitting to synthetic examples.\n\n### Recipe 3: Seasonal Events with Temporal Leakage Risk\n\n**When to use:** Predicting rare annual events (product recalls, flash sales, equipment failures) where temporal ordering matters and standard CV would leak future information.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `sampling_strategy` | 0.3 | Conservative ratio preserves temporal patterns in majority class |\n| `model` | `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=10)` | Captures non-linear interactions without extrapolation risk |\n| `cv` | `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=30)` | Respects temporal order with 30-day gap preventing leakage |\n| `scoring` | `\'roc_auc\'` | Time-ordered predictions need rank quality, not precision/recall |\n\n**What you get:** Validated performance reflecting true forward-prediction capability without optimistic bias from temporal leakage.\n\n**Trade-off:** Severely reduced training data per fold (only past available); early folds may have zero positive cases requiring careful fold design.\n\n### Recipe 4: Ultra-Rare Catastrophic Events (Anomaly Detection Alternative)\n\n**When to use:** Events occurring in < 0.01% of cases (system failures, sentinel diagnoses) where you have rich features but unsupervised anomaly detection has failed due to normal operational variation.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `sampling_strategy` | `{0: 500, 1: \'all\'}` | Cap majority at fixed count; use every rare example |\n| `model` | `XGBClassifier(n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.01, subsample=0.8, scale_pos_weight=100)` | Slow learning prevents memorization of tiny positive class |\n| `ensemble` | 50 bootstrap replicates | Stability through aggregation when positive class = dozens |\n| `cv` | Leave-one-out on positives | With n=20 positives, stratified K-fold fails |\n\n**What you get:** Ensemble predictions stable enough for monitoring despite training on perhaps 20–100 positive examples total.\n\n**Trade-off:** Model is fundamentally a highly-regularized pattern matcher, not a probability estimator; =============================================================================\n\ndef power_two_sample_ttest(n, d, alpha=0.05, alternative=\'two-sided\'):\n    """\n    Calculate power for a two-sample t-test.\n    \n    Parameters:\n    -----------\n    n : int\n        Sample size per group\n    d : float\n        Cohen\'s d (standardised effect size)\n    alpha : float\n        Significance level\n    alternative : str\n        \'two-sided\', \'greater\', or \'less\'\n    \n    Returns:\n    --------\n    float : Statistical power\n    """\n    # Degrees of freedom for two independent samples\n    df = 2 * (n - 1)\n    \n    # Non-centrality parameter\n    # For equal n per group: lambda = d * sqrt(n/2)\n    ncp = d * np.sqrt(n / 2)\n    \n    # Critical value(s) from central df, ncp) + stats.nct.cdf(-t_crit, df, ncp)\n    elif alternative == \'greater\':\n        t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha, df)\n        power = 1 - stats.nct.cdf(t_crit, df, ncp)\n    else:  # print(f"{n:<25} {power:.4f}")\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Example 2: Sample Size Determination\n# =============================================================================\n\ndef sample_size_two_sample_ttest(d, power=0.8, alpha=0.05, alternative=\'two-sided\'):\n    """\n    Calculate required sample size per group for two-sample t-test.\n    \n    Uses iterative search since closed-form solution doesn\'t exist for t-tests.\n    """\n    # Start with normal approximation\n    if alternative == \'two-sided\':\n        z_alpha = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha/2)\n    else:\n        z_alpha = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha)\n    z_beta = stats.norm.ppf(power)\n    \n    # Initial estimate from z-test formula\n    n_init = int(np.ceil(2 * ((z_alpha + z_beta) / d) ** 2))\n    \n    # Refine using actual power calculation\n    n = max(n_init - 10, 5)\n    while power_two_sample_ttest(n, d, alpha, alternative) < power:\n        n += 1\n    \n    return n\n\n# Determine sample sizes for different effect sizes and power levels\nprint("\\n\\nRequired Sample Size per Group")\nprint("=" * doesn\'t require pre-existing data—it\'s a planning tool you\'ll typically use *before* collecting data. experiment.\n\n1. **Drag a Power Analysis node** onto your canvas (find it under Statistical Analysis)\n2. **Select your test type** (e.g., "Two-Sample T-Test" for A/B testing)\n3. **Estimate your expected effect size** (start with 0.5 for medium effects if unsure)\n4. **Set your desired power** to 0.80 (the standard recommendation)\n5. **Click "Calculate Required Sample Size"**\n6. **Review Sensible Default | When to Change |\n|-----------|-----------------|------------------|----------------|\n| **Test Type** | The statistical test you\'ll perform (t-test, ANOVA, chi-square, etc.) | Two-Sample T-Test | Match this to your planned analysis—use Two-Sample for A/B tests, ANOVA for multiple groups |\n| **Effect Size** | How large a difference you expect to find (Cohen\'s d, r, or custom) | 0.5 (medium) | Use 0.2 for subtle effects, 0.8 for obvious ones, or calculate from pilot data |\n| **Significance Level (\u03b1)** | Your threshold for false positives | 0.05 | Lower to 0.01 for high-stakes decisions where false alarms are costly |\n| **Desired Power** | Probability of detecting a true effect | 0.80 | Increase to 0.90 for critical studies where missing real effects is 1:1, 2:1) | 1:1 | Adjust if control group is cheaper/easier to collect than treatment |\n\n### Node Outputs\n\n**Interactive Power Curve Chart:** Shows how statistical power changes with sample size. The curve helps you see diminishing returns—notice how going from 80% to 90% power might require 50% more participants.\n\n**Required Sample Size:** A clear number displayed at your specified power level. For a two-group study, this is the *per-group* requirement (double it for your total).\n\n**Sensitivity Table:** Shows power levels at various sample sizes (e.g., n=50, n=100, n=200). Helpful for budget discussions when you need to show trade-offs.\n\n**Minimum Detectable Effect:** If you fix sample size instead, this shows the smallest effect you\'d reliably detect. Useful when sample size is constrained by budget or population availability.\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\n**\u2192 Data Collection Nodes:** Set target sample sizes based on your power analysis results\n\n**\u2192 Experiment Design Node:** Configure group assignments using your allocation ratio\n\n**\u2192 Documentation Node:** Export power analysis charts for research protocols or stakeholder presentations\n\n**\u2192 Sample Size Monitor:** Track recruitment progress against your target during data collection\n\n### Practical Tips\n\n**Pilot data is gold.** If you have even 20-30 observations from a similar prior study, use those to estimate effect size rather than guessing. Connect your pilot data to an Effect Size Calculator node first, then feed that into Power Analysis.\n\n**Power analysis is iterative.** Start with conservative estimates, see the required sample size, then adjust. Maybe you realize you need to measure a stronger intervention or accept lower power for an exploratory study.\n\n**The 80% standard isn\'t sacred.** It\'s conventional, but 70% might be fine for preliminary research, while clinical trials often demand 90%. Match power to consequences.\n\n**Account for attrition.** If you expect 20% dropout, multiply your required sample size by 1.25.\n\n**Save your assumptions.** Use the node\'s notes field to document *why* you chose each parameter. Future you (or reviewers) will be grateful.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration for Pilot Studies\n\n**When to use:** You\'re designing a pilot study or preliminary experiment and need a fast estimate of feasibility before investing in detailed planning.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard threshold; no reason to deviate for quick checks |\n| `power` | 0.70 | Lower than production standard but adequate for go/no-go decisions |\n| `effect_size` | Cohen\'s d = 0.5 | Assume medium effect; adjust if domain knowledge suggests otherwise |\n| `alternative` | \'two-sided\' | Conservative default unless direction is theoretically certain |\n| `n_iterations` | 1 | Single calculation, no simulation needed |\n\n**What you get:** A minimum sample size estimate that tells you if your proposed study is in the realm of 50, 500, or 5,000 participants.\n\n**Trade-off:** Lower power (70%) means 30% chance of missing real effects; acceptable for screening ideas but not for final designs.\n\n### Recipe 2: Publication-Ready Research Design\n\n**When to use:** Designing a confirmatory study where results will be published, presented to stakeholders, or used for high-stakes decisions.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `alpha` | 0.01 | Reduced false positive rate for multiple comparison protection |\n| `power` | 0.90 | High sensitivity to detect true effects reliably |\n| `effect_size` | Empirically derived or d = 0.3 | Use meta-analysis estimates or assume small-to-medium effects |\n| `alternative` | As theoretically justified | Use \'one-sided\' only with strong directional hypothesis |\n| `n_iterations` | 10,000 | Simulation for precise confidence intervals around sample size |\n\n**What you get:** A defensible sample size with 90% probability of detecting effects and only 1% false positive risk.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires substantially larger samples (often 2-3× the quick exploration estimate) and more computation time.\n\n### Recipe 3: Non-Normal Outcomes in Healthcare\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing time-to-event data, count outcomes, or skewed continuous variables where standard t-test assumptions fail.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `test_type` | \'wilcoxon\' or \'logrank\' | Distribution-free or survival-specific tests |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 | Standard threshold |\n| `power` | 0.80 | Standard research threshold |\n| `effect_size` | Hazard ratio = 0.67 or rate ratio = 1.5 | Clinically meaningful effect in original scale |\n| `distribution` | Specify actual (e.g., Poisson, Weibull) | Match your outcome\'s true distribution |\n\n**What you get:** Accurate sample size for non-normal data without inflating requirements through inappropriate normal-theory formulas.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires specifying the correct distribution family; misspecification yields worse estimates than robust normal approximations.\n\n### Recipe 4: Equivalence Testing for Generic Products\n\n**When to use:** Proving two treatments are equivalent (bioequivalence, non-inferiority trials, A/A testing validation) rather than different.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `test_type` | \'equivalence\' or \'TOST\' | Two one-sided tests framework |\n| `alpha` | 0.05 per test (0.10 total) | Standard equivalence threshold |\n| `power` | 0.80 | Standard threshold |\n| `equivalence_margin` | ±0.2 Cohen\'s d or ±20% clinical | Smallest meaningful difference you want to rule out |\n| `alternative` | \'equivalence\' | Reverses null/alternative hypothesis |\n\n**What you get:** Sample size sufficient to demonstrate similarity within specified bounds, not just absence of difference.\n\n**Trade-off:** Requires larger samples than difference-detection tests and demands pre-specifying clinically meaningful equivalence margins.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender planning to test a new risk scoring algorithm faces a critical decision: how many loan applications must they analyse before confidently concluding whether the new model reduces default rates by the targeted 2 percentage points? alpha / 2))\n        ci_lower = 2 * point_estimate - q_upper\n        ci_upper = 2 * point_estimate - q_lower\n        \n    elif method == \'bca\':\n        # Bias-corrected and accelerated method\n        \n        # Bias correction factor\n        prop_below = np.mean(bootstrap_stats < point_estimate)\n        # Handle edge cases\n        prop_below = np.clip(prop_below, 1e-10, 1 - 1e-10)\n        z0 = stats.norm.ppf(prop_below)\n        \n        # Acceleration factor via jackknife\n        jackknife_stats = np.zeros(n)\n        for i in range(n):\n            jackknife_sample = np.delete(data, i)\n            jackknife_stats[i] = statistic(jackknife_sample)\n        \n        jack_mean = np.mean(jackknife_stats)\n        numerator = np.sum((jack_mean - jackknife_stats) ** 3)\n        denominator = 6 * (np.sum((jack_mean - jackknife_stats) ** 2) ** 1.5)\n        \n        if denominator == 0:\n            a = 0  # No skewness adjustment\n        else:\n            a = numerator / denominator\n        \n        # Adjusted quantiles\n        z_alpha_lower = stats.norm.ppf(alpha / 2)\n        z_alpha_upper = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)\n        \n        def adjusted_quantile(z_alpha):\n            numerator = z0 + z_alpha\n            denominator = 1 - a * numerator\n            if denominator <= 0:\n                return 0.5  # Fallback\n            return stats.norm.cdf(z0 + numerator / denominator)\n        \n        alpha1 = adjusted_quantile(z_alpha_lower)\n        alpha2 = adjusted_quantile(z_alpha_upper)\n        \n        ci_lower = np.percentile(bootstrap_stats, 100 * alpha1)\n        ci_upper = np.percentile(bootstrap_stats, 100 * alpha2)\n    \n    else:\n        raise ValueError(f"Unknown method: {method}")\n    \n    return point_estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper, bootstrap_stats\n\n\n# Example 1: Confidence interval for the mean\nprint("=" * 60)\nprint("EXAMPLE 1: Bootstrap CI for the Mean")\nprint("=" * 60)\n\n# Generate realistic data: customer purchase\n\n\n## Visualisations\n\n![](../../_static/figures/resample-confidence_fig1.png)\n\n![](../../_static/figures/resample-confidence_fig2.png)\n\n## Using This in Heuristix\n\n### What Data You\'ll Need\n\nThe Resample Confidence node works with any dataset where you want to estimate uncertainty around a statistic. You\'ll need:\n\n- **At least one numeric column** containing the values you want to analyze (revenue, conversion rate, response time, etc.)\n- **Optionally, a grouping column** if you want to calculate confidence intervals separately for different segments (region, product category, customer type)\n\nYour data should have at least 30-50 rows for meaningful results, though the node will work with smaller samples. Here\'s a simple example:\n\n**Input data:**\n| customer_id | purchase_amount | region |\n|-------------|-----------------|--------|\n| 1           | 142.50          | West   |\n| 2           | 89.20           | East   |\n| 3           | 203.10          | West   |\n| ...         | ...             | ...    |\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n| Parameter | What It Controls | Default | When to Change It |\n|-----------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|\n| **Target Column** | Which numeric column to analyze | (required) | Select your metric of interest |\n| **Statistic Type** | What to calculate: mean, median, standard deviation, or custom percentile | Mean | Use median for skewed data; percentiles for tail analysis |\n| **Group By** | Optional column to split analysis by category | None | Add when comparing confidence across segments |\n| **Confidence Level** | The certainty level for your interval (e.g., 95%) | 95% | Use 99% for high-stakes decisions; 90% for exploratory work |\n| **Number of Resamples** | How many bootstrap samples to generate | 10,000 | Increase to 50,000+ for very stable estimates; decrease to 1,000 for quick exploration |\n| **Random Seed** | Makes results reproducible | (random) | Set a specific number when you need consistent results across runs |\n\n### What You\'ll Get Back\n\nThe node produces three types of output:\n\n**Results Table** with columns:\n- **group** (if you used Group By): the category name\n- **statistic**: your calculated value (e.g., mean)\n- **lower_bound**: bottom of the confidence interval\n- **upper_bound**: top of the confidence interval\n- **std_error**: bootstrap standard error\n\n**Visualization**: An interval plot showing the point estimate with confidence bars for each group, making it easy to see which groups differ significantly.\n\n**Summary Metrics** panel displaying the margin of error and interval width, helping you quickly assess precision.\n\n### Quick Start\n\n1. **Connect your dataset** to the Resample Confidence node\n2. **Select your Target Column** (the metric you care about)\n3. **Choose your Statistic Type** (start with "Mean" if unsure)\n4. **Set Confidence Level to 95%** (the standard choice)\n5. **Leave Number of Resamples at 10,000** for your first run\n6. **Click Run** and examine the visualization\n\n### Connecting Downstream\n\nThis node pairs naturally with:\n\n- **Filter nodes** to subset data where confidence intervals don\'t overlap (indicating significant differences)\n- **Export nodes** to save intervals for reporting\n- **Comparison nodes** to test hypotheses about group differences\n- **Visualization nodes** to create custom charts with uncertainty bands\n\n### Tips from the Field\n\n**Start with fewer resamples during exploration.** Use 1,000-2,000 resamples while iterating on your analysis, then increase to 10,000+ for final results. This saves time without sacrificing initial insights.\n\n**Watch for overlapping intervals.** When confidence intervals between groups overlap substantially, you can\'t confidently claim they\'re different—even if the point estimates look separated.\n\n**Use the median for skewed metrics.** If you\'re analyzing something like deal size, session duration, or any metric with outliers, the median with bootstrapped confidence often tells a clearer story than the mean.\n\n**Check your interval width.** Narrow intervals mean precise estimates; wide intervals suggest you need more data or have high natural variability. The width itself is valuable information.\n\n**Combine with segmentation thoughtfully.** Very small groups (under 30 observations) will produce wide, unreliable intervals. Consider combining sparse categories before analysis.\n\n## Config Recipes\n\n### Recipe 1: Quick Exploration\n\n**When to use:** Initial data exploration when you need rapid feedback on whether an effect exists, working interactively in a notebook with datasets under 10,000 rows.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 200 | Minimum for stable CI shape without waiting |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.90 | Faster computation, acceptable for exploration |\n| `method` | \'percentile\' | Simplest method, no bias correction overhead |\n| `random_state` | 42 | Reproducibility during iteration |\n| `n_jobs` | -1 | Use all CPU cores for speed |\n\n**What you get:** Approximate confidence intervals sufficient to identify obvious effects or non-effects within seconds.\n\n**Trade-off:** Intervals may be 10-15% wider than necessary and won\'t hold up to skeptical review or publication.\n\n### Recipe 2: Production-Ready Reporting\n\n**When to use:** Creating statistics for dashboards, regulatory reports, or any output where stakeholders will make decisions costing >$10K.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 10000 | Industry standard for stability |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.95 | Conventional statistical threshold |\n| `method` | \'bca\' | Bias-corrected and accelerated for accuracy |\n| `stratify` | True | Preserve important subgroup proportions |\n| `random_state` | Fixed integer | Exact reproducibility for audits |\n| `n_jobs` | 4 | Controlled parallelism for server stability |\n\n**What you get:** Defensible, publication-quality intervals that will withstand technical scrutiny and reproduce identically.\n\n**Trade-off:** Runtime increases 50x compared to exploration settings; may take minutes on large datasets.\n\n### Recipe 3: Heavy-Tailed Financial Data\n\n**When to use:** Analyzing metrics with extreme outliers—financial returns, insurance claims, web traffic conversion rates, or revenue per user.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 5000 | Extra samples to capture tail behavior |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.90 | Avoid CI collapse in sparse tails |\n| `method` | \'percentile\' | BCa fails with heavy tails and outliers |\n| `statistic` | median or trimmed_mean | Robust central tendency estimator |\n| `smooth_bootstrap` | True | Add kernel smoothing for continuity |\n\n**What you get:** Stable intervals even when the top 1% of observations contain 40% of the total value.\n\n**Trade-off:** Median-based intervals don\'t speak to mean behavior that executives often want; requires explanation.\n\n### Recipe 4: Small-Sample Medical Diagnostics\n\n**When to use:** Rare disease studies, pilot clinical trials, or early-stage biomarker validation where n < 50 and every observation is expensive.\n\n**Settings:**\n\n| Parameter | Value | Why |\n|-----------|-------|-----|\n| `n_bootstrap` | 20000 | Compensate for small sample with more resamples |\n| `confidence_level` | 0.99 | Conservative for safety-critical decisions |\n| `method` | \'basic\' | BCa unstable with n < 50 |\n| `stratify_by` | outcome_variable | Maintain case/control ratio exactly |\n| `smooth_bootstrap` | True | Continuous distribution from discrete data |\n| `seed_samples` | Original data repeated 2x | Augment effective sample size |\n\n**What you get:** Credible intervals from 30-patient studies that appropriately reflect uncertainty without assuming normality.\n\n**Trade-off:** Very wide intervals honestly reflecting limited information; may discourage stakeholders expecting false precision.\n\n## Business Applications\n\n**Financial Services**\n\nA mid-sized UK mortgage lender struggled to set accurate confidence intervals around default probability estimates for non-standard loan products where historical data was sparse and violated normality assumptions.
